User: deliverthedawn Rating: 68

Okay. It’s good. But we already know CALAMITY is capable of writing incredible music after their debut EP, so why did their label insist upon pushing their creativity aside in favor of shoving their prewritten slop down our throats? It’s not bad, of course, but it’s not theirs, and it’s glaringly obvious.

Favorite tracks: Anything Goes, Glass Ghost

Least favorite tracks: Midnight (seriously, I know Mydei would never put a trumpet in one of his songs…)

~~~ August 29th, 3868. Eleven months before the release of Dreamscape.

Phainon’s tablet dings loud enough for the shrill notification sound to cut through his practice session. He instantly stops, hands forming a dissonant sort of chord as he leans forward and squints so he can read his new notification more clearly.

It’s from Hysilens. Her first text message is a link, and the second reads “New calamity interview. I think you gotta watch this one.”

Phainon sighs. He’s already made his decision before he thinks about it, really, and immediately presses on the notification. It takes him directly to their chat, sheet music long forgotten as he pulls open the link Hysilens sent. He rummages through his tote bag for his earbuds, pulling them out and connecting them to his tablet as the video loads. It opens with the interviewer’s obnoxious voice cutting through his ears far too loud as she introduces her guests.

Cipher, bassist and co-producer; Hyacine, guitarist and sub-vocalist; Castorice, drummer and songwriter; and finally Mydei, lead singer, producer, songwriter—every title under the sun. Phainon feels his blood run cold as she lists off his many talents. Someone who doesn’t even know Mydei, or his talents, not even in the slightest. She probably didn’t even know the first thing about music to begin with.

Her first question is about the band name. It’s a question Phainon can answer in a heartbeat—CALAMITY isn’t big enough for it to be common knowledge, but he was there. When it was just Mydei, Castorice, and Cipher, and they were all laying on the floor of Aglaea’s basement, laughing about their shared histories. The three titans of calamity, from Castrum Kremnos, Dolos, and Aidonia. So they named their band after old Amphorean mythology. Of course, Castorice answers this just as eloquently as ever, but leaves out the part where Phainon was there with them, too.

It’s not relevant. He knows that. He is not relevant.

Phainon stares at Mydei while Castorice and the interviewer engage in a casual back-and-forth about mythology. He looks different, and Phainon hates it. More rugged than he was in their undergrad years. His hair is longer, he has more tattoos, and he’s grown even more muscular. He watches Castorice speak patiently, nodding along to what she’s saying. Phainon hates that he’s still attracted to him. He wishes that, at least, would change.

They talk about instrument origins next—why they all play what they play, why they decided to start a band. Phainon doesn’t want to hear what Mydei has to say. His fingers linger beside his tablet, itching to turn it off, to switch back to his sheet music and keep practicing like nothing ever happened. But it’s like he can’t look away, as Cipher chimes in to talk about Aglaea adopting her and how she started playing upright bass for her orchestra.

Phainon knows the whole story inside and out, because he was there for that, too. He met her through Aglaea, when she started paying him to play with her orchestra. He knew her all throughout her rebellious streak, as her and Aglaea’s arguments grew more and more frequent, and more and more heated. He knew her when she left for Paperfold, and when he eventually followed her. She’s a talented musician, even if Aglaea would disagree due to where she’s wound up. She has an ear for little things most people don’t, and is much more intuitive than one might expect.

Hyacine answers next, with a story Phainon is not familiar with in the slightest. He doesn’t know her like he knows the rest of them, and was shocked when he discovered that she was a part of the band after Mydei signed with his new label. Last he saw her, she was his chemistry TA and was a pre-med student. He didn’t even know she played an instrument, and he thought he had known every musician at Paperfold.

Castorice explains how she, too, started playing drums with Aglaea’s orchestra, but Phainon already knows the details of how she and Cipher grew close after joining the Grove’s jazz band.

“I’ve been surrounded by music my whole life,” Mydei starts, and Phainon feels his chest lurch. It’s unfair. He knows the details of Mydei’s upbringing like he knows every key of the piano; not because he was there, but because Mydei trusted him with it like he trusted no one else. And now he tells the story like it’s no big deal. Not the details, but the story, and that’s bad enough. It feels like every last bit of Mydei that Phainon could hold onto are slipping through his fingers, slowly becoming someone else’s to hold.

“I got into rock music when I was a kid, started making it myself when I was a teenager. That’s when I taught myself guitar and started singing, but I didn’t actually work on my voice until it got serious and we actually started recording music.” Bullshit. Mydei always had a beautiful voice.

“You started on piano, correct?” The interviewer asks. Phainon groans out loud, resting his tablet against the keys so he can slam his forehead into the piano lid in front of him. For a brief second, Phainon thinks he can see the slightest hint of discomfort in Mydei’s face—which is a lot of discomfort by Mydei’s standards—but it goes away just as quickly as it was there. He still hates the interviewer all the same. “And you attended Paperfold University for a degree in piano performance?” As if it couldn’t get any worse. Phainon feels his distaste so deeply it hurts.

Mydei gives her a little curt nod. “We were all going to do something different,” he starts. “Cas was going to be an author, Hyacine was going to be a doctor, and Cipher…well, I don’t know—”

“Phishing scams,” she says without much thought. Mydei snorts a little bit at that, which doesn’t do much to alleviate the pit in Phainon’s stomach.

“Right,” he continues. “Anyways, I was going to be a pianist.”

“What changed?”

Mydei purses his lips, blinking a few times as he tries to come up with a suitable answer. Phainon could answer that for him a thousand times. He knew exactly what changed, because he was there. He was one of the things that changed. “We got the record deal,” is the answer he gives. Phainon bites his tongue so hard he thinks he might draw blood. “Being a rock musician was always my true dream.”

Of course it was. Phainon knows that. He always had. And he would have been there to support Mydei through all of it if he could have. But now their lives are too different, too separate, to ever make it work.

“Of course,” the interviewer says with a smile. “Will we ever see you showcase your piano talent in the future?”

Phainon freezes. He doesn’t know what he wants Mydei to say. No would mean no one else ever got to hear his prowess ever again. But yes meant that he could, because he wasn’t a part of Mydei’s life anymore, and never would be ever again. At least if he played it with his band, Phainon could watch from afar. It would mean that leaving wasn’t all for nothing.

Mydei doesn’t answer immediately. He opens his mouth, hesitant.

Cipher cuts in for him: “No.”

Hyacine backs him up, too, and Phainon’s jaw tightens.

“For now, no.” Is Mydei’s final answer. He doesn’t elaborate anymore than that, even though Phainon wishes he would.

Phainon knows he should respect that answer. But piano was far more than just an instrument to the both of them, and both of them knew it. Phainon hates seeing Mydei able to throw it away so easily, like it didn’t mean anything more than it was. Like it wasn’t the whole reason they had met, or fallen in love, like Mydei hadn’t poured a decade and a half of his life into perfecting it.

Phainon stares down at the keys and for the first time in his life, he wishes he could throw it away as easily as Mydei had. Maybe if he had left with Mydei when he’d asked, things would still be okay for him. He hates himself for yelling at Mydei for daring to ask such a thing. Now, he wishes he had just packed everything up and gone.

When the interviewer brings up Don’t Cry, Phainon considers turning it off for the second time. The only song of Mydei’s he could ever hate. The only song he turned off, where he would rather sit in his car and listen to silence instead of listening to that godforsaken song. It was devastating, when their debut EP came out, to listen to the way Mydei sang about the break up that was still fresh in Phainon’s mind, like rubbing salt in an open wound. He didn’t care what Mydei had to say—he could blame himself and claim he still loved Phainon all he wanted, but it wouldn’t make it any better. The only song Mydei had ever written for Phainon was about their break up, while he dug up old love songs about Hephaestion to rework in his EP. Phainon hated that more than anything.

The worst part of all was that it was public knowledge that Mydei had dated “piano virtuoso Phainon Khaslana” in his college days. Anyone that knew anything about Mydei knew that. Mydei was a private person, but that wasn’t. For whatever reason, he didn’t want to keep Phainon hidden.

Mydei explains the break up again now, though it lacks details and is watered down. He calls it amicable, mutual, a good thing for both of them. He says they both needed to follow their own dreams, and they couldn’t do that if they continued dating.

Phainon wishes more than anything that that was the full truth. He wishes they hadn’t fought, but at the same time he wishes he had fought more. He shouldn’t have allowed Mydei to walk away from him in the state he was in. He should have been there, no matter how much he had his own dreams to chase. He hates that he lacked the strength to abandon them for Mydei.

More than anything, he wishes it wasn’t devastating. The way Mydei talks about it now makes it seem like it wasn’t for him. Don’t Cry is a song full of pity, like Mydei could see the way Phainon took their break up horribly but still didn’t feel the same.

“This song is speculated to be about your ex-boyfriend, Phainon Khaslana,” the interviewer continues. “Is this true?”

Phainon wants nothing more than to throw his tablet across the room. He does not, though, and keeps watching. Mydei’s eyes flick towards the camera for a split second, and that’s all Phainon gets to imply that this is anything more to him. “Yes, it was.”

Phainon stops breathing. Mydei isn’t done, but he pauses regardless. None of his bandmates want to take this from him, and the interviewer doesn’t want to interrupt him were he to give away more information.

“Phainon is the most talented musician I have ever met. I respect and admire him immensely.”

Respect and admiration. That’s it.

If Phainon wanted respect, he would have gone to the little kids from his old village. If he wanted admiration, he would have spoken to the undergraduate piano students he was helping to tutor. Not someone who had seen him at his worst, who had seen every single part of him laid bare. He would have hoped he was a little more than just a talented musician to Mydei, even if they’ve both moved on.

Who was he trying to fool? Only one of them has moved on.

He turns his tablet off before he can hear what else Mydei has to say about him. He doesn’t want to know any of it. He doesn’t want Mydei to continue to reinforce Phainon’s deepest fear: that Mydei simply doesn’t love him anymore.

He should’ve known, and that’s the worst part. It had been years, and it was only normal to move on from a break up in that time. Phainon’s experience is abnormal, the only reason he kept any semblance of hope that Mydei might share his old feelings. His hope should have died at Rach 2. The piece Phainon can’t even listen to anymore.

He closes the tab when he turns on his tablet again, and tells Hysilens to go fuck herself. He regrets it immediately and apologizes, a message Hysilens instantly reacts to with a laughing emoji. And then he turns back to his sheet music, and pretends nothing ever happened.

“Do you have somewhere to be?”

The concert hall is empty at this hour. Things weren’t clicking in Anaxa’s office, so they walked to the stage to see if the issues would fix themselves. Evidently, they did not.

“No, Professor,” Phainon says. He runs his hands through his hair, trying to tame the mess for the nth time that day. He had forgotten to brush it this morning.

“Then why are you rushing?” Anaxa sits in the middle of the auditorium, arms crossed over his chest. Phainon thinks it’s somehow worse playing for one audience member than a thousand.

“My mind is elsewhere,” Phainon admits. “I’m sorry. I’ll get it done, I promise.”

“I know you will, that’s not the issue,” Anaxa answers. “If you’re distracted tonight, we should stop. It’s not worth either of our time.”

Phainon remembers the day Madam Herta kicked Mydei out of their lesson when he didn’t practice. That was the catalyst, wasn’t it? One of them, anyway. He knows Anaxa doesn’t suggest this from a place of malice, although maybe Herta hadn’t, either. Still, he shakes his head. He can’t allow Mydei and his stupid media-trained bullshit to win.

He sighs as he puts his hands on the keys. Remembers the concert clips he had watched just the night before, of Mydei’s closing show in Castrum Kremnos from a month ago. It was a performance Phainon was already all too familiar with, because he had already watched it a hundred times.

He always thought Mydei looked incredible on stage, but this was on a different level. Mydei was beautiful under the colored stage lights, as a crowd of thousands sang his own lyrics back to him. Phainon would never get that glint in his eye out of his head. The way Mydei grinned, all teeth, the way his hair flowed behind him, the way he looked so alive and carefree in the way Phainon had never seen before.

Mydei always loved performing, even when he was a piano student, but it was never like that. He came alive on stage, but he was always still trapped —he could never lose himself entirely when he didn’t really want it. He never wanted to be a pianist, and he and Phainon were always different in that way.

When Phainon stops playing, he already knows it wasn’t good. He doesn’t look at Anaxa as he takes in his feedback, which isn’t much different from what he just got. “Are you sure you don’t want to leave early tonight?”

This time, Phainon accepts his offer. It wasn’t like Anaxa was kicking him out. He wasn’t like Herta, not at all. He would never treat Phainon the way Herta had treated Mydei.

He’s never felt so alone as he trudges back upstairs, the repertoire folder hugged tight to his chest. He doesn’t allow himself to feel like a failure. He knows his talent, and he knows Anaxa won’t abandon him.

He meets Hysilens in the locker bay, fresh out of her own practice session. She raises an eyebrow when she sees him, closing her own locker and watching him begin to put in the code to his own.

“Someone’s in a bad mood.”

“Wasn’t a productive session,” Phainon mumbles.

“Have you looked at the Monti lately?”

Phainon glares at her as he pulls the lock open, and shoves his folder inside.

“That’s a no.”

Phainon slams the locker shut a little too loud. “My part of Csardas is easy. It’s you who should be looking at it.” He pushes the lock back through his locker and finally turns to leave.

“Okay, ouch,” Hysilens starts, trailing behind him as he heads for the fire exit. “Who’s fault is it if I can’t keep in time, then?”

Phainon shoots her a look over his shoulder. “It’s not a counting issue.”

“Well, I have been looking at it—a lot, actually. It’s a fun piece, unlike the Bartok.”

Phainon mutters something unintelligible under his breath as he pushes the fire exit open, holding it open just enough for Hysilens to get through, because no matter how frustrated he is, he’s not going to let the door slam on someone.

“Okay, I feel like I should apologize,” Hysilens starts, following him as he heads towards the fire exit. “I probably shouldn’t have sent you that video. I didn’t know you were still, well, you know.”

Phainon was never angry with her specifically, so the fact that she’s apologizing is rather surprising. “We can’t all marry our high school sweethearts.”

Hysilens turns, raising an eyebrow at him. “Are you comparing Mydei to Cerydra right now?”

“You don’t think they’d get along?”

“Stop changing the subject,” Hysilens answers, “and stop thinking about him.” They arrive at the bottom floor, so she pushes open the exit door and they leave, hit with the cool late summer air. Campus is peaceful at night, but they turn towards the parking lot and walk to Hysilens’ car instead.

“Like you’d know,” Phainon mutters, a little bitter. “This is your first and only relationship. If you don’t marry her one day, I don’t know what to believe.”

“I think I know well enough that you should be over someone nearly three years after your break up.”

Hysilens unlocks her car, and Phainon climbs into the passenger seat. “Stop.”

“Stop what?”

“Pretending like you wouldn’t be in the same boat if you and Cerydra broke up after everything.”

“Well, we won’t,” Hysilens starts, turning her key in the ignition as she sheds her jacket and tosses it to the back seat. “Besides, Phainon…you weren’t even dating Mydei for a year.”

Phainon knows this, and he knows that she’s right. There’s no reason for him to be as hung up about it as he is, but he can’t watch all of Mydei’s dreams come true and not feel the same way he did before.

“Why don’t you just go after him?” Hysilens suggests, after they’ve sat in their shared silence for too long and she pulls out of the parking lot. “Maybe you’ll get lucky and he’ll go after his favorite groupie.”

“I won’t,” Phainon pouts, and he knows he does. “His girlfriend.”

“Girlfriend?” Hysilens yelps, nearly speeding through a stop sign in her shock. “Sorry,” she says, after Phainon jolts forward when she slams on the brakes. “I think you neglected that minor detail.”

Phainon groans, leaning forward to rest his head in his hands. “He brought her to the Rach 2 concert.”

“Phainon, you never told me this.”

“I know.”

A beat of silence passes on her end. “Was it serious?”

“Is two months serious?”

“Oh, Kephale.”

“What!”

“Remind yourself where you were when Mydei promised you he’d watch you play Rach 2,” Hysilens says, reaching over the console to pat his thigh. “Yeah?”

Now Phainon leans back into the headrest, throwing his forearms over his eyes so Hysilens won’t see the way he blushes. “Stop, Hysilens. This is like torture to me.”

Hysilens clicks her tongue in disapproval. “Seriously, though. I know you’re somehow still mourning your first love, but you need to—okay, fine, we both need to work on the Monti.”

“The concert will be fine,” Phainon says, leaning his head all the way back against the headrest. Two weeks from now, in Okhema. They’d practiced throughout the whole summer, but rarely since returning to Paperfold. It wasn’t looking good, but they’d pulled together worse programs before.

“Let’s switch instruments and see how you feel about it, then,” Hysilens shoots back, giving him a quick glare before turning back to the road.

“Oh, god no. Never again.”

Hysilens laughs brightly, and Phainon can’t find it in himself to be upset again. Even though he knows that as soon as they’ve eaten dinner and he’s alone in his room, finishing up his homework or laying in bed wide awake, Mydei will inevitably occupy his thoughts again. As he always did these days.

“Are you alright?”

Phainon nearly jumps out of his skin as he sees Madam Herta standing before him, looking as polished as ever in her blazer. She still holds her baton as the student orchestra disperses around them, going to pack up while Phainon stays at the piano, alone. It had been a terrible rehearsal for him. He was planning on going over his music alone until he was inevitably kicked out of the concert hall.

“Yes,” Phainon scrambles to say, when he realizes he was silent for too long. “Yes, I—I apologize for my performance tonight. I will be prepared for the next rehearsal, I promise.”

“Alright,” Madam Herta says, and for a moment Phainon is shocked that she might simply leave it at that, but she looks at him like she has something more to say. “You’re an extremely talented pianist, Phainon. I wouldn’t want to repeat my past mistakes with you.”

“Right,” Phainon says carefully. “I understand,” he adds, so she’s aware that he knows exactly what mistakes she refers to.

“If you would like to come to my office hours to go over some things together, feel free.”

“Of course. Thank you.”

“Well then. I’ll leave you to it.” She walks off after that, and Phainon watches her go, left with a sense of odd bewilderment. He had both seen and heard of the worst parts of her. Like how she hardly ever applauded unless she was thoroughly impressed by someone’s performance, that time she kicked Mydei out of her office when he didn’t practice enough, how strictly she values her own time. He had seen her ask students to leave when they were out of tune, make the strings play stand by stand, and call on individuals to make sure they knew technical things on the spot. But no matter how much Phainon disliked her, she was damn good at her job. He had played five concertos with her orchestra and was currently on his way to a sixth, and every time her ear and interpretation of the music was impeccable. She got results. That was why she was still around.

To think Mydei had managed to pierce through her icy heart is a realization Phainon didn’t expect to have now, of all times. He had often suspected that Mydei was one of her favorite students, and that was why she treated him the way she had. She wasn’t the reason he dropped out—Mydei was far too headstrong to succumb to something as trivial as a mean teacher—but she must have felt deep regret for allowing it to happen.

Phainon curses as he leans his head forward, falling into his sheet music. To think he would feel camaraderie with Madam Herta, of all people. They both let Mydei leave. They both regret it.

His phone dings, and he digs it out of his back pocket, lifting his head and attempting to rub the exhaustion out of his eyes as he reads the preview of the email he was sent.

It’s from a music news channel he was subscribed to, following Anaxa’s instructions to keep up with music updates around the world. Even as a classical musician, it was important to keep up with the mainstream music industry as well, he claimed. Phainon wasn’t sure when that would actually become important for him, but he liked all types of music just as well and didn’t mind receiving updates about what was happening in the world. It was easy for him to become too laser-focused on his current project, pouring all of his time into his piano practice and forgetting what the bigger picture was.

Now, though, he regrets his decision to listen to Anaxa terribly. It’s innocent, on a first glance: the subject of the email reads “Anticipating Robin Oak’s fourth studio album…” and when he clicks on it, the rest of the subject line expands to show that she is titling said album Why Does Life Slumber? It’s an interesting album title, and with Robin being the biggest pop star in the world, Phainon is enough of a casual fan to skim through its contents once.

He’s known about the album since before this article, because Hysilens was featured on one of the songs. Robin had been looking for a classical violinist to feature on her track, and with Hysilens making rounds in the classical music industry last year, it was no big surprise that she would catch Robin’s eye.

She had been instructed to keep it a secret, but told Phainon anyway. It wasn’t hard for him to become suspicious on his own anyway, after he overheard her practicing music that was very obviously not classical over the summer. Still, he knows very little about the album as a whole.

He’s excited for its release, anyways. In the article, she claims to be working with lots of different artists, exploring genres and collaborating with all of her favorite musicians, leaving the album with more songs with features than not. Phainon, being the music lover that he is, couldn’t be more in support of the idea of her exploring her sound a little more. Mydei would always say there wasn’t a song or genre out there that Phainon didn’t like, which was one of the truest things that had ever been said about him.

Speak of the devil. Phainon can feel the blood rush from his face as he scrolls down to the end of the article, where Robin speaks about the different artists she’s working with. She mentions the High Cloud Quintet, and Phainon immediately knows where this is going.

“...she found a new band popular in Amphoreus, who cite the High Cloud Quintet as one of their biggest inspirations.”

CALAMITY isn’t mentioned by name. But Phainon knows immediately— how could he not? They’re a rock band, they’re talented, and they’re incredible, of course Robin would want to work with them. Who wouldn’t?

Phainon turns his phone off before he can finish the article, consumed with a whirlwind of emotions so conflicting he feels sick.

This was their way forward, their path to success. Being featured on a Robin album was the greatest thing that could befall a growing musician. This meant bigger stages, brighter lights—millions of fans screaming Mydei’s name. They would all know him. They would see his talent and appreciate it, just as Phainon had done first.

Mydei wasn’t his anymore. He needed to accept that once and for all.

Penacony Music, “Anticipating Robin Oak’s Fourth Studio Album ‘Why Does Life Slumber?’” 20 September 3869 O.W.L. Bert

Exclusive! Robin Oak makes her first public appearance in years to talk about her upcoming album, ‘Why Does Life Slumber?’

With the release of Robin’s debut album almost a decade ago, it was clear that the music industry would never have a pop star like her ever again. Her music had all the creativity listeners were craving, with the vocal talent to back it up.

Three years ago, the singer was tragically shot during a fundraising concert in Kasbelina. Thankfully, she survived, but was forced to take a hiatus from making music for an undisclosed amount of time, mainly to heal. Fans were unsure whether she would ever return, as she hadn’t been seen in public in years.

Rumors that she might have been coming back to music started swirling on Monday morning, where her marketing team posted on social media for the first time since the tragedy occurred. Today, she sits with us now, prepared to clear up any rumors and discuss the new album.

Robin claims that surviving such a tragedy was an experience she is ultimately grateful for. “My creativity was dwindling,” she explains. “This new album will explore these themes of mortality that I had never thought about before.”

Not only does she intend to explore thematically, but sonically, as well. While she loves the pop music she made in the past and everything it did for her, she’s ready to see what else is out there. “I’m working with all sorts of different artists,” the singer reveals. “There are a few songs I wrote and composed by myself, but most of them feature different groups.”

As for the identities of these groups, there are only a handful that she was able to reveal today. For example, the Astral Express, the jazz troupe her brother, Sunday, actually ended up joining. “They were so, so easy to work with, and welcoming, as well,” she says. “I love jazz. And I learned through working with them that I don’t know anything about it, either.”

Besides jazz, Robin also intends on exploring a genre of funk popularized in Edo Star. She visited the nation when her album was just being conceptualized. “There is so much music there, and it’s all so amazing,” she laughs. “It was so hard to decide which ideas I wanted to use.” In the end, she met a group of street performers more than happy to help her, and so it was decided.

It was a known fact that one of Robin’s favorite genres of music is rock, and everything under that umbrella. Now, she claims that she would have loved to work with the High Cloud Quintet but never got a chance before their notorious break up in 2016. Instead, though, she found a new band

popular in Amphoreus, who cite the High Cloud Quintet as one of their biggest inspirations. “I’m most excited to work with them,” she says. “I love their music, and I’m ready for the world to love them too.”

Robin says she was extremely honored at the opportunity to work with so many talented musicians, and that she hopes the world loves her new album as much as she does. “It’s experimental, for sure, but it’s the album I needed to make. Even if it doesn’t do well, I’ll be glad I did it anyway.”

~~~

September 12th, 3868. Ten months before the release of Dreamscape.

The whole team joins the band on their flight to Penacony’s west coast. It’s only been a couple weeks since they got home from their first tour, and somehow Mydei can’t find it in himself to be even remotely exhausted.

The possibilities of what this collab might bring him are all difficult to process. He has fame, and he had it growing up, too—but this could bring an unprecedented amount of fame. The world might know his name. Even if they don’t like his music, they would know him as a rockstar, and not a pianist.

Their team boards the plane after them. Aventurine first, their manager ever since they’d signed with the IPC. He was always the image of perfection: not a strand of hair out of place, with a different designer suit on every day. He used too much cologne and wore two luxury watches everyday. He was rich, had more money than he ever knew what to do with, and if he was trying to hide it, he was doing a terrible job. Sometimes, the sight of him brought Mydei back to his childhood, living in the mansion that was more a museum than a home. His father never let him wear the same suit twice. Mydei couldn’t help but think Aventurine must follow that same stupid rule.

Out of all of them, though, Mydei knew Aventurine the best. Despite what he had come to believe about the company they’d signed with, Aventurine at least made an effort to appear genuine. He was always in person for their meetings. Always flew with them, attended every concert with few exceptions. He listened to all of their gripes and did his best to appease them. When he couldn’t, Mydei could still believe him when he said he was sorry.

Jade boards next. She’s the band’s publicist—who probably is the publicist of a hundred other IPC musicians, because Mydei rarely ever sees her. Any message she has is always delivered to them through Aventurine. Now is only the second or third time he’s actually seen her in person, and “perfect” isn’t even an accurate enough word to describe her. She’s beautiful, in the way that tells Mydei he should stay away from her. Jade’s very presence on this plane is enough to send shivers down his spine. She ensures she’s the most important person in every room she enters, even if the reality is that she isn’t.

Topaz is right behind her, chattering away on her phone. Mydei hasn’t met her very many times either, but she’s much friendlier than Jade, which is interesting because the two of them seem to have a very close relationship. She’s fluent in four languages and greeted Mydei in Kremnoan when they first met, even though she only knew a couple words. Out of the three of them, while she does appear somewhat intimidating when you first meet her, she’s without a doubt the most approachable of them all. But behind her warm brown eyes and girlish haircut, her skills in business are not to be underestimated. She’s the kind of person Mydei’s father would have nothing but the utmost respect for. This alone makes Mydei more wary of her.

Ratio boards last, a minute or so after Topaz. He gives Mydei a curt nod as they make eye contact and moves to sit next to Aventurine. The two of them have an unlikely friendship: IPC’s star producer and CALAMITY’s manager. As far as Mydei knows, they only started working together when CALAMITY signed to the IPC, and even then, their fields don't overlap very often.

Ratio—or Dr. Ratio, his producer tag—was thorny when Mydei first met him, but they were eventually able to bond over their shared love of music once they found common ground. Ratio is simply someone who is very passionate about his craft, and it shines through in the way he interacts with his clients. Sometimes, he reminds Mydei of his old piano teacher from college: a musical genius.

Jade enters into a virtual meeting on her laptop mere minutes after she’s boarded, and Mydei can’t help but wonder why she’s even here. It must be a seriously important opportunity if she was willing to make the trip out in person. Topaz is still on her own call, and Ratio takes out a book to read while Aventurine scrolls on his own phone, no doubt doing something equally important.

Mydei sighs, leaning against the window as he takes out his headphones. He’s never particularly enjoyed flying, but this job forced him to get comfortable with it, and fast. He’s a quarter of the way through his third listen of the new Stellaron Hunters album as the plane takes off, before he pulls his phone out of his pocket and searches for Robin instead.

He’s never considered himself someone who dislikes any kind of music, but he’d always thought that Robin’s genre was not his first choice. He had nothing against pop music, he just thought a lot of it could be rather bland. But “bland” is not a word that comes to mind as he listens to her debut, and most popular, album. Of course, he knew a majority of the songs from hearing them on the radio, but he’d never actually sat down and listened to it.

The first song on the album is her most famous single, If I Can Stop One Heart From Breaking,  the pop song you couldn’t escape if you tried. Mydei had heard it in department stores, on every local radio station, in the soundtrack of every movie released around that time. It was overplayed, but it had to be good to get to that point first. The only criticism Mydei would have is that the lyrics are surface level at best, as she sings about some optimistic crap Mydei doesn’t really believe in. But then he thinks about their most recent EP, and the things his ghost writers made him sing about —maybe it’s not really his place to criticize the depth of her hit single, when the masses clearly didn’t care about that.

The second song strikes him because it wasn’t one he’d heard before. Instead of the generic pop beat he was expecting, it opens up with a balladic piano solo. He freezes, thumb hovering over the pause button. He can tell it was recorded live, by an actual pianist. They’re good, incredibly so, and the song just improves when Robin joins in, like whoever is on piano plays their best in collaboration with Robin.

He opens the internet, identifying who is credited for the piano part after a quick search. Sunday Oak. A name he had never heard before, but it’s clear that this is Robin’s brother. How he didn’t know him, Mydei has no idea, and he blanches when he opens images and sees the face of this mystery pianist. The resemblance is so uncanny it’s almost cruel. Mydei stares at Sunday’s image for longer than he should, pinpointing every difference he can put his finger on. His eyes are light brown, not blue. His hair is longer. He looks more subdued, like there’s a great weight on his shoulders. His smile is more offputting than charming.

And, of course, his playing. Mydei pauses the song so he can open a video link, watching a live performance of him with Robin. He’s good, and it annoys him. Mydei can’t stop thinking of the picture he saw, with that stupid condescending smile on his face. He probably thought he was the shit. Just because he could play Robin’s little pop song.

Mydei exits out of the video, turning his music back on again. He skips the song. Fuck Sunday, and his pretty face, and methodically perfect piano playing. He was nothing like Phainon.

Late summer heat hits Mydei square in the face as soon as he steps out of the airport. He’s used to the heat, having grown up in Amphoreus’ hottest city-state, but living in the eastern region of Penacony had forced him to grow accustomed to its milder climate. Regardless, he still prefers heat to cold, so he doesn’t mind all that much.

Still, the cold air of his hotel room is a welcome feeling after being outside. It’s late when they arrive, with no obligations until tomorrow morning, so

Mydei drops his suitcase on the floor, takes a shower, and immediately gets into bed.

He hates sleeping in hotels. The bedding is scratchy and uncomfortable, and the pillows are always too hard for his liking. He tosses and turns all night, never getting more than an hour of sleep at a time. Each time he wakes up, he can’t stop thinking about what meeting Robin would be like. To write a song with her. The inevitable fame that would come his way afterwards.

Eventually, his clock reads a time where it wouldn’t be unreasonable to be awake, so he gets out of bed. He takes his time, killing an hour and a half in the empty hotel gym before showering and heading to the lobby for breakfast. He piles a plate high with eggs and breakfast meats, then sits by himself in the corner. Barely five minutes pass before Aventurine slides into the booth across from him, nothing but a single coffee cup in hand.

“Good morning,” he says, too cheerily for this hour.

“Morning,” Mydei answers, currently emptying three packets of hot sauce over his eggs.

“You’re up early. Didn’t strike me as the type.” Aventurine takes a sip of his coffee. Black, it appears. Mydei fights the urge to make a face.

“Couldn’t sleep.” Mydei yawns, as if proving his point. “It’ll be a while before the rest are up. At least two hours for Cipher.”

“Well, your session with Robin isn’t until noon, so you have time.”

Mydei gives him an affirmative grunt before taking his first bite of breakfast. The eggs are hard and rubbery, and the sausage tastes more like plastic than meat. They should let him into the kitchen instead. “How’d you get into this industry?” Mydei asks. He really would rather eat his breakfast in silence, but Aventurine is here now, so he might as well make conversation.

He doesn’t show it outwardly, but it’s clear that the question upsets him a little bit. He shrugs in response, opening his mouth and closing it again

before he finally answers. “Luck,” he starts. “I’ve always been good at doing business. If it wasn’t the IPC, it would be some other corporation.”

Mydei nods. “You’re not a musician.”

“God, no. Not in the slightest. I have no talent for it, like you, or…Ratio.”

“It’s reassuring to know you think we’re talented.” Mydei opens a fourth packet of hot sauce and drowns his eggs even more.

“We wouldn’t have signed you if we didn’t think you were worth the investments.”

“Huh,” Mydei says. He takes another bite—it tastes a little better, now that the base flavors are completely drowned out by hot sauce. “Ratio, too. He knows his shit.”

“Of course he does,” Aventurine says, doing that soulless little laugh of his. “Before he got into music production, he was a professor at Paperfold.”

Mydei nearly drops his fork. “What?”

Like clockwork, Ratio slides into the booth next to Aventurine. “Good morning, you two,” he says, seemingly uncaring about the look of shock on Mydei’s face. He has a single croissant on a plate, and a cup of tea.

“Morning, Doc,” Aventurine says, giving Mydei a knowing smile. “We were just talking about you.”

“You worked at Paperfold?” Mydei asks, as calmly as possible.

“Oh,” Ratio says, raising an eyebrow. “Yes, for a few years, before I realized their music department didn’t align with my goals.”

“Did you know Madam Herta?” The question leaves his mouth before he can stop himself, and he clamps it shut afterwards, like it would change the fact that he had already said it.

Ratio clicks his tongue. “Herta, Herta, Herta.” He shakes his head, ripping the croissant in half. It looks too dry and dense in the middle, and once again Mydei wishes he was the one in the kitchen.

“So yes.”

“Naturally.” Ratio hands Aventurine half of his croissant, who takes it wordlessly. “Was she your piano coach?”

“Unfortunately.” Mydei shoves another bite into his mouth and tries not to think about it. “She was…very talented.”

“Talented, undoubtedly, but I doubt whether her talent is as helpful as she seems to think it is.”

Mydei doesn’t immediately respond, too busy mulling over Ratio’s words. He couldn’t place all the blame on Herta’s shoulders, but she was part of the reason he had dropped out, in the end. He couldn’t keep up with all her standards. He couldn’t ever live up to who she wanted him to be, to what he wanted him to be.

“Herta’s opinion of you doesn’t matter,” Ratio continues, when he doesn’t say anything. “Can she comment on your music now? No, because it’s not her field. But I can.”

There’s something Mydei wants to say, about how it’s technically not his music, and of course Ratio would think it’s good because he was the one putting most of the work in. He keeps his mouth shut, though, and nods instead.

The rest of Mydei’s breakfast is accompanied by boring small talk: Ratio’s PhD studies, Aventurine’s past education, Mydei’s life back in Kremnos. He talks about his friends, Krateros, how he met the rest of the band. Nothing that could be exploited for later, even though he thinks the IPC probably has the means of learning everything about his past if they really wanted to. He does not bring up Phainon. He doesn’t even think about Phainon.

He excuses himself when he’s done, cleaning his plate away before getting on the elevator and heading back up to his room. On the way, he passes by Topaz, who gives him a quick wave, once again busy taking a call.

When he was a kid, his father made it clear to him that he would either study piano performance and become a world famous maestro, or study business so he could take over as CEO of Kremnos Pianos. The second option flew out the window when he and his mother left, and Mydei couldn’t be more ecstatic that he would never have to worry about anything business related. Topaz seems to enjoy her job well enough, but such enjoyment is difficult for Mydei to wrap his head around.

Mydei returns to his hotel room with too much time to kill. There’s nothing planned for the band until noon, even though his managers probably all have packed schedules. He’s not entirely sure what any of them do all day, but they’re always busy.

Mydei makes his bed. Sits in the middle of it and turns on the TV, listening to the news for ten minutes before switching to a cartoon and eventually turning it off. He paces. He connects his wireless headphones and stares out the window. He wanders through the hotel hallways until he finds the pool, and, in his insurmountable boredom, considers swimming a few laps. But then he dips a toe in, almost slips, and retreats back to his hotel room in shame. Sometimes—rarely, but still sometimes—he wishes he was a good swimmer. Unfortunately, he’d have to stick to land sports until he learned to face his fears.

He scrolls through social media. He doesn’t follow very many people, so his feed is always boring except for Cipher’s horrible posts. She had been told multiple times to tone down her social media presence, and never seemed to listen.

As if he’s in a trance, he opens up the search tab and clicks on the most recent result: phainonkhaslana. He stares at the profile before him like he hasn’t already memorized it: the profile picture that looks like a model shoot, no doubt Aglaea’s doing. His thousands of followers, the following count that’s nearly double that. Nothing has changed, except he’s uploaded

a new post since the last time Mydei stalked him. He clicks on it without a second thought.

The first slide is a professionally done program photo: Phainon, donning a sleek black tuxedo, stands in the background with his hands in his pockets. He’s facing to the left, with a somber look on his face. Completely unlike his usual dimples and boyish charm. Hysilens is in the foreground, facing the right, with a long black dress on. She holds her violin, hair tied back into a long ponytail. They look incredible, both of them almost inhumanly attractive.

The second slide features both of them on stage, standing side by side. There’s a piano behind them. Hysilens holds her violin, free hand joined with Phainon’s. They have their joined hands raised in the air, both of them smiling wide at the audience.

The last slide is a picture of Hysilens alone, presumably taken by Phainon. She stands in what looks like a practice room of sorts, though it’s much nicer than the ones Mydei is used to. Her violin has a string loose and she glares at the camera with murderous intent.

Mydei’s eyes flick down to the caption:

Bartok violin sonata 2 🖒 Csardas 🖒 So so fun playing with

@hysil.phagousa last week. Thank you Okhema, always a pleasure :)

Against his better interest, he opens the comments. The top thread was started by Hysilens, mere hours ago.

hysil.phagousa: I hate this piece

phainonkhaslana: @hysil.phagousa csardas?

hysil.phagousa: @phainonkhaslana don’t insinuate that I have any criticisms of csardas ever again.

Mydei scrolls through the comments until he finds one that comments on how good they look together, which makes him upset enough to turn his

phone off. He knows better than anyone that Phainon and Hysilens are merely close classmates and good friends. But he doesn’t like that not everyone knows that.

He orders room service and eats in silence, letting his annoyance simmer. By the time he’s finished, it’s finally late enough that he can leave. Even so, he’s the first one in the lobby, and is forced to wait as patiently as possible even as his nerves get worse every second.

They’re driven to Robin’s house alone, where she told them they would meet. Aventurine, Topaz, Jade, and Ratio have a different meeting they need to attend, as far as Mydei’s aware. Robin had requested that they meet alone to work out the creative vision at first.

The drive isn’t very long, likely less than ten minutes, but it feels like an eternity. Mydei spends it staring out the tinted window and listening to Hyacine converse with the driver in the background. He can’t drown out his nerves, no matter how hard he tries. What if they don’t get along, and their visions don’t align? What if Robin doesn’t like them, or their music? What if her team had the wrong idea?

He’s pulled from his thoughts when the car stops, and he sees Hyacine get out of her seat. He climbs out expecting to see a lavish mansion similar to the one he grew up in, but finds a house much more modest than what he was envisioning. It’s still big and beautiful, but it doesn’t give the impression that Robin has allowed all her fame to get entirely in her head. It’s his first actual impression of her, and it’s a good one.

They walk to the front door, but it opens before they have to knock, and Mydei thinks his heartbeat nearly doubles when he sees the woman at the other side of the door.

He’s seen a hundred pictures of Robin—she’s at the level of fame where you can’t not see her, but seeing her in person is a completely different thing. Her long dyed blue hair is tied back into a bun, and you can see the roots of her natural hair color coming in. Her green eyes sparkle as she takes them in, and Mydei finds that the warmth each of her photos seem to emulate wasn’t fabricated at all. She wears long white feathers from her

ears and has big blue-framed glasses on. She’s even prettier in person than she is in a photoshoot, where she’s meant to embody perfection.

“Hi!” she starts, her voice soft and unbearably genuine as she fully steps outside to greet them. “I’m Robin, it’s so nice to finally meet you all! You must be Mydei?” she asks, and Mydei’s heart nearly jumps out of his throat. “Can I call you that?”

“Of course,” Mydei says, throat a little dry as he speaks. A beat of silence passes, and he offers his hand as an afterthought. She takes it, and he can’t help but note how soft her hands are.

“Hyacine?” she continues, moving to the girl to Mydei’s right. “Castorice, and then Cipher?” She shakes each of their hands, and Mydei squeezes the hand she had just touched into a fist. He’s embarrassingly clammy.

“I listened to all of your music over the past week, and I’m so happy my team was able to find a band like yours,” she starts, stepping back. “My favorite song is Taxidermy.”

Mydei can’t help the look that comes over his face. “Seriously?” he asks, and he can feel Castorice’s excitement, equally palpable, behind him. They wrote Taxidermy by themselves, and it was on their first EP, but no one ever spoke about it. Castorice always said it was her favorite song, and Mydei was inclined to agree. Cipher thought it was good, but her favorite song of theirs was Child’s Play. For reasons Mydei couldn’t quite understand.

Hyacine wasn’t there when they wrote the first EP, but she loved Taxidermy as well. It had their most ambitious guitar solo out of all their songs so far, and it took her over a month to learn.

Robin nods. “I was blown away when I first heard it. And to think you did all that on your own…it’s unbelievable. All four of you are so incredibly talented.”

“So are you!” Hyacine chimes in. “I’ve been a fan since I was in middle school,” she says earnestly. “Your second album was my favorite. I had tickets to the tour, and everything, I just couldn’t go because…something

came up.” Her smile fades slightly at the last part. Mydei wonders what she could be talking about, but realizes now is not the right time to pry.

“I’m so happy to hear that,” Robin says. “Don’t tell anyone I said this, but my second album is probably my favorite, too. I think it’s underappreciated.”

“It is underappreciated!” Hyacine exclaims. “The industry can’t handle something a little different nowadays.”

“That’s part of the reason why I’m writing this album,” Robin agrees, nodding. “Actually, why don’t you come in, and we can talk about it?”

She opens the door again, leading the four of them inside. Her house is even more beautiful on the inside, with intricate gold and blue wallpaper and polished marble flooring. She guides them through, all the way to a back corner, where she opens a door into her own personal recording studio. It doesn’t look that different from the ones Mydei is used to—maybe a bit bigger, with half of it turned into a seating area of sorts. A whiteboard hangs over one of the couches, filled with notes, song titles, and a couple artist names Mydei recognizes.

Mechanical Fever is what catches his eye the most—he knew Serval from college, when her band was a side gig and she was fully dedicated to her mechanical engineering degree. He didn’t think they were still playing at all.

“This is where we will be recording,” she says. “I have all the instruments you guys might need, but if you’re more comfortable with your own, feel free to bring them.”

Cipher has already made herself at home on one of the couches, and Mydei moves to sit beside her. Usually, she makes it a point to annoy him as much as possible when they sit next to each other, so he can only hope she wouldn’t pull anything weird in front of Robin.

“So, the album,” Robin continues. She flicks a couple switches to turn on the console. The speakers hanging from the walls make a faint sound as

they turn on. “I wanted to explore themes of mortality and humanity. My brother, Sunday—he studied philosophy in college, and always made it a point to ask me these questions he was studying. One that really stuck with me was ‘why does life slumber?’ That’s one of the biggest themes on the album, and I’m thinking of calling it that.”

Why does life slumber? Mydei doesn’t even know how to begin going about answering that. Philosophy was never his strong suit, always the kind of thing he hated talking about, because ultimately, who cares? He always took the questions too literally and didn’t think outside of the obvious answer.

Now, though, he’s struck with a memory from his childhood. His father was the closest thing to a Kremnoan conservative that existed in this time, even as someone with a very non-traditional career. He encouraged Mydei to exercise and tone his body like their ancestors did, so he would never forget where he came from. He had an old quote in his office that read “even blades must be laid down.” Mydei always thought it was stupid, and that his father was corny for hanging on to traditions that only existed millenia ago.

But he thinks of the quote today. Even though his father probably never thought about it too deeply, he supposes it’s a good enough answer to that question.

“I wanted to play you guys the rest of the album and a couple samples of what I’m thinking for this song,” Robin is saying. “The first song I wrote in collaboration with the country artist Boothill. Have any of you guys heard of him?”

Mydei hasn’t. He looks at Cipher—the only person in this room that he knows at least somewhat enjoys country music. He doesn’t hate it, but it’s never going to be his first choice.

“Don’t look at me,” Cipher says. “Okay, I know of him, but he’s more classic country than modern, so I think his stuff is boring.”

“Like modern country isn’t boring,” Castorice mutters under her breath.

Robin laughs before Cipher can start an argument. “Yeah, I didn’t like country music at all before I worked with him. But that’s the point of this album: stepping out of my comfort zone, and I knew if I really wanted to do that, I would have to study a genre I don’t like.”

She plays the first song, and the sounds of what sounds like three overlapping guitars fills the room. It’s not what Mydei was expecting, given that she had prefaced it by saying it was country music, and he’s surprised at how easily he’s able to get behind it.

He looks over at the whiteboard, at the tracklist written in one of the corners. Birds and Sky, featuring Boothill. He nearly jumps out of his skin when he looks down and sees Helektra Phagousa written beside one of the songs in the middle.

Hysilens. How in the world did she find Hysilens?

Robin’s soft voice comes over the speaker, and Mydei turns back around. So far, it doesn’t sound like she did much to alter the way she normally sings for this song. He knows that Robin is a talented singer, so she probably chose not to add an artificial “country twang” to her voice for reasons Mydei doesn’t know, but can appreciate nonetheless. The idea of it almost makes him laugh.

Near the end of the song, though, the instrumentals take over, and both Robin and a man’s voice can be heard yodeling in the background. He can’t help the smile that breaks over his face. Yodeling. Something Mydei wouldn’t be caught dead doing.

“He had to teach me how to yodel,” Robin explains. “It requires a lot of vocal control. I hadn’t sung in a long time when we recorded this, so it took longer than I’d like to admit.”

The next song is called Epsilon, which Robin says is the name of her hometown. A tiny island north of Penacony that few people have heard of. She sings most of the song in her native tongue, and says that the style of music was inspired by a band she stumbled across when she was visiting. They called themselves The Halovians, and did most of their performances

for free. Even though Mydei can’t understand what she’s singing about, she describes it as a love letter to her home. He thinks he can understand that, even though he does not know why he still loves Castrum Kremnos. There were few good memories associated with the place, and even fewer things to be proud of.

The third song is Fate in Dreamland, followed up with Night in Dreamland. Neither of the songs have a feature, being the first songs she wrote for the album. Fate in Dreamland is the most upbeat song so far, and sounds like a classic pop song. The kind of thing you would hear on her debut album. She doesn’t explain what it’s about in depth, but Mydei can tell it was written about her experience in Kasbelina three years ago. Or at least, partially, because it seems to be somewhat satirical in nature.

Night in Dreamland is a ballad, and Mydei thinks they must be connected due to the titles. He finds it odd that when Robin recounts her experience being shot in the neck during a concert, she doesn’t bemoan her own trauma. It’s something he respects regardless.

Pinion’s Aria is the fifth song, which features the Astral Express. Mydei only knows about the jazz troupe tangentially, given that he was sort of friends with Caelus and Stelle in college. Reaching out to them would be weird, he thinks, since they were obviously much closer with Phainon than they ever were with him.

Robin explains how Sunday was the Express’ newest member, and she wanted to explore jazz as another genre she knew very little about. Mydei admits that jazz is one of his favorite music genres, always preferring it to classical. He enjoyed the Express’ music as their original work put a modern twist to it, and their covers of classics were always incredible. Knowing that Sunday is their pianist, though, makes him like the group slightly less.

The next one is Hysilens’ feature, Moonless Midnight. From the beginning, Mydei is shocked at how different Robin’s voice sounds in this. Throughout the beginning of the album, her voice only rarely strayed from what he was used to hearing from her. The music styles differed, but her voice was

always the same. Now, though, she adopted a rougher tone, and belted the entire chorus with an aggression Mydei wasn’t expecting at all.

Hysilens plays throughout it, given a solo violin part after the first chorus. Mydei isn’t impressed by her prowess, he’s always known how talented she was. Throughout everything Robin has shared about the album so far, he’s come to admire her wholly as a person, but it’s this song that starts to make him admire her as a musician, too.

Harmony is next, and Mydei feigns indifference when she introduces Ruan Mei as the feature. Castorice and Hyacine both say they know her, which surprises Mydei, because he thought Castorice listened to mainly harder music like shoegaze and grunge rock, and Ruan Mei is far from it.

But he doesn’t know her, not well, anyways. He only knows Herta, her friend? Partner? Wife? Mydei is still confused about that. He doesn’t share that Ruan Mei shook his hand and said he was talented, but his pride surges when he hears her part in the song. Multi-instrumentalist, Robin said she was, and Mydei isn’t sure which instruments that encompasses, but he can hear her on the most beautifully placed saxophone part he’s ever heard throughout the song. Robin’s soft voice floats above the instrumental part, and Mydei feels like he’s dreaming as he listens to it.

The next song is called Had I Not Seen the Sun, and Robin explains it’s a cover of an old Penaconian classic. “I’m not from Penacony, obviously,” she says, finger lingering on the play button. “But I’ve been here for so long. Everyone I love is here. It’s just as much a home to me as Epsilon is, and I wanted to give this place some love. Even though it has its problems.”

The song starts with just her and a piano—Sunday, Mydei thinks bitterly. It’s a simple enough piano part that Mydei can’t be impressed. It’s a very intimate song, and he can feel the love that was put into it. Near the end, a chorus chimes in, which Robin says was recorded by a children’s choir in Kasbelina.

The last song is called The Eighth Day, the one featuring Mechanical Fever. Mydei explains his relationship to Serval, and Robin says she stumbled

across them in Belobog, but it’s still not much more than a hobby to any of them.

Once again, the song is related to Sunday in some way. Mydei would be irritated if it wasn’t so glaringly obvious how much he means to her. He can hear the rock influences in the instrumental, but it’s still different from their style. He had to admit he was unsure how different their song would be from Mechanical Fever’s if she chose to feature two rock bands.

“The next song is the one I want to write with you guys,” Robin says. “It’s the last song on the album. It has to close it out in a special way, I want it to be loud and grand and a perfect finale.”

Loud and grand. Mydei can do that.

Robin moves over to a computer in the corner, clicking the mouse a few times until she pulls up a folder filled with audio recordings. “I got help from Sunday to start recording the general idea I have,” she starts. “I want there to be a prominent piano part, and the rest will be rock instruments. You guys,” she clarifies, looking over at them.

Mydei feels Castorice’s eyes on him. He looks up, making eye contact for a brief moment. He isn’t sure what Robin means by that. He had just assumed he would be doing backing vocals, or something. He didn’t even want his own verse.

“Actually,” Robin’s mouse lingers over the play button on one of the audio files she had opened, but she doesn’t press it before she turns around. “I totally forgot to ask. Do any of you play piano? There wasn’t much of it in your music, so I figured if none of you knew I could just ask Sunday to do it.”

Now, Mydei can feel all three pairs of eyes on him. Poor Robin didn’t even know the can of worms she had just opened, and he can’t even deny it, with how obvious everyone else is acting. He swallows, and the sound practically echoes in the silent room. “I can,” he says quietly.

“You can!” Robin exclaims. “Oh, that’s so great! This worked out perfectly, then!”

“But I—” he cuts in, suddenly growing increasingly nervous. “I worry that my playing won’t be up to your standards.”

“Oh, bullshit,” Cipher interrupts, rolling her eyes as she leans further into the couch cushions. “You were only the best—”

“Cipher, stop,” Mydei hisses, clamping a hand over her mouth in his desperation. “Piano sounds great, Robin. I’ll get back to you on whether I'm willing to play it or not.”

“Okay! We don’t have to start recording right now, anyways. I was thinking we could just do lyrics today.” She plays the recording next, of a solo piano part obviously recorded on a phone. It’s simple, the kind of thing Mydei could easily sightread in his prime. Probably today, too. And he’s certain he could do it better than Sunday.

“I want it to be darker than my usual sound,” she says, once it finishes. “It’ll open with just the piano and me, and then the whole band will join in together afterwards.”

“I love it,” Hyacine speaks up first. Mydei nods. It does sound like a good idea. He just wishes it didn’t need to have the piano part, even though he knows deep down that scrapping the piano would make it significantly worse.

“It’s a very rough draft right now, of course. I don’t have any lyrics planned right now.”

“I can help with that,” Castorice says. “If you’d like, of course.”

“I did read somewhere that you write most of the lyrics,” Robin says, moving to pull a box of used notebooks out from underneath the coffee table.

“Not just me,” Castorice blushes. “Mydei wrote Don’t Cry.”

“Oh, did you?” Robin looks up as she selects one of the notebooks near the end of the box. “I liked that one a lot, too.”

Mydei thanks her. Even though Don’t Cry is one of his least favorite songs. It was the first song he wrote by himself and actually took seriously. It being their biggest hit was completely unprecedented.

Robin sits on the floor and writes down their brainstorming ideas into a blank page of the notebook. Since it’s her album, they mostly piggyback off of her original ideas. Escape, freedom, being trapped like a bird in a cage.

“There’s this children’s book I always read when I was younger,” Robin says. “It’s popular in Penacony, so I’m not sure if you have heard of it, but it’s about this artificial dream world anyone was invited to go to. It was actually quite a dark story, for a children’s book,” she laughs. “I was thinking something like that. Trapped in a land of dreams.”

“The last track is about escaping from the dreamscape,” Castorice murmurs.

Hyacine gasps, clapping a hand over her mouth. “Dreamscape! We can call it Dreamscape!”

“Oh, that’s perfect!” Robin rushes to write it at the top of the page, underlining it twice. “Oh, I just realized—I’m such a bad host. Do you want anything to drink?”

Mydei can’t just expect everyone to have pomegranate juice on hand, so he asks for a coffee instead. Cipher copies his request, Castorice asks for tea, and Hyacine asks for water.

“I’ll be right back. You can start on the lyrics then, if you want?” She hands the notebook and pen over to Castorice, who takes it and flips to a clean page.

Robin closes the door behind her as she leaves, and Hyacine and Castorice immediately start work on the lyrics. He has a couple ideas himself, but they’re so far in the back of his head right now. Cipher can clearly tell, staring at him strangely in the corner of his eye.

“Excuse me,” he says, nudging Cipher’s feet out of the way as he stands. “Bathroom,” he clarifies, met with their confused stares. Robin had pointed out where the nearest one was on their walk to the studio room, but he had no real intention of going there. He makes his way through her living room and into the kitchen, where she loads coffee beans into the machine with her back to him.

“Oh! Hi, Mydei, did you need something?” she asks, when she turns around. “The bathroom is that way—in case you forgot.”

“No, that’s not it,” he starts. “Robin, I wasn’t entirely honest with you.”

“Oh,” Robin says again, putting the bag of coffee beans down. Her full attention is on him now, and Mydei feels nervous under the weight of it. “What’s wrong?”

“I am a pianist,” he wets his lips, then swallows. “I am a very good pianist. Or…I was. I don’t really know if I am anymore,” he laughs as he says it, more out of nerves than anything. But even with his inexperience, he’s sure he’s at least better than Sunday.

“I went to school for it,” he continues. “It’s not a secret to the public, I couldn’t really cover something like that up, especially when there’s so many videos of me performing on the internet. But I’ve made it clear that I don’t do that anymore.”

Robin looks a little surprised, but doesn’t push it. “That’s fine,” she says. “I don’t want to make you do anything you’re uncomfortable with. I can always have my brother record it for us.”

The thought of having Sunday play on his track when he is more than capable sends shivers down his spine. Putting La Campanella in front of him would probably kill the man. He looked like his favorite composers were Mozart or Bach.

Mydei gathers himself, putting thoughts of Sunday’s probable incompetence to the back of his head. “I love your idea,” he starts. “I never

thought about including piano in my music before. If I was going to pick it up again, I see no better time than now.”

“Okay,” Robin says gently, nodding. “If you don’t mind me asking, what was the reason you quit piano?”

“A lot of reasons.” Mydei looks down at his hands. He doesn’t like thinking about that time in his life, even this far removed from it. “The biggest one, though, was that I didn’t like it enough. My teacher told me I would never make it as a classical pianist, because my dislike for it was so obvious.

“But this—” he shakes his head. “This is what I want to do. Make music like this. I can’t just go through the rest of my life as a musician ignoring the most prominent instrument in the world.”

Robin laughs, but she’s serious when she stops and looks at him. “You’re sure?”

Mydei nods. “Yes. I’m sure.”

“Mydei, why do you think life slumbers?”

Mydei looks up at her, but her back is turned to him again as she returns her attention to the coffee machine. “You know, I tried to answer that question when you first asked it, but all I could think about was this old Kremnoan quote. From when we still adopted a warrior culture.” Most people who don’t know very much about Castrum Kremnos tend to think of it as a land of brutes. Kremnoans rarely leave, and the rest of the world prefers it that way. He wonders if Robin thought that of him, when she first saw him. It’s not a rare reaction.

“‘Even blades must be laid down,’” he recites. “I’m sure sleep was important too, then. What good is a warrior who doesn’t rest?”

Robin presses a button on the coffee machine, and turns to look at him. “That’s a beautiful answer,” she says, smiling to herself. “Maybe now, when you pick up the piano again, you’ll be better than you ever were.”
