HALL OF STRIFE

Ptolemy Savalas, violin Perdikkas Katsanevas, viola

Peucesta Lytras, viola Hephaestion Axiotis, cello

Leonnius Goutas, bass Mydeimos Nikador, piano

Program

Sextet for Piano and Strings in D major, Op. 110……Felix Mendelssohn (2809-2847) Allegro vivace Adagio Menuetto agitato Allegro vivace

Grand Sextet in E-flat major……Mikhail Glinka (2804-2857) Allegro maestoso Andante Allegro con spirito

Piano Sonata No. 14 in C-sharp minor, “Moonlight Sonata”……Ludwig von Beethoven (2770-2827) Adagio sostenuto

Allegretto Presto agitato

About the Performers

Mydeimos Nikador is a Kremnoan pianist, who made his Hall of Strife debut when he was just seven years old. Born to virtuosos Gorgo and Eurypon Nikador, he has performed pieces by Liszt, Rachmaninoff, and many more. He currently attends the Gibranipar School of Music and plans to pursue a BA in piano performance at Paperfold University in Penacony. During his time as a pianist, Nikador has been recognized globally for his performance of Brahms’ Piano Concerto No. 1 in D Minor with the Symphonic Orchestra of Okhema and for his various appearances alongside the Castrum Kremnos Philharmonic Orchestra.

~~~

September 3rd, 3865. Sophomore fall semester.

“You did exceptionally well, Mydeimos.”

Madam Herta looks as put together as always, one leg crossed over the other in her seat that looks more like a throne than a desk chair. “And you’ve impressed me, which is not an easy feat.”

“Thank you,” Mydei says, fiddling with his hands in his lap from where he sits at the piano. He tries not to come across like those words make him feel giddy, even though he’s rarely felt pride so great in his life.

“So now begins the battle where we have to figure out how you’re going to impress me again.”

Mydei doesn’t care what she throws at him. He’s never been this determined to keep someone’s pride—not even his mother, or Krateros. But

if he really wants to be a good pianist, if this is really what he’s going to do with his life, he needs Madam Herta’s approval.

“I want you to play La Campanella.”

Mydei’s eyes widen. Now that’s a piece he actually knows—Phainon joked about it enough times for him to pick up on the title. He knows next to nothing about the actual piece. Just that it’s notoriously difficult, and Phainon doesn’t believe he could ever be capable of playing it, much as he wants to.

Mydei doesn’t quite know what he’s getting himself into, but he feels pride surge in his gut regardless. Madam Herta believes in him. Last semester, he wouldn’t have thought that was ever possible.

“Seriously?” he asks.

Madam Herta merely nods. “It would impress me,” she starts, leaning even further back into her chair, “if you perfected La Campanella in one semester. And you know what I mean by ‘perfected’.”

There were two things Madam Herta considered perfect. Herself was the first one. The way he had played his piece at the end of last semester was the other.

“Do you think you can do it?”

Mydei swallows all his doubts and nods. “Yes,” he says. “I can do it.”

Madam Herta smiles. She looks pleased, but there’s nothing nice about the look on her face. It’s something Mydei has had to get used to. Madam Herta is pretty much as eccentric as they come, but sometimes Mydei thinks she has to be some sort of sadist.

She hands him a small book of sheet music. The first page is the cover, written in some old font as if Madam Herta had time traveled and stolen the original hand-written copy by herself. He opens it, gingerly, and even looking at the first page makes him feel like he’s had an aneurysm.

“Scared?” Madam Herta laughs a little, and at this moment Mydei is even more convinced that she’s a sadist. “I performed this piece at thirteen. In fact, maybe it would do you some good to watch my old performance.”

Mydei merely nods, and places the sheet music on the rack in silence.

“Do your best,” Madam Herta kicks her feet up on her desk, leaning back. “You’re good at sightreading, I’ll give you that—but not good enough to play this easily right now. All I ask is that you improve every week.”

Mydei walks out of her office feeling like he’d just gotten run over repeatedly by an eighteen-wheeler. He’s not sure what kind of a psycho would sit down and write a piece like that, but he’s surprised it wasn’t Madam Herta herself. She’s the perfect amount of evil to come up with something like that—and while Mydei had no strong opinions on Liszt before, today he hates him.

It’s already late, around 8:30, and Mydei hasn’t had dinner yet. But that doesn’t stop him from locking himself in a practice room for an extra three hours. He leaves that session even more dejected, if it’s even possible, and feeling like he’s finally run into a wall he won’t be able to pass.

He checks his watch, and realizes how late it’s gotten without him even noticing. The dining halls close at ten, and he’s starving. He makes do with a bag of chips from a vending machine and sits on the music building’s balcony while he eats them in silence. He already feels like he’s losing his damn mind.

His phone rings, and the call almost goes to voicemail by the time Mydei digs his phone out from the bottom of his bag. He curses when he sees Phainon’s name on his screen, and scrambles to pick up. “Hello?”

“Mydei, hey, are you okay? Herta didn’t kill you, did she?” He laughs, awkwardly, the sound lingering in Mydei’s head.

“No, she didn’t.” Mydei swallows. He’d told Phainon he would text him after his lesson ended, and then forgot. He’s not sure if he even wants to explain himself to Phainon. What would he think, if Mydei told him that Madam Herta deemed him talented enough to play La Campanella? Wouldn’t that make Phainon jealous? Were their roles reversed, Mydei would absolutely be upset. “I was practicing.”

Phainon’s end of the line is silent for a few moments. “...It’s almost midnight.”

Mydei puts a chip in his mouth. “So?”

“You never practice this late. I thought you valued your sleep.”

“I locked in.”

“Mydeimos.”

“Phainon.”

“Did she give you a new piece?”

Mydei swallows the chip, pursing his lips slowly. It was his first lesson of the semester, so of course he would have gotten new repertoire to work on. “Yes,” he says, finding himself unable to lie.

“Would I know it?”

That is a stupid question, because Phainon knows every single piece of classical music ever written. Mydei could bring up some obscure composer who’s only written one piece for piano in their entire career and Phainon would still say he might have heard of them before. “No,” he replies anyway. “Really obscure.”

“What—are you being sarcastic, Mydei?” Phainon’s voice has a teasing lilt to it, the way it usually gets when he’s about to say something he knows will make Mydei mad. “Wait, let me guess. Hungarian Rhapsody.”

Mydei snickers. It’s his worst nightmare to play that piece. Phainon bringing it up now honestly helps him realize that it could always be worse.

“Anything by Liszt.”

“I told you it’s obscure.”

“And you were lying. La Campanella.”

“You got your guess for the day.”

“Mydei—”

“What are you playing?” Mydei continues, effectively cutting him off and changing the subject. Phainon was bound to figure it out sooner or later, anyway.

“Well, Mozart with the orchestra. And then I’m doing a Chopin waltz solo, and Brahms 1 with Hysilens’ quartet.”

Mydei exhales sharply. Being a junior and Mydei a sophomore, Phainon was much more involved with the music department than Mydei was. He probably could benefit from involving himself more, honestly—but he’s getting his credits. Phainon is just over-achieving. “I don’t know any of those pieces,” he says.

Phainon sighs loudly on the other end. “Yeah, we know.”

“I don’t like Chopin.”

“Or Mozart.”

“No, speak for yourself. Mozart is okay.”

“Ugh. He peaked at Requiem. Maybe if he’d lived a little longer.”

“He didn’t even write half of Requiem.”

Phainon laughs heartily on the other end of the line. It never fails to bring a smile to Mydei’s face. “Look at you and your composer knowledge.”

“Good point. I clearly need to spend less time with you.”

Phainon laughs yet again, making Mydei’s grin grow even wider. “Are you walking back, then?” He asks, and Mydei’s glad that the concern is out of his voice.

“Soon,” Mydei says.

“Will you text me when you get home? I need to shower.”

“What, worried I’m going to slip and fall?” Mydei asks. He stands, stretching a little before he heads back inside to throw away the empty bag of chips.

“Something like that. I know you’re very fragile.”

Mydei snorts. Last year, Phainon saying something like that to him would probably have genuinely pissed him off. Being around him so often has desensitized him to his relentless attempts to make Mydei mad. “Bye, then,” Mydei responds. “I love you.”

“Aw, I love you too—” Mydei hangs up, chuckling to himself as he pockets his phone and heads for the fire exit.

The next morning, he leaves his lesson music behind when he goes to class. His practice session that afternoon is spent doing dexterity exercises and etudes.

Phainon walks in on him, as he does many times. He’d always been able to tell when it’s Mydei playing, somehow, and has never walked in on someone by accident who isn’t Mydei. Though that was his word, and Mydei isn’t sure how much he believes that.

“What the fuck,” he says, effectively cutting off Mydei’s playing. The door shuts behind them, and Phainon stares at him like he has just walked in on someone else. “Mydeimos, you’re playing scales.”

“You don’t play scales?” Mydei asks, feigning innocence. Phainon does play scales. Every session, he warms up with an extensive scale and arpeggio worksheet in the key of the piece he’s working on.

Mydei, however, does not. He sits down at the bench and starts playing, because he doesn’t have time for all of that. Both he and Phainon are very aware of this fact. They had argued about it more times than Mydei could keep track of.

“G-sharp minor,” Phainon says blandly, peering over Mydei’s shoulder.

Mydei swallows. There are hundreds of pieces written in G-sharp minor. It’s not enough of a clue for Phainon to figure out he’s using it as La Campanella practice. “Picked a random key,” he replies.

“Why the fuck are you playing scales?”

“Don’t you think my fingers aren’t flexible enough?”

“What?”

“I mean—see?” Mydei stretches out his hand before Phainon, then places it back on the piano. He can hit a tenth comfortably, an eleventh if he really strains. He already knows damn well that Phainon can hit a twelfth if he really wants to.

“What exactly are you playing?” Phainon raises an eyebrow.

“I should be able to hit fifteenths, I think.”

Phainon blinks. “Mydei, no one can hit a fucking fifteenth. Not even Rachmaninoff could do that.”

“With jumping,” Mydei explains.

Phainon stares at him for a moment, and Mydei instantly knows he’s figured it out. “You’re playing La Campanella.”

Mydei’s hand goes slack, and he looks away with a dejected sigh. “Yeah,” he says. He’s not a liar, and it wouldn’t work on Phainon even if he tried.

“Holy shit.” The words leave Phainon’s mouth like an exhale, and he steps back a little. “I knew it. Why didn’t you tell me when I literally guessed that?”

Mydei bites his lip. “I didn’t want you to be upset,” he says, unable to look Phainon in the eye.

Phainon frowns. “Why would I be upset? I can’t believe I’m going to get to watch you perform La Campanella. Oh my god.” He runs his hands through his hair, eyes shining when he looks at Mydei.

“Yeah,” Mydei sighs. “You think I can do it?”

“I think you can do anything.”

Mydei doesn’t care all that much about what Madam Herta thinks of his playing at this moment. He finds himself constantly jumping between fighting for Madam Herta’s approval and being satisfied with the simple fact that Phainon has always believed in him. He isn’t sure which one is more powerful.

That weekend, Mydei is dragged to a party. It’s different from the first time last year, when he and Phainon got caught up in a challenge to see who could drink more than the other. It must have been divine intervention that brought him to his senses enough to leave before it got too late. Mydei doesn’t remember much about that night, which upsets him. It’s why he doesn’t like to drink anymore.

Phainon still manages to convince him to come with him sometimes, under the guise that his friends aren’t enough to entertain him. Mydei has met Caelus, Stelle, and Hysilens, and he’s somewhat close with Cipher and Castorice because of the band, and boring is the last word he would use to describe any of them. So the real reason must be something else entirely.

Sure enough, all four of them are already there when they arrive. Caelus is the host, apparently, this being his apartment. He lives with four other boys from the marching band and Mydei has no desire to be friends with any of them. Band kids were never his crowd.

There’s a group of them crowded around the living room table, playing a card game. Mydei knows none of them. Every once in a while, they scream and cheer so loudly that Mydei has to fight the urge to walk out immediately.

Cipher sits on top of a counter looking like she pays rent, and her jaw drops when she meets Mydei’s eyes. “No way you got him to come, Phangry?”

Mydei doesn’t know where that nickname came from. He asked Phainon about it once, and he said it was what his childhood friend used to call him. How it got into Cipher’s hands is anyone’s guess.

“I could get him to do anything, really,” Phainon laughs that awfully polite laugh of his. Mydei wishes they would hear the way Phainon laughs around him.

Caelus serves Phainon a drink that Mydei wouldn’t even trust knowing they’re friends. His sister, Stelle, leans against a corner countertop playing some game on her phone. She gives Mydei a quick nod as a greeting and goes back to her game.

“Good thing you’re here. I wanted to talk to you, actually,” Cipher says, while Phainon and Caelus are deep in conversation. “That song we recorded over the summer? I just sent it out to a few record labels—”

“What?” Mydei starts, eyes wide. “Seriously? That’s amazing, Cipher.”

Cipher laughs awkwardly. “Yeah…so anyways, I want you to cover the cost in full.”

Mydei’s smile fades. “…You’re serious.”

Cipher nods, like she’s ashamed, but Mydei knows she doesn’t feel an ounce of shame.

“They charged you to send a song in?”

“Penacony’s a fucked up place, man,” Cipher shakes her head. “I swear I’m not trying to scam you.”

Mydei honestly knows better than to trust her, but he gets her Venmo and pays her anyway. She grins, toothy, when she sees the money, and disappears soon after that.

Mydei met both Cipher and Castorice last year, during the spring semester. Cipher was introduced to him by Phainon, and they met each other when they both worked at the library. Cipher was a senior then, and Mydei isn’t entirely sure how she got into this college party (or graduated, for that matter), but most of what Cipher accomplishes shouldn’t be questioned.

Castorice was a junior literature major who worked for the writing center. Mydei met her after getting help on one of his History essays. She already knew Cipher very well, having met each other when they lived in Okhema. Cipher played electric bass, and Castorice played the drums. Mydei foolishly thought that the rhythm section of a band must get along very well, but with the two of them, that wasn’t exactly the case. They bickered a lot when the three of them worked together to write their first song, though most of that was Cipher’s fault. Castorice was hard to make angry, but Cipher tried her best.

All three of them, and Phainon as well, lived in Amphoreus, which was overseas from their college. It made it easier over the summer where they could see each other to record—all Mydei had to do was travel to Okhema, which wasn’t all that difficult.

The first and only song they’d ever written wasn’t a masterpiece by any means, but Mydei liked it. Castorice had written the lyrics, Mydei had written the music, and Cipher produced it, which she had no background in beforehand, but they figured it out together. It’s hard to create something perfect with limited materials, but it was the most fun Mydei had had in years. He didn’t think, at the time of recording, that they had any bigger plans for the little band they’d started for fun. And Cipher might have sent the song out, but that didn’t mean they were going to get a record deal.

“Mydei! My man!” Caelus cuts in, slapping him on the shoulder. He has a cup in hand that better not be intended for Mydei. “You drinking tonight?”

Mydei sighs. “I will if you hit the gym with us tomorrow night,” he responds, coming to stand beside Phainon.

Caelus looks over his shoulder to Stelle, who is offering him no help. “I’m kinda busy. Gotta do some homework tomorrow, you know how it is…”

“Your business homework?” Phainon asks, feigning innocence. Mydei disguises his laugh as a cough, turning into Phainon’s shoulder as he does it. “Did you fail the last color-by-number exam?”

Caelus rolls his eyes. “You guys are such assholes. The gym isn’t really my thing, okay?”

“...You’re a business major.” Phainon reiterates.

“We’re pianists,” Mydei adds.

“I’m in marching band!” Caelus defends himself, waving his arms around. “I have…that to worry about, and stuff…”

“Hitting the gym could help you hold your trumpet up for longer,” Mydei suggests, and Phainon nods furiously beside him.

Mydei sighs. “How many times do I have to tell you not to apologize for things that aren’t your fault?”

“But how is it not my fault?” Phainon asks. His hands are clenched into tight fists. His hair is a mess and there are bags under his eyes, like his insomnia is coming back. Mydei steels himself and bites his tongue. “You wouldn’t be pushing me away right now if I didn’t…do something, right?”

“Phainon,” Mydei says, annoyance creeping into his voice. He rubs at his temple, squeezing his eyes shut. “This doesn’t have anything to do with you. Please, just…let me deal with this myself.”

“But I’m supposed to be there for you,” Phainon says softly. It’s so reverent that Mydei isn’t quite sure how to react. “I want to be there for you.”

“I understand,” Mydei responds. He doesn’t feel like saying anything else on the matter. “Can you help me with this, now?”

Phainon looks down at the packet Mydei’s working his way through, then back up at him, confusion etched on his face. “Mydei—” he starts, and it already sounds like he’s not about to talk about music theory.

Mydei shoots him an obvious look, daring him to continue. He doesn’t.

Phainon visibly swallows, then slides the paper over to his side of the table. “You wrote a parallel fifth here,” he starts, taking Mydei’s pencil and beginning to erase part of his work. “You have to stop doing that. It doesn’t sound good.”

“I think it sounds good,” Mydei responds. A bit of peace settles over him as their relationship seems to have taken a tiny step closer to what it was before.

Phainon gives him a look. “It doesn’t sound good,” he reiterates, swiping eraser shavings off the side of the table.

Or maybe they’re just lying to each other.

By Mydei’s lesson on Wednesday, it marks exactly a week since he got the phone call. And exactly a week since the last time he practiced.

Usually, he practices every single day for at least an hour, though he does the bulk of his practicing on the weekend. This weekend he spent rotting away in his dorm room, and he was too busy catching up on the work he missed on Thursday and Friday to have time to practice.

Madam Herta notices instantly. Of course she does. She has the hearing of a bat, and Mydei would even say with confidence that she has something stronger than perfect pitch, if it was possible. She knows when Mydei has improved, which was pretty steadily a weekly occurrence up until this point.

This week, though, it’s like not only has he not improved, but he’s regressed, too. He messes up on phrases he could have sworn he could play perfectly last week. Madam Herta stops him fast, with a hand in the air.

“Mydeimos,” she begins, and Mydei begins to steel himself for the spiel he’s about to get. “Would you like to explain to me why you haven’t been practicing this week?”

Mydei takes a deep breath. He curls his hands into fists, and his palms are sweaty. “I didn’t get a chance,” he answers. He knows he can tell the truth —that it would be a valid excuse to most people, and hopefully that included Madam Herta. But he doesn’t want to succumb to it. Admitting the true reason he’s slipping would be like allowing it to defeat him. He’s stronger than that. He knows he is.

Madam Herta takes a moment before answering, pushing her glasses up so they sit on top of her head. She tosses her clipboard to the side, and it clatters against her desk. “Alright, then,” she says. “In that case, why don’t you get out of my office?”

Mydei opens his mouth, then closes it again, unsure of what to say. He knew he was going to get in trouble, but he didn’t think he was going to get kicked out. Does this mean she’s dropping him as a student? He knew Madam Herta didn’t like teaching students she didn’t see potential in, but dropping them entirely was unheard of for her. As far as he knew, anyway.

“Have you lost your hearing? Is that why you couldn’t practice?” she continues, and Mydei might have laughed at that if she wasn’t dead serious. “My time is precious, and I will not allow it to be wasted on your carelessness.”

Carelessness? Mydei has been called a lot of things, but careless is not one of them. Especially not when it comes to his love of music. Couldn’t she see how much time he had already put into this piece? How could she call it careless?

In what is a very strong contender for the most embarrassing moment of his life, Mydei feels his eyes start to sting. The last thing he would ever want to do is cry in front of Madam Herta because she was too mean to him. He stands up so fast the piano bench goes skidding into the wall, and picks his sheet music up haphazardly. The papers are probably not in order, but all he cares about is escaping right now.

“Thank you,” he mutters as he flees out the door. She doesn’t say anything else, and Mydei doesn’t look at her as he leaves.

He makes a beeline to the first practice room that’s open. On his first run through, his fingers are stiff and cold and he can’t see very well through the tears in his eyes. By midnight, his fingers are stumbling over themselves and all Mydei wants is to throw the piano against the wall. He’s still upset for his whole walk home, and even wakes up the next morning angry.

For the rest of the week, he gets up early to practice before his classes and doesn’t get back to his dorm until well after midnight. He’s averaging four hours of sleep a night. His goal is to double the amount that he would normally practice, and he thinks he’s making good work of it. The only thing he’s touched is La Campanella. He hasn’t been this desperate to please someone in his life.

He likes being this busy. It keeps his mind off things. Instead of thinking about his mom, which would just discourage him from practicing, he thinks of how humiliating it was to be kicked out of Madam Herta’s office on Wednesday. It’s the only thing keeping him going.

Phainon notices. Mydei knows that he does, because he makes it painfully obvious, even though he’s been good about not mentioning these things.

They meet for breakfast more often than they had before, because Mydei isn’t sleeping in anymore. He doesn’t have much of an appetite in the early morning, but Phainon does.

On Sunday morning, Phainon sits down in the booth across from him with a plate of pancakes. There’s a comment about eating healthy on the tip of Mydei’s tongue, but he stays silent. It was merely a passing thought compared to how often he thinks about La Campanella recently. He had even dreamt about it last night. He was on stage, for his final recital, and had sat down to start playing when he looked at the piano rack to see that he had forgotten his sheet music backstage. He had no choice but to play it from memory, and woke up with his heart pounding in his ears. He couldn’t fall back asleep after that.

“You know how I hate Mozart?” Phainon is saying, his mouth full of food. Mydei’s leg bounces restlessly under the table and he knows Phainon can

feel it, but can’t bring himself to stop. “I still do, but I think he might have one good song now. Besides Requiem.”

Mydei had heard the concerto—it was just alright, but Phainon had been so upset when he learned they were playing a Mozart piece.

“Mmh,” he says.

“And Herta is actually pretty nice to me. She’s a good conductor, you know. A little mean to the violas, but that’s obviously warranted.”

Mydei doesn’t particularly care for viola jokes on a good day, but the mere mention of Madam Herta shakes him to his core. He hadn’t told Phainon she kicked him out of her office last week. He would only ask why he hadn’t told her the truth, and Mydei was trying to avoid those kinds of conversations right now.

A tiny part of his brain whispers that Madam Herta is only nice to Phainon because she doesn’t see the same potential that she sees in Mydei. He immediately feels disgusted with himself for even thinking such a thing. Phainon is talented. He doesn’t deserve to be the target of Mydei’s insecurity.

He reaches for his cup of orange juice, and his hands shake a little as he raises it to his lips. His hands have been violently shaky recently, whenever he’s not playing.

He notices the exact moment that Phainon recognizes both the shakiness of his hands and the source of it, and can only pray to the god his people used to worship that he chooses not to bring it up.

Of course, he’s not so lucky. Phainon reaches across the table, taking Mydei’s free hand into his own. “Mydei,” he says, looking at him with his wide blue eyes. “Your knuckles are swollen.”

Mydei jerks his hand away, shoving both of them underneath the table. “I took a break,” is his weak argument. “They’re not used to playing this much anymore.”

“You didn’t play for a week,” Phainon shoots back. “How much did you practice yesterday?”

A lie is on the tip of Mydei’s tongue, but he bites it down. Phainon won’t believe him anyway, and he doesn’t deserve to be lied to as much as he has been recently. “All day,” he says.

“How much is all day?”

“Seven,” Mydei starts. “To, um, one?” He’s ashamed. He can’t seem to meet Phainon’s eyes.

“AM, Mydei?” Phainon demands. He’s leaning over the table more each time he speaks, as if getting closer will make Mydei more open to making eye contact.

Mydei’s face flushes. “I took breaks,” he says weakly. It doesn’t work.

Phainon goes silent, and Mydei sees him lean back into the booth in the corner of his eye. “Why?” he finally asks, the question breathless.

“What do you mean why?” Mydei asks, sounding more aggressive than he means to. “I need to get better.”

“Better?!” Phainon exclaims. “You’re already the most talented musician I’ve ever met, Mydei! You’re playing La Campanella, for fuck’s sake! You think any other pianist at this school can do that?!”

“That’s by your standards,” Mydei shoots back. It’s cruel, but he says it without thinking. Even if he had thought, he probably would have said it anyway. His hands hurt, he’s overstimulated, and every new word out of Phainon’s mouth is just annoying him more.

“Are you serious?” Phainon gawks, incredulous. “You don’t think all the opportunities you’ve gotten are any proof of your talent, Mydei? Herta clapped for you. Anaxa told me I could learn things from you that he couldn’t teach me as well as you could. You were invited to play with the PY Phil in two years. What is going to be enough for you?!”

“I’m not good enough,” Mydei reiterates.

Phainon groans, frustrated. “To who?!”

“Herta,” Mydei shoots back.

“Fuck Herta,” Phainon is frighteningly close to yelling at this point, and Mydei knows the others eating around them can hear their conversation. “Who are you doing this for, Mydei? Herta? Or yourself?”

Mydei can’t bring himself to unpack that question right now, so he doesn’t even try. “I need to be perfect,” he insists.

“Mydei,” Phainon’s voice is softer now, much to Mydei’s relief. “What good is perfection if you lose all the joy it gave you getting there?”

“I can tell you prioritize enjoyment,” Mydei mutters. He can see Phainon’s heart break just in the expression on his face.

“Oh,” he says softly. “I didn’t know you felt that way.”

Mydei immediately regrets it. But instead of apologizing, like he knows he should, he gets up. Slings his bag over his shoulder and walks away, out of the dining hall. For the first time since he’d known him, Phainon doesn’t chase after him.

He sits in the practice room he walked to in silence. His music is still in his bag, unpacked.

His mom would be able to give him good advice right now. Comfort him through all the pain but tell him it doesn’t give him an excuse to treat Phainon the way he had. But she’s gone, and if she wasn’t, Mydei supposes he wouldn’t be going through this in the first place.

Hephaestion is the second person he wants. He’d long gotten over that loss —his first best friend, his first love. It wasn’t easy, but he had his mother back then. But Hephaestion would always set Mydei straight. Tell him he’s being a spoiled asshole and that Phainon doesn’t deserve to be spoken to like that.

He hadn’t spoken to the rest of their friend group since he had gone to university. Nothing was the same after Hephaestion died, anyway. Mydei wouldn’t trust them with his issues anymore.

Everyone else he was friends with at their university was closer friends with Phainon. Truly, Mydei has never felt so alone in his life.

It doesn’t take very long for Mydei to start thinking about dropping out.

When it wasn’t Phainon motivating him to continue his major, it was his mother. And now, both of them are more or less gone. Herta’s blatant disapproval of him motivates him to practice, sure, but he knows that dropping out of college would also mean he wouldn’t have to deal with her ever again.

Maybe she would be more disappointed than ever with his decision to drop out. But that would be a one time thing that she would get over, and Mydei wouldn’t have to deal with the repercussions of her disappointment, since he’d be gone.

He misses when Phainon had given him a reason to improve when he felt like he didn’t know why he was in his major anymore. He misses the reverence in his voice and in his eyes when he watched Mydei play. Realistically, he would get that back with a single apology, if he just faced him and worked on their issues together, but for some reason Mydei enjoys being alone.

The night before Mydei’s next lesson with Madam Herta, Phainon calls him.

Mydei’s hands still on the keyboard when he notices who’s calling. He thinks it over for two rings before he picks up.

“Hello?”

“Hi, Mydei.” He sounds a little unsure, like he’s nervous. “Can we talk?”

Mydei swallows. He hates that part of him hopes Phainon is breaking up with him right now. That’s what he deserves, anyway—were their roles reversed, Mydei would have been gone by now. Mydei is convinced that the only reason Phainon is still with him is because of his own low self esteem. “Yeah,” he answers. And, then, before he allows himself to think himself out of it, “I’m sorry.”

“What?” Phainon sounds surprised. “For what?”

“For what?” Mydei repeats, a little incredulous. “I’ve been terrible to you, Phainon.”

“I thought you said not to apologize for things that aren’t your fault.”

“This is exactly the thing I should be apologizing for,” Mydei says. He moves to rest his elbows on the keys, which is bad for the piano, but he doesn’t really care.

“It’s not your fault your mom died.”

“But it is my fault I’ve handled it the way I have.” Phainon doesn’t say anything for a moment, and so Mydei keeps talking. “I know you wanted to help me, and I know you understand what I’m going through, but I…I just thought I could get through it by myself. And I thought it would be weak if I accepted your help.”

“Mydei…”

“And I think you were right,” Mydei continues. “I shouldn’t have kept going, because it’s making everything even worse.”

“I think that’s a great idea,” Phainon says softly. “Do you think you’ll take next semester off?”

“No, Phainon,” Mydei answers. He purses his lips, and his next words are so quiet they might not have been spoken at all. “I’m thinking of dropping out.”

It’s humiliating, to admit that everything has gotten to him to the point of quitting for good. But, realistically, this was bound to happen one day. He never liked piano enough for him to make a career out of it, and whatever he had with Phainon was never going to be enough to fix that.

“Oh,” comes Phainon’s reply, after enough time that it’s clear he was thinking about what to say. “Okay.” He doesn’t sound happy about it in the slightest, voice shaky and saturated with disappointment.

“It’s not final,” Mydei says, trying to give him at least some consolation. “You told me there was no point in perfection if you lost all the joy you had getting there,” he starts, and hears Phainon take a shaky breath on the other end of the line. “But that’s the problem, Phainon—I never had any joy to begin with. How am I supposed to believe I’m in the right major when I don’t even like it?”

“Lots of people don’t like their major,” Phainon tries. His words almost trip over themselves with how quickly he gets them out of his mouth. “For example, chemistry. No one likes it, but there are still people who study it.”

“Phainon,” Mydei groans, “no one studies music for money.”

Phainon doesn’t reply for a bit, so Mydei knows his rebuttal worked, even against the debate champion himself. “I just…” he starts, taking a deep sigh before continuing. “I don’t want you to leave.”

Mydei closes his eyes. Damn his incessant manipulation, even when he doesn’t mean to. Phainon has never been one to make anything easy for Mydei. “I don’t know,” is what he settles on. “I guess I’ll see how my next lesson goes.”

“Okay,” Phainon says quietly. Mydei wishes he would just argue with him normally instead of pretending to be okay with it while making his true feelings on the matter so obvious.

“Phainon,” Mydei replies, cautiously. “Do you want to break up?”

“What?!” Phainon’s voice is high with alarm. “No—Mydei, do you—”

“You can be honest with me,” Mydei whispers. “I haven’t been kind to you, I would understand it if you wouldn’t want to be with me anymore—”

“Mydei.” Phainon sounds desperate, borderline crazed, as he cuts Mydei off. “Mydei. Do you want to break up.”

Mydei takes a deep breath. “No,” he says. “Of course not.”

He can hear Phainon exhale on the other end of the line, his following laugh saturated with relief. “Okay…we’re okay, right, Mydei?”

“Yeah,” Mydei breathes. “We’ll be okay.”

Mydei’s legs shake as he sits down at the bench in Herta’s office the next evening. His hands are clammy, fingernails bitten down to nubs, and he’d torn at his cuticles until they bled with all his nerves. If Herta notices— which she does, as nothing ever gets past her eyes—she doesn’t say anything.

He can’t remember a single time in his life that he’d practiced as often as he had the past week, and he doesn’t know whether to hate or thank Herta for bringing him to this point. Even so, November is almost over, and his concert is only in a few weeks, and La Campanella isn’t even close to ready.

Dropping out crosses his mind again. He swallows the lump in his throat as Herta rolls her chair over to the piano, clipboard in hand. “Hello, Mydeimos,” she says. “Are you going to waste my time this week?”

Mydei bites the inside of his cheek. He wants to lash out, to tell her to go fuck herself and rip his sheet music to shreds right in front of her, but he doesn’t. If only she knew, he tells himself, even though it’s his fault he doesn’t. Madam Herta is his advisor, for god’s sake. Out of anyone at the school he should have told his issues to, it should have been her.

He can’t say no, because he’s not confident in his abilities right now, and that would be a lie. Saying yes might get him thrown out again, and any other answer would probably piss her off just as much. Thankfully, she continues before he has to answer.

“Why don’t we start with a run through today?” she suggests, leaning back in her chair and crossing one leg over the other. “Don’t worry about it being perfect. I just want to see what else we need to get done in the next few weeks, okay?”

There’s a gentleness to her tone that Mydei has never heard before. He wonders if she feels bad, but that’s impossible, so it must be something else.

He nods, placing his hands in position. He had tried a run through just yesterday. He got so annoyed he yearned for a gun to his head, then decided he needed to get some fresh air.

The beginning is fine. Perfect, even—by his standards, anyway. But it’s not the beginning that he’s worried about. The piece starts almost impossible for any sane pianist, and only gets harder as it goes. There’s not a single part of this piece beyond the first phrase that Mydei is completely confident in.

He stumbles through the rest of the piece, to silence on Herta’s end. The tempo is sloppy. He lingers on a note for too long, an amount of time that would be imperceptible to an audience member but is sacrilegious to Herta. He slows down significantly near the end, and it’s obvious that it isn’t a dramatic ritardando, but is instead a result of his own shortcomings.

But he finishes it. Once he’s held out the last chord for long enough, his hands slump down to his lap. He doesn’t even want to look Herta in the eye, and is already bracing himself for her to kick him out again.

“Alright,” is how she starts. Mydei already knows what that means. “Mydeimos, I want you to look at me when I say this.”

Mydei listens, turning his head until they make eye contact. “You’re a talented musician, Mydeimos. I’ve had faith in you ever since the first day I heard you play, but you’ve gotten to a point where I am not entirely sure what more I can do.”

Mydei licks his lips. He’s heard all about harsh music teachers hoping they can scare their students into improving. The worst part about those tactics is that most of the time, they work.

“Anyone can practice themselves to perfection, and you are not excluded from that. I can motivate you, I can give you tips, I can help you phrase in a way that can emulate emotion, but I cannot create passion.” Despite her words, Mydei finds that for the first time since he started taking lessons with her, he’s not scared of her right now. “Mydeimos, there is not a future in this for you if you don’t even like it.”

When Mydei doesn’t respond, she continues. “If it’s this piece that is putting so much stress on your shoulders, you don’t have to play it. Even as a performance major, you’re not required to play a recital every semester. We can take more time on it, and you can perform it at the end of next semester instead.”

Mydei still doesn’t say anything. Despite how comforting her words are, there’s still something weighing down on him. The end of next semester. He hadn’t been thinking that far into the future, and he knows what that means. Deep down, he doesn’t want to be here anymore. He’s already mentally dropped out.

“You’re right,” he starts. “I don’t like it.”

Herta smiles at that, and it seems somewhat genuine even if it’s tiny.

“Madam Herta, I…” he bites his tongue. Forces himself to take a deep breath. He can’t believe he’s saying this to her face right now. He can’t believe he’s already made this decision. “…want to drop out.”

Even in Herta’s genius brain, her reaction confirms that of all possibilities, that was not at all what she was expecting Mydei to say. “You…do?”

Mydei nods, firm. He’s already said it. He might as well go through with it now.

“Why?”

Mydei swallows the lump in his throat, taking a moment to gather himself before he answers. It’s harder than he thinks, because where does he even begin?

He opens his mouth, and starts with the first thing that comes to mind. “My mother passed away,” he says. His voice doesn’t shake as he says it, nor do his eyes tear up. “Two weeks ago. It’s why I didn’t practice last week. I…” he trails off. “She was my main motivator. I was doing it to make her happy, because I wanted to follow in her footsteps and she inspired me, but now that she’s gone, if I don’t like it, why am I still here? She wouldn’t…want me to be unhappy…for her sake.”

“Mydeimos,” Herta says, and her voice is back to stern again. “And you didn’t think to tell me this? I’m your advisor. There are ways we go about dealing with loss, but you have to start with letting someone know.”

“I know,” Mydei says. “I’m sorry. I thought I was—that I would be fine.”

“Typically, I would both recommend you for counseling and suggest you take a semester off. Are you certain you want to drop out?”

Mydei thinks about Phainon, and how crushed he would be if he knew Mydei had really gone through with it—and so quickly, too. He pushes that aside. Phainon just wants what’s best for him. He would accept Mydei’s decision either way. “Yes. I’m certain.”

“Did you consider other options?” Herta continues. “Perhaps, you can take a semester off and change your major when you come back.”

History, maybe. If Mydei wasn’t a musician, he would have studied history. But now, he’s sure he wants to go home. Go home, and find something else to do. Maybe he’d get lucky. Maybe the labels Cipher sent that song to would reply. “No,” he decides. “I want to drop out.”

Herta takes a deep breath. There’s something in her eyes akin to sadness, Mydei thinks. After all, she had just admitted to thinking Mydei is a talented musician. That’s a compliment he’ll carry with him for the rest of his life, he thinks.

“Okay,” she says. She rolls her chair back over to her desk and opens her laptop. “We can work this out now, then.”

It’s a boring process, with even more questioning on Herta’s end, but by the time he exits her office, it’s final. He will have officially dropped out by tomorrow.

Walking back to his dorm, an odd feeling settles over him. He’s relieved, lighter, even, but still not completely sure what his next steps will be. He will fly home, probably tomorrow, if he can get a plane ticket, and bring all his belongings to his mother’s house. She wrote in her will that the house and all of her inheritance would be left to him, with no one else to give it to. He’s not sure how he feels about that.

As soon as he gets back to his dorm, he texts Phainon and asks him to come over. They hadn’t spent much time together in person recently—at the beginning of the semester, Phainon would stay overnight more often than not. Mydei doesn’t know how this conversation is going to go, so he doesn’t tell him to bring his things.

Mydei takes a quick shower, leaving the door propped slightly open, and Phainon is in the room when he’s finished. He’s sitting awkwardly at Mydei’s desk, scrolling through some social media on his phone. “Hi,” he says when Mydei enters, sounding a little breathless.

“Hi,” Mydei responds. He can feel Phainon’s eyes on him as he changes silently. He knows what he has to say, but isn’t sure how to say it. It was just yesterday that he’d promised Phainon everything would be fine. This, he knows, is anything but fine.

He shakes his hair out a little, trying to pretend he’s not stalling, before he finally comes to sit on his bed.

“Mydei—” Phainon starts.

“I dropped out,” Mydei blurts out, effectively cutting him off. Phainon’s mouth drops open, but the look on his face is more of despair than shock. “I’m sorry, Phainon. I just,” he pauses, running a hand through his wet hair, “I can’t do this anymore.”

Phainon stands up, and walks over to Mydei to wrap his arms around his neck. He hugs him with so much force that Mydei is knocked onto his back, Phainon nearly crushing him with his full body weight. “I’m so sorry,” he whispers into Mydei’s neck.

Mydei wriggles beneath him until he can finally breathe, resting one hand on the back of Phainon’s head. “Again—”

“I don’t know how else to express my pity!” Phainon lifts his head, annoyed. “You don’t deserve to be going through any of this right now. I know it’s not my fault, but I’m sorry regardless.”

Mydei takes a deep breath. “...Okay.”

They stay like that for a while. Mydei thinks Phainon might be crying at some point, but he tries to hide it, so Mydei doesn’t comment on it. Finally, he sits up, Mydei following suit, and sure enough, the corners of his eyes are still tinged red.

“What are you going to do now?” Phainon asks.

“I’m flying back to Kremnos tomorrow,” Mydei swallows. “I’ll stay in my mom’s house, maybe find a job in the area. I can wait tables, or something.”

Mydei can see Phainon’s throat bob as he swallows. “So you’re just giving up?” he asks, and Mydei’s heart drops.

“No,” he insists. “I didn’t say that.”

“Mydei, you might not be passionate about piano, but you still love music,” he continues, like he wasn’t listening at all. “I can’t let myself just…let you

go, if you’re just going to let all your talents, everything you’ve worked for, go to waste—”

“I’m not,” Mydei shoots back. “I have the band, we have that song Cipher sent out. It’s not over, Phainon, I just have to wait it out—”

“Wait it out? Mydei, the label hasn’t responded yet. Do you seriously think they’re still considering it? If this is really something you want, you have to go out there and start putting music out by yourself. If you’re worth investing in, the labels will find you themselves.”

Mydei swallows. That had been in the back of his mind already, but he hadn’t admitted it to himself yet. He had thought they would at least get some sort of a rejection letter.

“Fine,” Mydei mutters. “I’ll go to Kremnos and I’ll…start making music full time.” Phainon smiles a little at that, before he continues. “And I’ll never have to touch a piano ever again.”

“That’s a little far-fetched, I think.”

Mydei doesn’t think it is. He certainly doesn’t want to. That would be his ideal life, really—making music full time with his band, no pianos in sight.

Despite the light-hearted lilt to Phainon’s voice, he can’t help but think it’s just a front. Phainon is devastated, he can tell. They both know where this is going. “Phainon,” he starts gently, placing a hand over his knee. “What about us?”

Phainon flinches, and his hand comes to rest over Mydei’s threading their fingers together. “I don’t know,” he admits. He bites at his lip so hard he could draw blood, and Mydei brushes his thumb over it, forcing him to soothe it out. “We could…do long distance,” he tries, but Mydei can tell he doesn’t actually believe that would work.

“You don’t want that,” Mydei says.

“Of course I don’t,” Phainon shoots back. “But I don’t want to lose you, either.”

“You could come with me.” Mydei regrets the suggestion as soon as it leaves his mouth, but he can’t take it back, and he can’t erase the look on Phainon’s face, either.

He unlaces their hands, pulling back a little. “What about me, then?” he starts, tone notably more aggressive than it had been just seconds ago. “I know you’re rich, and have everything you could possible want, but piano —this—is all I have.”

Mydei doesn’t say anything for a moment. “...Seriously?” he finally murmurs, his voice a little strangled. He doesn’t know how to refute Phainon’s comment about his life being easy without coming across like a spoiled rich brat.

“You’re asking me to drop everything I have for you,” Phainon shoots back. “That’s a little ridiculous, right, Mydei?” He’s standing now, hovering over where Mydei sits on his bed.

“I don’t have anything left, either.” Is all Mydei says. He doesn’t want to talk about his mother. And he sure as hell doesn’t want to talk about his father.

Phainon takes a step back, running a hand through his hair. He exhales deeply before responding, “I’m sorry,” he drops his hands to his sides helplessly. “I shouldn’t have said that. God, I’m sorry, Mydei.”

Mydei swallows, and gets to his feet, too. He doesn’t want to argue. They’re both hurt, and they’re both wrong. A winner is the last thing that matters right now. “I probably shouldn’t have suggested it in the first place.”

Phainon takes another deep breath. “Maybe,” he starts, chewing on his lip again before continuing. “Maybe we really should…go our separate ways.”

Mydei’s eyes sting at hearing those words out of his mouth. Words he should have heard weeks ago. Words he knew were coming from a mile away, and yet it still hurts. He nods, regardless.

Phainon chokes, and comes forward to wrap his arms around Mydei’s neck. “I don’t want to,” he cries, tears already wetting Mydei’s shirt. “I really don’t want to, Mydei.”

“It’s okay,” Mydei raises his hands, rubbing at his back. “Please don’t cry, Phainon.”

“I love you,” Phainon whispers. “I always will.”

Mydei laughs wetly, trying his best to hide the way he actually feels. “You’re going to have to move on eventually.”

“I won’t,” Phainon insists. “How could anyone move on from you?”

“You’ll find a way,” Mydei kisses the side of his forehead, just once, and Phainon seems to relax at least a little bit.

Finally, Phainon pulls away, eyes still brimming with tears. Mydei nods, and he takes a few steps backwards, wiping at his eyes carefully. “You have to promise,” he says. “You’re going to make this worth it. You have to.”

Mydei nods again. “I promise,” he says earnestly. “You too.”

“I will,” Phainon insists. “I’ll play Rach 2, and you’ll sell out stadiums, and I’ll be there when you do.”

“Rach 2 is a small goal for you.”

“I promise,” Phainon answers, with a hand over his heart. “I’ll do everything I ever dreamed of and more, but only if you do the same.”

“Are you seriously turning this into a competition?” Mydei asks. He can’t stop the fondness from creeping into his voice.

“Do you accept, Mydeimos?”

Mydei snorts, shaking his head. “Yeah,” he replies. “How could I not?”

Chapter End Notes

i wrote this chapter last semester when i, too, started slipping after being the best i'd been mentally in years my freshman year of college. sophomore slump or whatever. but that was for no particular reason, and mydei had more than enough reasons to crash tf out. he underreacted like crazy.

obviously madam herta is not nearly as bad as the whiplash guy, but this type of teacher is extremely common in music circles. the piano teacher i had for nearly ten years from the time i was four years old was like this, to the point where i was crying during lessons because she was so mean but regardless, i was still so, SO good. although i've learned recently that apparently she was much nicer to my brother and he liked her, so i'm not sure what that was about. maybe she saw more potential in me. haha.

~~~

September 14th, 3868. Ten months before the release of Dreamscape.

Mydei doesn’t sleep any better on the second night.

Phainon had a tendency to infiltrate his dreams more often than Mydei would like to admit, but it was never like this. Never to the point where he can’t fall asleep, too convinced he’s doing something terribly wrong.

He should have stayed in college. He should have gotten that damn degree, shouldn’t have dropped out the second it got hard. He should have married Phainon, and now it was too late. It had been three years. Why did it have to be Mydei who couldn’t move on?

He’d tried dating again, and the worst part was that it almost worked. He could have loved her, could have finally moved on, only for it to fall apart because of Phainon, of all people. He’d tried sleeping with other people, too, even though he didn’t like casual sex—only to discover that this opinion hadn’t changed.

He flips his pillow onto the cold side and tries to fall asleep again, but to no avail. His fingers are itching to play something for the first time in years. Maybe to prove to himself that he can still do it. That he might have been apart from it for a while, but that doesn’t mean he forgot. He’s still one of the best pianists in the world. He’s still the same musician who got applause from the Herta.

It’s just muscle memory. He hasn’t forgotten how to read the notes, so surely his fingers won’t forget how to move, right?

Decision made, he gets out of bed and slips on an easy pair of shoes, as well as a shirt. He takes the elevator down to the ground floor, which is empty at this hour. The lights are dim—there’s a receptionist sitting at the front desk, who looks very unhappy to be there. Mydei walks past him into the lounge, which is just as empty. There’s a public piano there. He saw it when they had first checked in, just out of the corner of his eye. He doesn’t remember what he thought at the time, but now he sits at the bench and tentatively presses down on middle C.

He plays a C major scale, and then its arpeggio. He feels a little stiff, so he takes a moment to stretch out his fingers before running through an old exercise Madam Herta used to make him do. It feels weird warming up, because he’d almost never done that in his college days, unless it was the beginning of his lessons. And yet, now he does. Maybe that meant he had matured.

And then, without thinking very much, Mydei starts to play the beginning of La Campanella.

It’s just as it always was, like not a day had ever passed since he last touched the piece. The beginning is near perfect, just like Madam Herta’s recording from when she was fourteen years old. The way he had subconsciously trained himself to play.

The longer he plays, the more confident he gets. He closes his eyes, and doesn’t miss a note. He’d poured so many hours of his life into this piece— time he would never get back, although at this moment he has no regrets.

The hotel is silent except for his playing, but he imagines Phainon beside him, watching. He always said he loved watching Mydei play—that it was his playing that he fell in love with first, and Mydei second. Back then, he thought that such a comment was just Phainon being annoying. Now, he wouldn’t want it any other way. Maybe Phainon wasn’t in love with him anymore, but maybe, just maybe, he hadn’t fallen out of love with Mydei’s music just yet.

Maybe he still listens to Mydei’s music, streams every single, just hoping to catch a glimpse of his first love in the remnants of what Mydei’s career turned into. Maybe he’s disappointed every time.

He forgets a note. His finger slips, and he curses quietly as he drops his hands to his lap.

A little cough sounds from beside him, and he scrambles to his feet, as if it wasn’t too late to pretend he wasn’t just playing the piano again.

It’s not, though. Castorice stands in the doorway, in a white t-shirt and butterfly pajama pants, and she stares at Mydei like she just saw a ghost.

Mydei thinks the way he stares back couldn’t have been much different. What feels like minutes pass silently between them, until Mydei finally realizes that Castorice was waiting for an explanation from him.

He clears his throat. Straightens his back. “Um,” he says, which wasn’t what he was planning to say, but it’s a lot more accurate to what he’s thinking. “Morning.”

“Good morning,” she whispers, eyes flicking back and forth between Mydei and the piano.

Mydei runs a hand through his hair, stressed out. “I couldn’t sleep,” he attempts.

“Me neither,” she says. She still looks at him like he’s a completely different person. “What do you normally do when you can’t sleep?”

“Not this,” Mydei says.

“Mm,” she hums. “Well, I was going to get some fresh air, if you want to come.”

Mydei nods, and they move towards the front entrance. Mydei holds the door open for her, and she gives him a sideways glance as she walks through.

It’s still warm outside, courtesy of early fall weather in southwest Penacony. Mydei’s hometown is hotter, even in late fall, so he doesn’t mind. They walk a little bit, Castorice at his side though a few feet apart. The city is empty at this hour, nothing accompanying them but the slight rustle of wind and the shuffling of their footsteps.

“I told Robin I would do it,” he blurts out into the silence around them. “I was going to tell you, I just wanted to make sure I still had it before I could disappoint you all, I guess.”

“I think you still have it,” is all she says.

Mydei purses his lips, considering his next words before he speaks. “Do you want to know why I dropped out?” Is what he settles on.

Castorice doesn’t say anything for a moment. They turn right, heading towards the beach—a subconscious decision on both of their parts. “I admit I’ve always wondered about it. It took me by surprise when I first heard.”

Mydei shoves his hands into his pockets, staring off into the ocean as the shore comes closer and closer into view. “I was good,” he admits. “I know that. Any classical musician would look at my best performances and think it’s a waste of my talent for me to move to rock music.”

“We all know you were good,” Castorice answers quietly. “But we appreciate your prowess here nonetheless.”

“I would never go back.”

That seems to surprise Castorice a little bit, as she turns to look at him with wide eyes. “Never?”

Mydei shakes his head. “I love making music with you guys more than I ever loved performing piano.”

“Did…you and Phainon break up because of that?”

“Not really,” Mydei says, staring at the path they walk through. The last thing he wants is for Castorice to figure out, well—what he wants. “We

fought, though.” He thinks back to that. The things he said. The things Phainon said. They had both apologized to each other, kissed and made up, but some part of Mydei can’t help but wonder if the reason their break up succeeded at all was intrinsically tied to that.

“I’m sorry,” Castorice says quietly. “I know he meant a lot to you. Both of you,” she corrects. “Both of you meant so much to each other.”

Mydei doesn’t give her more of a response than a half-hearted grunt, because what he feels in response to that statement is far more than he can trust himself to say eloquently. Phainon didn’t just mean a lot to him, he was everything. Still is. His heart lurches in his chest.

“I wanted to move on,” Mydei says, once he’s sufficiently regained his composure. “He was always going to be there, reminding me of the life I was trying to escape. Both of us had different dreams we wanted to pursue, and we weren’t meant to be in each other’s futures. Rock music and classical music, they’re not…they don’t mesh.”

“Oh,” Castorice says. She stares into space like there’s something she wants to say, but she doesn’t allow herself to say it.

“It’s childish,” Mydei mutters. “I know.” He pulls his hands from his pockets and crosses his arms over his chest instead, still annoyed at the way he chose to behave all those years ago. If only he had an ounce of maturity back then, maybe they would still be happy together.

“It’s how you felt,” Castorice responds. “People act on emotion all the time. There’s nothing wrong with that.”

Mydei turns her words over in his head. He’s not sure how to respond. “You’re still in touch with him,” he says instead. “Aren’t you?”

They stop walking when the path turns to sand, the sound of rushing waves much louder than it had been just a few feet ago. “I’m sorry,” she says, clasping her hands together at her hips.

“No, it’s fine,” Mydei says immediately. “He’s your friend too.” Castorice, Cipher, and Phainon all knew each other in high school, having attended the same school in Okhema. Castorice was closer to Cipher than Phainon was, the two of them making up the rhythm section of their high school jazz band, but they all got closer in college. “How is he?”

“Good, I think,” she says. “He’s back in Paperfold for grad school now. But I think he’s planning on getting an apartment in Okhema when he graduates.”

“That’s good,” Mydei nearly sighs, more wistful than he intended.

“Come on,” Castorice kicks her shoes off and steps into the sand, moving towards the ocean.

Mydei looks back at the street behind him, before sighing and following behind her. He doesn’t shed his shoes, and it proves to be a mistake as he trudges through the sand.

There’s a little log buried halfway into the sand a safe distance from the tide. Mydei sits near the middle, and Castorice next to him. She keeps her distance, though, as always.

“You don’t like water,” she remarks, curiously.

“Huh?” Mydei turns to her, a little bewildered. “Where did you get that idea?”

“We went to the beach in Okhema so many times, and I never once saw you get in,” she shakes her head. “You would just sit on the towel and read.”

“What’s wrong with that? I like to tan.”

She shrugs, and seems to accept that answer easily enough.

“There’s something I want to tell you,” she says suddenly, voice loud around them like she had blurted it out. Mydei gives her his full attention, watching her carefully as she fidgets with her hands in her lap. “I’m—” she starts, then breaks off, taking a deep breath. “I’m sick, Mydei.”

“What?” Mydei asks. He can’t think of anything else to say.

“I was born sick.” She looks down at her hands, and Mydei thinks her voice grows even softer with every word. “I practically grew up in hospitals. Whenever they thought I was free to get discharged, it would flare up again in a month and I’d just be back to a hospital bed.”

“Cas,” Mydei starts, then stops. He reaches out to touch her, to place a comforting hand on her back, but she shifts away from him on the log until he stops and drops his hand back down to the wood between them.

Castorice sighs, clenching her hands into fists. “Sorry,” she whispers, voice catching in her throat. “It’s not the disease that’s contagious, but I have a weak immune system because of it, so I get sick more than most people, and…” she stops, and shakes her head. “I’ve made people sick before, Mydei. I’ve…”

“It’s okay, Cas,” Mydei murmurs. “Don’t apologize.”

“Did you know I used to have a twin sister?” She looks up, regarding Mydei with tears in her eyes. He shakes his head, as gently as possible, and curls his fingers into a fist so he resists the urge to reach out and touch her again. “Polyxia,” she continues, a tiny smile breaking over her face as she says it. “She had the same condition, only worse. She couldn’t walk, was always in a hospital—at least I got to go to school sometimes. To see other people except for the doctors.”

Mydei doesn’t pull his eyes away, He hangs on to her every word, listening as intently as he can, even though he can’t bear to hear the rest of her story. He can already tell where it’s going.

“I got her sick, Mydei,” she rasps. She looks at him and her eyes are swimming with tears. “They didn’t say that that was it, but I know it was.” She bites her lip as a tear runs down her cheek. “I killed her.”

“Cas,” Mydei says, before she can continue. She clamps her mouth shut, chin quivering. “That’s enough. It wasn’t your fault.”

Castorice shakes her head, bottom lip caught between her teeth. “It was, Mydei,” she whispers.

Mydei lifts his hand again, bringing it to her shoulder carefully, as if he were trying to soothe a stray cat. She shifts away slightly, but he touches her anyway, and she lets him. “It’s okay,” he murmurs. He reaches slowly around the back of her neck, and pulls her into his shoulder. “It’s okay, Cas.”

She doesn’t say anything, burying her face into his neck even though she keeps her hands clasped tightly in her lap. Mydei snakes his hand to her other shoulder, sighing as he turns his head back to the ocean. He thinks it makes a lot of sense. Why she’s always been so inexplicably averse to touch. Why she writes, like she yearns for some semblance of normalcy in a life that is cruel with its abnormality. Her love of music, and why she picked up the drums, just another outlet for her escapism. She always said she liked how it took her mind off things.

He holds her for what feels like a near eternity, the crashing of waves drowning out the sound of her soft cries. She sniffles quietly, lifting her head and wiping her nose with the back of her hand. Mydei doesn’t let go of her.

“You were right, by the way,” Mydei breaks the silence, overcome with a sudden bitterness at the sight of the ocean. “I don’t like water.”

“I know,” Castorice says softly. “I just wasn’t going to pry.”

“I do like to tan,” he continues. “But I can't swim.”

“Oh…” Castorice pulls away, looking at him with wide, red-rimmed eyes.

Mydei bites his lip. The words are at the tip of his tongue, and he still can’t find it in himself to say them. Things he’s only ever admitted to Phainon, and even then, the only thing he hated more than Phainon’s pity was his own vulnerability.

“It’s nothing,” Mydei eventually decides. “I just never learned.”

He can tell Castorice doesn’t believe him. Mercifully, though, she doesn’t push it.

Mydei’s alarm wakes him up far too early the next morning, and he has half a mind to turn around and go back to sleep, uncaring of the deadlines he has to meet. All he knows is that no matter how terrible of a morning he’s having, Cipher’s is probably worse.

It’s that notion that motivates him enough to get out of bed. He was up late last night, talking to Castorice, but it was likely only a fraction of how late Cipher had stayed up playing video games. He didn’t understand her sleep schedule at all.

They meet up in the hotel lobby when the breakfast buffet starts, and him, Castorice, and Hyacine all have their own plates of food by the time Cipher makes an appearance.

She looks miserable, and slides into the seat next to Castorice with an obnoxious yawn that tapers off into a glare when she sees everyone staring at her. “It’s too damn early for this shit,” she starts, expression souring even further when no one says anything. “What. I’m up now, aren’t I? I wasn’t even that late, holy shit.”

“Cassie and Mydei have something to share with us,” Hyacine pipes up, scooping a portion of her eggs onto the empty plate set in front of Cipher.

She makes a face at it despite Hyacine’s hospitality, turning to scowl at Mydei now. “Oh, god. Are you two dating or something? Jeez, I don’t think I could handle that. I quit, guys, I’m done with this band.”

Castorice has her head in her hands, peeking at Mydei through the gaps in her fingers. “Don’t worry, Cipher, she’s all yours,” he says, delighted at the way that makes Castorice squirm further. Cipher seems to lighten up considerably, though.

“Then what’s your big secret, little prince? I won’t spoil it for Hyacine, you can do the honors.”

“Can you stop calling me that—” he starts, before processing the rest of her words. “Wait, what do you think I’m going to say, exactly?”

“That you’re playing piano on Robin’s track,” Cipher deadpans. Mydei ignores the way Hyacine looks at him in favor of staring at Cipher in disbelief instead. “Oh, come on, that one wasn’t even hard to figure out. I can’t wait to tell Phainon the news.”

Mydei’s heart lurches at the mention of him, but he tries to play it off like it doesn’t. “Yes, I’ll play the damn piece. Better than her brother doing it, anyway,” he mumbles.

“You don’t like her brother?” Castorice asks, in surprise. “He’s playing with the Astral Express now. I thought you liked them.”

“He’s not a good pianist,” Mydei starts, feeling a little more like he’s talking to himself than the others at the table. “And I don’t like his hair.”

“Oh my god,” Cipher groans. “Get over yourself, already. You know if you sent Phainon a text telling him you wanted to fuck, he’d be knocking at your door within the hour.”

“Not everything is about him,” Mydei retorts, unsure where else to start with that comment.

“Sure,” Cipher says simply, leaning back in her chair. Her feet knock against his under the table, and she refuses to move them, so Mydei does instead.

“I mean it,” Mydei says, to the rest of the table. He stabs a pineapple on his plate with so much force that it rings out in the room around them. “I’m my own person, we broke up, I’ve moved on. You might still be friends with him but that doesn’t mean anything for me.”

“You’ve moved on,” Cipher deadpans. Mydei resists the urge to kick her under the table, putting the slice of pineapple he had speared into his mouth.

“Three years, Cipher,” Mydei reminds her. “Three goddamn years. Of course I’ve moved on.”

Silence falls between the four of them, and Mydei is glad that at least Cipher doesn’t have anything else to say. No matter how unconvinced she looks as she stares at him across the table.

Hyacine is the one who breaks it. “Well,” she starts, voice bubbly as ever despite the obvious tension between them right now. “I think it’s exciting.”

Mydei glances over at her.

“All of this,” she clarifies. “Robin, piano, everything—you guys aren’t at least a little bit excited?”

Mydei doesn’t answer right away, looking over at Castorice who wordlessly gives him her encouragement. He doesn’t really know what to say—of course some part of him is excited, but the part that wins is more nervous than anything.

“It’s one track,” he says, sounding more like he’s trying to convince himself than anything.

“We know it means more than that,” Castorice says. “It’s okay, Mydei. We all believe in you.”

The reassurance is nice, but all that Mydei can think about is how real all of this is all of a sudden.

The next two days, they meet without Robin. It’s just the four of them and Ratio in a stuffy old recording studio, as Ratio messes with the buttons to get a feel for how it works. He has an mp3 file playing off his phone speaker, the demos Robin had sent him. It’s not the first time Mydei has

heard it, but knowing that the piano part is definitely his now changes things.

“Look at him,” he can hear Cipher whisper in Castorice’s ear. “I bet he’s already rewritten it.”

Not exactly, but his brain is already rapidly filling with improvement ideas. He’s not sure what it was, but his inspiration is back. This track has potential to become an instant hit, even if it wasn’t for Robin’s name already attached to it.

In fact, the sheer potential of it the more he thinks about it is enough to get him so excited he starts to feel a little sick. He jumps to his feet, startling Castorice, and heads over to the piano, pulling up the sheet music Robin had sent them on his phone.

It’s hard to read off his phone, the notes too small with not enough of an excerpt able to be on the screen at a time, but he leans in and squints instead, paying little attention to what his hands are actually doing.

Castorice and Cipher have heard him play before, having been dragged to Phainon’s concerts at Paperfold that Mydei was ultimately playing in as well. He doesn’t even think the base sheet music he was sent was all that difficult, even when sight-reading. It’s the kind of performance that only Phainon would praise, because he used to be too smitten with Mydei to do anything else.

But silence falls over the room as he plays through it for the first time anyway—even Ratio has stopped what he’s doing to watch. He can feel everyone’s eyes on him, but if it does anything, it only makes him play better. He’s his best self in front of an audience.

He abandons the sheet music at some point, making up a melody that he thinks would sound good. It does. He adds a little flair that’s impressive to non-pianists and is not all that crazy to someone who knows what he’s doing.

And then he messes up, leaving the key he was in on accident during his improv moment. He curses a little as he removes his hands from the keyboard, and doesn’t even want to look at his bandmates to see how they’ve reacted.

“Okay,” Ratio starts, a little slowly. “This is…a great start.”

Mydei looks over at Castorice, who is beaming. Cipher and Hyacine don’t say anything, but he feels as though he can tell what they’re thinking. No one wants this to be a one time thing.

He doesn’t address it. He replies to Ratio and they work through it together, figuring out which parts they want to change, which parts they want to add to, and which parts they want to keep. And then all four of them are playing together, changing up each part so they work together best. Mydei records the final thing so that he can write it down later, because he’s not skilled enough to change his ideas into sheet music on the spot like this.

Ratio leaves halfway through the session, having to attend an important meeting with Aventurine, and their productivity throughout the whole morning instantly dissipates.

“Play the hardest song you know,” Cipher requests.

La Campanella instantly jumps to the forefront of Mydei’s mind. He grimaces—yes, he had just revisited it last night, but he still hates that piece.

“You don’t have to do that,” Hyacine jumps in to defend him, as always. He appreciates her, but his hands are already in position for the beginning of La Campanella.

“This is the piece that made me drop out of college,” he explains, and then starts playing it. He thinks it’s the sort of thing that would sound impressive to anyone, but non-pianists would only understand the full extent of its difficulty by watching someone play it.

As he makes it through the piece nearly mistake-free, though not without the occasional blunder, he can’t help but feel oddly empty. It’s different from three years ago, when he walked into his first lesson of the semester with Madam Herta and saw the La Campanella sheet music on the stand. It’s different from the last time he had played it for her, and even the last time he had performed at Paperfold. Even when he hated it, he still felt something. Performance anxiety, frustration at his imperfections, a desire to be the best pianist in the world.

Now, he feels nothing. Playing La Campanella brings back none of those feelings, but it doesn’t bring him anything good, either. He stops, too distracted to continue, and realizes that he hadn’t felt anything particularly strong when he was playing through Robin’s song, either.

Part of him had thought that coming back to piano on his own terms, to make the music he loves instead of the music he was forced to make for so many years, would bring back the entire reason he had decided to study it in the first place. Madam Herta had always been right in her assessment of him, that he didn’t love it enough to make it in that industry, but that didn’t mean he never loved it. Anyone who puts that much work into learning something has to love it at some point.

But instead, it just feels like something he has to do. It’s not the big deal to him that it is to Cipher, Hyacine, and Castorice, but it’s not something he’s against, by any means.

Regardless, he looks over to see Cipher speechless for the first time in his life. Hyacine says something he barely processes about how amazing he is, before stepping forward and requesting her own song.

“Do you know Piano Man?”

Mydei just barely restrains his snort, nodding as he reaches for his water bottle. At least he’s making someone happy, he thinks, as he puts his hands on the keys and begins to play.

Still, after they’ve killed nearly an hour making Mydei play for them, he can’t help but think that this must have been what they thought this whole

time. All the time they spent defending him to interviewers, giving every question regarding Mydei’s potential return to piano a hard no, was all a guise for how they really felt. They wanted him to play this whole time, they just weren’t saying it out loud.

They finish up their version of it the next day, with Ratio there the whole time to keep them on track. Mydei listens to Ratio’s request that he reel it back in some places.

“It’s not about you,” he tells Mydei, as blunt as ever. “This song doesn’t want you showing off. It wants you as support.”

He’s right, so Mydei responds with a nod as he takes a moment to scratch out any of the lines that were too complicated for the song. It’s a new exercise now, trying to write something where he isn’t at the front of it. His whole life, he had performed pieces where he was the center of attention, and now, writing a rock song with one of the biggest pop stars in the world, he has to change this mindset greatly to match these new goals.

When they play the recording of their new version for Robin the next day, Mydei can’t help but smile a little to himself at the sound of Robin’s high praise. It gets even better when she sings along on the second time, and Mydei realizes just how much better it will be when they record everything together for the first time.

It doesn’t disappoint. Mydei’s part isn’t the easiest thing in the world, but they cut down on a lot of the parts he had written to show off. Still, he can’t find himself to be bored by it when the whole song comes together.

They then record each part separately. Robin goes last, and Mydei is immensely impressed by her vocal talent. The tone she uses on this track is glaringly different to the vocals Mydei remembers from her. It’s darker, less suited for pop and more for rock. He didn’t think she had a sound like that in her, but her voice is incredibly mature this time around.

They add their final touches the next day, making little changes in production and adding strings in the background. And then they spend the rest of the time they have playing it live together. It takes longer than usual to sync every part up with each other, with a few frustrating mistakes on Mydei’s part. This is another thing he’s going to have to get used to—with every solo he’d played alongside a massive orchestra, the orchestra and conductor changed what they were doing to match him. When he took time, they took time. He could do whatever he wanted with it, and they would follow.

But now, he needs to be steady, because Robin wasn’t going to change her part on his behalf. All four of them were supporting her, not the other way around.

Regardless, they get through it, and Mydei finds himself so in the zone that he doesn’t even realize they’re nearing the end of the song until it’s already over. It’s a far cry from the catharsis he thought he might feel, returning to piano after so long, but it’s a step in the right direction. For the first time in years, he’s really, truly proud of something he’s created.

Chapter Notes

shorter chapter today before the rest of them start averaging 10k+ words. think of it as a palatte cleanser of sorts. before it all starts going downhill. and then uphill. it will go uphill eventually.

I’m going to play it one day. Rach 2. I’m going to play it one day.

Okay.

Promise me you’ll be there when I play it. And I’ll be there when you’re selling out stadiums and have three charting rock albums.

You think I’m going to be a rockstar?
