Okay.

Promise. Promise me you’ll be there.

I promise.

~~~

July 19th, 3869. Two days after the release of Dreamscape.

Mydei has never felt concert anxiety this brutal in his life. Between all the shoots, interviews, and travel, he had no idea what he was actually getting himself into until this very moment: backstage at the festival Robin is headlining, patiently waiting it out as she goes through the rest of her set. He can hear the audience screaming as if he was in the middle of the crowd. He can hear Robin perfectly, as she hypes up the crowd and her performance goes perfectly.

It feels like it’s just been months since CALAMITY was booking gigs at empty bars, singing to three drunk men and a bartender, none of whom knew a single one of their songs. In reality, though, it’s already been nearly a year since they first flew out to west Penacony to record with Robin.

It hasn’t hit until right now. Even though his social media follower count has skyrocketed, and he’s been recognized in the street for the first time, and people seem to know who he is now. It’s just been days since the album was released, and CALAMITY’s streams have already tripled overnight.

“Do you realize how many people are out there?” Cipher whispers to him, like she’d be heard outside if she spoke too loud.

Mydei covers his face with his hands, taking a deep breath. His hands feel cold against his cheeks, and it makes him feel the tiniest bit better. “I don’t know, Cipher. At least a thousand.”

“At least a thousand?! Mydei. Bro, I think there’s more people than there were at Cerydra’s inauguration.”

“What?” Mydei pulls his hands off his face, squinting as he looks at her. “Cerydra is, like, twenty?”

Cipher whacks him across the shoulder, gawking like he’s said something offensive. “Dude, that’s so rude. Just because she’s short doesn’t mean she’s that young.”

“Is she forty?”

Cipher frowns, looking away. “Hm. No.”

“Then she couldn’t have been inaugurated, dumbass.”

“Oh shit, you’re right. Who the hell am I thinking of, then?”

“Can you leave?”

“Deep in thought, are you? Don’t let it mess you up on stage!” Thankfully, she leaves to bother Castorice instead, but the whole experience has left Mydei so baffled that some of his nerves have begun to dissipate.

He pulls out his phone instead, which is never a very good idea nowadays if he wants to calm his nerves. Robin’s post had already alerted lots of fans to the fact that she’s bringing a guest on stage at her festival performance, leading a lot of people to suspect that it might be them, since they’re the only ones known to be in the general area.

Those that are sure it would be them already know they will be performing Dreamscape, leading to speculation about whatever else they might play. Obviously, Mydei knows they’re only playing Dreamscape. It’s Robin’s show, and they don’t have any other song good enough to perform, anyway. Still, that won’t stop his phone from being blown up from people convinced they will be playing Don’t Cry, too.

Out of all the music they’ve released, Don’t Cry remains their most famous song. Before Dreamscape, it was so popular and the rest of their music was so unpopular that CALAMITY was believed to be a one-hit-wonder. Mydei had thought that with Robin’s album out now, it would cause people to realize they had made other music, too—but apparently that had been wishful thinking. He’s grateful for the engagement, of course, but would like to be recognized for something else for once.

He turns his phone off, throwing it to the side. Don’t Cry always has him thinking of Phainon, and now is no different.

This festival isn’t in a stadium, but the amount of people in the crowd may just as well be able to fill one up. Either way, it’s easily the biggest concert he’s ever played. It’s a milestone. There are musicians who spend their whole careers waiting to play a show of this size.

He had been there, for Rach 2. He still remembers it like it’s yesterday. It had been in April, near the end of Phainon’s first year at grad school. He saw the posters, happened to be in the area, and remembered their promise immediately. Even through everything—the break up, the distance, the resentment—he still felt like he needed to go.

He had brought Phoebe, the girl he was dating for two months before she inevitably dumped him that very night. He foolishly thought he was far enough removed from Phainon and their relationship to date someone else. He foolishly thought he would be okay to go to that concert—to see Phainon’s biggest dream come true right in front of him while he was in the middle of producing an EP he didn’t even write.

After everything, it would be ridiculous of him to seriously expect Phainon to attend. Those promises meant nothing, in the end. They had broken up and weren’t a part of each other’s lives anymore. But he had upheld his end of the deal, and naturally wished Phainon would do the same.

He’s pulled from his thoughts by a sudden soreness in his back, and instantly sits up straight, tossing his phone aside.

“Fuck,” he mutters under his breath. Why now?

It wasn’t pain debilitating enough to render him unable to perform, but he would much rather perform without it. Without the constant reminder of all the ways Phainon used to soothe him when it would act up, raking his nails over the spot and pressing light kisses into his vertebrae like it was something to be protected.

“Mydei,” Hyacine says, and his eyes fly open to the sight of her standing before him. “We’re on in a minute. Are you okay?”

Mydei nods, grimacing a little as he stands up. He stretches his back twice, which is good enough for now, and ignores the way Hyacine looks at him strangely.

“Are you sure you’re okay?”

So much for trying to ignore it. “Yes, Hyacine, I’m fine.” It’s enough for her to drop it, and they walk over to where Castorice and Cipher stand near the entrance to the stage.

His back issues have been something he’s dealt with for enough years now for it to be normal to him, but that doesn’t mean an answer wouldn’t be nice. He had never seen an actual doctor about it, but Hyacine, as an ex-med student and his friend, might be able to give him an explanation.

He considers it briefly and then pushes it aside after all. Even if he went through with that, now is not the time.

“Ready?” Aventurine asks, as he sneaks up behind them and claps his hands on both Mydei and Hyacine’s shoulders.

Mydei nearly flinches, taken by surprise, but nods regardless as he turns to look at Aventurine.

“For this last song,” Robin says, voice echoing through the speakers outside, “I’ve invited some friends.”

“You are going to do great,” Aventurine reassures them, pushing both Mydei and Hyacine forward a little bit. “They already love you. See?”

He points forward, to where Mydei can hear the crowd chanting Mydei, Mydei, Mydei. His name. He understands CALAMITY is hard to chant given that it’s three syllables rather than the typical two, but he still doesn’t think a single one of their band members deserves full credit for their work. He swallows, suddenly feeling bad for the three girls now getting less credit for achievements that are equally theirs.

“Go, Mydei,” Castorice says, stepping aside.

Mydei nods, swallowing his guilt and nerves as he pushes through the curtains and walks out to the center of the stage. It’s nearly deafening, even with his in-ears, how loud they scream. He can’t help but grin as he takes in their cheers. It’s a scene out of his wildest dreams. He would be ridiculous not to soak it in.

Robin gives him a hug as a greeting, whispering good luck in his ear with her microphone off to the side. He nods, and moves to take his seat at the piano.

He starts by raking his fingers over the keys, getting a feel for the instrument he’s never played before. Sunday was on it earlier, so he knows it should be in tune—assuming, anyway, that Sunday knew what an out of tune piano sounded like.

He takes a breath, as the crowd around him begins to fade. None of them matter. Robin doesn’t matter. The only person he wants to hear this is Phainon—whether or not he’s in the crowd doesn’t matter, either. His imagination is strong enough.

He starts to play. It’s not the opening to Dreamscape, not yet, because he had arranged a solo piano part, sort of like a cadenza, at Robin’s request. It doesn’t even start in Dreamscape’s key, written with inspiration taken from both his favorite classical pieces with a mix of jazz and rock thrown in. It’s the kind of thing Phainon would call him a genius for. The kind of thing that traditionalists like Krateros would grimace at.

The relief he felt when Robin asked him to write something for their festival was almost overwhelming—the opportunity to convince Aventurine that they can do it, too. That just because he dropped out of college and didn’t finish his piano degree doesn’t mean he didn’t know what he was doing. He has less experience writing lyrics than writing arrangements, but with Castorice’s literature degree, he knows they’re capable of making art.

But more than anything, he still wants to make Phainon proud. Make him see that his talents aren’t being wasted on rock music. That their worlds can still coexist.

The change into Dreamscape’s key is subtle, and then he shifts to a melody that slightly resembles the opening of Dreamscape. He thinks he can faintly hear people start to cheer. Behavior like that would be ridiculed at a classical music concert where you can’t even clap between movements. Now, though, Mydei smiles at the sound of it. People clap when there’s

something they want to appreciate. Why would he ever stop anyone from doing that?

And then, finally, he transitions into the first piano part of Dreamscape. Robin pauses longer than usual before her entrance, and Mydei listens to her as they’d always practiced before coming in again.

Castorice comes in, signifying the faster tempo as Mydei switches to his arpeggios, and then Hyacine and Cipher join together, too.

It’s perfect. Mydei doesn’t think he’s felt bliss like this in years. He doesn’t think he felt it when they signed with the IPC, or got the Robin feature, and he certainly never felt it while playing piano in his life.

The crowd knows every word. They scream it like they’re the ones performing, like they feel each word like a knife to the chest. Mydei can’t help but smile at the pure ecstasy he feels in his gut, so powerful he could choke on it.

This is, without a doubt, where he is meant to be. Making music he loves, performing it for people who love it almost as much. He doesn’t think he needs anything else after this.

The song ends, and he is instantly reminded of the pain in his back again. He finds himself wondering, once again, if Phainon is in the crowd—but he can’t see individuals. And even if he was, Mydei doesn’t think he would be in the front.

“Thank you,” he says, caught off guard after Robin offers him her microphone and asks if he has anything to say. “It’s an honor to share my music with you.”

Robin beams at that, and Mydei stands up to join the rest of the band as they’re given a chance to say something, too.

There are very few things Mydei allows himself to truly want. This, everything he has right now—the crowd screaming for him, loving him and

his music—is something he only ever wished for quietly. He thought that if he wanted it too much, it wouldn’t come true.

Phainon is the second thing he wants, and he feels like there are weights in his heart with this realization. The only thing he can do is hope that somewhere, somehow, Phainon is listening. That would be enough.

None of them have calmed down from the adrenaline and pure disbelief at it all by the time they’re in the back of a tour van, pulling out of the cramped parking lot to begin the long drive back to east Penacony. The festival hadn’t been far outside of the city, especially considering how Robin had to fly all the way from the west coast, but it was still a few hours.

Mydei’s eyes are closed as he leans against the window, willing his heart to relax. If playing for audiences so large is what he’s going to have to do for the rest of his life, he hopes he never gets used to it.

He can hear Cipher laugh at something Hyacine says, and it sounds so distant, like in the background of a dream. Even through the simmering adrenaline, he feels like he’s started to drift off.

Until the bus comes to a harsh stop, and he jolts awake.

“Oh, good, you’re awake. Just in time,” Hyacine says.

Mydei doesn’t think he was asleep, but now that his eyes are open, he feels like he might have been. Everyone is looking at him now, even Aventurine, who had climbed back from the passenger seat.

“What’s going on?” He asks. Looking out the back window, he can spot a long line of cars piled up behind them.

“Traffic,” Cipher explains, like that wasn’t obvious. “Probably a car accident.” She shrugs, then looks back at Aventurine. “Anyways, you were saying?”

“I just got off the phone with Diamond.”

Diamond. What a stupid name. Sometimes Mydei thinks that all of the IPC workers he knows must have code names, because it was just too perfect. But that would make no sense, he just has no better theory right now.

“Reception to the concert is already incredible. Your names have been skyrocketing even before Robin’s album was released, but now it’s finally confirmed that the four of you have serious star quality.” Aventurine begins. Mydei tries not to let himself get excited prematurely, but this is really sounding like good news.

“I’ve been pushing for this since we signed you, but Diamond is the one who actually calls the shots here,” Aventurine continues. “But I digress. Point is, we want an album.”

Mydei genuinely thinks he could cry. He leans back as far as possible in the seat, heart back to racing a thousand beats a minute. Part of him thinks this might not be real, but it is, and he’s here, and he can think of very few moments where he’s felt happiness this great.

“Wait, really?” Hyacine asks, the first to speak up out of the four of them. He’s never seen Castorice smile this big, or Cipher this speechless.

Aventurine nods. “We want to arrange for you to start as soon as possible. You will not be assigned any third party writers or producers unless you ask for them. Ratio will help you record and edit studio versions, but you will be in full control of any and all creative decisions.”

Mydei exhales. He doesn’t know what he did to deserve this, but it must have been something good.

“We want the album to be released before next summer, for multiple reasons: one, scheduling tours will be better, and two, we don’t want to allow the hype from Robin’s album to die down for too long before release. When do you think you can realistically finish writing this album?”

“September,” Cipher says immediately.

“No,” Mydei answers, just as quickly. “That’s a month and a half, Cipher, are you crazy?”

“I figured that wouldn’t be realistic,” Aventurine says. “Any other suggestions?”

“End of the year?” Hyacine asks, looking at Mydei for confirmation.

He thinks it over. That’s a little over five months, which doesn’t sound like a lot of time. But then he thinks about all the songs he’s written, that he’s already itching to revisit. All of the songs he wants to write. And that’s not even taking into account the lyrics Castorice has, or the ideas Hyacine and Cipher have.

“Yeah,” he says, shrugging. “Why not?”

“I like end of the year,” Castorice chimes in, nodding slightly.

“Then it’s settled.” Aventurine types something quickly on his laptop. “Finally, all of you need to stay active on your social media accounts. I’ll try to book interviews to do here and there to keep people interested, but most of the work will have to be on your end. Promote old music, show people who you are, and most importantly, hint at writing an album but don’t confirm anything until we have a release date. Understood?”

Mydei hates posting on social media. Too many strangers. The idea of having several million people following him that he doesn’t even know irks him. But he can talk about music. He can post cryptic photos with no caption. His most recent post, with a long paragraph for his caption, was already too much for him. He would never do that again, even though the reception had been mostly positive.

“Alright. Sounds good.” Aventurine closes his laptop, getting to his feet. “Anyways, I have to return to the front. I have a game of Blackjack going with Francisco.”

“The—the driver?!” Hyacine exclaims, eyes wide.

“Don’t worry, I’m playing for him.” Aventurine winks and climbs back into the passenger seat, officially out of their sight.

Mydei doesn’t even care a little bit about Aventurine’s apparent gambling addiction. He’d always had a hunch, anyways, just no proof. The only thing that matters right now is this album.

“So,” Cipher says, lifting her leg up so she can kick him in the knee lightly.

“What?” Mydei asks, moving out of her reach.

She blinks. There’s a stupid little half-smirk on her face, like he’s supposed to know what she wants to say without her saying it.

“What?”

“...Piano?”

Penacony Times, “How the ‘Astral Express’ is reviving jazz” 29 December 3867 O.W.L. Bert

An introduction to the visionary jazz troupe and their illustrious members.

In 3862, when Himeko Murata and Welt Yang joined forces with one common goal in mind: to study jazz music lost to time, they didn’t expect the success they’ve achieved today. Murata is the troupe’s talented vocalist, trained in both operatic and jazz styles throughout college and beyond. She sang for an opera house in Lushaka for ten years before meeting Yang, a decorated saxophone player from Earth.

The troupe didn’t take off immediately, though. Murata and Yang spent a good amount of time working one-on-one, fine-tuning their abilities and playing small shows when they could. Now, with the Express harboring many more members than it had upon its genesis, the troupe has been on tour for a year now, with no signs of stopping any time soon. “It’s unprecedented,” Murata explains, “how many people out there actually love jazz. Young people, too.” Both she and Yang agree that they love the opportunity they have been given to inspire future generations to pursue jazz, as well.

Their supporters aren’t the only young people they’ve found who love jazz, though. The other three members are all fairly young, two of them fresh college graduates. Caelus Aron is their trumpet player, who started playing seriously in high school for the social aspect. He continued throughout college for the same reason, as a revered member of Paperfold University’s marching band for all four years. When asked if he saw himself playing trumpet full time at any point in his life, his answer is intentionally ambiguous. “I can’t remember anything before I was, like, sixteen,” he admits. “It’s like my life started then. So I don’t really ever know what I wanted to be.” He loves jazz, though, and says that proudly. The Astral Express has welcomed both him and his sister with open arms.

March 7th is the troupe’s drummer, who grew up in Amphoreus. She admits that she also suffers with minor amnesia issues from her childhood, but found Murata and Yang during the Amphoreus leg of their tour. “I love live music, so I thought it would be fun to go to the concert,” she explains. “I loved it so much I went up to them after the show and begged them to let me join.” Both Murata and Yang confirm this story, saying that at that point in time they would let anyone in if they had talent and asked.

Dan Heng is their final member, and the oldest of the three. He plays the upright bass, though he will occasionally play the electric bass as well. Neither he nor March went to college, choosing to dedicate their lives solely to spreading music instead. Dan Heng joined the Express only a month before March, deciding that jazz was a fitting path to follow as he attempts to find himself.

“It’s all fun,” Murata declares. “All our concerts are free, we don’t make money outside of donations. So we don’t care very much about the music being perfect, as long as everyone is having fun.”

~~~

July 16th, 3869. Eight hours before the release of “Why Does Life Slumber?”

Phainon is running late. The highway was backed up with some of the worst Okhema rush hour traffic he’s ever seen in his life, turning a fifteen minute drive into thirty, and what’s worse is that he looked at the invite instructions and the venue claims they take absolutely no latecomers under any circumstance.

He supposes that at the end of the day he can always reconvene with his friends after the show, but he isn’t just going so he can see them. He wants to hear the music, too, especially as someone who isn’t very well-versed in jazz music at all.

He speeds into the parking lot and parks crooked, but he’s just in the lines, so no one can really complain. He practically scrambles out of his car, hearing it beep to confirm that it’s locked when he’s already run several yards away. He hopes he isn’t sweaty when he barges through the front doors, and takes a moment to gather himself before he heads downstairs, to where the entrance doors are.

It’s a small venue, nothing like what he’s ever played, but the Astral Express exclusively plays in intimate places like these. The doors are glass, blocked by a man on a stool with a scanner in hand. Phainon pulls his phone out of his pocket so quickly it almost slips out of his hands, his hands shaking as he searches for his email. “Sorry I’m late,” he says, pulling up the QR code and turning his phone screen towards him.

The man hums, examining his ticket as he scans it. “Phainon Khaslana?” he asks, raising an eyebrow. Phainon nods. “You can go in. They’re just about to start.”

Phainon rushes through a very enthusiastic thank you, and pushes through the glass doors as quietly as possible.

He was given a single table, with a white tablecloth and an intricate candelabra on top of it. It’s near the back, so he doesn’t draw too much attention to himself when he walks in and takes a seat. Sure enough, the troupe begins to play their first note the second Phainon sits down.

Phainon knew Caelus after they were random roommates their freshman year of college and chosen roommates their sophomore year. Junior year, Caelus got an apartment with his friends from the marching band, and Phainon got a single, but they remained friends ever since. He was a business major who somehow managed to finish his degree despite how little he tried and how much he disliked it. He seems much more content playing trumpet full time now.

Being friends with Caelus, he naturally met Stelle as well, though didn’t see her as much. Stelle was a communications major, which she always said she picked because she had no idea what she wanted to do. Sure enough, she dropped out of college after their sophomore year and decided to start Twitch streaming instead. Now, she travels with their jazz troupe even though she doesn’t play an instrument, and does Twitch streaming full time. Phainon’s never been very big into video games, but she’s supposedly very successful there.

He’s known March for the longest time—the drummer, one of the girls Phainon grew up with for a couple years after the farm burned down. He wasn’t as close with her or her twin as he was with Cyrene, of course, but Phainon’s obsession with learning piano as a teenager was one of the things that motivated March to learn an instrument, too.

Then there was Dan Heng, who was Caelus’s new best friend (which Phainon definitely doesn’t mind at all). Dan Heng used to go by Dan Feng, who was the bassist in the High Cloud Quintet, a band Phainon never listened to, but an old friend of his was a huge fan. (He doesn’t think about how overjoyed Mydei would be if he knew that Phainon was mutual friends with one of his idols. He never thinks about that.) Now, Dan Heng plays

upright bass for a much less popular jazz troupe, and says he’s “finding himself” whenever he’s asked about his past.

Phainon knows all about the band’s extremely messy break up. How they were once a tight-knit group of best friends, until Baiheng, their pianist and guitarist, died in a freak accident. Dan Feng and Yingxing, the drummer, were so unable to cope with her death that they released a disastrous comeback album not even a year after the incident, which heavily relied on AI generated vocals made to sound like Baiheng. It was terrible and painfully obvious as the amount of recordings of Baiheng singing circulating the internet could have been counted on one hand. The actual lead singer, Jingliu, tried desperately to salvage their public image, but it was short-lived and ultimately resulted in her public arrest when she finally lost it, successfully ending her career. Yingxing fell off the face of the earth following her arrest and was never heard of or seen ever again. Jing Yuan, the lead guitarist, was seemingly the only normal one, who was able to cope with his grief in a healthy way. According to Mydei, he’s raising a child now, and has a fairly successful solo career. Phainon loves his solo music much more than he ever loved the High Cloud Quintet’s discography, but he thinks Mydei had the opposite experience.

Given that this is all the previous information Phainon had on Dan Feng and his nature, he was surprised to discover that Dan Heng actually comes across as a polite, and well-adjusted man. If Phainon didn’t know any better, he would have thought they were two different people.

Himeko is the lead vocalist, who sometimes plays guitar if the piece calls for it. He doesn’t know very much about her personal life at all, but the two of them get along fine.

It was a similar situation with Welt, an older man who played the saxophone. Phainon didn’t know anything about him except for that, but he was very polite in all their interactions. As a musician, Phainon respects him greatly.

Sunday was their final and newest member, older brother to the famous pop star Robin. He’d worked with her for years, as her pianist, but ended up joining the Astral Express when they stopped in Penacony for the first time.

Phainon doesn’t know the details, but Caelus was, at the very least, wary of him right now, so it must have been a little messy.

Phainon thought he was a very talented pianist. Both he and Mydei were better, of course—especially Mydei, Phainon still dreams about his music— but he was good at what he was doing. Phainon never really dabbled in jazz, and he respects Sunday for his improvisational skills.

The song they’re starting with is far too slow for the beginning of a concert, in Phainon’s professional opinion, and he feels like he’s about to fall asleep. Regardless, it’s nice, with barely-there drums and soft acoustic guitar and a beautiful sax solo that sounds perfectly unpredictable, like it was never written down and Welt is merely making it up as he goes. Phainon supposes most of jazz is exactly that.

That’s what Phainon likes about jazz—he might not know much about the technical side of things, but it’s always striked him as a music genre that is impossible to play by musicians lacking passion. He’d trained for six years to get his master’s degree in piano performance, had studied his ass off to grasp music theory to the best of his ability, only for all his knowledge to be thrown out the door the second he speaks to a jazz musician. He’s always regarded it as something out of his reach.

Phainon believes every musician has a genre they can’t touch, no matter how much they might admire it. For Hysilens, it was folk and bluegrass— anything with a fiddle. She would often complain about how she wished she wasn’t classically trained from such a young age. For Phainon, it was jazz, without a doubt.

As for Mydei, well—he might be the only exception.

The first song ends, and Welt thanks the crowd briefly after they applaud for him. He seemed to be wearing a leather jacket when he first came into class, but now it’s abandoned and draped over the back of his seat instead. The tank top he wears shows how muscular he is, as well as the red tattoo climbing up his right arm, and Phainon is kind of pissed off that he has the nerve to show off like that.

When he turns around, looking back at the chalkboard to whatever nonsense Anaxa is writing, Phainon lets his gaze linger a little longer. His resting expression is stoic and borderline mean. No wonder no one wanted to sit with him.

He tries not to pout for the rest of class, but it’s difficult. Especially with Hysilens just across the room from them, sitting next to Raiden Mei. The two of them certainly look like they’re having a whole lot better of a time than Phainon is. He doesn’t even know Mei very well, just that Hysilens

played a violin duet with her last year, and he still bets that she’d be way more fun than this egotistical grouch.

A week later, he walks into Mydei’s practice room, falsely assuming it was empty. It takes Mydei a few seconds to realize there’s someone watching him, and in those few brief seconds Phainon’s ears are filled with the most wonderful music he’s ever heard, and that’s all it really takes for Phainon’s opinion of him to do a full one-eighty.

Mydei stops abruptly, and Phainon mourns the loss. “Um,” he says, looking up at Phainon and blinking once, slowly. “Occupied?”

“Right,” Phainon says, but he doesn’t move. Nor does he say anything. Mydei’s wearing glasses, his hair pulled back into a sloppy ponytail. He has a hoodie on today and Phainon doesn’t know why that sort of pisses him off. There’s a pencil tucked behind his ear, and that just pisses Phainon off more. Put it on the stand like everyone else instead of trying to be performative.

“Do you need something?”

“No,” Phainon desperately hopes his face isn’t as red as it feels like it is. “Um, sorry, I’m sorry, I’ll go.”

He stands outside the door and listens to him play for another fifteen minutes before he finally drags himself away.

Phainon wants to marry Mydei one day. It would be on the most beautiful day of the year, in Castrum Kremnos. They would grow old together and adopt a daughter. She would grow up to be the best pianist in the world, he thinks—until it dawns on him just what he’s thinking, and he wipes the thought out of his head just as quickly.

Mydei doesn’t do anything special when it finally clicks to Phainon just what he’s experiencing. They’re simply in Phainon’s dorm together, watching a movie while Caelus is busy at rehearsal, and Phainon says something that makes Mydei laugh.

It’s a stupid joke. But he laughs like it was the funniest thing he’d ever heard, and Phainon realizes that seeing any of his other friends laugh like this doesn’t make him feel this way.

The amount of romantic experiences Phainon has had at this point could be counted on one hand, and yet he can’t help but think that this must be exactly what it feels like to love someone.

~~~

Phainon gets the same feeling now, watching the camera’s close up shot of Mydei’s hands on the piano keys. His playing is still as beautiful as ever— fuck whatever Madam Herta had to say on the matter. Phainon still believes that Mydei could lay on the keyboard and it would sing out a melody. Ever since that day that he realized he loved Mydei, every time he saw him play it was like he fell in love with him all over again.

Phainon’s so focused on the original melody Mydei performs that he doesn’t recognize the key change into D-sharp minor, matching that of Dreamscape. He doesn’t register that the rest of his band has now walked out on stage, taking their respective places with Robin standing right in front of Mydei’s piano, until the crowd starts cheering again.

And then Mydei launches right into the Dreamscape piano solo, and Phainon thinks he finally loses it.

Robin starts singing, and then the drums kick in, and Mydei’s solo picks up. The guitar and bass are added, and Phainon wants to kill whoever is controlling the screencast for focusing on anyone but Mydei.

He can barely hear the piano part over the screaming of the crowd now, but he knows that it’s happening, and the way the music comes together live is almost overwhelming.

He can’t stop himself from crying, uncaring for how dramatic he might seem. Mydei never seemed to mind how weak he was, anyways. Maybe, if they could see each other, Mydei would step off stage and come console him. Hold him in his arms and run his fingers through his hair like he always did when Phainon’s insomnia hindered him from sleeping back in college.

And then reality hit him: Mydei couldn’t see him, and Phainon was probably the last thing on his mind right now, anyway. If he knew Phainon were here, he probably wouldn’t think much of it. He had a beautiful girlfriend at home that, if everything worked out in his favor, would be his wife someday.

To Mydei, Phainon was in the past. And Phainon was okay with accepting that.

The song finishes. Phainon doesn’t stay for the rest of the set.

Even once he’s waded his way out of the crowd and begins the walk back to where he parked his car, he can hear the low rumble of Mydei’s voice speaking to the crowd, even through their earsplitting screams.

It’s not nearly as busy on the outside of the festival as it was when Phainon had arrived, so it doesn’t take long to walk to where he parked. Just as he’s getting into his car, he gets a phone call from an unknown number.

It’s from outside Penacony, he can tell by the way the numbers are laid out before he even reads the country it’s tracked to.

Castrum Kremnos. He almost drops his phone, then scrambles to accept the call before it goes to voicemail. There’s only one person he knows from Castrum Kremnos, and it can’t be him mid performance. He’s not entirely sure why he picks up—his phone number still has the Aedes Elysiae area code, anyways, so it could very well be Amphoreus spam.

“Hello?”

“Hello. Is this Phainon Khaslana?” It’s a man’s voice. Deep, but not as deep as Mydei’s. He speaks in Kremnoan-accented Okheman. Phainon blinks a couple times, caught off guard as he forces his brain to switch back into Okheman, too.

“Yes?” Phainon says, suddenly extremely confused. “Who is this?”

“I’m calling from Kremnos Pianos. We’re reaching out to you for a sponsorship opportunity. Would you be interested?”

Phainon’s brain short circuits. “What?” The word comes out harsher than he intended, but he’s in no rush to take it back. He swallows as the man keeps talking, yet fails to wash down the bitter taste in his mouth.

“It won’t take much from your end. We would pay you five hundred thousand dollars upfront to use one of our pianos in every performance for the next year, as well as a 50% cut of all revenue made from an advertisement you’re featured in.”

Phainon’s brain is moving at a snail’s pace. First, Kremnos Pianos is calling him—Mydei’s father’s company—and they’re willing to pay him five hundred grand just to play on one of their pianos for a year.

Phainon isn’t poor like he was after the fire and in college, when all the money he made was from the occasional concert and each minimum wage job he worked, and his college tuition was mostly covered by a scholarship he still doesn’t think he ever deserved.

But he’s not rich enough to think five hundred grand is beneath him. He’s happy with where he’s at, but he can’t even fathom where that sort of money might get him.

He can’t believe it, but he’s actually considering saying yes—until a cold hang drags him back as if forcing him to remember. It had been so long since he’d allowed himself to think about the ugly parts of Mydei. Like his

past—like his father. Things he hated thinking about then, and hates just as much today.

The man on the other end is still talking, but he doesn’t know what he’s saying. Something about other options and how they’re open to negotiation.

Phainon doesn’t care how flexible Eurypon Nikador is willing to be. “No,” he says, a little too quietly.

“...Sorry?”

“I said no.” It’s more forceful the second time around. He swallows the lump in his throat. “I won’t do it.”

He doesn’t seem to be willing to take that as an acceptable answer. A few beats of silence pass on his end, and Phainon considers hanging up, but decides against it. He wants them to know just how little he’s willing to take this sponsorship. “Er…we can up the price as much as you want, sir. How about seven hundred?”

“No,” Phainon says again. He’s starting to get a rush from denying Mydei’s father this. He feels genuinely good about himself for the first time all week. “I don’t care how much you’ll give me. I have no interest in working with your company.”

“Well,” Phainon can hear the man swallow thickly on the other end. “That’s…not an acceptable answer, sir.”

“Oh, is it?” Phainon laughs. “I’m the one you’re begging to work with. I don’t think you’re in any position to tell me what is and isn’t acceptable.”

“Our company is willing to take matters into our own hands if this is your final answer, sir. You will receive a check in the mail for all the money we owe you regardless.”

“What the hell are you talking about?” Phainon doesn’t think he’s talking to Eurypon right now—it would be weird if he was, but this is exactly the kind of manipulation he imagined he used to run his business. Suddenly he’s

getting weird images in his head of edited pictures of him smiling next to a Kremnos piano.

“Have a good day, Mr. Khaslana.”

The line clicks off. Phainon stares at his phone screen, immensely confused. Was that actually what they were going to do? Make it look like he supported their company, when he didn’t agree to a sponsorship? Did they seriously think they would legally get away with that?

Regardless, he does the first thing he can think of, and posts something to his public Twitter account—a disclaimer about his refusal to collaborate with Kremnos pianos. It comes across a little meaner than he might intend on a different day, but he doesn’t think he’s felt such hatred for a man in years.

~~~

Summer in Okhema was always unbearably hot. Somehow Phainon managed to drag Mydei, Cipher, and Castorice to the beach for a day while Mydei was visiting to record music for the band. Phainon thinks he has the worst heat tolerance out of any of them, but he would never admit that to Mydei, lest he find something else to hold over his head.

At some point, Phainon leaves Castorice and Cipher in the water to talk to Mydei. He lays on his back underneath the burning sun, eyes closed and hair like a bright yellow halo around him. For a brief moment, Phainon thinks he might really be asleep, but he stirs as he feels Phainon approach and sits up onto his elbows.

“Hey,” he says casually, squinting up at him. “Having fun?”

Phainon just shrugs, coming to sit beside him. “It would be more fun if you went out there with us,” he says, smiling at Mydei sideways.

Mydei’s carefree expression falters a little. He looks away, at the ocean, and there’s clear pain in his eyes. Phainon instantly feels bad for prodding. “I can’t swim,” Mydei finally admits.

“What?”

Mydei turns to look at him. He doesn’t repeat himself, because they both know Phainon heard. That was just never something he considered before— Mydei was so strong, athletic, and he grew up rich, in a large estate with an outdoor pool. He’d mentioned it in the past. How was it possible that he was never taught how to swim?

“I was seven,” Mydei begins, sitting up fully and crossing his legs. There’s tension in his shoulders, and without thinking, Phainon reaches up to soothe it. Mydei’s flinch is almost unnoticeable, but he relaxes instantly. Phainon doesn’t ask.

“My father…” Mydei continues. “He was an asshole to me.” He takes a deep breath, and tells the rest of the story without pausing once. “The bigger his company got, the more he drank. The alcohol changed him until he wasn’t the same even when he was sober. When I started taking piano lessons, he got this idea in his head that I would overshadow him one day. And that was a big enough problem to him that he wanted me gone. My mother fought with him all the time. She wasn’t one to let him speak to her the way he did, and she wasn’t one to let him hurt me, either. But one day it went too far. He was the drunkest I’d ever seen him, and he threw me into the pool. I would have drowned if my mother didn’t pull me out. We left him that night. But I haven’t been able to swim since. So I just…I never learned.”

~~~

Phainon turns the car on and tosses his phone aside. He pulls out of his parking spot a little too fast, just as his car connects to the local radio

station. He practically bruises his knuckle with how hard he mutes it. He does not have the patience to listen to the Fools right now. He’s not sure why such a terrible band ever even got a record deal.

The traffic is moving too slowly in the city for him. Phainon usually praises himself for being a safe driver, but he’s overcome with the urge to crash head on into the car in front of him right now—a feeling he’s completely foreign to.

He’s gripping the steering wheel so hard his knuckles are turning white. He’s never had tunnel vision this bad before, too lazer-focused on what’s directly in front of him, that he doesn’t notice the light turn red before he’s speeding through it, and he doesn’t notice the car hurtling into his driver’s side until it’s too late.

~~~

July 27th, 3869. Ten months before the release of Oracle.

The band takes a few days of rest after the festival. Aventurine informed them they weren’t required to write their album in an IPC building, but needed to record it in one—which was easy enough. Mydei knows he’s supposed to use these days to take a break, but it doesn’t feel very well deserved after only playing one show. Robin brought out two different guests for the other two nights of the festival, and besides, it was her album that was out, and not theirs. All Mydei really had to adjust to was his skyrocketing popularity.

And now Don’t Cry is charting again. Mydei even heard it on the radio once. And speaking of Phainon, one of his posts was trending on social media to the point where Mydei had actually gotten a notification about it. His feed usually doesn’t include anything related to pianists or the classical music world as a whole, but what really caught his eye was the mention of Kremnos Pianos specifically.

Phainon released a statement publicly denouncing the brand and stating that he had been boycotting them. What Mydei finds especially interesting is that he never elaborates as to why, not even in the replies when people press him for further comment. In fact, he was oddly silent under this post, not answering a single comment. Mydei knows enough about Phainon’s social media presence to know how friendly he was with all of his followers, and Mydei has a hard time believing he would be the type of person to stay completely silent online. Especially when talking about an issue that is clearly very important to him.

Mydei, of course, has a guess as to why he’s chosen to boycott the company. It’s a personal thing, without a doubt—a lingering connection to Mydei, and his father, and Phainon’s stubborn hatred of the man. Mydei never understood why Phainon insisted upon hating Eurypon for him.

And there’s no evidence out there that Kremnos Pianos is an unethical company. While Mydei has no knowledge of their business practices, disconnected from all of it as he is, he doesn’t have any reason to believe Eurypon is an asshole beyond being a drunk old man with a short temper. So he chalks Phainon’s silence up to a simple lack of evidence.

That is, until he receives a phone call around noon, a couple days before the band had agreed to start working on the album together. It’s from a number he doesn’t recognize. He picks it up anyways.

“Hello?”

“Hi, we’re calling from the Feldspar Hospital of Penacony. Is this Mydeimos Nikador?”

“Yes.” Mydei suddenly feels a wave of nausea overcome him, thrown back to that terrible phone call he received in college. Was Castorice sick again? Did Hyacine get in an accident? Cipher? It all seems so unlikely, everything was going so well recently. But that was also the case the day his mother died.

“Do you know a Phainon Khaslana?”

“Oh,” Mydei can’t help it from coming out of his mouth, the word so small in the air around him. He takes a seat on his couch, accidentally sitting on his cat’s tail. She yowls and runs away, but it’s hardly at the front of his mind. “I…do. Did. We—is he okay?”

“He was in a car accident last Wednesday. His condition was stabilized, and he has been recovering. We cannot allow him to fly back to Amphoreus, as he is foreign, and he says you are the only person he has a connection with in the area.”

Mydei almost doesn’t hear the end of her words after processing the first part. A car accident. It must have been him on that day, after the festival. What the hell was he doing in Penacony in the first place? All his family and friends still lived in Amphoreus, as far as Mydei knew. Unless he was here for the concert—which is a possibility Mydei doesn’t allow himself to ruminate on for too long.

He was safe, at least, and that was all Mydei needed to hear. Only once he’s calmed down a little bit does he process the second half. Phainon wants to stay with him until he can fly back home.

God, Mydei wants nothing more. He spent the last three years of his life inadvertently chasing him down, anyway—attending every concert in his area, watching videos of his performances late at night, wondering whether or not he’s moved on, and not thinking too hard about why he so desperately wants the answer to be no.

Regardless, it doesn’t matter. They were friends first, were they not? The closest friend Mydei had ever made—he always hates himself for how easily he let him go.

“Sir? Are you still there?”

“Yes,” Mydei rushes to say. “Are you saying he wants to stay with me?”

“Of course, something like this cannot be done without your consent, and it is an atypical situation, as the two of you are not family. There are alternatives to this, if you don’t have the means or desire to take him in.”

“No,” Mydei says, a little too loud. “I can do it. I will do it.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes. You said he’s alright now? What are his injuries?”

“His hands and fingers were crushed, he dislocated a hip, and fractured a collarbone. He is also recovering from mild whiplash.”

“What?” Mydei practically whispers. “He can’t use his hands?”

“That’s right, sir.”

No matter how hard he tries, Mydei cannot think of a more devastating way Phainon could have injured himself. Something like that, Mydei thinks, might be a fate worse than death. He had always loved piano more than anything else in the world.

His phone call with the nurse ends soon after that. He asks if he needs to pick Phainon up, and they say the hospital will transport him to Mydei’s

apartment themselves. He would be discharged by the weekend, which only gives Mydei a couple of days.

He stares at the baby grand piano in front of him. Ever since writing Dreamscape, he’d been playing here and there again. Not learning any new pieces, just recalling ones he used to know. It was as frustrating an experience as it was cathartic—now, after being so far removed from all the bad things he had come to associate with it, he realized that he really did like being so good at an instrument few can say they’ve mastered. But it’s not as much muscle memory as he had thought it was. Trying and failing to play pieces he knew how to play mere years ago only served to piss him off, not to relax.

He wonders how Phainon would feel, seeing it. Would it make him happy to see that Mydei still had a piano in his apartment after all these years, or would it just sadden him, being so close to an instrument he wants to play, but can’t?

Before doing anything else, he texts Phainon. He doesn’t expect him to respond, knowing he probably can’t, but doesn’t think the first time they’ve spoken in years should be on the day Phainon moves in with him. He makes sure to clarify who he is, just in case Phainon had gotten a new phone or deleted his contact. He wouldn’t blame him if that was the case.

Phainon responds a minute later with a message that reads “Hi mighty I’m on like so many drugs right now and I just I love you.” Mydei stifles his laugh and types back a few more messages that Phainon doesn’t respond to. He doesn’t think about it too hard—even initiating voice text must seem impossible when you can’t even hold up your phone.

As soon as he puts his phone down, finally able to process the information he was just given, he can’t help the giddiness he feels pooling in his gut. Worry is there too, of course—Phainon’s message was lighthearted enough for him to believe he was doing fine, but that was most likely just the painkillers speaking. And Mydei knows Phainon. He knows he would rather die than pile his burdens on anyone else, even if they’re asking for it.

But he’s going to see him again. They’re going to reconnect. It’s ridiculous that it took something so terrible for that to happen, but Mydei is glad regardless.

The day of Phainon’s arrival comes much quicker than Mydei was anticipating. He had spent the last few days until the weekend doing his best to prepare—he could have the guest room, which up until now Mydei was using as his office, so he moved all the clutter into the living room instead. The band had initially agreed to do their work together in the studio, but after the change of plans Mydei had to ask that they work in his apartment instead. He then spent an entire afternoon moving all the soundproofing boards from the guest room to the living room.

Phainon is brought to Mydei’s apartment at the beginning of the next week. The nurses ensure Mydei knows exactly what he needs to do to make sure Phainon heals properly. He’s more or less off the strong painkillers by now, but the first time he actually addresses Mydei alone is after the nurses are gone.

“Hi,” he says. He sits on the edge of the couch, and Mydei isn’t sure if he looks more uncomfortable about being in Mydei’s apartment, or his injuries. He had been kept in the hospital for a little under two weeks, until he could walk on his own since he wasn’t able to use a crutch. His hands are in splints, his left arm in a sling. Mydei was already given all the information for the physical therapy sessions he had already been attending three times a week.

“Hi,” Mydei replies. He swallows thickly. He had already spent several hours fantasizing about this moment, wondering if they would click back into being best friends like no time had passed, or if too much would have changed for them to even reach that point ever again. Right now, it’s looking like the second option is more plausible. “How do you feel?”

“Fine,” Phainon’s response is immediate. “It’s really not that serious, I just have to keep the brace on because they tell me I have to.”

And all of a sudden, Mydei’s already annoyed. He fights the urge to click his tongue at him, or cross his arms, or do anything to reveal how he truly feels. But the last thing Phainon needs right now is to misread his irritation. “Phainon,” he says, as gently as he can manage. “You can be honest with me.”

“Of course, Mydei.” He gives him what Mydei assumes is the biggest smile he can manage right now, but it doesn’t look that convincing. Mydei sighs, quietly, and sits down on the coffee table across from him.

“Why were you in Penacony?” He gently places a hand over his knee. “Did you have a concert?” He doesn’t admit to the fact that he knows Phainon did not have a concert in the area. He always knows when Phainon is coming near him.

“No,” Phainon says. “I was visiting a friend.”

Mydei knows he’s lying. “A friend?” He questions, in an attempt to get something more out of him. “And yet you chose to stay with me?” He stares at Phainon in a way he knows is intimidating. Phainon can’t look away, even though Mydei can tell he wants to.

He worries at his lip, and then exhales. “It was you,” he admits quietly. “I went to the festival.”

Mydei already knew that was probably it. He just didn’t want to admit it to himself in case it was merely wishful thinking. He tries to stop himself from smiling, and fails miserably. “You did,” he murmurs. “You were there.”

“Of course I was,” Phainon says, frowning a little. “I promised.”

“Rach 2 wasn’t the only performance I went to,” Mydei admits. “I saw you play with Aglaea’s orchestra when I was in Okhema last.”

“Oh my god,” Phainon starts to laugh, but it doesn’t last very long. “Didn’t I play Hungarian Rhapsody as an encore?”

Mydei fights back a smile of his own. He hated that piece—it had caused one or two arguments in college, as it was one of Phainon’s favorites. Watching him play it live had almost been enough to change his mind. “I was proud of you, because you said you didn’t think you’d ever be able to learn it.”

Phainon settles for a simple smile this time, though the twinkle in his eye tells Mydei that he wants to laugh. “It wasn’t that hard once I finally sat down to do it,” he says, and then his smile fades as quickly as it had appeared. “Wait, Mydei, you don’t…live alone, do you?”

Mydei can’t help but laugh, a little in disbelief. “What?”

“Well, because—”

“Who would I possibly be living with? Cas? Cipher? Although, Kephale knows she probably needs help with rent—”

“I meant your girlfriend.”

Mydei closes his mouth, caught off guard. “My girlfriend?” It takes too long for him to realize that Phainon means Phoebe, who he had brought to his Rach 2 performance over a year ago now. He almost forgot about that completely. “Phainon, we broke up. We’ve been broken up.” Since the day Phainon met her. It didn’t take Mydei longer than a couple weeks to get over it, but he’s still riddled with shame whenever he thinks about that night now.

“Oh,” Phainon murmurs, so soft the word is barely even there. “I’m sorry.”

Mydei remembers what he used to tell Phainon in college whenever he apologized to him unnecessarily. Don’t apologize for things that aren’t your fault. He almost laughs at the irony of it now, thinking about all of it. It would be a lie to tell Phainon it wasn’t his fault. “It was a while ago,” he says instead. “We went our separate ways, and I’m past it now.”

“That’s good, then.”

“What about you?” Mydei prods, leaning forwards a little. “How’s your love life going?”

Phainon half-snorts. “Just as bad as you’d expect. You know who I am.”

“Huh.” Mydei thinks he might know what Phainon means by that. Phainon didn’t fall in love easily. Piano always came first in his life, and he might have been in love with Mydei once, if only for the fact that they shared that priority.

But they didn’t anymore. And Mydei supposes that’s okay.

“Huh,” Phainon echoes.

They fall into silence. He had known what Phainon had grown up to look like, of course. The slightly messy way his hair sits on his head, fluffy and sticking up in several stubborn places he can never seem to tame. His bright blue eyes that almost feel overbearing sometimes. The pink undertones of his skin and the rosy blush on his cheeks. It’s all the same. And yet, he looks a thousand times more mature now, and infinitely more handsome, even through the circles under his eyes and fresh scar on his cheek.

Mydei sighs, finally breaking his gaze away. “I’m happy you’re here, though,” he admits. “Even though the circumstances are terrible. I wanted to talk to you again.” He shocks himself with how vulnerable he is so quickly. Leave it to Phainon to bring it out of him.

“Me too,” Phainon agrees. “You know, you could have just called me. I would have picked up without a second thought.”

Mydei snorts, head hanging low. “I could say the same to you, you know.”

“Yeah,” Phainon chuckles softly, and Mydei lifts his head to look at him again, at the way his eyes twinkle with mischief and relief and a thousand positive emotions, without a single negative one in sight, even in such circumstances. “I guess we’re both just fucking stupid.”

“Okay,” Castorice sighs, as Mydei sets down the final case he had dragged out of her car. “That’s the last of it.”

“I didn’t know you had a kit this big,” Mydei mutters, staring at the mess they had just turned his living room into. Hyacine and Castorice had been slowly unloading every box Mydei had dragged out of Castorice’s car, setting up her drum kit in the living room. Cipher was supposed to be helping, but she wasn’t.

“I brought everything,” Castorice explains. “For options.”

“Right,” Mydei stands in the archway between his kitchen and living room, hands on his hips. “Options.”

“When can we meet the lovely delivery boy?” Cipher chimes in, and Mydei almost jumps at how easily she was able to sneak up on him.

“Delivery boy?” Mydei snickers.

Cipher comes to stand before him, smiling like she was trying to feign innocence. “Yeah, he used to deliver pizzas in high school. You didn’t know that?”

Mydei pinches the bridge of his nose and walks past her, exasperated. “He’s in his room,” he answers. “He’ll be out soon. He did say he wanted to meet you all.”

“Meet?!” Cipher scoffs, turning away. “Bastard gets a little lick of fame and pretends he doesn’t know us anymore.” She huffs, exasperated, before stalking off to perch herself on Mydei’s couch and watch Castorice and Hyacine do actual work.

Mydei shakes his head, moving to the kitchen to retrieve the plates of food he had prepared last night. He sets them down on the coffee table, choosing not to comment on the very obvious bite that had been taken out of one of

the dishes. Cipher, no doubt—Castorice and Hyacine wouldn’t do such a thing, and Phainon wasn’t even able to feed himself with both his hands in a cast.

He knocks on Phainon’s door, hoping to retrieve the whiteboard he forgot was still in the spare room. It was the best thing he could think of to start brainstorming with.

“Come in?” Phainon's voice comes on the other end, laced with uncertainty.

Mydei pushes the door open, and Phainon audibly sighs in relief when he sees it’s him. “I need the whiteboard,” he explains, closing the door behind them. “You okay?”

Phainon is shirtless, and the room is a mess. Eve had sent over a suitcase full of his clothes, and he wasn’t able to empty it out very neatly. There’s a t-shirt halfway on one of his arms, and he stares at Mydei helplessly. “I’m useless,” he shakes his head, slumping as he sits on the side of the bed.

“Here,” Mydei walks over to him, lifting the shirt and opening it so Phainon can stick his head through. It’s more of a hassle to get his other arm through, but they manage. “You can ask for my help, you know,” he says. “It’s nothing to be ashamed of.”

“I know,” Phainon mutters, but he still sounds bitter.

“It’s temporary,” Mydei says. “You’ll heal.”

Phainon chews at his lip, but doesn’t say anything.

“Come,” Mydei sits up, offering him a hand. “They want to meet you.”

Phainon doesn’t accept his hand, looking up at him despairingly. “Mydei, I…look like shit.”

Mydei takes him in—his hair is a mess, unable to tame his bedhead, and there are even worse bags under his eyes than yesterday, but there’s still something almost devastatingly attractive about him. Mydei shakes it away.

It’s the outfit, it has to be—jeans and a solid-colored t-shirt, much more mature than the horrendous things he would throw together in college. He doesn’t look like shit at all.

“You just got in a car crash, Phainon, no one is expecting you to be model ready,” Mydei shakes his head, gripping his arm and pulling him up to his feet. “Come on. You look fine.” Fine is an understatement, but he can’t say any more than that.

Mydei grabs the whiteboard by the wall, and by the time they both enter the living room, Castorice’s drum kit is almost entirely set up.

They all look up as the two of them enter. “Hi guys,” Phainon says from Mydei’s right, a little sheepish. “It’s been a while…”

Cipher gives a low whistle from her seat atop the couch cushions, with Kokopo III on her lap. “Shit, Mydei, you weren’t lying.”

“About what?!” Mydei demands, alarmed. He’s horrified, for a second, that he said something he shouldn’t have, until Cipher continues.

“He really did get fucked up. I thought you just wanted an excuse to live with him.”

“Why would I lie about that?”

Cipher doesn’t respond, and Mydei turns his attention back to Phainon, who is currently trying to figure out a way to shake Hyacine’s hand.

“Do you remember me?” Phainon asks, when they part. “From chemistry?”

“You asked more questions than any other student, of course I remember you,” she answers. “And, I graded your final. It was…disappointing, to say the least.”

Phainon’s whole face flushes, and he looks away. “I only failed it because I didn’t study!” he jumps to defend himself, like that’s an acceptable excuse. “He said the finals would only count if they helped, and I had a ninety!

Pretty good for chemistry, if you ask me.” Sometimes, Mydei thinks Phainon must be a genius.

Hyacine giggles. “Yes. It’s not for everyone.”

They move to sit around the coffee table, making idle conversation as Mydei sets up the whiteboard. Now, it was clearer than ever that although Cipher, Castorice, and Phainon had kept in touch, they hadn’t seen each other since he and Mydei broke up. Mydei thinks that is probably his fault. He never said anything about allowing them to meet Phainon despite them not being on speaking terms, and would feel terrible if he was the sole reason they hadn’t seen one of their closest friends in years.

“How’s Agy doing?” Mydei catches Cipher asking while he’s in the kitchen, rummaging through one of the drawers for a dry erase marker.

“Aglaea?” Phainon asks. “Last I saw her, her vision was getting a lot worse,” he says. “She’s handling it just fine, though. But I think she would appreciate a call from you.”

Mydei doesn’t hear her response, and by the time he’s back in the living room, the conversation has moved on. Cipher doesn’t talk about Aglaea often. He thinks they must have been close, given how Aglaea was Cipher’s legal guardian, but their relationship is somewhat strained nowadays. He has no idea why that is.

“Are you still living with Cyrene, Phainon?” Castorice asks next. Mydei sits on the couch beside Phainon and unlocks his tablet. He has all his old music on here somewhere, he just has to find it.

“No,” Phainon answers. “I have my own apartment in Okhema. She’s abroad right now though, doing her book tour.”

“She published it?” Castorice’s eyes light up, hands clasped together. Phainon nods, beaming.

Mydei had heard about the book Cyrene was writing in passing; when he and Phainon were still close, she had already been working on writing it for

years. From his understanding, it was a long retelling of ancient Amphorean epics titled As I’ve Written. She studied history and anthropology in Janusopolis for years in preparation for this novel.

“It’s gone really well so far. I’m sure she’d ship you a free copy if you wanted, Cas. All of you, actually.” Phainon looks at Mydei specifically, and he’s not entirely sure why.

“Nah, I don’t read.” Cipher stretches out from her spot atop the couch cushions, hitting Phainon’s shoulder with her foot. Kokopo III jumps off her lap. “Can we clock in now?”

“I didn’t think making music was such a chore for you, Cipher,” Hyacine admonishes. She scratches the top of Kokopo III’s head like she’s a dog.

“I’ll leave you guys to it, then,” Phainon says. He carefully stands from the couch, giving Mydei a light nod as they make eye contact. “I’ll be in the guest room if you need my help with any theory stuff, Mydeimos.”

“Very funny. Get out.”

Phainon goes, soft laughter trailing behind him as he disappears around the corner.

“You two seem close,” Hyacine says once they can hear his door shut. She wears a pleasant smile on her face when Mydei whirls his head around to look at her.

“Seriously?” He demands.

“Yeah, what exactly did reconnecting entail with you two?” Cipher chimes in. She’s rolled off the top of the cushion now, legs thrown casually over Castorice’s lap. “He might not be as spry as he once was, but surely you can put some work in now and then.”

“What does that even me—”

“The album,” Castorice chimes in, as if trying to remind everyone why they are here in the first place.

Mydei shoots to his feet, uncapping the marker in his hand. “Yes, Cas. The album.”

“The album,” Hyacine agrees, shifting the way she’s sitting until she faces the whiteboard Mydei had hung on the wall. The only open space was over one of his windows due to all the soundproofing equipment he had installed. He writes the word album on the top of it in all caps.

The one thing they all remember very quickly is that none of them have ever written an album before. Individual songs are different—they can be anything, but an album must be at least somewhat cohesive. In theme, or sound.

They mess around on their instruments until they find a general sound they like, before deciding they don’t want to be confined to one sound. Cipher turns one of their old basslines into funk, and Mydei plays an improvised jazz lick on the piano. Hyacine points out that they’re technically still a rock band, after which they all unanimously decide that while they don’t want to lose this origin, they don’t want to be tied down by it, either.

They brainstorm themes next, Mydei writing each one on the whiteboard. Hyacine’s first suggestion is that they write a social commentary, right before spitballing “romance” while looking very pointedly at Mydei. He shakes his head but writes it down anyway. Cipher follows that up with “heartbreak” and a wink. Mydei writes that down, too, because he has a lot of songs about heartbreak he already knows he wants to workshop.

Castorice suggests a concept album, where they wrote a story along with characters and based the songs after their experiences. She claims she already has a couple ideas, paging through her notebook at vague sketches and half-written stories.

“I like the idea, but I still want this album to be more personal,” Mydei confesses, thinking about the promises he had already made to himself.

“What the hell happened to you?” Cipher demands. “You never tell us anything.”

“Well, neither do you,” he responds. “I couldn’t waterboard details about your relationship with Lady Aglaea out of you.”

“Okay, you could definitely waterboard it out of me—”

“I find that hard to believe considering—”

“That’s enough,” Hyacine juts in, getting up from her seat. “We’re never going to finish a whole album by the end of the year if you’re going to keep starting all these petty arguments.”

Hyacine rarely scolds them, but when she does, Mydei can’t help but feel ashamed each time, without fail. He didn’t think his banter with Cipher was ever that serious, even if he always said how he felt.

“It’s true,” Castorice chimes in. “Neither of you ever tell us anything.”

“I tell you things,” Cipher crosses her arms, closing herself off as she looks at Castorice with an expression akin to a pout.

“You’re bad at telling the full truth,” Castorice answers softly.

“If you want an honest album, Mydei, you have to be honest with us,” Hyacine says. “At least a little bit.”

Mydei sighs. He knows that’s true. Even if he doesn’t want to talk to them about it, giving them the music would be enough to let them know. And it’s the knowing that he’s scared of, not the conversation. The potential of them looking into his past, his deepest feelings, and thinking of him as weak because of it.

“Fine,” he concedes. “I’ll be right back.”

He goes to his bedroom, lugging out the case filled with his old music from under his bed. He brings it back to the living room, dropping it onto the carpet and sitting before it, legs crossed. “All my old music,” he explains, gesturing to it like it’s some sort of treasure chest. “Help yourselves.”

Cipher pounces on it almost instantly, digging through the case for whatever scores she thinks speak to her. Castorice crawls beside her, equally curious but much more toned down.

“Are you serious?” Hyacine asks. She hasn’t gotten up, but Mydei can tell she wants to. “You’re really trusting us with all of this?”

“Isn’t that what you wanted from me?” Mydei crosses his arms. “I can’t guarantee all of it is worth workshopping. But it’s a start. Right?”

“Mydei, is this a song about golden honeycakes?” Cipher asks, holding up a single sheet of paper. It’s crumpled, tossed to the bottom of the case, but Mydei knows exactly what she’s talking about regardless.

“Yeah,” he closes his eyes. The regret is starting to kick in. “I think I was high.”

“Dude, just get some honeycakes delivered,” Cipher tosses the draft to the side. “You don’t need to write a whole song about it.”

Mydei pulls his knees up to his chest and watches them as they sift through the papers, trying not to let his nerves get the best of him. The honeycakes song was one lighthearted example in an ocean of songs he never intended to see the light of day. The amount of songs in that case about Phainon alone is enough to make him hold his breath, knowing the man in question was just down the hall. Even his most generic romance songs, not written with any muse in mind, always circled back to him in the end.

“This one looks interesting,” Hyacine holds up two pieces of paper stapled together. “You rarely write songs this stripped back.”

“Oh, god,” Mydei reaches over to snatch the paper out of her hands, panic ringing in his ears. “Did you look at the lyrics?” He demands, eyes wide.

“Oh, uh, no?” Hyacine shrugs. “I’ve just been looking at the instrumentals to see if anything catches my eye.”

Mydei nods, squeezing his eyes shut. “Good, good,” he breathes. “You weren’t supposed to see that one.”

“Give it to me,” Cipher puts down whichever song she was looking at and reaches one hand out, trying to grab the papers from him.

“Cipher—I would actually rather die than let you read this,” Mydei’s voice shakes a little with alarm. “It’s not personal, it’s just…”

“Then what’s the problem?” Cipher cocks her head to the side, feigning innocence. She knows damn well what the song is about, and Mydei hates it. “C’mon, we’re all adults here—”

“Sit down,” Castorice urges, tugging at Cipher’s wrist. “There are so many other songs to look at. You don’t have to torment him over one.”

Cipher huffs in annoyance, but gives up for now anyways. Mydei makes a mental note to shred it later, just in case she decides to go through his garbage in her desperation. Because a song like that was not sticking around now that Cipher knew it existed.

Mydei crumbles the draft up, and stuffs it deep into his back pocket. Cipher wasn’t above attempting to pickpocket him, but now she would have to touch his ass to do it. He doesn’t think she wants it that badly, and if she did, that’s just sad.

“How about this?” Hyacine asks, having analyzed another selection during Mydei and Cipher’s bickering. “It’s in the early stages of development, but I think it looks promising.”

Mydei moves over to her, looking over her shoulder at the song she had picked. He vaguely remembers starting this one, and recently, too. It was just a couple days after he had watched Phainon’s performance of Rach 2— he was inspired by the orchestra and decided to try composing a rock song that included an orchestra.

He only got to writing a somewhat simple string part to play before the chorus, and had a little bit of an acoustic guitar part planned, as well. At the

bottom of the second page, he had written “trumpet solo?” as some sort of reminder, even though he never continued it after that.

There were no lyrics, and the base was just simple enough to give them a starting point. It was the perfect selection.

“Yeah,” he says. “Yeah, let’s start with this.”

By the time the sun starts to set, they have almost the entire instrumental part worked out and in the beginning stages of being transferred to the online site Mydei uses for demos. The trumpet solo, which Mydei still thought was a good idea, took some convincing on Cipher’s part, but she acquiesced eventually. Now, all he needs to do is find someone to record it for them, because fake trumpets added in production never sounded good.

They play what they have together before parting ways, Castorice left with the task of starting to add lyrics to it. There’s no specific direction they want to take the song. All they know is that, right now, it sounds good, which, based on their past experiences, was all the IPC really cared about.

Phainon comes out to say goodbye to them, eyeing the mess in the living room as he does. “What’s all this?” he asks, gesturing to the papers strewn across the floor. “I didn’t think your writing process was this horrific, Mydeimos.”

Mydei scoffs at how he speaks about the mess like it’s closer to a murder scene than what it actually is. “Most of that wasn’t my fault,” he answers. “I let them go through my old music. That was actually horrifying.”

“You did?” Phainon turns to him, eyes wide. “Can I?”

Mydei holds his gaze for much longer than necessary as the memories of what he’s written about come back to him in an instant. The songs about his grief and trauma were one thing, Phainon probably knew to expect those. The countless songs he had written about Phainon, both when they were

dating and when they weren’t, were a whole different beast he wasn’t quite ready to tackle. Not even by himself.

“No.”

“Aw, I really thought you were going to say yes for a second,” Phainon pouts, but it’s not enough for Mydei to relent. Nothing would be. “I heard you guys playing,” he adds, as Mydei turns his back to him.

“I thought you said you were going to put your headphones on?” Mydei moves to the kitchen, surveying the contents of his fridge as he debates what to make for dinner.

“Couldn’t,” Phainon says, from behind him. “My hands.”

“Oh.” Mydei pulls out a few vegetables and closes the fridge. “Next time, I’ll help you.”

“No need,” Phainon takes a seat at one of the barstools before the island, watching Mydei pull out a cutting board. “I liked listening to you. It sounds great so far.”

“You know I don’t like people listening to my works in progress,” Mydei huffs.

“Well, I doubt my headphones would drown out much of anything to begin with.” Mydei can feel Phainon’s eyes on his back as he washes the vegetables, one by one, in the sink. He tries not to think much of it, but can’t help the slight shiver that runs down his spine.

He continues the conversation before he can think for too long. “Are you still in touch with Caelus?”

“Yeah, of course. Why?”

“Could you get him to record something for me? I want an actual trumpet part, so it doesn’t sound fake.”

“You’re putting trumpet in your song?” Phainon sounds like he’s on the verge of laughing, but pulls himself back. “Sorry. Didn’t you say that was your least favorite instrument?”

Mydei shrugs. He might have said something like that in the past, but how Phainon remembers all these years later is beyond him. “It fits the song.”

“I can’t wait for this album,” Phainon says wistfully. Mydei dumps his handful of washed vegetables onto the island, right beside his cutting board. He unsheathes his best knife, one he had gotten shipped directly from Edo Star. “Your last EP—”

“I don’t want to talk about it,” Mydei cuts him off, chopping the stem off an heirloom tomato. “We didn’t write that record, we didn’t even produce it. I want to prove myself with this one.”

“I know you didn’t write it,” Phainon says. “I’m on album of the year. I gave your EP a sixty-eight.”

“A sixty-eight,” Mydei almost laughs, taking a break from cutting up his tomato to look at him. “That’s gotta be one of the highest user reviews it has.”

“The top one was the first to give the IPC that stupid nickname,” Phainon says matter-of-factly. “They didn’t like it. But you’re lucky they took it out on your label, and not you.”

“I guess that’s true.” Mydei resumes his chopping.

“It’s okay, Mydei. Only the best of us write bad albums.”

“I don’t think it’s bad,” Mydei shoves his chopped up tomato to the side, reaching for the next one. “And judging by your score, you didn’t think it was bad, either.”

“No,” Phainon admits. “It just wasn’t Bleed Gold.”

“What did you give Bleed Gold, then?”

“A ninety,” he responds immediately.

“Hm.” Mydei will accept that, he supposes—Bleed Gold wasn’t perfect in his eyes by any means, but he would have liked to think Phainon found it so. “What’s your favorite song?”

“Of yours?”

Mydei nods.

Phainon hangs his head, presumably in thought. Mydei knows it was probably a selfish question to ask, but he couldn’t help his curiosity. He doesn’t know what he expects—perhaps Don’t Cry, the only song that’s explicitly about him, but Phainon is too niche to consider Mydei’s most famous song his favorite.

“One you haven’t written yet, I guess,” Phainon murmurs. It took him long enough that Mydei finished chopping up all his vegetables, turning around to dump them in a pan.

“Huh,” Mydei turns up the heat, leaning against the stove to survey him properly. “So you don’t like any of my music, then?”

“You really have to stop twisting my words, Mydeimos,” Phainon scolds, shaking his head. “I didn’t say that. I simply mean that I think your music will only ever get better.”

“Right,” Mydei shakes his head. Phainon’s manipulation truly held no bounds. “I’m sure that’s exactly what you meant.”

“I would never lie to you, Mydei.”

“Oh, you wouldn’t? That’s a new one.” Mydei turns back to the pan, pouring in some vegetable stock he had retrieved from the fridge before covering the pan to let it simmer. “If you don’t have a favorite, do you have a least favorite?”

Phainon makes a noise close to choking. “I do,” he says quietly, once he’s recovered.

“Would you share?”

There’s undeniable pain present in Phainon’s eyes as he looks at Mydei, but he covers it up better than he did when they were students. “Don’t Cry,” he finally admits.

Mydei swallows. A whole conversation could pass between them as they just look at each other. But Mydei doesn’t ask the questions on the tip of his tongue, and Phainon doesn’t answer them, even though his feelings are so obvious.

Mydei turns, retrieving a pot from one of his cabinets and moving to the sink to fill it with water. “Understandable,” he finally says, breaking the silence with as lighthearted a tone as he could manage. “It’s too overplayed. I don’t like it anymore.”

“Yeah,” Phainon agrees. “It’s overplayed.”

Mydei knows that’s not why he dislikes it. He might not know what the real reason is, but it’s obviously much deeper than he’s letting on, so Mydei doesn’t pry.

He finishes filling his pot up with water, and carries it to the stove to boil. There’s leftover pesto cream sauce in his fridge, so he microwaves it and sets it aside as he waits for the water to boil.

“Tell me,” he says, when the silence starts to grow too awkward for him. “What have you been up to? Besides playing Rach 2 and accomplishing all your dreams.”

Phainon laughs, but it’s still a little strained. “Not all my dreams,” he says sheepishly. “I graduated, obviously, and then went back to Paperfold the next year for my master’s.”

Mydei knows this. He saw the post he made after he got his master’s: a shot of him walking across the stage, robes weighed down with all his cords. Mydei never thought all the extracurriculars he was in were going to pay off in the end, until he saw that photo.
