“Hysilens and I did a lot in between those years. She was still playing with her quartet, but we booked a lot of venues and small gigs playing for more intimate crowds. My Rach 2 performance started getting me followers on social media, so I started posting on there, too.”

Mydei knows this, as well. His following wasn’t something to laugh at—he had enough for brand deals, even though his videos were mostly educational—teaching his audience the most fascinating parts of music theory, as he put it, or little minute long videos of the pieces he was working on. Sometimes he would take requests and cover popular songs. Most of the time he played obscure classical music no one had ever heard of before.

“When I graduated, I was desperate for opportunity, because even though I was making a lot more than I could ever have expected, my income was not enough to maintain rent at my apartment in Okhema. I ended up signing with the orchestra I played Rach 2 with as an official member.”

This, Mydei didn’t know. He had never heard of the orchestra when he watched the performance, but he had seen little of Phainon’s performances over the last couple months.

“I never liked them, or the conductor, very much,” Phainon admits. “But they promised opportunity, and even though I was with them for a short time, they did bring me it. We performed a lot in Adlivun, and the pay was good enough for me to stick with it, even though there was no one I clicked with—seriously, Mydei, they were all insufferable. And then I found out how much they got funded in Adlivun, and how underpaid I was compared to literally everyone else, so I left. I think they replaced me in a week with some guy named Zephyro. Weird names they have over there.”

“How recently did you leave?” Mydei asks. He sprinkles some salt into the steaming water.

“Just last month,” Phainon answers. “I didn’t know if I wanted to leave, at first. They gave me enough money to live on, and I was fine with that, until Cyrene told me I didn’t deserve to be treated like that. I listened to her because of how much I didn’t like them.”

“How bad were they?” Mydei knows it takes a lot for Phainon to truly dislike someone. Once he does, there’s almost no changing his mind, but this hatred does not come easily to him.

“Cartoonishly evil,” Phainon says. “It was a weird group, Mydei. I can’t even believe they actually liked any of the music they played in the first place. But I’m free now, and I can’t even play to begin with, so it doesn’t matter anymore.”

Mydei dumps in the remnants of a box of pasta without measuring, hoping it’s enough for both him and Phainon’s big appetites. As he covers the pot, he can’t quite pull his thoughts away from the obvious: Phainon can’t play anymore. And even if the way he mentions it is casual, he knows this can’t be anything less than heartbreaking for him.

“You will heal,” Mydei turns around, making sure Phainon is looking at him as he says it. “And you will play again.”

Mydei can see Phainon’s jaw tense as he bites down on his tongue. He and Mydei were similar in few ways, but they were always one and the same when it came to the way they handled their grief. Phainon always pushed it to the side and pretended it didn’t exist. Not that the events didn’t happen, but that they didn’t hurt him as deeply as they did. It infuriated Mydei to no end, and he wonders only now if this is how Phainon felt about him, too.

“Thank you,” Phainon looks away. “But I know that, Mydei.”

He’s lying. Normally, Mydei might call him out on it. Today, he cuts him some slack.

Mydei takes the top off his pot as it starts to boil over, stirring through the noodles until the water calms down. He tastes one, and deciding they’re ready, pours them into a strainer over the sink.

Phainon doesn’t say anything as he finishes preparing the dinner. He carefully drains the broth from the vegetables, too, then adds the noodles to the pan and mixes in the sauce he had just heated up.

Mydei halves it, preparing two plates. He’s not used to cooking for two people, and even though it looks like too much food, he thinks the portions are more likely to be too little than too much.

He gives Phainon his with a spoon, before sliding his own across the island to the seat next to Phainon’s. “This looks incredible, Mydei,” Phainon says, carefully balancing his spoon between his thumb and pointer finger.

“Really? I think it looks like shit,” Mydei grumbles, retrieving two glasses from one of his cabinets. “I haven’t gone grocery shopping in a bit. This probably won’t even taste good.”

“Stop being modest. Everything you make tastes good.”

“You knew my cooking in college, Phainon.” He fills them up with filter water, then gets a straw to place into Phainon’s cup.

“Exactly. So you can only have improved, then.”

“Believe what you will,” Mydei says, passing Phainon his water, and then finally taking his seat beside him.

“Mmh,” Phainon mumbles, trying to talk with his mouth full. “I was right.” He swallows his food, then leans over to drink some water.

Mydei shakes his head, trying the food himself. It’s nothing special, but it’s far from his best work. “I wanted to ask,” he starts, swallowing. “How much do you know about Cipher and Aglaea’s relationship?”

Phainon sighs. “Not very much,” he admits. “Neither of them like to talk about it. All I know is that Cipher doesn’t really talk to her anymore, not for no reason, but the reason they haven’t spoken for so long is because both of them are too stubborn to reach out first.”

“I see,” Mydei looks down at his food, swirling it around with his fork. For the brief two weeks he had known Aglaea, he always felt like she disdained him, somehow. Cipher reassured him that that was just the way she was, but he couldn’t shake the feeling that she disapproved of the music they were

making to her very core. “Cipher doesn’t really talk to us about anything. I thought maybe things would be different with you.”

“If anyone actually knows her thoughts on the matter, it’s Cas,” Phainon says. “They’re best friends. Of course, that doesn’t guarantee anything. Cipher’s like a slimy fish.”

“I think she’d kill you if she heard you say that.”

“Good thing you’re not going to snitch on me. Right?”

“Don’t push your luck,” Mydei says. He turns back to his food.

“Your life, then,” Phainon presses. “I want to know what happened when you went back to Castrum Kremnos. You did, right? Go home?”

Mydei nods. He feels as though he’s lost his appetite for a moment, and puts his fork down. He doesn’t like talking about this. His mother. His grief. The way he had spiraled. He’s brought back to Hephaestion’s words time and time again, about how crying doesn’t suit a man like him. Grief doesn’t, either.

“It was hard,” he admits. Saying it without looking at Phainon makes it easier. Like he doesn’t have to face his pity. “I had the house to myself and too much money than I knew what to do with. I spent a month doing nothing. I didn’t leave. I ordered food to be delivered whenever I got hungry, which wasn’t often. I lost so much weight, it was humiliating.”

Mydei’s breath hitches when he feels Phainon’s injured hand press lightly against his back. He settles right over the middle of his spine, over the vertebrae that always aches under his touch. “Eventually, Krateros came by. He told me I needed to get off my ass and do something, so I got a job at a bakery. Slowly, I started going to the gym again. I reconnected with my old Kremnoan friends, and they knew my mother, so they had heard. But comfort was the last thing they offered, and honestly, the last thing I wanted.”

Phainon’s hand stays still on his back, grounding him. Mydei knows it must hurt him to lift his arm in such a way. Selfishly, though, he wants him to stay. “When Cipher and Castorice graduated, they reached out to me and I traveled to Okhema for two weeks, staying at Aglaea’s place with both of them. We recorded our first EP together, and released it without much thought. I went back home, and we had our record deal by the end of the summer. Moving to Penacony, and working with the two of them, and eventually Hyacine…” Mydei trails off, shaking his head. He doesn’t know how to articulate the sheer magnitude of his gratitude. Even if he didn’t like the music they were making then, it healed him anyway. He’s not sure how he would ever be able to repay them for something like that.

Phainon exhales sharply through his nose. Neither of them eat, letting the silence settle between them instead. “I’m really happy for you, Mydei,” Phainon finally says. “I’m happy you’re happy now.”

Mydei can’t think of a better word to describe the way he feels about how his life has ended up in this moment, but something else still lingers under the surface. A hole in his heart that he had never quite been able to fill. It had been there since he left Phainon, but even now, with Phainon right by his side, the emptiness stays.

Phainon is already awake when Mydei gets up the next morning. He sits in the living room, staring at the TV like he’s not actually watching whatever random channel he had turned it to. It’s set to a low enough volume that Mydei couldn’t hear it in his room, captions flying across the bottom of the screen instead.

“Good morning,” Mydei says from the doorway. Phainon flinches out of his thoughts, eyes wide as he turns to look at Mydei. His gaze lingers on Mydei’s torso for a beat too long, before flicking back up to his face. “How did you sleep?”

“Fine,” he says.

He’s lying. Mydei sighs and heads into the kitchen. “Do you want coffee?”

“Yes, please,” Phainon replies. Mydei can hear him struggle to get to his feet, then limp back over to the kitchen. “I tried to make some myself, but couldn’t figure out how your coffee machine worked.”

“It was out of coffee, dumbass,” Mydei laughs, pouring more beans into the top compartment. “Black?”

“Yes. Thank you.”

Mydei resists the urge to roll his eyes, and makes his coffee for him.

“You have more tattoos,” Phainon blurts, when Mydei hands him a mug of steaming black coffee. “When did you get them done?”

“A little over two years ago,” Mydei answers. He busies himself with his own coffee, trying to hide his growing embarrassment with his careless decision to not put a shirt on before he left his room.

Phainon hums. Mydei can feel his staring as he pours coffee creamer into his mug, and puts it back in the fridge. As soon as he turns around, Phainon’s eyes dart away, and he hides behind his coffee cup.

“You want breakfast?”

Phainon shakes his head. “I’m not hungry.”

Mydei knows that’s a lie, so he makes enough breakfast for two people, and pretends not to act surprised when Phainon inevitably steals his share.

He has to drive him to physical therapy at noon, so Phainon goes to take a shower first. Mydei helps him out of his splints and sling. His hands are red and swollen underneath and he tries not to wince when he sees it.

Phainon goes impossibly stiff underneath the shower water, as Mydei forces shampoo through his hair because his hands are too weak to do it himself. They don’t say a word. Phainon tries to get out of it multiple times, and insists he can do the rest alone, effectively kicking Mydei out.

Mydei stands outside the bathroom door for a couple seconds, listening to the running water. He knows why Phainon refuses his help, but that doesn’t mean he likes that he does.

He shakes his head, and leaves to get ready himself.

Ten minutes later, he’s knocking on the bathroom door. Phainon lets him in, though not without an obvious amount of frustration. Mydei helps him get dressed as Phainon once again grows stiff and eerily silent beneath his touch.

“You don’t have to—” Phainon tries, once he’s fully clothed and Mydei starts working on putting his splints back on again. “You don’t—”

“Yes, I do,” Mydei interrupts, fastening his left splint and putting his arm back through the sling. “There’s no one else here, is there?”

“I’m sorry,” Phainon whispers. “I was high off my ass when I mentioned you. If I was thinking even a little bit straight I wouldn’t have—”

“I’m glad you did,” Mydei says, finishing fastening the straps on his right splint. “Let’s go now. Alright?”

Phainon nods, and doesn’t push it. Mydei helps him into his shoes, then puts his own on, grabs his keys, and they head out of the apartment. Phainon is still limping a little, but won’t let Mydei touch him when he tries.

The drive there is silent, until they arrive and Phainon tells Mydei he can do the rest himself. So he drops him off, and Mydei drives to the grocery store instead.

His usual grocery store of choice is an organic private-label one which he’s found he is very rarely approached in, but it’s too much of a drive from the physical therapy office, so he settles for one closer.

The fame he had gotten after the Robin collab was not enough to stop him from being able to live his life, but getting recognized in public was much

more common now than it had ever been for him. Still, he does his grocery shopping mostly in peace, turning up the volume on his headphones and ignoring the obvious stares of other patrons.

Mydei arrives at the physical therapist five minutes early, and gets out of his car as he sees Phainon approach the front door. He opens the car door for him, and Phainon gets in wordlessly.

“How was it?” Mydei asks, after he climbs back into the driver’s side and shifts the gear out of park. “Any progress?”

Phainon shakes his head. He leans his head against the window, face gaunt as he stares at the road as they pull out of the parking lot. “It was fine,” he mumbles, a stark contrast from what his expression implies.

“Alright,” Mydei answers. He lets them sit in silence for the rest of the ride back.

Mydei carries the groceries up to his apartment, even after Phainon offers to help. He retreats into his room as soon as they get back, so Mydei is left putting his groceries away in silence.

The band comes over shortly after, though not for as long as they had the day before. Hyacine asks how physical therapy went, likely just as invested in Phainon’s health as Mydei was due to her medical background. Mydei doesn’t let her see him when she asks, thinking the last thing he probably wanted right now was to talk about something that was very obviously bothering him—and to someone he barely knew, no less.

Hyacine doesn’t seem to mind this decision, so they gather in the living room and get straight to work. Castorice presents the lyrics she had written the night before, and they start rehearsing it with lyrics this time. They spend much longer than Mydei would have expected working on backing vocals. Mydei had layered his vocals in the past to create a harmonizing effect, but decides this time that he wants the others to do them instead, so there are different voices present.

What he finds is that none of them are terrible singers by any means, and they all have very unique voices. Cipher has the deepest range, probably an alto or even a tenor if she tried. Her voice is the roughest, the most stereotypically “built” for rock besides Mydei. Castorice’s is similar to Jingliu’s, which doesn’t surprise him much in retrospect given how much of a High Cloud Quintet fan she was as a teenager. She has the most versatile range and the richest tone. Hyacine’s is the highest and breathiest. It’s clear she has the least practice with singing in the past, and Mydei thinks her voice could be a very interesting touch if she worked on her chest voice instead.

After he spends too much time giving singing lessons, Cipher brings forward a song she and Castorice wrote together a couple months ago. Mydei’s not sure what he’s expecting, but it’s not this: a song they called Cat Food about the Amphorean economy (or, at least, that’s how Mydei interprets it) coated in a heavy layer of sarcasm.

“It was mostly a joke,” Cipher explains. Mostly. Mydei, as he’s grown so used to, doesn’t press. “We thought the instrumentals could be a joke, too.”

“You want to write a bad song,” Mydei deadpans.

“No, we want to write a funny song.”

And that’s where they leave him, four pages of extremely messy sheet music in Mydei’s hands with the singular mission of writing some sort of piano part that Cipher would deem “funny”.

It’s not until he checks his phone after they’re gone, fully intending to find a recipe for dinner tonight, that he sees it: pictures of him from earlier in the day, going viral on social media.

He’s been spotted by paparazzi in public without his knowledge before, only to come across the candid photos later on, but they’re never quite this talked about online. Because if it were just him grocery shopping, there wouldn’t be much to say. But instead they got pictures of him outside of his car, holding the passenger side open while Phainon climbs in, of both him

and Phainon inside the car. He can feel the tension he felt earlier return tenfold through his screen.

He swallows as he scrolls through his feed, holding his breath for anything too bad. It’s not like Phainon wasn’t known in the public eye, either—there are people who know him, who approach him in public. He’s not the kind of celebrity that needs to worry about paparazzi, but he exists online. He’s not a secret.

While Mydei has talked about their past relationship before, but never in depth. As far as their respective fan bases are aware, they have very little knowledge about the other besides the fact that they exist. It’s not exactly bad that they were seen together, it just leaves Mydei with more questions to answer than he wants to.

He gets caught off guard when he sees his first post by a fan and not a paparazzi account: “i’m starting a rumor”, it reads, though Mydei isn’t entirely sure what that means. He thinks it reads like the account knew of both of them somehow, which he thinks is a rare crossover. He opens the comments to try to get some sort of an explanation, and doesn’t find anything helpful.

The post underneath that is a fan of Phainon’s, writing a heartfelt message about how they were happy to see Phainon was okay. The crash had become public knowledge in the last couple of weeks, though any confirmation about injuries or how he was doing hadn’t been released. Mydei smiles at the sight of someone who clearly cares a lot about Phainon, and scrolls past it. The next post is one which very obviously implies that they believe he and Phainon would make an attractive couple.

He exits social media immediately after this revelation, vowing not to open it again until this mess finally subsided as he returns to his recipes.

Phainon doesn’t say he minded being spotted together, and having the whole world know that they reconnected—whatever the nature of that may

be—but the next time Mydei picks him up from physical therapy, he gives the parking lot a thorough scan before getting into Mydei’s car.

August flies by, between band rehearsal and being Phainon’s personal chauffeur. He rarely asks to leave outside of doctor visits, but they catch an orchestra performance of Dvorak’s ninth symphony when Mydei sees a flyer about it. It’s one of the most famous symphonies in the world, as far as Mydei is aware, and he finds himself dragging Phainon with him when he refuses to go. He desperately needs to get out more.

Phainon ultimately ends up enjoying it more than Mydei did, but seeing him happy for the first time since he’d arrived was enough to put a smile on his face, too.

The band focuses on the two songs they have for a while. Mydei, with Phainon’s help, gets Caelus to send a recording of him playing the trumpet part Mydei had written, and they finish their first song of the new album, titled City of Thieves.

Cat Food takes slightly longer, even after all the hours Mydei pours into writing a suitable piano part for it. Phainon ended up being a lot of help in the end, once Mydei worked up the courage to ask him. Together, they wrote a part that was inspired by jazz, though it was much more random and much less relaxed than the jazz Mydei listened to. He added an acoustic guitar part as well, and they decided the rest of it could be done in the studio.

Their first meeting after finishing Cat Food, Castorice explains to Hyacine what she had told Mydei almost a year ago now.

“I’m telling you this because I wrote a song about it,” she finishes. The room had been silent the whole time. Even Cipher listened intently, and didn’t interrupt to say anything stupid. “I don’t just want you to make up ideas for what you think I wrote it about. I want you to know the truth.”

“Cassie,” Hyacine starts. She reaches out to grab one of her hands, and Castorice doesn’t pull back. Through Cipher’s help or not, she had gotten

better at accepting touch from other people recently. “You didn’t kill your sister, Cassie.”

“How can you say that?” Castorice whispers. “It was me. I got her sick, I know I did, because I realized I was sick afterwards. It must have been me.”

“Hospitals are careful about these things,” Hyacine explains gently. “If your sister was extremely immunocompromised, they wouldn’t have let a child attending school visit her without taking all the necessary precautions beforehand. Do you realize how many germs and sick children you’re exposed to every day in an elementary school?”

“That’s what…my mother tried to tell me, too.”

“I think you should have listened to her,” Hyacine shakes her head, moving closer to her on the couch. “Instead of carrying all this guilt with you for so many years.”

“Sorry,” Castorice mumbles. “I know you’re right.”

“Come here,” Hyacine says, pulling Castorice close to her chest. “This better be a good song, if you had to suffer for it for so many years.”

Castorice giggles, turning her face into Hyacine’s neck. “Thank you, Hyacine.”

Mydei glances at Cipher, who is staring at them with the most serious expression Mydei has ever seen on her face. She catches him staring, and it’s gone in an instant.

Mydei’s first read of the song she had titled Fever has him thinking about Hephaestion for the first time in years. Castorice has a way of writing in which her words tend to be very flowery, roundabout ways of getting her point across instead of saying her feelings outright. This, however, is the most honest song Mydei has ever seen her write.

Hephaestion died of an illness he never told Mydei about, one he never found out about until Hephaestion was breathing his last. He pleaded for

forgiveness and then asked Mydei not to cry for him, an impossible request.

Castorice knew exactly what Polyxia was going through. Mydei never did. Castorice spent years finding reasons to pin Polyxia’s death on, before eventually deciding that it must have been her. Mydei spent years in a state of confusion as to how he never realized something was wrong.

“This is beautiful, Cas,” he says, turning back to the first page and handing it off to Hyacine.

“You think so?” Castorice asks. “You like the music I wrote, too? It was my first time doing something like that, I didn’t really know what I was doing…”

“It’s good,” he nods. “We’ll look at it together. I don’t think we’d have to change much, though.” It was already clear that Castorice had spent years alone on this song, ever since they wrote their first EP and Mydei taught them basic music theory and how to read treble clef.

After Fever is finished, they spend the first few weeks of September going through Mydei’s old music again. They experiment with some songs that never really go anywhere, before Cipher pulls one out that he had almost forgotten about. It’s not the oldest one in the box, but it’s far from the newest—he had likely written it in college, when he had first come to Penacony.

“It’s about Kremnos,” he explains, when Cipher asks. “Kind of, anyway.”

The song was his first attempt at satire, something he eventually realized he wasn’t very good at, which led to him ultimately scrapping it. People in Penacony had a fixed view of Kremnoans, one that wasn’t very educated outside of ancient Amphorean myths no one really followed anymore. Their view of Okhemans was already misguided, but they still thought of Kremnoans as war-mongering brutes, even though Kremnos hadn’t been at war in centuries, and Penacony had.

He thought it was amusing, if not overwhelmingly frustrating, that people overseas still thought of them in this way. That was why he started the song.

He explains this to them now, and Cipher nods like she knows exactly what he’s talking about. This reaction is, somehow, a little relieving when she reminds him that sarcasm is one of her strong suits. She gets her hands on the lyrics and somehow manages to rewrite them exactly how Mydei wanted when he first started this song.

So they finish it together, titled Berserker. It takes a little over a week. The night they call it done, Mydei forces Phainon into a celebratory movie night after finishing four whole songs. He had to do a lot of forcing on him recently. Phainon spent most of his time in his room, coming out only for meals. Seeing him in such a state is the last thing Mydei wants, and he’s starting to wonder how long he can keep pretending to buy his excuses.

Just like old times, they argue over Gnaeus and Flame Reaver of the Deepest Dark, and eventually decide on both. This time, though, they start with Flame Reaver, and Phainon has fallen asleep on Mydei’s shoulder halfway through Gnaeus.

He mutes it as soon as he notices, turning the captions on so he can keep watching. Phainon hasn’t been getting very much sleep lately—that much is as glaringly obvious as the rest of the problems he pretends doesn’t exist, but just as with those, Mydei doesn’t bring it up. He’s not sure if this development is a result of his pain or insomnia, or both, but having him soundly asleep is not an opportunity Mydei is going to pass up on.

It’s here, with Phainon asleep on his shoulder, trying his hardest to remain as still as possible, that he gets an idea. A drill sergeant is yelling at his soldiers, barking questions that they respond to with a repetitive and deeply annoying holler of “aye, sir”. Mydei can practically hear them clear as day from how many times he’s watched this movie, even though the screen is muted, and he can imagine those lines perfectly as if they were included in Berserker.

He reaches for his phone as carefully as possible, and immediately texts the idea to the band’s group chat. Cipher is the only one still awake, and she gives him some stupid response about how she “doesn’t know anything about that nerd movie”. Mydei shakes his head, turns his phone off, and makes a mental note to include the excerpts during production anyway.

The band takes a short break from meeting every weekday near the end of September, forcing Phainon to spend more time with Mydei than he might have liked. Mydei sits down at the piano Friday morning, recovering an old piece he used to love in an attempt to lure Phainon out of his room. He clearly harbors some disdain for the instrument, but would still never pass up an opportunity to watch him play.

Sure enough, he can hear his footsteps coming down the hallway until he reaches the living room and makes himself comfortable on the couch. His hip is almost completely healed, no longer needing to limp. He doesn’t need the sling anymore, even though his collarbone still faces some issues. His hands were by far the worst injury, though today they are in lighter splints than they were a month ago.

Mydei plays through the rest of the song, pretending that Phainon’s presence wasn’t the whole reason he started to play it in the first place. Phainon pats his thigh lightly with one of his hands, in lieu of applause as he finishes. “Fantaisie Impromptu,” Phainon comments. “Good job. Show off.” He smiles as he says it, but some bitterness is there anyway.

Mydei spins in his seat until he’s facing Phainon directly. “You finally decide to keep me company,” he tries to keep it equally lighthearted, but much like Phainon, is unable to keep the bitterness out of his voice. “I finally have a roommate, and then I never see you. I’m getting lonely, Phainon.”

“Lonely,” Phainon scoffs. “His Highness Mydeimos Nikador of Castrum Kremnos, lonely. Whatever is he going to do?”

“Just as I kept my promise and never called you Deliverer, you vowed never to call me that.”

“That,” Phainon rolls his eyes, “is your real title, Mydeimos. The Deliverer is just some stupid roleplay.”

“My real title. So I’m a prince now.”

“Cipher calls you prince.”

“Cipher is an asshole,” Mydei stands up, getting even closer to him until he sits on the edge of the coffee table, and Phainon can’t run away. “Tell me why you’re avoiding me.”

Expectedly, Phainon doesn’t look at him as he answers. “I’m not avoiding you.”

Mydei bites down his debilitating irritation, taking a moment before he responds so he has time to calm himself. “When will you finally stop lying to me?”

This time, Phainon looks at him. “I’m not lying to you.”

“Stop it, Phainon,” Mydei snaps. “You know I can see right through you.”

Phainon’s jaw tenses. He exhales, frustrated, and turns away, attention stolen by Kokopo III as she runs down the hall and leaps into his lap. She had grown fond of him during his stay. Probably because he was less likely to get up than Mydei was. He places one of his scarred, broken hands on top of her back and Mydei’s own frustration almost dissipates as he sees the beginnings of tears in Phainon’s eyes.

“I have tried to be so attentive to you, Phainon,” Mydei continues. “I gave you time. I guess I thought that one day you’d finally be honest with me on your own, but I’m losing my patience. It’s a miracle I’ve kept it for this long.”

“I can’t—” Phainon starts, then shakes his head. “I can’t just—I’m not like you, Mydei. I don’t want you to think I’m weak.”

“Are you serious?” Mydei leans forward. “Weak? Phainon.”

“I know,” Phainon hangs his head. “I know, Mydei. Please don’t start.”

Mydei isn’t sure what he’s talking about, so he continues anyway. “You’re a lot of things, Phainon. Most of them infuriating, but I have…” he shakes his head in disbelief. “I would…never in my life consider you weak.”

Phainon doesn’t say anything to that. Mydei can see his chin quiver, his hand on Kokopo III’s back tense a little bit.

“Do you think I would judge you for reacting to an injury like this?” Mydei continues. “Phainon. Do you think I would like it if I had my tongue cut out, and I couldn’t sing anymore?”

“I don’t know!”

“You don’t know?”

“Obviously, yes,” Phainon bursts, distressed. “But that would never happen to you, would it? And this happened to me.”

“And I am trying to tell you that you have every right to react to that how you have been. But I don’t like being useless, Phainon. I’m supposed to be here to help you.”

“Do you really want me to be honest, Mydei?” Phainon finally turns his head to look at him, eyes alight with determination, or something else.

“Of course,” Mydei says, leaning back a little bit. He doesn’t show the raw excitement he feels. How that was everything he ever really wanted from Phainon.

“I think I’ve been enough of a burden on you,” Phainon’s voice is harsh, despite his words. “I live here, I don’t pay rent, I don’t pull my weight in housework. I don’t leave. I make you drive me to PT, to the doctor. I don’t think you need all my emotional baggage on top of everything I’m already making you deal with.”

“Phainon,” Mydei exhales, exasperated. “I’m happy you’re here,” he admits. “Even if you avoid me, and don’t come out for dinner until you

think I’m asleep. Even if you don’t tell me anything, and think pretending everything is fine is enough to fool me. I’m just happy I get to be your friend again.”

Phainon blinks rapidly, then lowers his steely gaze to set on Kokopo III. “My friend,” he mutters. “You want to be my friend.”

“Why wouldn’t I?” Mydei asks. “You might think yourself a bad roommate, but I don’t mind all those things, because it’s you, Phainon.”

“Mydei,” Phainon murmurs. “Please.”

“No,” Mydei continues. If Phainon isn’t going to burden Mydei with his emotional baggage by himself, then Mydei will just have to force it out of him. “I know that you spoke to my father.”

Surprisingly, Phainon doesn’t jump away from this accusation. “Not your father,” He says, voice growing even more bitter at the mention of him. “One of his sales representatives.”

“And what did they want from you?”

“A sponsorship.” The tears are gone from Phainon’s eyes. He glares daggers into Kokopo III’s head, gaze near murderous. “An advertisement. Five hundred grand.”

“Five hundred grand.”

“And half the revenue made from the ad.”

“Are you—”

“And then he offered to up it to seven hundred.”

Mydei feels like his head is about to explode. “Are you fucking serious?”

“I didn’t take it, Mydei.”

“Why not?!” Kokopo III scatters, claws scratching at the floor as she runs out the room. Phainon doesn’t seem to mind, though, meeting Mydei in kind.

“Because I hate your father, Mydei!” He bursts. “I fucking abhor that man like nothing else—”

“And yet you have no reason to!” Mydei shoots back. “A deal like that could have gotten you—”

“Yeah,” Phainon spits. “I know what it would have gotten me. And you know what the best part of all of this is?” He sits up in his seat, glaring not quite at Mydei but at the space between them. “I wouldn’t have crashed that goddamn car if I hadn’t been so goddamn angry.”

He gets up, storming down the hall and back into his room before Mydei can so much as call out for him, blinded by shock.

One thing Mydei knows for sure is that he doesn’t hate his father. Perhaps in the past, he had. When he was a child, maybe—when hatred was an easier emotion to feel towards someone than something this complicated. But the older he got, the more he understood just how complicated it actually was.

Phainon still finds hatred easier than facing his true emotions. Perhaps his hatred for Mydei’s father was a guise for something much deeper than he was ready to face. Whatever that might be, Mydei wouldn’t know.

But he does know one thing: if it was Eurypon who led to Phainon crashing his car, however indirect his involvement might have been, for that, Mydei hates him.

He’s pulled from his daze by his phone ringing. He stands, fishing it out from his back pocket, met with Aventurine’s contact name. Without thinking about why he might be calling, he picks up.

“Hello?”

“Hi, Mydei, how are you? Are you busy right now?”

Mydei’s brain lingers on how he should go about answering the first question before he processes the second, and realizes that he can ignore it altogether. “No,” he says, even though he feels like he’s lying.

“That’s great! Is the album going well?”

“Very, thank you. Is there anything you need?”

There’s a bit of commotion on Aventurine’s end of the line, before he answers. “How soon can you be at the office? I’m sorry this is so last minute.”

“Um—about ten minutes, probably. Why?” He doesn’t feel like he should leave right now, not after an argument, not after learning what he’s just learned. He would say he was busy were it any man other than the one who gave him his career.

“We have a company representative here to talk about future sponsorship opportunities,” Aventurine says. “It’s a piano manufacturer. I think it would be a great deal, after you recently came out playing piano for the Robin collab.”

“Aventurine,” Mydei says, voice rising in panic. “What company?”

“Kremnos Pianos. I’m sure you’re familiar, given your background.”

“Aventurine,” Mydei’s voice is the closest to pleading he’d even let it get without embarrassing himself. “Please deny it.”

“Deny it?” Mydei can hear the disbelief through the line. “This would be a fantastic opportunity, Mydei. I can’t do that so easily.”

Mydei’s grip on his phone is so tight he can feel it shaking, unsure of how to respond in a way that maintains professionalism. What are the odds that this happens now?

“Will you come then, Mydei? We can talk about this in person.”

Mydei moves the phone away from his ear to take a deep breath. “Okay,” he says back into the receiver, though his voice still shakes a little bit. “I’ll be there soon.”

Mydei does not crash his car on the drive to the IPC office, though it’s a near thing. He parks in his usual spot, which is surprisingly empty this late into the day, scans his badge to enter through the back door, and makes his way to the elevator. Aventurine’s office is on the seventh floor, and by the time Mydei stands outside his door his heart is throbbing so hard he can feel it through his whole body.

He knocks. Aventurine calls for him to enter, and when he does, he can practically feel his heart fall through the floor.

“Mydeimos!” The man standing in front of Aventurine’s desk lights up at the sight of him, and Mydei recoils like he’s been shot. “My boy.”

It’s Eurypon Nikador, in the flesh. To think he actually flew all the way to Penacony for this makes Mydei’s stomach twist.

Age has done him no favors. When Mydei was a kid, his looks and all the ways they differed from his mother’s led him to believe that he must have simply looked a lot more like his father. He knows that’s not entirely true now, but can only hope he doesn’t age the way Eurypon has.

“Father,” Mydei glowers. Eurypon tries to pat him on the shoulder, and he steps away, forcing him to drop his hand awkwardly.

“Ah,” Aventurine says from his desk, just as awkwardly. “It seems he needs no introduction. I did think there was a little bit of a resemblance.”

Mydei wants to throw up. That’s the worst thing he’s ever heard.

“Long time no see, Mydeimos. I’m glad to see you’ve grown into a real man. You look a far cry from the frail little kid you used to be.”

Mydei swallows. He doesn’t pull his eyes away from him, ensuring Eurypon knows the depth of his distaste.

Aventurine clears his throat. “Let’s talk business, shall we, gentlemen?”

“I want nothing from him.” Mydei says this more to Aventurine, though his eyes stay glued on Eurypon. “I don’t care how much it is. I doubt he even has the money upfront, given that he’s here now.”

Mydei expects anger from Eurypon at this, and is even prepared to dodge whatever punches he might throw at him. To his surprise, though, he gets none of that. “You are not incorrect, Mydeimos. Sales have been dropping recently. A famous piano maestro publicly denounced my company a few months back…Strife knows why.”

“Praying to Strife won’t give you a more peaceful death than you deserve,” Mydei sneers. “Why don’t you go back to stealing money like you did ten years ago?”

“Didn’t Gorgo ever teach you not to speak to your elders that way?” Eurypon answers. “Now that I’m your legal guardian, maybe it’s time we revisit some basic manners.”

Mydei steps closer to him so they’re eye-to-eye. He takes some pride in the fact that today, he has grown to be a couple inches taller than him. “How dare you talk about her?” he starts. “The last thing she ever would have wanted is for anything of hers to fall into your hands. She hated you until the day she died.”

“You know that’s not true, Mydeimos.”

Aventurine clears his throat again, and Mydei bites the inside of his cheek before he chooses to ignore Aventurine and respond to Eurypon anyway. “Business, gentlemen,” he reminds them. “Mydei, Mr. Nikador requested that you feature in an advertisement and play only Kremnos pianos until your partnership ends. As a result, you would receive a 15% cut of all revenue Kremnos Pianos receives for the rest of the partnership, and a 50%

cut of all revenue made directly from the advertisement you are featured in.”

Mydei clenches his jaw. He’s hardly listening to Aventurine as he speaks, just barely processing the amount of money he would probably make by accepting this. He knows it’s a lot. Of course it is—Eurypon needs it to be convincing.

“We think this would be extremely beneficial in promoting your new album to a wider audience. Fans of classical music would be introduced to you and invested because of your background in it. And your endorsement of Eurypon’s company would help Kremnos Pianos sales increase greatly, which only means you would be making even more money from the deal.”

Mydei stares at him. “I can’t accept this, Aventurine,” he says. “I don’t care about the benefits. I just can’t.”

To his surprise, Aventurine actually nods. He moves to say something else, too, but Eurypon beats him to it.

“Refusing this deal, Mydeimos…” he starts, shaking his head. “Would be… unwise.”

“Are you threatening me, Father?” Mydei demands. “Is that what you did to Phainon, too? Because I know he would never have said yes.”

Eurypon raises an eyebrow. “So you know him.”

“Phainon hates you,” Mydei continues. “You might not remember that night, but I do. All of us do.”

“I was trying to protect you.”

“You were trying to protect yourself!” Mydei bursts, incredulous. That was the best explanation Gorgo could ever come up with as to how her husband, who she had once loved deeply, had lost himself so greatly. He was a prideful man. Your talent challenged that, Mydeimos. He liked to remember those words before every performance. Let it challenge him.

Eurypon takes a deep breath, before turning all the way to face Mydei. Aventurine tries to cut in again, but neither of them are listening to him anymore.

“Is that why you keep Mr. Khaslana around? To protect you?”

“I don’t need anyone to protect me,” Mydei sneers. Even the idea of it is enough to make him squirm. “Least of all you.”

“You think just because you’re tall and fit, you’re any more of a man than you were fifteen years ago?” Eurypon demands. “I still remember the way you cried when I took you hunting, Mydeimos. Your heart is soft, no matter how hard you try to hide it.”

Mydei bites his tongue so hard he tastes blood. He clenches his hands into tight fists, resisting the urge to lash out. The ringing in his ears is so loud he can barely hear his surroundings anymore.

“You want to hit me.” Eurypon urges, leaning in even closer. Mydei can smell cigarettes and alcohol on him. He didn’t even have the decency to show up here sober. “Do it, Mydeimos. Hurt me, I dare you. Prove me wrong.”

Mydei swallows. He digs his nails into his palms and calms his breathing, until he’s at a place where he no longer thinks he would genuinely give in to Eurypon’s relentless instigation.

Mydei doesn’t notice that Aventurine has stood up until he’s between them. “I have to ask you to leave, Mr. Nikador,” he’s saying. “I can escort you out, if you would like.”

“This isn’t over,” Eurypon shouts at Mydei, over Aventurine’s shoulder. Mydei doesn’t say anything. He watches Aventurine lead him to the door, and then he’s alone.

Mydei takes a deep breath, running a hand through his hair. He sits down in one of the chairs before Aventurine’s desk, trying to calm down. He needs

to apologize. He hadn’t been that close to losing his cool since he was a hormonal teenager who hated the world.

Aventurine comes back in soon, sitting at his desk. He doesn’t say anything for a bit, until Mydei lifts his head to look at him. “I’m sorry,” Mydei starts. “You shouldn’t have seen that.”

“No, I’m sorry,” Aventurine smiles apologetically. “I shouldn’t have made you speak to him when you clearly didn’t want to.”

“I didn’t think it would be him,” Mydei explains. “He’s too lazy to actually do things himself.”

“Regardless, some of the things he said were horrible,” Aventurine offers. “I couldn’t stand for that. He has no place here.”

“No,” Mydei says. “Thank you.”

“If you want to talk about it—”

“I don’t,” Mydei says immediately. “I’ll be fine.”

Aventurine nods. “Well, then, there was one more quick thing I wanted to mention.” He opens his laptop, navigating somewhere before turning the screen around to show the paparazzi photos of him and Phainon. “Phainon Khaslana,” he starts. “These photos were taken a while ago, but when you mentioned him, I remembered.”

“Yes,” Mydei says. “He was in the area and got in a car crash a few months ago. He’s staying at my place now, and I’m helping him recover from his injuries.”

Aventurine nods again, turning the screen back towards him. “That’s all fine, I just thought I’d let you know that these images have caused some dating rumors to circulate online.”

Mydei swallows. “I know,” he starts. “I don’t really care. They can think what they want.”

“Very well,” Aventurine says. “Then you’re free to go, Mydei.”

Mydei nods. “Thank you.” He gets up from his seat, making his way over to the door before Aventurine stops him abruptly.

“Just to clarify,” he says, and Mydei turns to face him. “Your father. If he really does try something like this again—”

“I don’t want to see him ever again.”

“Then you won’t.”

Mydei thanks him again, and leaves. He drives back to his apartment in silence. There’s already a new bass riff at the back of his mind that he can’t wait to get his hands on.

He sits in his living room, spare bass in hand, and attempts to play exactly what he had heard earlier. It would undoubtedly sound better if Cipher were playing it, but she’s not here. He pulls out his electric guitar next, much more accustomed to six strings than four. Attempting to play the riff on guitar goes much smoother than on bass, and even though it doesn’t sound perfect to what he’s envisioned, it’s enough to allow his imagination to thrive.

Phainon pads into the living room at the sound of him working on something. “Where did you go?” he asks. “I’m sorry I yelled at you, Mydei. I was upset and wasn’t thinking, and I don’t want to fight anymore.”

Mydei puts his guitar down. Some things about him were drastically different from college, but this had remained constant—Phainon always seemed to apologize first, mere hours after they would fight. He never seemed to want to argue until Mydei forced it out of him. “Me too,” he says. “I just…” he takes a deep breath, pressing the heel of his palm into his forehead. “I went to the office,” he starts. “My father tried to get me on a sponsorship after what you said had sales dropping.”

Phainon’s eyes widen. He looks horrified. “What…?” he closes his mouth, then opens it again. “Was he there?”

Mydei nods.

“Oh my god.” Phainon moves forward, slowly lowering himself to sit on the floor, facing the spot Mydei sits with his legs crossed. “You just spoke to your father.”

Mydei nods.

“And?” Phainon whispers. “How did it go?”

Mydei swallows, looks down, and shakes his head. “I almost lashed out,” he admits. “It’s been a while since anyone has made me that angry.”

“You should’ve,” Phainon’s eyes flash as he says it. “Bastard deserves to get the shit kicked out of him.”

“No, he doesn’t,” Mydei insists. “It wouldn’t have made me any better than him. Would it?”

Phainon doesn’t say anything to that. Mydei picks his guitar back up, strumming a quiet cord that plays through the nearby amplifier. “I’m never going to see him again,” he continues. “Aventurine. My manager. He promised me I wouldn’t have to.”

“So you didn’t take the deal.”

“Of course not,” Mydei breathes. “I couldn’t. I would never accept something like that.”

Phainon’s jaw hardens. “Then you should be able to understand why I rejected it, too.”

“No, Phainon, I don’t,” Mydei says. “You have no ties to him. That deal could have changed your life.”

“No ties to him?!” Phainon demands, incredulous. “I have you, Mydei.”

“I don’t need you to hate him for me,” Mydei shoots back. “I don’t even hate him.”

“Just—” Phainon sighs, his head falling back onto the couch cushion. “I don’t want to argue, Mydei. I really don’t.”

“Fine,” Mydei says. He looks down at his guitar, positioning his fingers to match the riff he had just been working on. “Make yourself useful and help me with this arrangement, then.”

They call the song Wrath of Man, and Mydei writes the lyrics last, once he’s calmed down enough. He thinks they still come across as angry, even though the emotion he was trying to emulate wasn’t anger, but something more complex than that.

Phainon is helpless with rock music, but he sits on the couch making little comments here and there when he has something to say, and Mydei is glad that he’s at least not hiding in his room anymore.

After the break, Mydei gives each member a copy of their part and they play through it together. It’s almost perfect on the first playthrough, and they add it to the working list of songs on the whiteboard. Cipher especially likes it, but Mydei thinks that’s just because her part is so prominent.

Hyacine reads them a poem she had written during their break on the same day. Inspired by everyone pitching their own songs, she asked Castorice for help writing poetry, since she wasn’t the best at it.

Mydei wasn’t expecting her poem to sound so bleak.

Throw it all away Let’s lose ourselves There’s no one left to take the blame And it’s a shame we’re all dying Do you think you deserve our freedom?

How could you send us so far away from home? When you know that this is wrong I would still lay down my life for you

Do you think you deserve your freedom? No, I don’t think you do

There’s no justice in the world And there never was.

“It’s about a couple things,” she explains. “My ancestors were warriors like yours, Mydei. The nation of Skyfolk was just as destructive as Castrum Kremnos in its prime.”

Mydei swallows. He had interpreted her poem in the same way. Thoughts of his father plague him recently like they rarely had in the past. What would he think if he heard Mydei singing an anti-war song? The thought just makes him want to include it on the album even more.

“Just like you, Mydei, I hate war,” she says. “I went to med school because I wanted to bring people the happiness everyone deserves. Maybe it would have been different in Okhema, but the industry in Penacony was so… unfair,” she admits. “I had a summer internship at a hospital in a low income area, and the amount of patients we were forced to turn away because they couldn’t afford their medical bills, and didn’t have insurance, I just…I couldn’t do it.”

Mydei looks down at his hands. He’s never been poor. He doesn’t know what it’s like to be denied something you need. He doesn’t even know that much about how Penacony differs politically from Okhema, but he thinks it’s much more unjust, based on what he’s heard.

“It made me lose all the hope in humanity that I used to have,” Hyacine continues. “But music changed that. Guitar had been a hobby of mine since I was very young, but it wasn’t until the IPC scouted me that I realized I could actually do something with it. And seeing people come together because of the music that we made is better than anything I could have asked for.”

Turning Hyacine’s poem into a song—now titled Bleeding Out—becomes more of an exercise on singing and harmonies. Mydei is the main voice, but they layer everyone behind him, like a choir. The instrumentals are fairly stripped back, just guitar and a little bit of drums. Cipher says she could add upright bass in the final version, but for now they use her electric bass.

The song turns out to only be a little over a minute long, so they decide to keep it as an interlude somewhere in the middle of the album.

With that, they’ve written six songs, which is about half of the length they’re intending the album to be. Cipher says thirteen, Castorice says twelve. Mydei thinks they should just write until they have nothing more to say. But if that were the case, they might have nothing to write about in the future, and just one album that’s forty songs long, so he’s more on Cipher’s side.

Even though Phainon had been improving ever since their conversation last week, he’s still silent as Mydei drives him to physical therapy on Wednesday. With his hands getting better, their appointments have gone down from three times a week to twice a week. Phainon has been able to do more, and needs Mydei’s help with simple tasks less. The pain has gone down too, Mydei thinks, but his insomnia remains. Mydei doesn’t know what he could possibly do to remedy that.

“Hey,” Mydei says, as Phainon climbs into the passenger seat. He doesn’t look at Mydei as he enters, dropping his bag into the space between his legs and beginning to fumble with his seatbelt. “How was it?” Mydei continues, reaching over the console to help him buckle himself in.

Phainon presses the back of his head firmly to the headrest, clearly frustrated as he allows Mydei to help him. “It was fine,” he finally says. His voice is hollow, betraying none of what he truly feels.

“Yeah?” Mydei clicks his seatbelt into place and unpauses his music. It blares through the speakers, alarming them both, and Mydei rushes to turn it down almost all the way. “Sorry,” he mutters, as he shifts the gear into reverse.

The quiet music does little to ease the awkward silence between them as he pulls out of the parking lot. Mydei taps the beat of the drums against his steering wheel and it’s louder than the actual music. He stops at a red light, and looks over at Phainon beside him. He stares into space, unaware Mydei is even looking at him. His lips are pressed into a tight, thin line. He looks like he’s being driven to his own funeral.

“Phainon,” Mydei starts, and he flinches out of his trance. “What did she say?”

Phainon swallows hard. Mydei observes it in the bob of his throat. “Nothing,” he answers. Just as expected.

The light turns green. Mydei presses on the gas, making a left turn down the road his apartment is on. “Didn’t we decide you were going to start being honest—”

“It was fine, Mydei,” Phainon doesn’t snap, but it’s a near thing. “Okay? I said I was fine.”

“Alright.” Mydei pulls into the parking garage. They’re silent as he searches for a spot, finally finding one on the third floor. They remain silent as they both step out, and he locks the car, and they walk to the elevator. Phainon trails behind him like a storm cloud all the way to his apartment building, and all the way to his door.

He helps Phainon out of his coat, and bends to untie his shoes. Phainon gives a frustrated sigh above him as he does. Mydei understands. He doesn’t say anything.

When Mydei rises to his feet, Phainon’s shoes set neatly under the rack, he meets Phainon’s eyes and sees that his are wet with unshed tears. “Phainon,” he murmurs, concern softening his voice. He lifts one of his hands to set it on Phainon’s shoulder before he can run away. “Evidently, you’re not fine.” Phainon doesn’t cry often, and Mydei hates it every time he does.

He hangs his head, messy bangs obscuring his face, as if that would make Mydei forget he had just seen the tears in his eyes. “I wish I had just died in that crash,” he mumbles.

“What?” Mydei whispers, setting his other hand on his free shoulder, too. “Phainon—”

“I don’t have anything to live for anymore, Mydei,” Phainon laments, lifting his face and bringing their eyes to meet. “Nothing.”

“Phainon.” Mydei moves his right palm to press against Phainon’s sun tattoo, his fingers light as they brush against the back of his neck. “What are you talking about?”

“She said—” Phainon starts, then stops, sniffling, before trying again. “I finally told her I played piano.”

“Oh,” Mydei murmurs. Dread settles deep in his gut. He waits for Phainon to elaborate, and finds he doesn’t want to know what she said in response.

Phainon presses his forehead into Mydei’s shoulder. His voice is muffled as he continues. “She said it’s unlikely I will ever be at the level I was at. Ever again.”

Mydei doesn’t say anything. Comfort has never been something he was all too good at offering. He thinks it must be a Kremnoan thing, because his mother was the same. She would always hold him wordlessly when he was upset, and that was enough.

He does the same now, wrapping his arms around Phainon’s back and holding him upright as he puts all his weight onto Mydei’s shoulder. He cries silently, even as sobs wrack his body violently. “I’m sorry,” he finally whispers, voice nasally and wet. “I shouldn’t have put all this on you.”

“Do you think I would have agreed if I didn’t want to?” Mydei asks, into the crown of his head. “This isn’t a burden on me, Phainon. I’m glad I was here for you.”

Phainon sniffs, and lifts his head. His eyes are bloodshot, cheeks stained with tear tracks. “Mydei, this is…” he shakes his head, and wipes his nose with his sleeve. “This is almost the biggest loss of my life.”

Mydei swallows. He resumes his rubbing at Phainon’s upper back, wiping away the tears with his other hand that Phainon couldn’t get himself. There are lots of things Phainon has lost. His parents. His hometown. His childhood dog. He carried no small amount of grief on his shoulders everyday, taking each loss honorably. And still, today he cries. “Almost?” The word catches as it leaves Mydei’s throat. He doesn’t know why he asks. It’s a question he can safely answer by himself, and yet he still wants to hear Phainon’s answer.

Phainon doesn’t say anything, looking at him through the silence that falls between them. His chin quivers. And then he falls forward again, resting all of his weight atop Mydei’s shoulder.

He never elaborates. Mydei holds him anyway.
