@eeeeeeeejjjj • 1m ago Who’s Phainon Khaslana?

~~~

November 3869. Seven months before the release of Oracle.

Mydei wakes up with a sore throat and a splitting headache. He opens his eyes to the unbearable sunlight filtering in through his windows, squinting as he sits up.

He’s in his room. At home. He has no memory of getting here, or what happened last night. All he remembers is all of the drinks he had—and Phainon. He was dancing with someone else. Which is fine. He’s perfectly welcome to dance with whomever he likes.

Mydei feels sick. He doesn’t know what, exactly, causes this nausea for him, but he stumbles out of bed and runs to the bathroom to empty his guts out into the toilet.

He doesn’t know how long he’s throwing up, but he feels warm hands on his neck, pushing his hair out of his face to the best of his ability. His hands are too stiff, and a few strands of hair still fall out of his grasp. But Mydei’s stomach flutters at the gesture alone. “Good morning, Mydei,” Phainon says. “Are you feeling okay?”

Mydei groans, resting his hands on his thighs. He’s not confident he’s done. “No,” he grumbles.

Phainon laughs lightly. “Yeah, you had a rough night,” he says, pressing the palm of one of his hands to Mydei’s forehead. Mydei can feel his scars, rough against his sweating skin. He needs to shower.

“What happened?” Mydei reaches for the toilet paper, rolling out a few sheets of it and using it to wipe his mouth clean.

“Um,” Phainon sounds sheepish, letting go of Mydei’s hair completely and sitting down fully beside him. “We found you in the bathroom,” he explains. “Hyacine told us to put you on your side and give you water. Serval came in, saying she was looking for you, and that you had done some shots together. Do you know how much you drank?”

Mydei closes his eyes, flushing the toilet. He thinks he feels a little bit better now. “I think so,” he says. “It wasn’t that much.”

Phainon sighs. “You know you’re a lightweight.”

“Yes.”

“I’ve never seen Hyacine so upset. Didn’t think she had it in her. She thought Serval was pressuring you, or something.”

“No. I’m sorry.”

“Tell that to Hyacine,” Phainon huffs. “I think she lost years off her life ensuring you got home safe.”

“Fuck,” Mydei groans. He closes the toilet seat so he can lean on it, elbows crossed in front of him. He knows it’s gross. He’ll shower later. “This is why I don’t drink.”

“Yes, maybe you should take a break for a little while.” Phainon puts a hand on his back. Mydei’s throat tightens at the comfort it still seems to give him. Comfort Phainon knew he was offering. “By the way, how has your spine been recently?”

“My spine?” Mydei squints as he turns to him, resting his cheek on his arms. “Oh, yeah.” It had been so long since the last time he’d felt the pain in his vertebrae, that he had forgotten all about it. “Good,” he says. “It hasn’t hurt since, like…July. I think.” He swallows, as the irony of that statement is not lost on him. But if Phainon doesn’t notice the correlation, he has no reason to bring it up.

“Does your throat hurt?” Phainon asks next, tilting his head to the side. “Your voice sounds rougher than usual.”

“Yeah,” Mydei says. “I need water.”

Phainon nods, getting to his feet in an instant. Mydei watches him leave, staring at his back as he heads down the hallway and disappears into the kitchen.

Whatever he felt for him wasn’t platonic, he knew that now. But he also knew that on Phainon’s end, it was. That much was clear as day.

He puts his head back down. He’s starting to feel sick again.

Phainon comes back moments later, before Mydei has managed to calm his stomach back down. There’s a big glass of water he’s holding with both his hands, carefully handing it to Mydei before sitting beside him again. “Try to finish it, yeah?”

Mydei nods, taking it from him. He downs half of it in one gulp. It makes his throat feel slightly better, but he still feels like he could throw up any second. There’s a strong possibility that it’s Phainon’s presence alone causing him to feel this way.

“Do you think you could eat something?”

Mydei’s stomach rumbles. “Yeah, but if you make me a salad, I’ll kill you,” he says, before drinking the rest of the glass.

Phainon is as good-natured as always, and laughs. “Of course not, Mydei. And I won’t burn down your kitchen, either.”

“You better not,” Mydei growls, pulling himself up to his feet. “I need to shower.”

Phainon nods, closing the bathroom door behind him as he leaves. Mydei drinks another half glass of tap water as he waits for the shower to heat up, staring at himself in the mirror. He looks rough. Most of the makeup on his face has been washed off, though some of it remains in the form of dark, running eyeliner under his eyes. His hair is a mess, but thankfully someone —probably Phainon—had changed him out of his costume.

He’s shirtless, and at the sight of faint hickeys on his neck, he feels his blood run cold.

He has no memory of receiving those. No memory of whoever it was who gave them to him, but he knows it can’t possibly be Phainon, or he would have mentioned something by now. If he had gotten to that point with Phainon, he would have confessed his feelings under the influence. Things would have been different this morning. Mydei knows how his own body reacts to alcohol well enough by now.

He doesn’t know what he said to whoever gave him these. He doesn’t know what else they did, but he hopes it’s not what he thinks it is, given the ache in his throat.

His thoughts continue into the shower. Phainon hadn’t said anyone was with him when they found him, which implies he hadn’t seen. But the hickeys on his neck were so obvious, with him shirtless like this, that he had to have known by now.

The worst part is that he doesn’t seem upset. If Mydei had hooked up with someone else, and Phainon reciprocated his feelings, he wouldn’t have acted like this. He would have distanced himself, moped around and flashed fake smiles when Mydei asked. He wouldn’t have been this caring and gentle, even if he knew he had to take care of Mydei as per Hyacine’s instructions.

Mydei’s eyes burn, and he can’t tell if he’s crying or got shampoo in his eye. He hopes it’s the latter. He can’t deal with something like this right

now, on top of everything else he’s supposed to do.

Or, he can. He freezes as the realization comes to him that something like rejection this intense would be the perfect thing to write a song about. Or multiple. Or a thousand. However many it takes until he’s finally over him, and for good this time. He’s determined for it to be “for good” this time.

He leaves the bathroom in a towel, having forgotten clothes in his bedroom. He picks out jeans and a t-shirt, before searching for his phone. It’s plugged in on the floor, and Mydei turns it on to find that it’s almost two in the afternoon.

He has missed text messages from nearly everyone he had seen at that party: Castorice, Serval, Cipher, Caelus, and most notably, Hyacine. Despite Phainon’s warnings, her messages are the ones that sound the least concerned. She has written a couple paragraphs to him that are almost clinical in how they read, with detailed instructions of what to do to feel better, before finally reprimanding him and telling him he was very stupid. She then requests that he text her when he wakes up, so he does. Then he takes some time replying to everyone else as well, before leaving his phone where it is and returning to the bathroom.

When he emerges, Phainon has cooked him breakfast, despite the time of day—two eggs, sausage links, and oatmeal with bananas and honey. He has another large glass of water set out, as well as a smaller one filled with pomegranate juice.

Mydei stares at the meal before him. Phainon rarely cooked for him in college, given that neither of them had access to a kitchen, but Phainon always called his own cooking “mediocre”. Either he was lying about his skill level, or he had greatly improved in their years apart.

Regardless, it’s such a loving gesture. Mydei would give anything for that to be the intent behind it, too.

“Do you have to go anywhere today?” Phainon asks. He’s wearing Mydei’s apron that often hangs in his kitchen, unused.

Mydei feels near to tears. “No,” he says, softly. “Thank you for breakfast, Phainon. It looks amazing.”

Phainon beams at that, hands reaching behind him to gingerly untie the apron. He hangs it back up on its peg near the fridge and turns to the sink, beginning to do the dishes.

“Phainon, was I…” he swallows, halfway through cutting up his eggs. “With anyone…last night?”

The pan makes a loud clanging noise as Phainon drops it into the sink, pulling his hands away so as not to injure them further. He curses, grabbing a nearby kitchen towel to dry the counter. Mydei would offer to clean the kitchen for him, but that would only upset him. He’s found that Phainon is much more amicable when Mydei mentions his injury as rarely as possible.

“Sorry,” he mumbles, and Mydei can just barely see him blushing, unable to look at him directly.

Well, that was as good an answer as any. Mydei bites his lip, willing his heartrate to slow. It wasn’t productive to dwell on someone who didn’t like him back—but dwelling seemed to be all he was able to do when it came to Phainon.

“Briefly,” he admits. “I don’t know who he was. I don’t know what you two did, um, but you were fully clothed when we found you.”

Mydei looks back down at his plate. “Right.” He supposes it’s enough reassurance to know that his dignity remains somewhat intact. He resumes cutting up his eggs, then takes a bite of one along with some sausage. He bets it would taste incredible if he was in the right headspace.

“How do you feel?” Phainon asks. He clears his throat before he continues. “About him.”

“Indifferent, I suppose,” Mydei says breezily, though indifference is the last thing he feels right now. “I don’t know the guy.”

“He took advantage of you.” Phainon says firmly, nearly cutting Mydei off. He says it like he had wanted to say it all day. “He’s a dick.”

“Hm,” Mydei looks down at his food. So the only reservation Phainon had about the whole thing was about consent. Right.

“I’m serious, Mydei,” Phainon says, turning around to look at him. “You could barely stand when we found you.”

“So?”

“So?!”

“You don’t know what happened.” Mydei stabs one of the sausages so hard that his fork clangs against the plate. All the food tastes like rubber now. Mydei doesn’t know if he’s more annoyed about that, or Phainon’s bullshit this morning.

“I know enough,” Phainon says. His voice is tight. He’s been scrubbing at one spot in the frying pan for what feels like minutes now.

“No, you don’t. You weren’t there.” Mydei puts his fork down. Now he’s lost his appetite altogether.

Phainon drops the pan into the sink, uncaring as the sound of it rings out around them. He shuts the water off with more aggression than was ever necessary, turning around to look at Mydei. “So, what, you wanted it, then?”

Mydei huffs under his breath. “Of course I did. So what?”

His gaze hardens, and Mydei can see it from all the way across the kitchen. That upsets Phainon. Mydei can’t possibly fathom why.

“It was a one night stand, Phainon,” Mydei continues. “You seem awfully preoccupied with a stranger for someone who has no reason to care.” He regrets saying it immediately.

“What the hell is that supposed to mean?” Phainon’s brow is furrowed now. Mydei hates that he always seems to be most attracted to Phainon when he’s angry. Damn him—to think he’s feeling this now, of all times.

“Nothing.” Mydei looks away. Back down at his plate, where he picks up his fork again so he can pretend to pick at the food.

“Don’t lie to me, Mydei,” Phainon’s tone might be near pleading if it wasn’t already so rough with anger. “You’re acting weird. It’s not nothing.”

“You’re the one acting weird.”

“Because I’m upset!” Phainon bursts. His movements are jerky, like he doesn’t know where to put his hands. “Some asshole drags you into a bathroom to go fuck when you’re blackout drunk, of course I’m going to be upset!”

Mydei’s stomach twists. He doesn’t think they fucked, but then again, neither does Phainon. It’s only the intent that he cares so much about. “Right,” he mutters bitterly.

“Mydei.” Phainon tries. He’s sounding more distressed by the second. “Can you—”

“If I wasn’t drunk,” Mydei starts, quietly. It’s enough to cut Phainon off completely. “You wouldn’t care.”

Phainon inhales sharply. “That’s bullshit.”

“Is it?” Mydei looks up at him. “You’re not upset about the fact that I was with someone last night. So drop it. I wanted it, it doesn’t matter.”

Phainon goes still. He’s staring at Mydei in disbelief, and then something in his gaze softens ever so slightly. When he speaks, his voice is careful, like he’s choosing each word as it comes. “Would you want me to be upset about that?”

Mydei knows where this is going. He can’t allow it to pass. He can’t stand to embarrass himself more than he already has. “No,” he says. His throat is

tight. “I’m just saying you’re making this too big of a deal.”

Phainon laughs, but it’s completely devoid of any humor. “You—” he closes his eyes, running both of his injured hands down his face. “You are unbelievable.”

“I’m unbelievable—?”

“Yes, Mydei!” Phainon shouts. “Think about it. If it were me last night, you can’t tell me you wouldn’t be pissed off.”

“I wouldn’t care,” Mydei responds, as calmly as he can manage right now. “If you want my permission to go get laid, you have it. Do whatever you want.”

Silence blares between them. Phainon’s eyes are still wild, but he doesn’t move. He’s angrier than Mydei has ever seen him.

“Oh my god,” he mutters, disbelieving. “Whatever. You win.”

Phainon walks off without another word, and Mydei hears the guest bedroom door slam seconds later. The dirty dishes are still in the sink. At least now Mydei can do them without feeling guilty.

He swallows thickly. It doesn’t feel like a good win. If anything, now he feels even worse.

“Cipher, you have to tell me,” he groans, when they meet up at the cafe the next day. “Who did I hook up with at that party?”

Cipher nearly pisses herself laughing, and she’s still recovering by the time the barista has delivered their orders to them. “You forgot?” she cackles, completely disregarding the barista. “You forgot about Big Phainon?”

“Big Phainon?” he demands, leaning over the table and lowering his voice. “What the hell are you talking about?”

“You made out with him—in front of everyone, mind you—and then dragged him into the bathroom. It was quite the spectacle, actually.”

“Oh my god,” Mydei thinks this is the closest he’s ever gotten to becoming suicidal. “What’s with that nickname? Phainon is already big.”

Cipher feigns gagging. “Not what I wanted to hear in front of my brownie.”

“I’m not talking about his—” Mydei picks up the specials menu on the table and smacks her over the head. “He’s tall, Cipher,” he hisses, leaning forward and hoping no one around them has heard their conversation.

“Yeah, well, this guy was even bigger,” Cipher states. “And he had the hair. Light blond, you know? And a little charming. And—wait, you didn’t actually hook up, did you?”

Mydei closes his eyes. He’s not about to explain to her how far he suspects they went, and he thinks she wouldn’t appreciate it if he did, anyway. “Fuck,” he groans.

“Mydei—did you fuck that guy?”

“No, Cipher. Enough.”

“Oh, thank Kephale,” she whispers. “You were gone when we found you, dude. Like, scary shit. Hyacine was in full doctor mode.”

“Fuck,” Mydei mutters. “I probably thought he was Phainon.”

“Wouldn’t put it past you, in that state. I thought he might have been Phainon, too, when I saw you with him, until I saw Real Phainon watching.”

“So he saw.”

“Yup,” Cipher says. She picks the cherry off the piece of cake Mydei had ordered and pops it into her mouth. “Didn’t look like he was enjoying the show.”

Mydei furrows his eyebrows. He didn’t think Phainon would have enjoyed it, necessarily, but the way Cipher puts it makes it seem like it was glaringly obvious. “He didn’t?”

“Of course he didn’t, dumbass,” Cipher gives him a look like she can’t believe she has to say it. “Phainon was pissed. He was about to kick the shit out of that guy when we found you.”

Mydei rests his head in his hands. That much was, unfortunately, clear. Phainon just wasn’t upset about the right thing.

“I mean, you were really out of it, Mydei,” Cipher continues, face dropping a little. “He thought—well, you know. You know what he thought.”

“I didn’t—say anything, right? When you found me later?”

“Nothing that made any sense,” Cipher reassures him. “I don’t even know if you recognized us.”

“That’s probably for the best,” Mydei mutters. He’s been stirring his coffee up mindlessly for a couple minutes now, and finally sets the spoon down on the side of his plate.

“So you finally came to terms with it, then?”

Mydei knows exactly what she’s talking about. He feigns ignorance anyway. “Came to terms with what?”

“Your love for Phainon, obviously?”

“I…” Mydei runs a hand through his hair. “...don’t know what you’re talking about.”

“Oh my god.”

“Anyways, you and Cas—?”

Cipher rolls her eyes, collapsing forwards until her forehead hits the table. “No,” she mumbles, voice muffled. “She got drunk, too. I didn’t want it to

happen like that.”

“Makes sense,” Mydei says, shrugging. “Well, I think you should have a pretty big chance if you just talked to her.”

“Hm,” Cipher muses, before snapping her head back up. “Do you know something?”

Mydei smiles, shrugging.

“Mydeimos. Do you know something.”

“Talk to her, Cipher. I’m not going to wingman for you.”

“Stupid, boring Kremnoan,” Cipher mutters. “Fine. Choose the least helpful option.”

“Whatever, man,” Mydei answers. “Are we going to finish this damn song, or not?”

The song, called Lies Will Always Be Lies, is not finished by the end of their session, though it’s ready to present to the rest of the band. They do so at the start of the next week, and Cipher elects not to tell the story behind it. Despite her experience being at the forefront, helping her to write it caused Mydei to develop his own connection to it, as well. He’s not sure what it’s about to him, but it still feels like it’s his song, too.

They’ve started meeting at the IPC building again. All their equipment has finally moved out of his living room, so he’s back to his own space. Castorice, who lives closest to his apartment, drives him to work every morning so that Phainon can use Mydei’s car while he’s gone. They decided that he would stay in Mydei’s place until physical therapy ended, which would run until the end of the year. Mydei doesn’t know which he feels more: dread for that day to come, or excitement.

Now that they’re writing and recording in the same space, the two things have started to happen at once. Mydei coaches Cipher throughout her recording session of Lies Will Always Be Lies, and—as Madam Herta once

said—he cannot emulate emotion, but she finds it without him during her solo bridge. A year ago, he would never have expected to say that he witnessed some of the most touching singing out of anyone in the band from none other than Cipher herself. Maybe she wasn’t lying about being emotionally intelligent after all.

“That’s great, Cipher,” Ratio says, when she finishes her first recording session. “Mydei, I think you’d make an excellent professor one day.”

Mydei snorts laughing, and finds that he rarely feels as happy as he is in moments like these. “I think I’d have to go back to school for that, doc.”

Ratio shrugs. “Maybe if you studied production, you’d be motivated to get a PhD.”

“Yeah right,” Mydei says. Why would he do anything else, when he could do this for the rest of his life?

They listen to Cipher’s every instruction as they continue to record. Allowing himself to get bossed around by Cipher while he records the acoustic guitar is not something he ever thought he would do. And then she proceeds to tell him that the tone of his voice isn’t right. She doesn’t know what he needs to change to get it right, but she knows what she wants. Mydei appreciates that.

Hyacine and Castorice get significantly less shit from her during their turns —she merely tells Hyacine that the electric guitar needs to be “bloodier”, which neither Mydei nor Ratio understand. But eventually, she gets it. Castorice plays her part perfectly, and Cipher only interrupts to ask if they can add a tambourine. Ratio obliges in production.

It takes about a week for them to finish it, but listening to Lies Will Always Be Lies in full at the end of production has Mydei thinking it might end up being one of his favorites on the album. It’s good. It wouldn’t be nearly as good if it weren’t for Cipher and everything she had added to the track. Her voice alone is one thing, but her vision for the song is strong.

As Castorice is driving him home, he gets a group email from Aventurine. He notifies her, and she turns her music down so he can read it aloud.

Promotional Christmas Concert Aventurine Kakavasha To: Cifera Mnestia; Mydeimos Nikador; Hyacinthia Seliose; Castorice Thanatos Cc: Jade Evelyn; Topaz Jelena; Veritas Ratio; +3 others

Greetings and good afternoon,

I hope this email finds all of you well. Dr. Ratio informs me the album is coming together splendidly, and I am writing to inform you of an incredible opportunity I have just secured. In order to promote the album, I would like to do a small concert around Christmastime. It will be recorded in the studio, in an intimate setting, and all videos will be posted online.

As for the songs you choose to perform, it is completely up to you. You could do old songs, or mostly covers, which might be more beneficial if they are popular songs. As for new songs, one should be sufficient. Make sure you choose this one wisely. I will ensure Dr. Ratio agrees with your choice before we move forward with the preparations.

More information will come soon regarding costuming and set design. Please inform me or Dr. Ratio as soon as you have your final setlist picked out, and accommodations will be made to fit. All additional backing instrumentals and vocals will be recorded by you beforehand.

Best, Aventurine Kakavasha Band Manager | Tour & Operations Manager CALAMITY

“Oh my god,” Castorice says, the closest to a squeal Mydei has ever heard from her. “This is so exciting. I love shows like these.”

“Do you have any ideas?” Mydei asks, turning his phone off.

“Crucifixion,” Castorice says instantly. Mydei laughs, as it’s the song currently playing from her car radio—the title track of High Cloud Quintet’s most famous album.

She turns the volume back up, and Mydei listens to it—it’s far from the first time he’s heard the song, but he somehow feels like he’s using a fresh pair of ears. They could actually do this song. He’s not the biggest fan of the High Cloud Quintet anymore, and neither is Castorice—both of them are much more casual listeners than they were when they were teenagers, when they were actually the band’s target audience. But a lot of their audience is High Cloud Quintet fans. Even though they don’t make music anymore, it’s like a rite of passage for all teenagers to become superfans of that band at some point.

Regardless, it’s a tribute that wouldn’t go unappreciated. It’s not a bad idea at all.

Castorice drops him off soon after that. Riding high off another day of success, he’s in a fantastic mood as he unlocks the apartment door.

He nearly jumps as he’s met with music the second the door cracks open. Phainon had an infuriating tendency to keep to himself in Mydei’s apartment, a habit Mydei was hoping he would have broken by now.

He’s overjoyed to discover that Phainon isn’t just playing music, he’s making it. He toes his shoes off and sheds his jacket as quietly as possible, coming to stand in the doorframe as he watches Phainon play in the living room.

It’s a simple piece, one most beginners can play after being acquainted with the instrument for no more than a year. Phainon plays slowly, careful not to strain his fingers too much. It’s clear he’s trying to get used to it again with

his new skin, but Mydei can’t stop himself from grinning ear to ear nonetheless.

Mydei claps when he finishes, and Phainon jumps when he looks over his shoulder. “Shit, Mydei—warn a guy next time, will you?”

“I didn’t want you to stop,” Mydei explains. “You sound good. It’s been so long since I’ve heard you play.”

Phainon sighs. He looks dejected when he turns back to the keys, chewing at his bottom lip. “I guess it’s a start.”

“Even without the injury, you wouldn’t be at the level you were at before if you didn’t play for four months,” Mydei says.

“And I never will be,” Phainon mumbles under his breath.

“Keep practicing,” Mydei drops his bag on the coffee table and takes a seat on the couch. “You never know what might happen.” Mydei knows Phainon will never stop practicing. Even if he’s never at the level he once was at, being able to hold onto some part of it will still be enough for him. Even if he can’t make money off his performances anymore, that doesn’t matter, because it was never about that for him. As long as his fingers can still move, even if it’s only a little bit, Phainon will keep playing.

Phainon doesn’t look very happy, but he turns back to the keys anyway. Mydei pulls out his laptop and listens to him continue his practice as he starts his search for songs to cover.

There’s no sheet music in the apartment at the level Phainon is playing at, so Mydei knows he’s going through these songs from memory. Both of their childhood piano coaches insisted on having them memorize their pieces, and yet Mydei does not think he could do what Phainon does now.

“What are you doing?” Phainon eventually asks, spinning around on the bench.

“Picking out songs for a mini show we’re doing soon,” Mydei explains. “We’re doing covers.”

“That’s so cool,” Phainon says. “Can I come?”

Mydei looks up, studying him for a moment. He doesn’t know why, but it’s not what he expected him to say. “I don’t know,” he says finally. He doesn’t. He always assumed these sorts of things just had crew members in the audience, rather than being an actual live concert. “I’ll get back to you on that.”

“Okay,” Phainon says. He spins around once. Mydei gets the sense that he wants to ask something, so he stops what he’s doing and looks up.

“What?”

“Huh?”

“You want to ask something. So ask.”

“Okay,” Phainon says, laughing nervously. “I was just wondering if, um, you needed your car tonight…?”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “Are you going somewhere?” There’s a pit forming in his stomach. He tries to swallow down his rising dread.

“I,” Phainon starts. “Well. I. I have a, um, a date.”

“A date,” Mydei deadpans. He forgets to feign excitement.

“Yes,” Phainon says. “Is that…okay?” His eyes are wide, hopeful.

Mydei gives him what he wants. “Yes,” he says. “I’m not going anywhere.”

“Right,” Phainon stands. “Okay.” He clears his throat. “I’ll go get ready, then.”

Mydei stares at the spot where he just was. He’s overcome with an unbearable desire to rip something apart. It’s admirable, how he’s

maintained his composure so well thus far.

He can’t even go to the gym, because Phainon is taking the car. He’ll just have to go tomorrow morning, and hope he restrains himself well enough until then.

He looks back down at his computer, at the working list of cover songs he was typing into a new document. Now, it’s the least of his worries. There’s a new song he has to write—excerpts of it have already been floating around his head for nearly two weeks now. Since the Halloween party, really. He has working lyrics in his head and one piano riff he wrote into Sibelius so he wouldn’t forget it.

He plugs in his headphones and works on expanding the piano part, barely noticing Phainon come out of his room half an hour later with his hair slicked back and a suit on. The sight of him puts a lump in his throat. It’s unfair, the way he looks.

“Bye, Mydei,” Phainon says, voice faint through Mydei’s earbuds. He sounds a little apologetic, but Mydei can’t fathom why that might be.

“Have fun,” Mydei responds. He doesn’t look up from his computer. The less he sees of him in that suit, the better.

The door closes, and Mydei finds himself engulfed in impossibly lonely silence. There can’t possibly be anything worse than this, he thinks. His apartment empty, darkened by Phainon’s absence, every wall closing in on Mydei along with the devastating realization that any hope he might have had left has officially dissipated entirely.

Just the thought of Phainon at some fancy restaurant, sitting across from another man or woman, charming them past the point of no return with that killing smile of his. It makes Mydei feel sick. The first person Phainon expresses interest in should marry him if they know what’s best for them. Mydei just happened to be too late to do it first.

He turns back to his computer, giving the silence around him nothing more than an annoyed sigh. Phainon was perfectly welcome to date whoever he

wanted. It was Mydei’s own fault for being a coward and refusing to at least try to get him back first.

Lyrics come quickly. He writes like his hands are on fire, uncaring for rhyme schemes or making it sound pretty. He just needs to say what he needs to say first—he can make it good later.

Halfway through the bridge, he calls Castorice. Not because he needs inspiration from her, but because he needs to calm down. He’s worried that he’s making it too aggressive, to the point where Phainon would drop dead on the spot if he heard it.

She picks up on the fourth ring. Mydei can hear faint rock music playing in the background, as well as what sounds like an oven fan. “Hi, Mydei,” she says, a little breathless. “I’m cooking dinner. What’s up?”

“What are you making?” Mydei asks. The mention of cooking makes him temporarily forget his grievances in the first place. He hasn’t had dinner yet, either, but he’ll probably just have leftovers at this point.

“It’s soup day!”

“Soup day?”

Castorice makes a noise of affirmation. “The day before I get groceries, I make a soup with all my leftover ingredients. I’m roasting broccoli but I think it’s gonna burn—hold on, Mydei, let me put you on speaker—”

She cuts out for a minute, and then Mydei can hear her surroundings in much more perfect clarity than before. “Broccoli cheddar?” he asks.

“Not quite.” She laughs, then continues, “That’s what I’m trying to do, but I’m adding a bunch of other stuff to it too. It might be bad.”

“It sounds good. I haven’t had soup in months.”

“Mydei, you’re missing out!”

He’s not that much of a soup guy. He tries to eat meat with every dinner, and he much prefers it in its original form, where he can tear through it like a wild animal. It brings him a great deal of joy. “Anyways, Cas, I’ll let you go if you’re busy—”

“No, stay!” She sounds far away from the microphone, and stressed out. Mydei understands the feeling. Cooking always stressed him out when he was just beginning, and he knows that Castorice doesn’t have as much experience with it as she does baking. “Why did you call me?”

Mydei groans, as the previous events of his night come back to him. “Phainon,” he admits.

“Oh!” Something loud clangs in the background, and Castorice coughs. “Sorry, I’m trying not to burn my kitchen down. What did he do this time?”

“He’s on a date.”

“...Oh.” Mydei can hear a faint beep, and then the sound of the oven fan disappears. The resulting silence on her end is devastating. “Shit, Mydei.”

Hearing Castorice curse is almost funny enough to make him laugh. He hopes that he can laugh about it later, once he’s calmed down. But nothing is very funny right now. “I want to kill him. I’m serious.”

“Okay, well, maybe that’s not—exactly—the move—?” There’s rustling on her end, now, followed by a little shriek that cuts out on Mydei’s end. “Sorry, Mydei, I really do feel bad for you but I’m getting broccoli everywhere.”

Mydei laughs at that, a little bit. Really, if he wanted to calm down, he’s already got that.

“I do get it, though,” Castorice continues. “I want to kill Cipher sometimes.”

“Well, me too,” Mydei answers. “Not sure if it’s for the same reason, though.”

“She has a penchant for being annoying.”

Mydei snorts. “And yet you still like her.”

“Doesn’t Phainon ever annoy you?”

“Like you wouldn’t believe,” Mydei says, rolling his eyes. He tosses his laptop aside and lays against his couch cushions entirely. “He is the most infuriating man I have ever met, and yet—”

“You’re in love with him.”

“Did I say that?” Mydei says faintly, struck with intense deja vu from a very similar conversation with Cipher.

“Maybe not, but I can see it.”

And Mydei knows it. He knows in himself that he’s in love with Phainon, but admitting it to anyone else would allow a level of vulnerability that he isn’t ready to face. Even if they can all see it—even if they knew before he did.

“Do you think you’re in love with Cipher?”

There’s a few beats of silence on Castorice’s end before she replies. “I don’t really know what it would feel like if I was.”

“But you know you like her.”

“I know that I don’t feel the same way about her that I do about you, or Hyacine.”

“Could be…a strong friendship?” Mydei knows he’s grasping at straws. He just wants to make sure that they both feel the same way about each other.

“But you’re my best friend, Mydei.”

“Oh.” Mydei doesn’t know why, but he almost thinks that Castorice saying that makes him feel the same way reciprocation from Phainon would. It

alone makes him want to give up on Phainon altogether. Why was he wasting so much time lamenting on romantic reciprocation from Phainon when he had the best friends he’d ever had, surrounding him all the time? “I —thank you. You’ve already made me feel so much better,” he admits.

“I, um,” she starts, then sighs deeply as she cuts herself off. “I don’t know about Cipher.”

“What?”

“A lot of things,” she murmurs. “Whether or not she likes me back is one thing. But I feel like, even if she did, I won’t be what she actually wants in someone. You know?”

“No,” Mydei says earnestly. He’s never felt that way, personally. Up until now, with all Phainon’s signals that he’s obviously moved on, he’s never doubted his relationships before. “But keep going.”

“I don’t think I’d be able to make her happy. I know love can be…blind, I guess. If she likes me, she might not see who I really am.”

“I really don’t think you need to be worried about that,” Mydei says. “Cipher has been your friend for, what, a decade now? I think she knows who you are.”

“...Maybe, yeah.”

“Cipher has a million reasons to like you for you,” Mydei continues. “You’re so kind, and so strong to manage everything you’ve been through with so much grace. You have every reason in the world to lose it, and yet you don’t. Kephale knows I would’ve broken down years ago if I was you.”

“Mydei…”

“I mean it. You’re one of the strongest people I know, by a long shot.”

“Well, I don’t know about that—”

“I’m serious, Cas.”

“Okay, Mydei.” Castorice finally acquiesces, voice quiet. “People don’t give you enough credit for your kindness.”

“Wow, okay.” Mydei might actually be getting a bit teary-eyed, now. Phainon feels so far away. He can only hope that, for Castorice, Cipher does, too. Even though he knows in his heart that the two of them are going to work out. No matter how much work they might have to put in to get there.

“You’re a lot like Cipher, in that way. The things she does for others often go unnoticed.”

“Mm. I can’t believe you just compared us. I’m going to go throw up now.” Mydei knows that Castorice is right, as she always is. But he says it anyway.

Castorice laughs, and the sound brings him great relief. “She really likes you, you know.”

“...Ah.”

“I’m serious! She loves spending time with you. And she thinks you’re the funniest person ever.”

“I’m not sure if that’s a good thing.”

“It is a good thing. Cipher doesn’t make fun of people who can’t handle it.”

Mydei laughs for a bit, staring at the window as the sun begins to set over the city skyline. Nothing really seems to matter that much anymore. “I’m rooting for you two, you know.”

“Well, I guess we’ll see. I’ve already written her a terrible love song.”

“Actually?” Mydei can feel his whole face light up at that admission. “Like an actual love song?”

“Erm…maybe not.”

Mydei laughs again. One thing about CALAMITY was that a true, genuine love song seemed to be something they could not accomplish. Mydei would, given that he has the perfect muse, but Phainon pissed him off far too often for him to finish anything he started. It was unfortunate that it seemed Castorice was in a similar situation.

“I’ll send it to you when I finish it, and you can look over it, okay?”

“What are you going to tell Cipher if we put it on the album?”

“That I wrote it about someone else.”

“Oh.” Mydei thinks about Phainon and his date again. There’s a tinge of bitterness in his mouth, but it doesn’t stick around for as long as it did before.

“Not in that way. I mean I would tell her it was a story I wrote.”

“Or you can tell Cipher how you feel, and then you wouldn’t have to lie.”

“Very funny. I’ll tell her the moment you tell Phainon.”

“Suffer, then.”

They sit in a few moments of silence, before Castorice continues. “I think my soup is getting cold. Do you feel better now, Mydei?”

“A lot better,” Mydei says earnestly. He still has the song to finish. But writing a song with a clear head was always going to be better than writing it drenched in emotion, even if the song itself was inherently emotional. “Thank you, Cas.”

“I feel better, too,” she confesses. “I’m…” her next exhale is a little shaky. “I’m really happy you’re my friend, Mydei.”

“Me too,” Mydei says quietly.

Castorice hangs up, leaving him engulfed in silence once more. Only this time, it doesn’t feel so lonely.

The song is nearly finished when Phainon gets home. It’s still one of the most emotionally charged songs he’s ever written—besides maybe Conqueror of Lions. If anything, he’s glad this is happening to him since it means that such an amazing song would come from it.

“You’re still awake,” Phainon says from the doorway, matter-of-factly.

“As you see,” Mydei answers. He drops his hands from the piano keys to his lap—he had just played it in full, but the ending was just instrumental. Thankfully, Phainon hadn’t heard any of the lyrics.

“Did you write something?”

“I did,” Mydei swallows, belatedly realizing how suspicious it might sound if he suddenly was struck with inspiration while Phainon was out on his date. “An old song I’ve been meaning to revisit,” he adds, hoping that’s enough for damage control.

“Ah,” Phainon pauses, staring at him like there’s more he wants to say. “Can I hear it?”

Mydei stands, closing his computer that had the notes open. “No,” he says. “I’m going to bed.”

“Oh…okay,” Phainon murmurs. Mydei leaves him where he is, walking past him and into his bedroom.

He doesn’t fall asleep quickly. He thinks of Phainon, in the room across the hall, and wonders if sleep comes easily to him tonight. He hopes it doesn’t, even though he knows how horrible that sounds.

Phainon isn’t awake before Mydei leaves the next morning. He puts leftovers from breakfast in the fridge and leaves a sticky note on the island, telling him that they exist. He swallows down all the lingering bitterness. Despite how it might seem, he does think he’s beginning to head towards acceptance.

“I wrote a new song last night,” he says, once they’re in the studio. Ratio isn’t there yet, busy with another group he’s producing for.

“Me too,” Castorice says instantly, eyes lighting up as she turns towards him. “I’m not sure about it, though, so I was going to send it to you first.”

“That’s, what, ten songs, now?” Hyacine says, looking at the white board they had brought in from Mydei’s living room. “We have to hurry up with the last two if we want to reach our deadline.”

“The last three,” Cipher corrects.

“Does the deadline matter?” Castorice asks. “I don’t think anyone wants to rush us.”

“The song isn’t final,” Mydei cuts in, sitting at the keyboard. “I mean, I think you guys are going to like it, but I don’t know if I want to include it just yet.”

“Then maybe you shouldn’t play it for us until you’ve made your decision,” Cipher answers. She leans over as Castorice sits on the couch next to her, and rests her head in her lap. It’s such a casual action, one Castorice hardly flinches at. Mydei can’t fight the little smile that breaks over his face when he sees it.

Mydei rummages through his bag until he pulls out his laptop. Truthfully, he does want to put the song on the album. He knows it’s an experience many people can relate to. But he doesn’t want Phainon to see. Even if he didn’t realize it was about him, its hopelessness is so palpable that Phainon would have no choice but to see him as weak for writing it. It even feels too vulnerable for his band. Phainon was one thing, but they had already seen the worst parts of him.

The working title is Become the Dawn, which he already knows is too obvious. But it’s the best he has, and part of him doesn’t care if Phainon connects the dots. By the time they debuted it, Phainon would already be going back to Okhema in five days. Mydei could handle living in shame for those days if it meant Phainon would eventually leave and they would never

have to see each other ever again. Even though just the idea of that alone hurts.

And then there’s just the fact that he loves this song. He thinks it’s beautiful. He thinks it’s some of his best writing. It has single potential. “I want you to convince me,” he tells them.

So he starts playing it for them. The whole song isn’t written to have a piano part, but he plays the root chords along with the guitar part instead. He’d written it for piano first anyways, and just transposed it to other instruments afterwards. Honestly, he doesn’t know what it sounds like as written yet—he needs the whole band for that, which is why he doesn’t consider a song done until they’ve looked at it together and tweaked what was necessary.

The keyboard in their studio isn’t very good. It lacks the quality and emotion of a grand, its sound muted and fake. It doesn’t play very loud, no matter how hard Mydei tries, but it’s the best he has, and he hopes it’s good enough to get the point across.

The second chorus leading into the bridge is his least favorite part, because the vulnerability in it is palpable. He almost wants to stop right here and tell them never mind, he can’t. He’s come so far already, with them, with everything. He keeps going.

I love you still, that’s my sentence No appeal, no way to repentance Banish me to the pits of hell I’ll fight my way out, even if I always lose I don’t know why I always choose you It’s not my fault you’re so easy to love

I know you’ll light up another’s life one day Their sun, their stars, their moon in the sky You’ll become a dawn that isn’t mine

But why, why? Why can’t it be?

Why can’t you be mine?

The rest of the song is mostly piano. Mydei finishes it, almost two minutes of instrumental that eventually fades out, opening his eyes only to double check the sheet music. He does not look at them. He can’t bring himself to see their faces met with his raw vulnerability, the feelings he had denied for so long.

He stops when he sees his written-in notation to fade out. That’s something they can add in production, but he can’t emulate. He can hear his heart racing when he finally lifts his fingers from the keys, lifting his head to look at the rest of them.

They’re still in the same positions they were in when he had started— Hyacine cross-legged on one end of the couch, Castorice sitting politely in the middle, Cipher sprawled out with her head in her lap. None of them look particularly happy with him. They don’t even applaud, and Mydei thinks, for one awful moment, that they didn’t like it at all.

“Mydei,” Hyacine starts gently. “Who is this song about?”

Mydei looks at her, wordlessly begging her to understand. Because who else would it be, really? There’s no one else for him. He thought, based on Cipher’s incessant comments and Castorice’s knowing looks, that it had been quite obvious.

“It’s Phainon, Cinny,” Cipher answers. Her voice doesn’t match Hyacine’s care, but it lacks her usual tease. “Who else?”

Mydei looks at his hands. Who else? He had been so blind to his own feelings for so long. He thought he knew himself better than that.

“Well,” he says, snapping his computer shut so he can see them more clearly. “What did you think of the song?”

“It’s beautiful, Mydei,” Castorice says. They share a knowing look. Hers is filled with pity, and even though Mydei hates being pitied like nothing else, he can’t bring himself to feel upset with her at this moment.

“Are you sure?” Hyacine says. “That Phainon doesn’t feel the same?”

Mydei swallows. He knew a conversation like this was unavoidable, but he would still like to try to avoid it. “Do you like the song, or not?”

“It’s good,” Cipher says, yawning. She sits up, and comes over to steal Mydei’s computer so she can look at it herself. “But you knew that already.”

“You don’t have to tell us anything,” Hyacine continues, moving closer to Castorice on the couch so she, too, can look over Cipher’s shoulder at the score.

“Uh, don’t say that, I think he should,” Cipher argues. “What the hell happened to Phainon giving you heart eyes all the time? Where did this ‘woe is me’ of a song come from?”

“He was never giving me heart eyes,” Mydei closes his eyes, leaning back in his seat until his head hits the wall. “He didn’t care about the guy I—” he clears his throat. “Whatever. It doesn’t matter. He went on a date last night.”

“No he didn’t.” Cipher’s eyes are wide, the look on her face somewhere between utter disbelief and anger.

Mydei merely nods in response.

“Oh, I am going to kill him,” she growls. “That flakey, inconsiderate son of a bitch—”

“Stop, Cipher.” Mydei shakes his head. “It’s not his fault he doesn’t feel the same.”

“So it’s yours, then?”

“It’s no one’s fault. You don’t control who you fall in love with, do you?”

“We must be missing something,” Castorice replies. “Phainon isn’t like… that.”

“It’s fine, guys,” Mydei sighs. “He doesn’t like me. It’s okay.”

“Well…” Hyacine starts. “I don’t know. Phainon saw Mydei with someone else at the Halloween party, despite Mydei liking him. Should we really be taking Phainon’s going on a date with someone else as absolute proof he doesn’t feel the same? First dates are generally pretty casual, aren’t they?”

Mydei swallows. Of course, he hadn’t thought of that. But he knows Phainon better than most, and he knows how he is when something upsets him. Perhaps he’d been a little awkward recently, but not upset. It would be painfully obvious, were he upset.

He’s not able to respond before the door swings open, and Ratio walks in. “Good morning,” he says, shedding his jacket and throwing it over his chair. “Are we alright? You all look like someone died.”

“We’re fine,” Mydei says.

“We have a new song to record,” Cipher pipes in, sitting up straight. “Don’t we, little prince?”

Mydei sighs into his palm. With Ratio’s intrigued hum as he strides over to the couch and he, too, takes a look at the score, he has no choice but to acquiesce. He’ll do it. He can deal with the consequences later.

The consequences, it seems, come as early as the end of the week. He manages to get through the full recording process without many questions —or comments, for that matter, from anyone he doesn’t particularly want to explain himself to. Ratio cares about the music, not the lyrics. Mydei wouldn’t be surprised if he hadn’t even listened to an actual word this

whole time. And even if he did, it’s unlikely that he would have much to say on the matter. Ratio was the most cerebral man Mydei had ever met.

It might be this ignorance of sensitive subjects that leads him to suggest they perform this song at their upcoming concert. He gives a long speech about why he believes it’s best suited for something like this—it being one of the best songs on the album, but not significantly better than the rest of its songs. He also says it would be a great opportunity for Mydei to showcase his skills as a pianist and writer, as the song with Robin was not an original from him.

His arguments are too good. It’s a massive difference from how secretive he wanted to keep it when he had first pitched the song to the rest of the band. Were it to be released with the album, he was hoping they could stick it in the middle and hope it flew over most people’s heads. If a song was given extra promotion before album release, it didn’t matter where you put it. People were going to remember it anyway.

And now, it would likely be the main song used to promote their album. It would go viral, were their performances successful. It could easily become the lead single.

“Okay,” Mydei says, his face betraying none of the nauseating cocktail of emotions he feels. “If everyone else agrees, I’m okay with that. We can start preparing to play it live, then.”

Ratio nods. “The rest of the songs, too. We’re due to start rehearsals for that soon, so I suggest you focus on finalizing your setlist sooner rather than later.”

“Mydei,” Hyacine says quietly from where she sits beside him. “You’re really okay with this?”

“I am,” Mydei’s voice doesn’t shake as he says it, like he fears it would. He can’t wait until he’s home and can freak out about this in solitude.

“Then, I’m okay with it,” Hyacine offers, smiling.

The others agree soon after that, and it’s decided. Ratio stays with them for a bit, helping suggest other cover ideas that he thinks would work well for them. They end the day with a long list to look over for homework—mainly Mydei, to see if any of the songs would be out of range for him. There are a couple songs on the list by female singers, one of which he’d really like to do, even though he’s not looking forward to transposing it into a key more comfortable for him. He prides himself on his ability to hit higher notes, despite where he sings comfortably—but with a whole song in a higher register, it was a lost cause.

“Also, if there are any additional instruments required, we can hire people to cover it, or just add it to the backing track. It’s up to you,” Ratio adds. Mydei thinks there might be a song with accordion on the list. Where they were going to find an actual accordion player, he has no idea.

Mydei takes a picture of the list once they’re dismissed, and they decide to go to a restaurant together to celebrate the weekend. Castorice plays through the first couple of songs on the list as she drives them there. The first one is too slow for him, and Castorice doesn’t like how boring her part would be, so they eliminate it. The next few remain possible contenders, though Mydei has no strong winners just yet.

The majority decision once they’re shown to their booth in the restaurant is that they are not allowed to leave until they’ve narrowed down the list to its final stage. Mydei thinks that could mean they’re here for hours, and hopes they’re all more or less in agreement.

They get to work as soon as they’ve ordered. Castorice pulls out one of her notebooks, copying down all of the songs from the photo Mydei took.

They have only crossed out four options before they start adding more.

“Apotheosis - Argenti Idrila,” Hyacine blurts out.

All three of them snap their heads up to look at her. “Idrila?!” Cipher demands, incredulous.

“You’re not serious,” Mydei says.

“Come on!” Hyacine grabs the notebook and writes it in herself. “He has such a beautiful voice. Yours would be perfect for that style of music, Mydei.”

“You’re out of your damn mind,” Mydei retorts. “Our music styles aren’t even in the same universe. He went through a completely different kind of training than me, Hyacine.”

“I agree with her, Mydei,” Castorice says. “I think it would be a perfect opportunity to showcase your range.”

“Oh my god,” Mydei mutters. “Fine.”

“And we’re not changing the genre of the backing track,” Hyacine adds. “Maybe we can translate the strings into acoustic guitar.”

“I’ll work on it,” Mydei decides. “If we choose it. Don’t get your hopes up.”

They keep making their way through the decided list, arguing over this and that. Hyacine seems set on showing off their range, which Mydei only agrees with to an extent. It’s a good way to prepare listeners for what will come their way with the new album, as it introduces a new sound many old listeners probably won’t be used to. But Idrila is a bit too far, which is where they start to disagree.

Castorice wants to do tribute music, to other artists they take their inspirations from. She’s set on Crucifixion, no longer much of a joke, but Mydei worries his voice won’t be a good fit for it. He’s already of the impression that songs written for female singers are much worse when a man covers it, even though songs written for male singers are often better when a female singer covers it. He can’t explain it. Some songs he thinks he can cover, but Crucifixion just isn’t one of them. His voice just doesn’t have the right color, and color is so necessary for a High Cloud Quintet track.

That said, a voice built for rock isn’t going to have a very easy time covering Idrila, either.

“I want to do this one,” Mydei says, pointing to the one he had already liked when Ratio mentioned it. It’s by an artist named Acheron, which is a name he vaguely recognizes, though he’s not sure from where. It’s called Self-Annihilationism and Mydei doesn’t know how he’s never heard it before, because it’s incredible.

He pauses for a moment, then continues, “I don’t have anything else to say. Cas?”

He looks back at her, and she stands, coming up to share his microphone. “I forgot I’m singing this one,” she says shyly. “Okay. This is, um, Crucifixion. By the High Cloud Quintet.”

Mydei picks his guitar back up, slinging it over his shoulder as the second drummer walks out. She’s an IPC employee Mydei had never met before, but they ended up getting along very well.

Crucifixion’s studio version starts with ambient noises and a little bit of keyboard, and their modified version of it plays through speakers before the full band joins in for the beginning. The instruments fade back out as Castorice starts singing, beautiful voice ringing out perfectly through the room.

He knows this is probably wildly unexpected for whoever would eventually watch this video when it’s posted, but he’s not the only one singing on the album. He might be the leader of the band on paper, but they all work together to make this music. It isn’t just Mydei and his backing track.

Castorice is a talented singer. He’s known this for months, now, and is overjoyed at the prospect of the rest of the world realizing this, too.

The song finishes, and Castorice is smiling brighter than he’s ever seen her. He doesn’t think he’s ever been more proud.

“Thank you,” she says, breathless. “And thank you to our drummer for filling in,” she gestures behind her, and Mydei steps out of the way so the backup drummer can wave at the camera before moving offstage.

“Spoiler alert,” Mydei says into the mic, after Castorice goes back to her kit. “I’m not the only one singing on the new album.”

A couple laughs. Cipher cheers, a muted whoop as she doesn’t have a microphone in front of her.

“Okay, our next song is a little different,” Mydei warns them, pulling the stool up and lowering the mic stand so he can sit on it. “We have Cipher on upright bass, Hyacine on acoustic guitar, and Cas on drums. Surprise.”

He gives them a couple seconds to get situated. “Okay,” he starts. “We are going to play Apotheosis by Argenti Idrila.” He looks straight at Phainon as he says it, and thinks the mic might pick up a little bit of his laugh when he sees the shock on his face.

The original song starts with drums, bass, and harp, which he had translated to work for acoustic guitar. Hyacine plucks the notes, and it doesn’t sound like a CALAMITY song, but it sounds more like one than it originally did.

Mydei takes a deep breath before his cue, and starts singing. His voice is deep enough to hit it without having to transpose the key, thankfully, but the style of the original vocals was hard to achieve with training like his. They spent the most time preparing for the live version of this song by far because Mydei could never quite get it right. He wanted to scrap it several times, but Ratio kept reassuring him he could get it, so they kept trying.

He thinks it sounds good now, and hopes he’s right about that.

The original song builds to horns and strings near the end, but they keep it more subdued to match the intimate setting. Hyacine plays most of the melody on her guitar again, demonstrating a difficult picking technique she hadn’t shown off before. Though Mydei doesn’t think the average person would be paying much attention to that, no matter how much he wishes they would.

He holds out the last note alone, until he feels it’s sufficient. The applause when he finishes goes on for a little longer than it had previously, and he thinks they might have found it genuinely impressive.

“Thank you,” he says, because he feels like he has to. He looks at Phainon, who looks back, eyes shining with remarkable pride. Mydei feels a swell in his chest at the confirmation. “That one was definitely a stretch.”

He pauses for a drink of water as Hyacine talks for a minute, answering a question that Mydei didn’t quite catch. They transition into Transcendence next, where Mydei finally takes his seat at the piano.

Hyacine starts this one on acoustic guitar again, and continues to be the only one playing throughout half of the first verse, until Cipher joins on bass. Castorice kicks in leading into the pre-chorus, along with Mydei.

The piano part for this song is relatively simple, mainly chords. As he leads into the chorus, Hyacine joins him singing with that beautiful bright voice of hers.

Transcendence is one of the most ethereal love songs Mydei has ever heard, more similar to Castorice’s style than her own. The lyrics are artfully crafted, and the instruments all come together to create a nostalgic, pleading melody. The singer tells a story that is not his own, of two people acting out a marriage in their final moments as they drown together in a wrathful river.

These hazards of love, he sings, as both Hyacine and Cipher join in on backing vocals, never more will trouble us.

Mydei wishes he had the right to think of Phainon as he sings it, but he does not. He hopes, in spite, that Phainon is left to wonder who Mydei might possibly be dedicating such a love song to. He hopes he sits in the audience and is moved by the beauty of Mydei’s pseudo-relationship. He hopes it makes him jealous. Not that it couldn’t be him in Mydei’s pretend lover’s shoes, because such an outcome would never be possible. But simply that it couldn’t be him in Mydei’s shoes.

He finishes with his hands off his keys, Hyacine playing the final chord on her guitar.

They only pause briefly between songs this time, Mydei taking his space back in front of the upright microphone, Hyacine handing him the acoustic guitar. She starts Suns Subdued with an electric guitar version of the harmonium intro to the original track, before fading out so Mydei takes over on acoustic, joined immediately by both Castorice and Cipher.

He starts singing with his voice soft. He has his eyes closed, so he can avoid making direct eye contact with Phainon. He knows if he were to open them, he would have nowhere else to look.

He doesn’t know who Phainon thinks of when he hears this song, but it must be someone. Part of him hopes that this performance has ruined Suns Subdued irreversibly for him. He hopes that every time it comes on the radio, on his playlist, he is forced to skip it lest he allow his brain to wander so cruelly to thoughts of his very first love.

Mydei knows that songs are best received by an audience when an emotional impact on the performers is evident. This has been clear since his college days—Herta constantly trying to get him to play with feeling. To be asked that back then was akin to being asked to torture himself, only now it comes almost too easily to him. Had he admitted that in college, he would have thought it made him weak. Now, he’s not so sure what it makes him.

He thinks the audience must be able to feel it. This isn’t just a song he sings out of love and appreciation for the music, it’s a song he sings out of passion. This is personal, and he thinks anyone in the room who might attempt to deny it must be a fool.

He can vaguely hear his bandmates harmonizing behind him as he heads into the final verse, but that’s hardly his focus. How he’s keeping up with his part on the guitar, he has no idea—his fingers and hands move on his own. He thinks he might forget the next lyric, and then sings it perfectly anyway. There is nothing clear in his head but thoughts of Phainon, and even those are not entirely clear.

Finally, he gets to the final lyric, and allows his voice to fade out. He plays the last couple of chords, Hyacine plays hers, and the music ends.

There’s a torturous few moments of silence after they stop, and finally the crowd gives them their applause.

Mydei dares a glance at Phainon. He thinks, even in the dim lighting of the room, that he looks near to tears. Mydei hopes they're angry tears. Bitter tears. He hopes he’s ruined the song for him forever.

He puts down his guitar, sitting down as he takes another couple sips of water.

“That was Suns Subdued,” Hyacine says. “By none other than Jing Yuan.”

“Ex High Cloud Quintet member,” Castorice supplies quietly, and a couple people in the audience chuckle. Mydei thinks they must have been paid to laugh at their jokes. Then he mentally kicks himself for being internally mean to Castorice, as his bad mood was no excuse.

“Our final song will be one from our upcoming album,” Hyacine continues. “Mydei, would you like to introduce it?”

“It would be my pleasure,” Mydei says, standing so he can reach his microphone. His voice is a little unsteady. He swallows, placing his water back down, before he continues. “I don’t have very much to say about this song. I think you will like it very much.”

He moves to the piano, and pushes the microphone back a little bit as it was uncomfortably close to his face. “This song is called Deliver the Dawn.” He thanks his awkward angle at the piano, because he could not look at Phainon even if he wanted to. Which, if he ever did, it would have been an accident.

The song starts with an electric guitar solo from Hyacine. He has vocals behind it, though they’re quiet, and her part is the focus.

The rest of them come in together after her solo is done, though the melody from it continues into the main part of the song. His piano is in the background starting at the pre-chorus, and he plays the main theme as they launch into the chorus.

He makes it through the first half of the song without giving so much of a thought to its muse. Right at the start of the second chorus, though, he fails. He grows bitter, just as the lyrics do. He hates himself for writing such a song. He hates Phainon more for forcing his hand.

He knows he’s slamming too hard on the keys. He doesn’t think he’s ever played so angrily, and he opens his eyes and can’t help but glare directly into the camera pointed at his face as they reach the bridge. You’ll become a dawn that isn’t mine, but why can’t it be?

He’s not speaking to Phainon. He pretends he isn’t, because admitting that he is would only make him angrier. Luckily, the instrumentals as he exits the bridge only get louder and more convoluted, so he can disguise his vocals in the background as an artistic choice and not a genuine reflection of the bitterness he feels just as strongly as he had that first day he sat down to write it.

He doesn’t think he’s ever been so happy for a performance to end. He takes his hands off the keys, they clap, he thanks them one last time. Hyacine promotes their album again, and they wish the cameras a merry Christmas together before they finally cut out, and more clapping fills the room. This time, Mydei thinks it’s genuine.

He can’t find Phainon in the crowd. He was already in the back, and now people are standing, discussing various things, preparing to review footage, dismantling equipment. He’s nowhere to be seen, and Mydei soon gives up on trying to catch his reaction. He will leave, and Mydei can deal with the inevitable fallout when he gets home.

Aventurine steps onto the stage, shaking Mydei’s hand. “That was great,” he says, before giving Mydei the first smile he’s ever seen from him that he actually believed. “All of you were truly incredible. Castorice, your singing —”

Mydei is interrupted by Ratio, who he hadn’t seen in the crowd earlier. “Was your muse here?” he asks, calculating as ever.

Mydei chokes on his spit. “What are you talking about—”

“No one sings like that unless they’re singing to someone,” Ratio says. “Well, I hope whoever it is knows how lucky they are to be loved so deeply by someone as talented as you.”

Mydei feels his face go hot, and can’t imagine how flushed he might be. He can handle compliments well, he thinks, but a compliment to his talent by someone equally talented will always mean more to him than the general, shallow ones. Not to mention it was from Ratio, who Mydei had previously thought had the emotional capacity of a rock.

He’s brought back to the dressing room once they’ve reviewed the footage and audio and declared the band good to go. Mydei is forced to stumble his way through no less than ten thank yous as several audience members pull him aside to congratulate him, or his talent. It’s refreshing, to be in a room full of people who all care for music as much as he does.

“Why do you seem so glum?” His stylist says, as she sits him down and starts wiping at his face and undoing his hair. “You did great!”

“I know,” Mydei says. “I mean—I don’t mean to be conceited, but I like to think I know what good music sounds like.”

“I’d say you do, too,” she laughs, putting down her wipe before moving to take off his jewelry. “Well, then? Spit it out.”

“It’s nothing,” Mydei chews on his lip. He wasn’t going to tell her, but now he wonders who she is to him that he has to worry about her knowing. “I just worry I’ve ruined my relationship with a close friend of mine.”

“Ah,” she shakes her head. Mydei hopes he doesn’t have to explain himself further than that, but it seems she understands. “I wonder how solid the friendship was on their end if such a thing as you loving them differently than they love you is enough to ruin it for them.”

Mydei looks down. “I guess,” he mumbles. He isn’t entirely convinced of her words. He doesn’t even know if he’s fully processed them yet.

“Well then. Go change, and then go home. But don’t let such a small adversity ruin your successful night.”

“I won’t,” Mydei promises, and he finds that he means it. What he had done tonight was something to be proud of, and he knows it. If Phainon wanted to ruin it by rejecting him, then that was on him.

December 20th, 3869.

Mydei’s apartment is silent when he arrives. It’s almost eerie, like the calm before the storm. He doesn’t know where Phainon is, but his shoes sit by the door and Mydei’s car keys are hung up on the coat rack. His heart is pounding as he sheds his coat and begins to untie his boots, resisting the urge to throw up what little food he had eaten after the show.

Part of him hopes Phainon did not understand. Deep down, though, he knows that he will. Now, it was all up to whether or not Phainon reciprocated Mydei’s feelings, which Mydei already knew was a no. He’s already accepted the ensuing rejection, and braces himself for it as he walks into the living room.

Phainon sits on the couch. He’s hunched over, head hanging in his hands. For a moment, Mydei reads this as despair—though he can’t imagine why —and then he lifts his head, and that’s unmistakable anger in his eyes.

Mydei sighs, turning towards the kitchen. “Can you let me eat something before you start yelling at me?”

“What?!” Phainon bursts, and Mydei can hear him stand up and start to follow him across the hall. “Mydei, you—Deliver the Dawn? Really?”

Mydei scowls as he opens the fridge. There’s one yogurt left. He was saving it for Phainon. Now, he tears the lid off so he can eat it in front of him out of spite.

“Are you serious right now?”

Mydei doesn’t entertain him with much of a response. “Yes. I’m hungry.”

“You wrote that whole fucking song about being in love with someone else and you have the audacity to name it after me?!”

Mydei pauses, spoonful of yogurt hovering just before his mouth. “What?”

Phainon looks like a mess—hair sticking up in every direction, eyes glassy and bloodshot, lips flushed and bloody from chewing at them relentlessly. “What do you mean, what? What the hell was I supposed to think?”

Mydei blinks. He’s not quite sure what Phainon’s conclusion is just yet, so he doesn’t know where to begin with a response.

“Did you think I was going to enjoy that?” Phainon continues. “This… confirmation that you’re always going to be out of reach for me? That you’ve moved on, leaving me to lament in your absence knowing that I’m never going to get to? Do you even know how much that hurts?”

“Phainon,” Mydei starts carefully. The magnitude of his stupidity is almost enough to offset the beginnings of giddiness in his chest, if Phainon means what he thinks he might. “You think Deliver the Dawn is about me moving on from you?”

“Don’t do that,” Phainon sneers, brows furrowed as he glares at Mydei. “Don't act confused like you’re not the one who wrote the fucking song!”

Mydei sets the yogurt down on the counter. “I did write the song,” he starts, “so I think I know what it’s about.”

“Look, Mydei,” Phainon continues, like he’s not listening to a single thing Mydei says. “I know that…that we are—”

“I don’t think you know anything,” Mydei interrupts, crossing his arms.

“Oh, I don’t?” Phainon argues, eyes wild. “Look, I’m sorry that taking me in was such torture to you, Mydei. If I had known how you really felt this whole time I would’ve been out of your place months ago.”

“What—”

“You know I’m in love with you,” Phainon confesses, voice barely above a whisper. “Don’t you?”

Mydei’s lips part. He thinks the amount of conflicting emotions he feels in this moment must be enough to send him into shock.

“I’m sorry,” Phainon breathes. “I’m sorry, I know I’m too late, I know, but I just…fuck, I’m sorry.”

The giddiness in Mydei’s chest slowly starts to subside into anger. How dare Phainon misinterpret his song so badly? How could the smartest man Mydei had ever met possibly be so stupid? It’s so baffling, that Mydei isn’t quite sure how he’s stayed in love with Phainon for so long.

“Look, I know this is awkward for you, but I’d really appreciate it if you would say something—”

“Are you serious?” Mydei starts, and Phainon reels back like he’s been struck. “You went on that date a month ago. You’re the one who hates every song I’ve written about you. You’re the one who said you’re incapable of loving anyone more than you love music. Aren’t you?”

“God forbid I try to move on,” Phainon shoots back. “Like you clearly already have, with Phoebe, and with that guy at the party—”

“I thought that guy was you.”

Phainon blinks. “What?”

“I wanted you, Phainon,” Mydei confesses. “It’s always been about you.”

“You…” Phainon exhales, face softening. He looks more hopeful than Mydei has seen him in a long time, and it’s this quickly that all of Mydei’s

ire dissipates. “You do?”

“Yes,” Mydei confesses, quietly. “I do, I…I have.” For how long, Mydei doesn’t know. He thinks, now, that he never stopped.

“Can you say it?” Phainon requests. His eyes are wide, like he’s hands Mydei his heart of glass and prays that he doesn’t break it. “I need to hear you say it.”

Mydei swallows. “I love you,” he murmurs. “I wrote every song for you, because even if they’re not about you, I want you to like them,” he admits, and this confession is somehow worse than the first one. “You’re really the only critic who matters.”

“And Deliver the Dawn?” Phainon prods.

“I thought you were moving on,” Mydei explains. “It’s about you. Not me.”

“Fuck,” Phainon groans. “I would ask you how you thought that, but I guess I did a good job pretending to—”

Mydei steps forward, and Phainon stops. He can see the bob of his throat as he swallows, then lifts his eyes to meet Mydei’s. He looks a little scared. Mydei licks his lips. “Are we done?”

“With—” Phainon wets his lips, too. “With what…?”

“Discussing asinine topics.”

Phainon slowly starts to nod, like he’s hypnotized. “Yes.”

Mydei doesn’t waste a second longer. He steps forward, determined, and kisses him.

Phainon meets him halfway, hands gripping Mydei’s hips so tightly it almost hurts. Their bodies slot together, just as perfectly as they did all those years ago. It feels familiar and different and everything in between, Phainon licking into his mouth with an urgency that was never quite present

back then. Like he didn’t know, the last time they’d kissed, that it would truly be their last.

His hands are everywhere, hot against Mydei’s face, neck, slipping under his leather jacket as he forces it off his shoulders and to the floor. And then they’re underneath his shirt, and Mydei nearly hisses with such immense heat against his stomach. He nips at Phainon’s lips, trying to get him to stop, but he doesn’t, not until Mydei grips his shoulders and shoves him off.

“What’s gotten into you?” Mydei asks, laughing a little at how red Phainon has gotten. “Has it really been that long?”

“Stop it, Mydei.” Phainon steps forward and grabs Mydei’s wrist, before promptly dragging him down the hall.

“Oh my god,” Mydei laughs in disbelief. “Phainon. You haven’t slept with anyone else?”

“You have?” Phainon demands, pausing for a moment in between both of their bedroom doors.

“Sorry to disappoint,” Mydei says, still amused. “I wasn’t going to go celibate just because we broke up, Phainon.”

“And?”

Mydei snorts. “I know what you want to hear.”

“So? Say it.”

“No, Phainon. It wasn’t as good.”

Phainon pulls Mydei close, squeezing his back tightly in a near-possessive embrace. “You’re going to kill me, Mydei,” he groans, voice muffled into Mydei’s shoulder. “And…for the record, I haven’t been entirely celibate either.”

Mydei shakes his head in disbelief. “And?” he asks, partially as a joke, partially serious.

“It wasn’t as good either.”

Mydei laughs, shaking him free and pulling him into his bedroom. He flicks the light on, kicking the door shut behind them. “You’re clean, then?”

Phainon wastes no time in pushing Mydei onto the bed, immediately pinning his hands down to the sides of his head. “Yes,” he murmurs, kissing him lightly. “You’re that eager to go raw?”

“Ew, what is wrong with you?”

Phainon doesn’t seem remotely deterred by such a comment, simply pulling Mydei’s shirt up over his chest. It’s a bit of a struggle, but he manages to get it over his head and tosses it to the floor.  All of the fear from earlier is thoroughly gone. “Then who is going to make love to you so—”

“Phainon.” Mydei grabs the hair against the nape of his neck and pulls him down, silencing him with his lips instead.

“Yes, yes, Mydei—” Phainon manages between kisses. “How dare I forget how impatient you are.”

Mydei laughs softly against his lips, a little breathless as Phainon’s hands wander lower and lower, unzipping his fly and then sliding back up to his waist to rub little circles into the sides of his hips. When they finally part, there’s hardly any space between them, foreheads pressed together.

Mydei’s head spins with giddiness. There’s unwritten melodies clouding his brain, and he can hardly wait to sit at the piano and write about him how he had always wanted.

“You’re so beautiful, Mydeimos,” Phainon whispers, hands trailing up over his chest. Mydei’s whole body tingles with it, the feeling of his rough scars against his skin.

Mydei exhales, the sound somewhere between a scoff and a laugh. He pulls Phainon’s hand from his neck and laces their fingers together. “Stop talking,” he requests, and Phainon leans back in.

Mydei wakes up when the sunlight filtering in through his curtains hits his face. He squints, shifting a little, only to be trapped in place by a pair of warm arms.

He can hardly contain his joy as the memories from last night fly back to him. Phainon was his again. It was as he had always wanted.

He lifts his head up as much as he can, searching for his phone, only to find an empty nightstand and his charger disconnected. He sighs, unable to find it in himself to be annoyed—he must have fallen asleep too quickly last night. But he needs to know what time it is, so he carefully ejects himself from Phainon’s hold and moves to his dresser to put some clothes on.

His phone sits on the kitchen island, and he turns it on to find that it’s not dead, but is getting to that point. He has an unread email from Aventurine congratulating them on a great performance, and a couple missed texts from the CALAMITY group chat.
