Mydei sighs, unsure how she was able to figure that out so quickly. He goes back into his bedroom, plugging his phone in and sitting down at the edge of the bed.

Phainon has never looked more at peace, face perfectly relaxed. His mouth is slightly open, hair mussed, snoring quietly. Watching Phainon sleep has always made Mydei happy, with how rarely it seemed to come to him.

He pushes Phainon’s bangs out of the way so he can press a soft kiss to his forehead. He stirs slightly, mouth closing, but he doesn’t wake.

Mydei wants to spend the rest of his life like this. Phainon in his apartment, in his bed—he wants to wake up every morning with Phainon’s body heat warming his bedsheets. He wants Phainon to attend all of his shows, and he wants to attend all of Phainon’s. Just him, really, was all he ever wanted. The album doesn’t matter. Fame and money don’t matter. Nothing else matters.

He leaves to shower, and can hear faint music playing from the kitchen when he steps out of the bathroom.

“I made breakfast,” Phainon says, when he hears Mydei come around the corner. “How do you feel?”

Mydei takes in the two plates of food laid out on the island. It’s a similar feeling to the one he got when he had first cooked for him, when he was recovering from that awful hangover. He thinks he could be with Phainon for the rest of his life.

“I love you,” he says, coming up behind him and planting a kiss to the back of his neck.

Phainon flushes a little, but grins at Mydei as he turns over his shoulder. “I love you too, Mydei,” he says softly. “Can you imagine if we had just told each other this five months ago?”

Mydei laughs, pulling Phainon away from the sink to sit at the island together. He takes his first couple bites of the egg, potato, and sausage hash he had made in silence. Phainon had already seasoned it perfectly, with extra hot sauce on Mydei’s portion. Such a feeling never quite fails to send butterflies through his stomach.

“Am I going to have to meet your dog now?” Mydei finally speaks up. It’s a much less vulnerable question than what he really wants to ask.

Phainon stops chewing, staring at his plate for a few moments. “Really?” he asks, voice deadpan.

Obviously, he wasn’t fully serious. He wasn’t about to let something like a stupid mutt ruin this for him. “Yes,” he says, just to make Phainon sweat a little.

“Mydei, I’m not getting rid of my dog.”

“Fine,” Mydei starts. “But if I recall correctly, you implied that you hate my music last night.”

“Mydei, what?”

Mydei frowns, taking another bite of his food. When Phainon looks at him, mouth open in shock, he merely shrugs.

“Oh my god.” Phainon laughs, disbelieving. “I’m sorry. I obviously don’t actually think that.”

“Maybe so.” Mydei shovels the rest of his food into his mouth, washing it down with the pomegranate juice-and-milk concoction set out for him.

“Mydei.” Phainon’s voice is more serious now, as he watches Mydei move to the sink. “I’m serious. I love your music.”

“You better, because I’d break up with you if you didn’t.” Mydei puts his plate into the dishwasher, then loads his silverware in as well.

“So we’re dating?”

Mydei sighs. “I’d hope so.”

“Is that a yes?”

“How about you answer that one for yourself?” Mydei asks, then leaves to unplug his phone from his room. Castorice texted that she’s on her way two minutes ago, so he needs to hurry up.

When he walks back to the kitchen, Phainon has finished as well, and is in the middle of clearing his plate away. “Yes,” he says, turning to look at Mydei.

“Yes…what?”

“We’re dating.”

Mydei snorts, putting his phone in his pocket as he goes to the front door to begin putting his shoes on. “Good to know.”

“You’re in a good mood today,” Castorice says, as Mydei climbs into the passenger side of her car.

“Yeah?” Mydei clicks in his seatbelt, and puts his bag on the floor between his feet. “What makes you say that?”

“I don’t know. You seem lighter.” Castorice shifts the gear of her car, and heads down the road. “Has anything happened with Phainon?”

Mydei sighs, leaning his head against the window. “Why is everyone saying that?” he mutters.

“You sang him the song you wrote about him last night,” Castorice says, shrugging. “I think he’s smart enough to figure it out.”

Mydei hums. Not quite, but it’s a kind thought.

“So?”

“So…?”

“So, did you talk with him?”

“About what?”

“Stop playing dumb, Mydei.”

Mydei laughs, sitting up straight. He can’t help but smile just thinking about it. “We argued,” he says instead, continuing to laugh a little at the memory. Phainon tended to jump to conclusions that Mydei didn’t even know were possible.

“So he did figure it out.”

“No, not really.”

“What?” Castorice turns to stare at him in bewilderment as her car rolls to a stop before a red light. “What did he think it was about?”

“Me moving on…I think.”

Silence falls between them. Castorice blinks at him, wide-eyed, before she snorts, and starts laughing. Mydei can’t help but join her, still in disbelief about the absurdity of it all. “You told him he was wrong, right?” she asks, through her laughter.

“Yes.”

“And now, you’re…?”

“Dating. Yes.”

The light turns green, and they start moving again, Castorice smiling a little. “That’s really great, Mydei. I’m happy for both of you.”

“I’m happy for you too, you know,” Mydei turns to her, watching her carefully as she continues to drive. “You’ve opened up a lot. It’s nice to see.”

“You think so?” Castorice asks. “I am happy,” she continues, shaking her head a little. “I was thinking last night that I don’t really care how well our album does. I just love making music with you guys.”

“Funnily enough, I was thinking something similar this morning,” Mydei admits. “Regardless, I’m sure it will do well. If it was bad, I hope someone would have told us by now.”

Castorice laughs again, as she pulls into the IPC parking lot. “Yeah. I’d hope so.”

They arrive first today, swiping into the building and heading up to their recording studio. Mydei stares at their white board, still with hardly any songs placed into spots on the setlist. They still have to record Castorice’s song, and after that, they have nothing.

It’s not like Mydei is lacking inspiration, though. He could have written a thousand songs about Phainon before they got together, and he still can today.

Perhaps spurred on by the overwhelming success of their Christmas special, they start what slowly but surely becomes their most productive day yet. Ratio joins them late, already a quarter into recording Castorice’s song by themselves. He enters quietly, in the middle of one of Mydei’s takes. He can’t quite get the tone of voice right. The song calls for something softer, something he’s not incapable of but is less used to.

Hyacine has told him they got a good take four times already. It’s Mydei’s fault alone that they’re dragging it out as long as they have.

Mydei pushes the headphones down to sit around his neck as the music stops, already frustrated. Castorice has handed Ratio a copy of their score, explaining it to him quietly during the last take.

“That was good, Mydei,” Hyacine’s voice is muffled from the outside of his recording booth.

“One more time,” Mydei calls back. He takes a sip of water, puts the headset back on, and picks up the score from off the music stand before him.

“Uh—the whole thing?” Hyacine sounds slightly concerned. Mydei doesn’t look up from the music, crossing out one of the notes he had written in previously.

“Yes, just the main vocal line, please,” Mydei answers.

“Alright…” A couple mouse clicks, and the beginning of the computerized instrumentals begin to play again. Mydei starts singing on his cue, careful to keep his voice as soft as possible this time.

Even on their less classic rock-adjacent tracks, Mydei has never had to fight to keep the roughness out of his singing voice before. It was part of their sound, and while Hyacine and Castorice would both probably tell him that it was okay for this song to sound as he usually does, he doesn’t entirely agree with that.

Castorice wrote this song for Cipher. For Mydei, it was about Phainon—but it wasn’t bitter, like Deliver the Dawn. He could be as angry as he wanted while performing that song because it only enhanced it. Castorice, discouraged as she might have been while writing it, would never write out of a place of anger. He doesn’t want to do that to her song.

He steps back once the vocal part is done, dragging a hand down his face. It was better that time. It will do, for now at least.

“Was that it?” Cipher asks. She sounds bored as ever.

“Yes,” Mydei answers. “Sure.”

Ratio speaks up next, the first he’s heard his input during this session. “Sure doesn’t sound too convincing to me.”

“Oh my god, that was the fifth fucking take,” Cipher groans. “He sounded good the first time.”

Mydei relents, setting down the headset and exiting the booth. “It’s enough for now,” he says, moving to collapse onto the couch. There are only so

many times he can sing the same song in a row before his takes stop improving entirely.

“Alright,” Ratio turns the page to the packet he’s been given, scrutinizing all the parts before he decides who should record what next. “Hyacine, let’s do both guitar parts.”

Mydei would usually record the acoustic guitar part, given that it’s the part he’d usually play for their tours, but Hyacine is perfectly capable of playing both. So he sits on the couch and observes, trying to finish his water bottle before it’s his turn again. He never does his best work when he’s annoyed.

Hyacine gets both parts done in a little under twenty minutes, given that it’s essentially her first time reading the music. Cipher and Castorice go together, which they usually do. Mydei loves listening to the rhythm section record. Those two always seem to be so in tune with each other, despite their glaring differences. Cipher might take pleasure in annoying Castorice to no end, but the second they’re playing together, it’s like they’re speaking a language only the two of them know.

“Good,” Ratio says, and they exit the booth. Cipher gives Castorice a high five she only half-heartedly returns, but it puts a smile on Mydei’s face anyways. “There are a lot of instruments here that could be added in production, then,” Ratio continues, clicking through his production software until all the recorded tracks are added to a new save. “Accordion, for example. If you really want to find someone to record that part for you—”

“God, no,” Cipher drawls, collapsing next to Mydei in a heap. “Accordion players are the last people in the world I’d ever want to interact with.”

“Accordion is not too different from piano,” Mydei retorts, shooting her a glance.

Cipher snorts. “Exactly.” Mydei should have expected that.

“Anyways, it doesn’t sound super artificial if I add it in here,” Ratio says. He clicks a few buttons, putting the part Castorice had written into the software, before clicking play.

It does sound good. Mydei turns to Castorice, and she’s smiling. “I think that’s perfect,” she says, once it’s over and Ratio looks at her expectantly.

“Alright,” Ratio resumes his clicking, even though he can somehow talk through his focus. “Mydei, if you’re ready to record again, you’re up, and then we can do backing vocals.”

Mydei nods, downing the rest of his water bottle before standing up.

“Won’t you tell us what was so wrong with that take?” Hyacine asks.

“Too rough,” Mydei says. Cipher snorts, and he shoots her a glare. “I don’t know. I think my voice should be softer for this song.”

“Aw,” Cipher snickers. “So cute. What changed?”

“Can you shut up?”

“It’s all ready for you, Mydei,” Ratio says, giving him a small smile that’s almost apologetic in its nature. “Just relax. That’s all I can really tell you.”

Mydei nods, and pulls on the headset as he steps into the booth. He has to note that as soon as the instrumentals start playing, he feels instantly better than he had before, when all he had was a computerized score to accompany him.

He closes his eyes as he starts singing. It’s always better for him to pretend there’s no one watching. By the time he’s done, he’s almost surprised at how that had been so difficult for him just an hour ago. Were he singing a song about unrequited love, still thinking Phainon had someone else in his heart, he thinks it would have been a hundred times more difficult to soften his vocals than it had been today. Now, there’s no reason to worry anymore. Phainon had always been his.

“Yeah,” he says, once the music cuts out. “That’s the one.”

“Fucking finally,” Cipher groans. He’s honestly surprised at how impatient she’s being today, given that six total takes was far from the most amount of times Mydei has asked to redo something.

“Cas? You’re good with that?”

“I think that was perfect.” Mydei has never seen a bigger smile on her face, and it doesn’t fail to put an equally big one on his own.

Hyacine is sent into the booth to record backing vocals next. There was a bit of debate about who should do it, between the three of them—Mydei was always an option, of course, to match his own voice, but sometimes the song sounded better with a different color behind it. In this case, Mydei thought Hyacine was the obvious choice, even though Cipher thought it should have been Castorice. Castorice was ultimately the tie-breaker, who agreed that Hyacine would fit better.

Backing vocals take almost longer than Mydei’s main vocals, with the amount of layers and retakes they have to do. Mydei coaches her a bit on how to phrase her harmonies. Ratio, as always, listens to every single request they make.

They break for lunch, Ratio promising to finish it up while they’re out. They pick a fast food restaurant to go to quickly, and Castorice drives all four of them.

Mydei’s quiet the whole drive there, while Phainon texts him about groceries. Despite how much he loves the band and the music they’ve been making recently, he wishes he had the day off.

“You miss him that much, huh?” Cipher asks, sitting down across from him after she picks up their orders. “Stop smiling at your dick, dude, it’s weird.”

Mydei makes a show of turning his phone off, placing it face-down on the table. “How do you even know who I was texting?”

“All three of us are here,” she scoffs. “The only other person you talk to is Phainon.”

“You make it sound so sad,” Mydei says, as Hyacine hands him the burger he ordered. He has fast food so rarely that he allowed himself something unhealthy, just this once.

“So it was him,” Cipher grins, and Mydei can see that her mouth is full of food. He shudders, turning back down to unwrap his food.

“Stop it, Cipher,” Hyacine says. Mydei thinks he can feel her kick Cipher under the table. “It’s none of our business.”

Cipher looks at him, raising an eyebrow.

“Fine,” he sighs, exasperated. “Yes. We’re dating. Is that what you want to hear?”

Hyacine gasps, but Cipher just looks unimpressed. “He told me that already, little prince. From you, I want the details.”

Mydei is going to kill Phainon for betraying him like that, but that’s for later. He pushes it aside. “If it’s details you’re after, I think you’re better off asking him.”

“And I’d prefer not knowing,” Castorice speaks up.

“Thank you, Cas,” Mydei says. He hides the way he blushes, even if slight, behind a bite of his burger.

Cipher huffs. “You all are so boring.”

“You just called your girlfriend boring,” Mydei points out.

“You two are so boring,” Cipher corrects, pointing at both Mydei and Hyacine.

“What did I do?!” Hyacine exclaims.

“Oh my god,” Cipher mutters. “Fine. Mydei, you are boring.”

All because he doesn’t want to share his sex life. He thinks that’s a little bit of an unfair accusation, but he’s willing to accept the insult for now.

“I’ll ask him, then,” Cipher adds, almost quiet enough that Mydei couldn’t hear it. But he does, and he immediately picks up his phone to tell Phainon

not to give her a single detail.

The entire building is nearly empty by the time they have a good idea. Usually, Mydei would be itching to leave—they rarely stay past five, especially during their recording sessions. And if inspiration wasn’t striking, the best solution would be to go home and try again tomorrow.

Unfortunately, today is loads of fun. Ratio is gone by the time they get back, so they sprawl out on the floor together and bounce ideas off each other. According to the deadline set up by them months ago, they really only have a couple days to finish their album. But realistically, good art takes time. So no one in this room feels rushed to throw together a good song, because good songs are never thrown together.

“If you guys weren’t musicians, what would you be?” Hyacine asks, filling up a moment of silence. It’s questions like these that have been hindering the four of them from writing down an actual song idea.

“Pianist,” Mydei says immediately.

“That’s still a musician, dumb fuck,” Cipher replies, smacking him in the back of the head. It actually hurts, but Mydei doesn’t say anything.

“Historian, then.”

“Ew, okay. Guess we know who’s going broke out of the four of us.”

“What would you do to make so much money then, Cipher?” Hyacine prompts.

“I don’t know, rob a bank?”

“Like you’ll get away with that. You’re not nearly intelligent, intimidating, or agile enough.” Mydei has never thought very in depth about robbing a bank before. But he thinks he could get away with it if he did.

“If I get caught, would you bail me out with daddy’s money?”

Mydei laughs so hard he shocks himself with it. “Maybe with my mother’s money.”

“What if I killed someone?”

Mydei squints at her. “Are you trying to see how far I would go for you?”

Cipher shrugs, leaning all the way back on the couch until her head hands off the arm rest. “I’m just saying, if you killed someone, I would help you cover it up.”

“Kind of you.”

By the time the sun has begun to set, Mydei isn’t quite sure why he’s exhausted enough to leave just yet. After all, Phainon is waiting for him, but Mydei knows that Phainon will understand.

Hyacine’s hair has started falling out of her ponytail, Cipher is on her third energy drink, and Castorice smells heavily of weed. The result of her last “bathroom break”, no doubt. But they sit in the darkening room, no one with any strong desire to leave.

“I love you guys,” Castorice confesses, into the carpet her face is pressed into. Mydei’s stomach tumbles with giddiness. He’s so overcome with joy that he almost can’t contain it in a normal way. Because he thinks that when he’s inevitably on his deathbed, it’s these moments that he will look back on and miss the most.

“I love you too, Cassie,” Hyacine says, patting Castorice’s shoulder lightly.

“Wait, idea,” Cipher suddenly sits up straight, eyes wide. “We should write a happy song.”

“What?”

“Come on,” Cipher says. “Every song on this album is bleak as fuck. Our audience will have no other choice but to believe we hate each other.”

“Will they…?” Hyacine asks, voice doubtful. Castorice has lifted her head now, and even with her eyes glazed over she looks like she might like Cipher’s idea.

“Cat Food isn’t bleak,” Mydei attempts, determined to disprove her. They recorded him laughing outside of the studio and added it to the track, what about that was bleak?

“Yes it is, if you’re less dense than a brick,” Cipher shoots back.

“City of Thieves?”

“Shut up, Mydei, it’s about the vibe. None of our songs sound fun.”

No one says anything, silently playing through the track list in their heads. She’s sort of right. There are very few songs on the album that Mydei would consider “fun”. But maybe that was for a reason. Maybe it just wasn’t for them.

“Fun,” Castorice mumbles. “Sure.”

Mydei doesn’t remember Hyacine getting a hold of her guitar, but all of a sudden she’s strumming a pattern off the top of her head on all open strings. It’s fast, much faster than any of the acoustic guitar parts they’d ever written. Honestly, Mydei didn’t even know she could do that. Her skills are so much more recognizable on electric guitar.

“Woah,” he says. That’s all it really took to be on board with Cipher’s idea.

“That is perfect, Hyacine,” Cipher scrambles to go unpack her bass, which she had never even opened until now.

“You think so?” Hyacine blushes a little. Mydei moves over to the piano.

“F sharp,” Mydei suggests, and Hyacine plays the same strumming pattern, this time on an F sharp chord. When she repeats it, he joins in on piano, playing a melody off the top of his head. When he switches to a G chord, it takes Hyacine moments to shift her chord to a G, as well. Mydei smiles

wide when he hears it. To think the three of them had such minimal theory knowledge just mere months ago, and now their ears are just as good as his.

“That is it,” Cipher cheers, while they continue. It doesn’t take long for them to fall apart, but it doesn’t matter. It’s more of a start than anyone was expecting.

Cipher writes a simple bassline to go underneath Hyacine. As they play together, Mydei hums the beginnings of a melody above them. He doesn’t even notice Castorice pulling herself off the floor and moving to the drum kit until she, too, joins in. The line she adds is much less polished than what she usually writes, shocking Mydei with how uncharacteristic it sounds. Her eyes are fully closed, and Mydei can tell that this is exactly what she feels at this moment. And it’s perfect.

Hyacine ditches her acoustic guitar, picking up her electric one to add a solo of her own. Inspired by all of it, Mydei joins back in on piano. Her solo ends, and he picks it up—playing whatever he wants, but remaining in the key. He thinks, unable to keep the smile off his face, that this might be the most fun he’s had in months.

Hyacine vocalizes on top of everything once he ends his piano solo, causing Mydei to join in on harmony. And then, somehow, they all cut out at the same time.

Mydei doesn’t know what to say. He doesn’t think anyone else does either, if the way they stare at each other in shock is anything to go off.

“I fucking told you we had it in us.” Cipher breaks the silence. “Are we kidding? That was amazing!”

Polishing it is a breeze. The lyrics come quickly, oddly enough, though no one is one hundred percent sure what it’s about. Maybe it’s about something different to everyone, and Mydei thinks that’s beautiful.

It’s nearly midnight by the time they finish. Mydei’s stomach hurts from how much he’s been laughing tonight. He can’t name a single thing in his

life that upsets him anymore, and the final recording of Argonautica (Castorice’s title) perfectly expresses exactly how he feels now.

They part ways in the parking lot, saying their goodbyes for the next few days. Talks about spending New Year’s together were already in question, but they all had prior plans for Christmas. Mydei didn’t, when they had first talked about it, but now he supposed he would be with Phainon.

He wishes Castorice a merry Christmas as she drops him off outside his apartment building. His family had never been one to celebrate the winter holidays very much, but the festive decorations in the apartment lobby and overplayed Christmas music on the speakers somehow manages to fill him with a warm sort of contentment. He doesn’t think he felt the same way about it a year ago, though.

The hallways are silent as he walks to his apartment, quietly humming the tune of Argonautica, which he was unable to get out of his head.

He’s promised Phainon to play him the album before its release, but hasn’t allowed him to hear a single studio recording, no matter how much he begs. While Phainon’s input would be extremely valuable were he recording a collection of original classical pieces, the man doesn’t know the first thing about rock music.

He’s met with the unmistakable sounds of piano music gracing his ears the second he opens the door to his apartment. He’s so shocked by the raw emotion that strikes him that he stands in the doorway for a second, afraid that moving will disturb Phainon into stopping. He rarely practiced with Mydei at home these days; Mydei knew from the sheet music piling up in the living room that he had been practicing, but Mydei rarely heard it.

He had no idea Phainon had improved this much. The last piece he knew of him working on was the medium-difficulty Chopin étude he had told him about at the grocery store, and now Mydei is met with an almost perfect piano rendition of Tchaikovsky’s pas de deux.

It had always been Phainon’s favorite piece from the Nutcracker. Mydei never quite understood his fixation on it. He wasn’t a very big fan of large, emotional pieces when they weren’t as fast as he might have liked it. Now, though, he thinks he knows perfectly well what Phainon was talking about.

He shuts the door as silently as he can, before bending down to untie his shoes. The music is almost enough to bring Mydei to tears—even when Phainon stumbles over the notes, even when he makes a mistake. He doesn’t stop, or go back to correct himself, and when Mydei takes off his jacket and walks forward to see the inside of the living room, he can see Phainon with his eyes closed, no notes on the stand. He’s playing from his head—or heart, maybe—and such a thing as an incorrect note is not enough to stop him.

Phainon isn’t playing to learn the piece, he’s playing because he wants to, because he loves it. A skill Mydei always wished he had. He wished he could play piano like Phainon did. He wished he loved it as much as Phainon did. But alas, there was little Mydei loved more than the music he made today—and even less that he loved more than Phainon.

The moon casts a silvery, ethereal sort of glow over the room. Phainon’s hair shines white, glowing as if lit by a halo sitting behind his head. It’s almost funny, how perfectly romantic this scene is. How Phainon looks when kissed by the moon is akin to Mydei laying his eyes on a god. The music he creates swirls around them, and Mydei has never felt like this in his life. Not when they were dating in college, not with any potential partner he had ever met between then and now. Loving Phainon was not foreign, but loving him this much was. Like he’d die for him. A thousand times, if that was what Phainon needed. A million, or multiple millions. Whatever Phainon asked for, whatever he wanted, Mydei would give. If it was something he could not give, then he would sooner cut his own throat out than give up trying.

Phainon stops, hands resting on the keys as he holds out the last note. And then his shoulders relax and his posture slumps, breathing out a soft sigh as his hands come to rest on his thighs. He flexes them once, twice. Mydei feels like he can’t talk without crying.

He tries, anyway. “Phainon,” he murmurs, his voice catching a barely noticeable amount. He’s quiet, but the room is even quieter.

Phainon startles, nearly jumping out of his seat as he turns to Mydei. “Mydei,” he says, louder than he most likely intended. “I—I didn’t know you were here,” he continues, eyes wide. Then, quieter, “Why didn’t you tell me you were coming home early?”

Home. It’s such a simple word, the kind of thing that doesn’t really mean anything unless you choose to give it meaning. He had never thought, before today, that he would hear the word from anyone and allow it to affect him in such a way. Regardless, shivers run down his spine as he hears it. He would like Phainon to be home with him. For the rest of their lives.

“I’m in love with you,” Mydei confesses.

Phainon breathes out a little laugh. “I thought we clarified that already.” Despite his retort, he still blushes at Mydei’s words. Like he’s not used to hearing them.

“I don’t know how else to put it,” Mydei says. “I love you.”

“Did I put a spell on you with that piece, or something?”

“Was that what you were trying to do?” Mydei knows that’s not the case, but he wouldn’t be surprised if it was. He certainly feels like it worked, anyway.

“No,” Phainon frowns. “But I played it for you.”

“For me, when you didn’t even know I would be home.”

“For you, Mydei,” Phainon confirms. “I just. Thought of you, and played what I felt.”

The irony of Phainon throwing Mydei’s old words back at him isn’t lost on him, and he wonders if this is the way Phainon felt when he had said it to him, all those years ago. “Pas de deux,” he muses. “That’s quite an honor.”

“You know, I’ve listened to that song almost every day since you left me.”

“I just started to understand why you like it so much, the second I walked through the door.”

Phainon laughs, standing from the piano bench. “Did you ever wonder what such a piece is doing in the middle of an otherwise upbeat ballet?” Of course Mydei hasn’t. Phainon knows this, so he continues without waiting for an answer. “His sister died mid writing it,” he says. “It was to commemorate her.”

Mydei raises an eyebrow. “You are likening me breaking up with you to your sibling dying.”

“Stop it, Mydei,” Phainon huffs, moving forward until they’re mere inches away. “The point is the loss, not the relationship.”

“You could have reached out to me at any point,” Mydei says. He’s unable to stop his eyes from flicking down to Phainon’s lips. “That’s your fault. Not mine.”

“Stop it,” Phainon says again, and kisses him. It’s light, but Mydei’s lips still tingle from the loss when they break apart.

“You’re too stubborn,” Mydei says. “That’s what stopped you, wasn’t it?”

“You said I reminded you of everything you were trying to forget,” Phainon’s voice is heavy when he says it, and it sends a pang through Mydei’s heart. “I would have reached out to you in a heartbeat if I thought there was even a small chance you would respond.”

“I did not say that,” Mydei says, shaking his head. He’s pretty sure he didn’t, anyway. He thinks he would feel more guilty if he had really said something like that.

“The point is, I wanted to give you your peace,” Phainon argues. “I might have made more of an effort after Rach 2, if…” he trails off, expression hardening out of nowhere.

“If Phoebe wasn’t in the picture,” Mydei finishes for him.

“No,” Phainon says immediately. Then, something a little closer to the obvious truth, “Maybe.”

“You need to stop bringing her up,” Mydei says.

“I didn’t bring her up—”

“We both know I said what you wanted to.” Mydei shakes his head. “Phainon, Phoebe broke up with me because she could see that I was still in love with you.”

Phainon’s mouth parts, eyes widening. He shakes his head, like he doesn’t quite believe it, and Mydei shushes him.

“I didn’t believe her,” he says. “I let her go, obviously, because she wanted that, but it wasn’t until recently that I realized how right she was.” Mydei frowns. “And how blind I’ve been.”

Phainon looks distraught, taking a tiny step backwards as he begins to process everything. “Was she upset?” Is the first thing he asks. Mydei almost grimaces at such a reaction. It’s not what he was expecting at all.

“Of course she was,” he answers. “What I did was wrong. She reacted as anyone would.”

“And you haven’t spoken since.”

“No, Phainon. We were never really friends.”

“And we were?”

Those words catch Mydei off guard. He doesn’t really know what to say, opening and closing his mouth like a fish. “Yes,” he tries to say, but it sounds just as forced as it feels. He’d always thought Phainon was his best friend both before and during their relationship. He still thinks Phainon is his best friend today, but if he’s really being honest, they’ve always been something a little bit more than that. Even when their relationship wasn’t

inherently romantic, it was like their souls had been tied together somehow. Meeting Phainon for the first time felt, in retrospect, like every decision in his life had led him up to that point. He didn’t feel that way with Hephaestion.

“Mydei,” Phainon says, and Mydei can tell by the tone of his voice that he knows Mydei is lying. “It’s why I never called,” he continues. “Trying to reconnect could only mean…one thing, really. I didn’t want to disturb what you had, or—or make you think I was trying to get in your pants, or something.”

“I never called, because…” Mydei stops, chewing at his lip. “I don’t know, I guess. I knew that if you never did, I never would have.”

“But if I did,” Phainon lifts his head, eyes swirling with desperation. “If I did, would you have picked up?”

“Of course,” Mydei says without hesitation. “Would you?”

“Mydei.” Phainon is near whispering, and Mydei knows exactly what he means. The answer is obvious. “I’ve loved you since the day I met you.”

“You’re lying,” Mydei says, smiling. “You told me you thought I was arrogant.”

“Did I say that?” Phainon jerks backwards, blushing. “I’m pretty sure I said your playing…sounded arrogant?”

Mydei laughs, tugging on Phainon’s arm to bring him in closer. “I’m pretty sure you hated me,” he whispers, teasing, into the side of Phainon’s neck.

“What—don’t even say that, Mydei,” Phainon argues, pulling back to study Mydei’s face like he’s trying to drink all of him in. “Maybe I was intimidated. That’s as far as it goes.”

“Intimidated,” Mydei muses, raising an eyebrow. “I think that’s worse.” Mydei has been called intimidating before. Even when he was a teenager, before the hair dye and tattoos and piercings, his mother had told him that

people probably were wary of him because of his perpetual scowl and blunt way of speaking. It was the case both inside and outside of Kremnos—even in his hometown, he was outcasted in the same way. From Phainon, though, it’s new.

“You know I didn’t mean it like that,” Phainon says, as if vocalizing Mydei’s thoughts. “I liked you…eventually.”

“I know,” Mydei responds. His arms come up on instinct, pulling Phainon impossibly close and slotting his chin against Phainon’s neck, like two pieces of a puzzle coming together. Sometimes he thinks their bodies were molded with each other in mind.

Phainon sighs heavily, like the feeling of Mydei’s arms around him have freed him from a weight on his shoulders. He presses his hands into Mydei’s back, one of them coming to settle right over the spot on his spine. Mydei shudders at such a familiar feeling he didn’t know he was missing. Perhaps it’s subconscious when Phainon lifts one of his fingers, nail scratching directly over the bone as he’d done so many times.

“Phainon,” he whispers, voice muffled with the fabric of Phainon’s shirt.

“It doesn’t hurt anymore,” Phainon whispers back. “Right?”

“No,” Mydei responds. He squeezes his arms even tighter around Phainon as his nail turns into the pad of his finger, soothing over the vertebrae, touch so light it’s more a caress than anything. “Not since you’ve been back.”

The room has dimmed significantly when they pull apart, the moon hidden behind a thick cloud. “Stay,” Mydei requests, or demands. He regrets the words as soon as they leave his mouth, but doesn’t take them back.

Phainon nods. They don’t talk about the logistics of that. They don’t bring up the flights that were already booked, or his belongings, or his dog. He nods, and Mydei knows they’ll figure it out.

They buy a Christmas tree the next morning. Phainon’s parents always had a live tree that they planted in the farm after it was up for a week. They would decorate it together on Christmas Eve, and take it down on New Year’s. Mydei’s mother had the estate decorated by her staff. The main tree was always massive, and fake.

Living in the city means they can’t have either of these things, so they settle on a tiny potted cypress tree and each of them buy one ornament, since it can’t handle much more than that. Phainon’s is the head of a stupid stuffed animal—some blue creature with sunglasses and a sunhat. He calls it Bubbles and selects it the second he sees it, like it was meant to be. Mydei’s is a sharp sphere of red crystals. Phainon says it looks like it could kill someone, but Mydei thinks it’s pretty.

They set the tree on the living room coffee table. Not two minutes have passed before Kokopo III is chewing at the leaves, and Mydei scolds her before feeling bad and giving her a treat.

The next morning, it’s knocked over, dirt spilling from the pot. Mydei’s red ornament is shattered on the floor, and he’s only irritated for a minute or so before he decides that it was his fault for foolishly buying a glass ornament.

It’s snowing too heavily to leave, so he spends the morning super-gluing it back together and puts it back on the tree. This time, they set it on the kitchen island. Kokopo III isn’t allowed up there, and she knows this, but Mydei supposes that won’t stop her from going up there when she has the apartment to herself.

On Sunday, Christmas Eve, they attend the matinee showing of the Nutcracker. They had bought last minute tickets after Phainon saw an advertisement for it and begged Mydei to go. Mydei can only deny him so much, so of course he obliged.

They exchange gifts when they get back, instrumental Christmas music playing on the TV. Phainon’s choice, not Mydei’s, but again, he can only deny him so much. He makes two mugs of hot chocolate and they sit together on the couch, as more snow begins to fall outside.

They each get each other two presents. Phainon starts by handing Mydei a little box, which he opens to find a beautiful golden guitar pick.

“Gold,” Phainon says, suddenly sounding shy. “To match all the gold you wear.”

Mydei nods, but looking at it, he can’t help but be reminded of the little flecks of gold in Phainon’s eyes, or the way his hair looks under the sun. He turns it over in his hand, and almost drops it when he sees the little engraving on the back. HKS, it reads, above a little heart.

“Oh my god,” he laughs, at the old Kremnoan word, one of his favorite insults in college. “Thank you, Phainon. I’m never going to use any other pick.”

“I’ll hold you to it,” Phainon smiles. Mydei isn’t sure if Phainon knows that he rarely used the word on anyone else.

He gives Phainon his first present next, a set of piano finger trainers. It was advertised as being for pianists, to train dexterity and strength, so he tells him that. He doesn’t say it’s mostly to help him recover further from his injury. When Phainon thanks him, his voice is soft. They both know what it’s for, and Mydei thinks he appreciates the way he doesn’t bring it up outright.

Phainon’s next present is a beautiful leather bound notebook. When Mydei opens it up, he finds it filled with page after page of staff paper. He doesn’t know for sure, but he thinks Phainon might have replaced the original lined notebook paper with staff paper all by himself. Mydei thanks him, already knowing exactly what song he’s going to use it to write.

Mydei’s final gift to Phainon is an old wooden metronome he had found from an old antique shop. Phainon looks at it like it’s a treasure, before the wrapping paper is even fully off of it. “Holy shit, Mydei,” he breathes. “Where the hell did you find this?”

Mydei shrugs, leaning over the coffee table to take a sip of his hot chocolate. “It looks old, but I promise it works,” he says instead.

“Hm,” Phainon adjusts the weight, then pulls the bar to one side before letting go. Sure enough, it clicks out four steady beats before Phainon stops it. “This is amazing,” he says, turning it over. “I hate using my app.”

“I know,” Mydei says. “Also, you were rushing pas de deux.”

“Mydei.” Phainon turns, shooting him the meanest glare he can muster. Mydei smiles a little, before Phainon tackles him down, metronome discarded to the side. “Take it back.”

“Or what?” Mydei asks. “You’ll prove me wrong?”

“As much as I would love to, there’s something a little more pressing right in front of me.”

“Hm.” Mydei hums, then pushes him off, sitting up. “That’s unfortunate, because I’m not having sex with you until you play pas de deux in time for me.”

Phainon doesn’t say anything, staring at Mydei in disbelief. “You’re not serious.”

Mydei shrugs, and gestures over to the piano. “Go, maestro. Show me what you got.”

They spend New Year’s Eve in Cipher’s apartment, drinking shitty champagne and listening to even shittier music. She can afford better champagne and she can make better music, but Mydei doesn’t complain.

He allows himself no more than one glass of champagne, then fills his cup up with pomegranate juice she “happened” to have in her fridge. It’s a nice gesture, but Mydei knows that if he brings it up, she would just say something mean in response.

They play a game of cards that’s entirely luck-based and Phainon wins nearly every round. He smiles through it all, even as Cipher’s insults grow

more and more personal and even Castorice shows the first signs of irritation.

They switch to a video game after Phainon’s fifth win, Hyacine’s suggestion. It’s a dancing game that Mydei thinks she might have picked on purpose, because Phainon is atrocious at it. He’s dared to do one on his own, and Cipher cackles as she watches his stiff attempts at dancing. Mydei can’t help but laugh at such a sight, either. He needs to move his hips more —it’s truly a horrible sight.

Castorice and Cipher do a tango dance next, telling Phainon to “watch and learn.” Mydei doesn’t think their attempt goes much better than Phainon’s, honestly. Cipher is just as confused, and Castorice has to keep directing her when they bump into each other and step on each other’s toes.

Mydei and Hyacine go next, to a pop song Hyacine picks out. He’s just comfortable enough to give it his all, determined to show up both Phainon and Cipher, and he and Hyacine tie with five stars each.

“Let’s go, Mydei!” Hyacine squeals as their scores are calculated on screen, jumping up and down to give him a high five. Mydei looks over his shoulder to see Phainon and Cipher, both equally shell-shocked.

Midnight comes, everyone somewhat calmed down as the night grows late. Phainon is curled into Mydei’s side, shaking Mydei’s shoulder every time he laughs at something Cipher says. Mydei is mere seconds away from falling asleep as the clock resets, and nearly jumps out of his skin at the ensuing celebration. He hardly processes it until Phainon’s lips are on his, a quick peck before he pulls back and wishes him a happy new year.

Mydei wakes up the next morning curled up with Phainon on Cipher’s couch. Phainon is already awake, hands threading through Mydei’s hair, and he can smell the beginnings of breakfast coming from Cipher’s kitchen.

“Is Cipher cooking?” Mydei mutters groggily, rubbing at his eyes.

“Don’t worry,” Phainon reassures him, kissing the top of his head. “Hyacine is helping her.”

That is enough to put Mydei’s mind at ease, burrowing further into the blanket thrown over the two of them. It’s freezing in Cipher’s apartment. “Where’s Cas?” he asks, voice muffled.

“Showering, I think,” Phainon answers. “Do you guys have to go back to the studio tomorrow?”

“Yeah,” Mydei says. “I have to write my song today.”

“Your song,” Phainon shifts beside him, lifting his head to look at Mydei properly. “About what?”

“Secret,” Mydei murmurs.

Phainon frowns, about to say something, but they’re interrupted by Cipher before he can. “Wakey wakey, lovebirds, breakfast is served!” She yells from the kitchen. Mydei groans, and he can vaguely hear Cipher yelp after Hyacine, most likely, hits her with something.

The two of them made pancakes, though Mydei thinks it was probably more Hyacine’s doing than Cipher’s, because they taste good. She doesn’t have a dining table, so they stand around the kitchen as they eat. Cipher sits on one of her countertops, and Castorice joins her when she gets out of the shower.

They talk about the album for a while, all the things Aventurine has already scheduled for them once they finish recording. It’s a conversation Mydei can tell Phainon is soaking in, given how little Mydei had told him about all of it so far.

They leave soon after that, Phainon complaining all the way to Mydei’s car. “I mean, seriously, I think your fans know more about the album than me at this point,” he says, exasperated. Mydei’s car is covered in a layer of snow, having made the mistake of parking outside last night.

“Are you not a fan?” He asks, retrieving the brush from his trunk. He moves to the windshield first, brushing it off while Phainon watches.

“Um, I think you and I are a little closer than artist and fan,” Phainon pouts, crossing his arms. “Besides, you’ve barely posted about it. Your fans who follow only you probably have no idea.”

“Then there you go,” Mydei argues. “At least you know I’m recording an album.”

“Just one song,” Phainon begs. “Come on, Mydei.”

“You’ve heard one song,” Mydei deadpans. He opens the passenger door and slams it shut, watching the snow fall down to the sidewalk.

“That’s the same song everyone else has also heard,” Phainon says.

“You barely let me hear you practicing.” Mydei puts the snow brush away, then moves to the driver’s side to do the same before finally climbing in. Phainon does the same, blowing on his hands to warm them up. “Think of it as payback for that.”

Phainon groans in response to that, but he doesn’t say anything back, so Mydei considers it his win.

Mydei starts writing as soon as they get back, sitting in the living room as Phainon takes his usual spot at the piano.

He gets the lyrics done in under an hour, accompanied by the sound of Phainon’s practicing. He doesn’t recognize the piece he’s working on, but he hums the melody in his head on top of it. He thinks the two songs end up in the same key by accident.

When the room goes quiet, I can still hear you play The music hangs in the air, I wish I never walked away Because every road I took just led me back home

“I’ve been using the gift you gave me,” Phainon says, cutting through Mydei’s thoughts. “I think it’s helping. Watch this.” He proceeds to play the first few lines of Moonlight Sonata’s third movement, even faster than how Mydei remembers the written tempo.

“Hm,” Mydei looks back down at his notebook, hiding his smile. “Adequate.”

“Oh, fuck you,” Phainon says, laughing. “You couldn’t do that.”

Mydei shrugs. He’s right, but he’s not going to admit that.

However long it takes, I will always love you Ten million heartbreaks, I will always love you

Mydei looks up, watching Phainon carefully. He pretends not to notice Mydei’s gaze, eyes too focused on the sheet music in front of him. He’s back to the piece Mydei doesn’t know, that he’s subconsciously harmonizing with.

“Phainon,” he says, and he stops. “Can you play this for me?” He hums a short piano melody that was in his head, after which Phainon looks down at the keys for a minute before playing exactly the notes Mydei was asking for. “Brighter than that,” Mydei guides, and Phainon does it perfectly the second time. “That’s good,” he grins, opening the notebook Phainon had gotten him for Christmas. “What notes were they?”

“Starts on an A,” Phainon answers. “It’s all whole steps from there, except the final interval is a second.”

Mydei haphazardly scribbles it into his staff paper, then looks over at his second notebook, where he had been writing the lyrics. “Thank you,” he says, reading over the lyrics one more time as Phainon resumes the piece he was working on before.

“Is your song in A minor?” Phainon stops halfway through a phrase to ask the question, like it had been forced out of him.

“I think so,” Mydei says, not looking up from his notebook. He scratches out one of the words, unsure what to replace it with just yet.

“That’s funny. So is my piece.” Phainon looks over at his sheet music for a split second, before focusing his gaze back on Mydei. “And it’s my favorite key.” It’s added quietly, like an afterthought.

“Huh,” Mydei mutters. “I thought C major was your favorite key.”

Phainon’s gaze loses any of the softness it just had, staring at Mydei as if he had just insulted his entire lineage. “Stop it, Mydei.”

“What? Aren’t they the same thing?”

“Oh my god.” Two very dissonant chords come out of the piano as Phainon rests his elbows on it, head falling into his palms. “You did not just say that to me.”

“No sharps or flats. Isn’t that the same thing?”

Phainon groans very loudly, so obviously irritated that Mydei decides to put him out of his misery and stop messing with him. They turn to their respective projects, Mydei finishing up the lyrics so he can go back to writing out the music in his new notebook.

When he’s done, he transports it into his computer so he can listen to it. Even though part of him doesn’t want to tune Phainon’s playing out, he plugs in his headphones anyways.

He emails a copy of the song to Ratio when he’s done, and copies the rest of the band. He asks them all to take a look at it and let him know if they like it or want to change anything.

He gets a text from Cipher first, which is surprising because Mydei didn’t think she checked her email very often. “wtf loverboy,” she writes. “and here i foolishly thought you’d lose ur magic touch when you fell in love.”

The rest of the responses trickle in while he cooks dinner, water boiling over on the stove as he rushes to defend himself in a minor argument over tempo with Castorice. Their fights over these things never last very long. They trust each other, and know that a music suggestion is never personal.

And then work resumes the next day, back to the studio as if nothing ever changed. In two days, the new song is recorded, and Ratio officially tells them that while his work is done, theirs is far from it.

They spend the rest of the week, and the week after that, pushing off Aventurine’s incessant questioning about a release date while they find themselves in argument after argument over track order, minor tweaks, or things completely unrelated to their music altogether. Mydei has listened to the album so many times at this point—in different orders, or individual songs as they decide some need finishing touches—that he doesn’t even know if he likes it anymore.

City of Thieves, the first song they wrote, is now his least favorite. It feels like an entirely different group of people wrote it, like it’s not fully theirs anymore. Mydei spends hours at a time hunched over his laptop, messing with mixes and soundbites, until he feels like he’s going insane. Phainon is constantly reminding him that it’s okay, that music is something he loves and there’s no point in agonizing over it to such an extent. Mydei would listen more if Phainon followed his own advice once in a while.

Phainon, finally cleared by his physical therapist, gets a job at a local cafe. It’s temporary, and they both know this. Just a way to get his own money to spend as he works towards performing again. He insists upon paying Mydei back for rent, but the last thing Mydei wants is compensation for something that was never much of a burden on him.

It’s nearly February by the time they finally finalize the track order. Mydei spent more time than he would like to admit fixating on the tiny details of every single track, but he thinks it pays off when he leaves the studio with a finished album saved to his files and officially sent to Aventurine.

They call it Oracle, after holding a vote on the top titles everyone had contributed during another session of brainstorming. The title is the last

thing they settle on, and the album is officially done.

Phainon gets home late from his shift, and he can somehow tell from the way Mydei looks at him what he means to say.

“You finished it,” he breathes, halfway through taking his shoes off.

Mydei nods.

Phainon wants to listen immediately. Mydei makes him wait until after they’ve both eaten dinner, and then he hooks his laptop up to the TV and they lay together on the couch as he broadcasts each file to the big screen.

Phainon clings to Mydei throughout all of it, like he’s afraid of him leaving, somehow. Mydei holds onto his shoulder and taps along to whatever part he likes the best. Sometimes it’s the bass, or the drums. Most of the time it’s the piano.

His face lights up with laughter when he hears Caelus’ trumpet solo in City of Thieves. A lot of the song had been touched up, but Mydei didn’t change a single second of that part. It was perfect from the first day he heard it in the studio.

He squeezes Mydei so tightly during the studio version of Deliver the Dawn, that Mydei can hardly breathe. He laughs at the piano part of Cat Food, but any of Mydei’s shared lightheartedness fades the second the beginning instrumentals of Love Song come on. It’s a stupid title. He had tried so many times to think of something better, but at the end of the day, listened to Hyacine when she told him the bluntness of it suited him.

Phainon catches on as soon as he hears what key it’s in. “A minor,” he whispers, lifting his head a little. His eyes are practically shining. Mydei can’t do anything but smile. “This one’s mine, isn’t it?”

Mydei pulls him back down. “They’re all yours,” he answers. “But yes.”

Phainon is near to tears by the end of that song, and Mydei would be lying if he said he wasn’t close. Somehow, he holds it together until the final

track, Conqueror of Lions. Phainon sucks in a breath as he hears the first piano chord ring out, and Mydei is glad that he can’t see the pain so blatantly obvious on his face from the angle of his head.

He bites back his tears until the song ends, and the silence that comes with the final track fills the room. “Mydei,” Phainon prods, sitting up. “That was beautiful.”

Mydei doesn’t trust himself to speak without crying, so he nods instead. He had avoided listening to that song for as long as he could for this exact reason. He trusted his earlier self for believing it was perfect and hadn’t touched it. It remained the final track throughout all of their workshopping, and he always stopped when he got to the start of it.

“I’m so proud of you,” Phainon continues. “You’re just—god, I’m so lucky. I’m so lucky, Mydei.”

Mydei nods again, biting his tongue. Phainon looks almost distraught at such a sight, and pulls him in so his head rests against his chest. “She would be so proud of you,” he murmurs into his hair, as his free hand settles right against that vertebrae again. “You know that, right?”

Mydei thinks he does. He nods a third time.

The work doesn’t stop. If anything, it gets a hundred times worse—they’re even more busy than before, doing the worst part of the preparations.

They sit in stuffy meeting rooms, being talked at about creative ideas they have little say in. They’ve taken Castorice’s original idea of modeling characters after old Amphorean myths, and ran with it. Mydei is at least happy they’re following the idea instead of doing what they think would work better. They plan music videos for Wrath of Man and Deliver the Dawn, which are projected to be the highest charting songs off the album. Wrath of Man for being the first track, and Deliver the Dawn for being familiar.

Then the meetings talk about more boring things—their tour schedule, opening acts, interviews, photoshoots. Album cover designs. If they want it to be a photoshoot, or an artwork. For some reason, Mydei wants neither— he doesn’t want to be in it, but he wants it to be some sort of shoot, anyway.

He spends a whole day doing fittings, and doesn’t see a single member of the band once. He knows it’s because they’re off doing fittings of their own, but he feels like he’s going insane after being surrounded by IPC workers the entire time.

For whatever reason, they seem to want him shirtless. Mydei thinks he might know why that is, but it doesn’t bother him enough to protest. He worked hard for his body, so he might as well show it off.

The photoshoots are the worst part. Mydei has no idea why in the world they need so many promotional photos for one album—Cipher has plenty of candids in her camera roll that would do the trick just fine. But alas, it’s not his decision to make. They take a hundred pictures of Mydei as “Mydeimos”, and then they put the four of them in matching suits and take photos that Mydei is sure would belong more on the front of a program than the back of a CD.

Then they do weird ones. They put Mydei in heavy make-up and then make him stand under a sprinkler until his shirt is sticking to his stomach. They put the four of them in casual, grunge clothes and take pictures of them from above a staircase. They bring in props like monkey bars or chairs that are edited to look like they’re in an empty movie theater. They make Castorice and Mydei pretend to arm wrestle while Hyacine and Cipher cheer in the background. Mydei really wants that one to be their new artist picture on music streaming platforms. He hopes he can convince the other three of this later.

Phainon spends hours laughing at him later that night, as Mydei clicks through the emailed files. They see all the outtakes, the ones where Mydei is blinking, or isn’t making quite the right expression. And then, perhaps feeling bad for making fun of him, Phainon pulls out a few of the old photoshoots he had done with Aglaea the first time he’d played with her orchestra.

There are a few shoots Mydei has seen finalized versions of from Phainon's social media, but most of them are new to him. Aglaea seemed to have a very specific image with Phainon that she executed perfectly. Somehow, she managed to capture his charm in some shoots, and his beauty in others. Mydei’s favorites highlight both.

Until he swipes to one photo in particular, and Mydei feels like all the air is knocked out of his lungs.

He grabs the phone from Phainon’s hands instantly, so he can see the picture better. It’s absolutely ethereal, the kind of thing you’d see in an Okheman museum. Phainon’s arms are perpendicular to the rest of his body, head tipped back and turned to one side as if he’s mimicking a crucifixion. There are massive angel-like wings behind him, and the tip of a halo behind his head. He’s dressed in hues of white and gold, lit by raw sunlight filtering in from the bottom of the image. There are clouds all around him, like he’s rising from them.

Mydei has never seen anything like it in his life. “Phainon.” Is all he can manage, as he finds himself unable to tear his eyes away from the photo.

“What?” Phainon asks. “You like it?”

There’s only one coherent thought in Mydei’s head. This is their album cover.

It takes more convincing on Phainon’s end than the rest of the band. They all agree almost instantly, and when Phainon is finally on board after Mydei says they would edit it to make it more ambiguous about who it is, he says he would ask Aglaea to give the IPC the rights to use the photo.

Aglaea agrees with little trouble, and he sends it into Aventurine for editing. It’s finalized a few days later. The editors added even more of a golden hue to it, on the darker end of the original. The shadows and highlights are more pronounced, and there’s a grainy sort of filter over all of it. You can’t tell it’s Phainon in the final photo at all.

The music videos are filmed during what’s close to the worst two weeks of Mydei’s life. He’s never been so busy, or so drained, in his life. A small part of him is undoubtedly glad that they’re putting so much time into promotion for this album—more than they ever put into their projects in the past. He’s glad they think it’ll perform well.

Still, Mydei is shuttled around from set to set for these music videos. They film outside in short bursts, then move inside to perform in front of a green screen. By his tenth time summoning emotion for the shoot, Mydei doesn’t think the songs mean as much to him as they once did. And he’s okay with that. He’s ready for them to mean something different to someone else now.

Aventurine pulls him aside after they finally wrap the music video for Deliver the Dawn. “The next few weeks are booked with interviews,” he explains, just as corporate as ever. Mydei hasn’t experienced the same camaraderie from him since he had Eurypon escorted out of the office. But true to his word, he hadn’t heard a thing from the man since.

“Yes,” Mydei says, wiping sweat from his forehead. “More travel.”

Aventurine gives him a look Mydei could easily misread as apologetic. “There are always topics interviewers aren’t allowed to ask about. I’m going to go through the questions tonight and over the weekend, and wanted to see if you had any requests first. I will ask your bandmates as well, I just thought this would be a better conversation to have one-on-one.”

Mydei thinks carefully. He knows, now, that the dating rumors with Phainon are in full swing. Even when he doesn’t check social media, Cipher makes sure to remind him of it. He hadn’t confirmed nor denied this, and he had only posted something once or twice since Phainon started living with him. He was bound to get at least one question about it.

Now, though, he shrugs it off. Let them ask. He wasn’t ashamed of Phainon —quite the opposite. If he confirmed the rumors, maybe he’d open up a whole new audience of listeners to Phainon’s work that might not have checked it out otherwise.

“My father,” he says instead. “I don’t want to deal with a single question about him, or the company, or anything like that.”

Aventurine nods. “And you know what to say if they find a work-around.”

“Of course.” How could Mydei forget the weeks upon weeks of media training he had been put through when he was first signing with the label? He had almost spent the longest amount of time in those classes out of the four of them, second only to Cipher. It was practically torture, being forced to learn how to portray himself the way people who didn’t even know him wanted him to be portrayed.

All things considered, the interviews don’t end up being that bad in the beginning. They ask the same manageable questions a thousand times. Where did this album come from? How does it differ from the last EPs? Is this your most personal work yet?

They always give the same answers. It was the album they needed to make. They had the time of their lives writing it and can’t wait to do it again. Yes, absolutely.

It’s with the solo interviews that the worst questions start. They ask him about college. About piano. About how it feels coming back to it. And finally, one brave interviewer asks him about Phainon.

“I’m a big lover of classical music myself, you know,” he says, laughing a little. He had done an incredible job of making Mydei feel safe with him, and he wonders how much of what he says is actually true. “I loved Phainon Khaslana’s work before his injury.”

Mydei nearly jumps out of his skin, and he’s tremendously thankful that this isn’t a recorded interview. “Right,” he says awkwardly. Where are you going with this remains unsaid.

“It’s no secret the two of you have been living together lately,” he continues. “How did you meet? How long have you known each other?”

Mydei sighs. He knows the last time he knew he was photographed with Phainon wasn’t the last, but he didn’t care to investigate it further. To think it was common knowledge that they lived in the same apartment—the rumors would be hard to dispute, were he a fan.

“I met him in college,” he says, swallowing a little before continuing. His heart is racing in his chest as he realizes he’s doing this. “We…” he clears his throat. “We started dating at the end of my freshman year. And then we broke up when I dropped out, and reconnected after his injury.” He hates how many people in the room he’s confessing this to. Aventurine stands in the corner, with the band beside him and what seems like countless corporate workers as well. He hates how many more people will read this article, or learn of its contents one way or another.

The interviewer does a very good job of seeming impartial to this information, typing something in his laptop while nodding along calmly. “And the status of your relationship now…?”

Mydei smiles. He asks it almost like he feels like he shouldn’t, and that somehow makes Mydei feel a little bit better about answering truthfully. “Yes,” he confesses. “We got back together in December.”

And with that, the worst of it’s over. He won’t have to hide Phainon anymore—not that he necessarily was in the past, but now he can freely post pictures of the two of them and the whole world would finally know that Phainon is his.

The interviewer continues to ask a couple more questions about Phainon’s status and whether or not he would be returning to piano, which Mydei thinks are more self-indulgent than anything. He answers as truthfully as he can, which is that he is working towards making his debut with Aglaea’s orchestra over the summer.

His favorite interviews are the ones where the four of them are asked to break down the music together. They talk about growth, collaboration, finding their sound through trial and error. They mention the inherent messiness of the album, despite its coherent sound. Mydei does not say Conqueror of Lions saved him, or that Love Song was a song his heart

yearned to write. Even though his relationship with Phainon will be public knowledge the second that article is released, he does not mention him once.

With the release date—May 4th, 3870—in sight, Mydei starts posting more on his social media. He asks Cipher for some of her candids and posts those, along with a few of his own. He even posts a picture she had taken of him and Phainon kissing at their New Year’s party, not thinking about it very much until he sees the reception afterwards. They’ll calm down about it eventually, though, and that’s how Mydei wants it to be.

He even starts posting short-form content of classical piano songs played on electric guitar or rock songs played on piano, and he thinks Aventurine should be very proud of all the work he’s putting in.

And then, finally, the night of May 3rd arrives.

Mydei doesn’t think he could sleep if he tried. He’s buzzing with anticipation, jittery and nervous as he types out the caption of his final post promoting the album that’s about to drop.

Mydei nods, and pulls him back to settle on his chest.

Okhema, he thinks.

That’s not so bad. He can make it that far.
