~~~

June 2nd, 3870.

Okhema doesn’t feel like home anymore.

Phainon steps out of the airport hit with blistering heat, so intense he instantly breaks out a sweat. He squints as he takes in his surroundings, trying and failing to remember where he was supposed to go. To think it had almost been a year since he was back here. A year with Mydei. He misses him immensely.

“Phangry!” He turns at the sound of the nickname, unable to prepare himself as a ball of pink hits him square in the chest, nearly tackling him to the ground with the sheer force of it. He laughs as he hugs Cyrene back, squeezing her almost as tightly as she squeezes him.

“Have you gotten taller?” She asks, hands on her hips as she pulls away. “Ugh, that’s so unfair. I don’t even look older than you anymore.”

“You won’t complain when I’m old and wrinkly, and—”

“Ew, stop. I don’t even want to imagine that.”

Phainon laughs, his chest squeezing a little as he takes her in. Her hair is still dyed the same shade of pink—it had been since they were kids, for so long that he had forgotten what her natural hair color even was. She looks the same, and yet so different, like she had matured a hundred years in the length of one. The same kindness still lights up her eyes, but now they shine with the faintest hint of wisdom, too.

“So, you and Mydei,” she says mischievously, as she latches onto Phainon’s arm and drags him in the direction she had come from, presumably her car. “You need to tell me everything.”

Phainon sighs. “I already told you most of it.”

“Not enough,” Cyrene shakes her head. “How is it? How is he? How does it feel to finally get the love of your life after years of—”

“He’s great,” Phainon cuts her off before she embarrasses him, even though there’s no one but the two of them to listen to their conversation. “I couldn’t ask for a better partner.”

“Ah,” Cyrene sighs wistfully. “You’re practically living in a romance novel. How lucky.”

“Stop,” Phainon says, shooting her a glare he doesn’t mean. “It’s not…like that.”

“It’s not?” Cyrene raises an eyebrow as she clicks the unlock button on her keys. A few feet away, her tiny pink car beeps twice.

“It’s normal,” Phainon argues. “Not…I don’t know. I don’t read romance.”

“Right. You only read erotica.”

“Cyrene.” Phainon lifts his suitcase into the trunk of the car after Cyrene opens it, thankful that he can turn away so she can’t see how furiously he’s blushing.

There’s a bit of silence as they both climb in, Cyrene giggling quietly as her phone automatically connects to the speaker to reveal that she had just been listening to Mydei’s new album. She keeps it on, at a low volume as she pulls out of the parking lot.

“I read other genres,” Phainon says, too loudly in the space between them as she slows to a stop at a light.

Cyrene bursts out laughing. “Right, right.”

“I like to read about antiques,” Phainon continues, like it’s a good argument.

Cyrene giggles at that, too, and Phainon’s face flushes even further. “Antique appraisal and erotica,” she tuts. “What an interesting man you are. It’s no wonder you’ve scored a man like Mydei.”

“How’s your new novel going, Cyrene?” Phainon asks, overdoing the brightness of his voice to force the subject to change.

“It’s still in the planning stages right now. You can’t rush perfection.”

“Of course,” Phainon says. Her debut novel was successful enough that Phainon figured she was probably making enough money from it to support her lifestyle by now. When they were kids, she was always telling him the stories she made up in her head. She had no shortage of ideas, Phainon was sure.

They had seldom gone longer than a week without talking to each other during his stay in Penacony, but that didn’t mean he hadn’t missed her all the same. Even when they lived apart, he would still make time to visit as often as he could.

“So, Eve moved out?” He asks, as Cyrene parks her car in the closest spot she can find to her place, which is still quite a walk away. Okhema’s streets were always bustling, so much so that he’d been disappointed by how tame Penacony was in comparison.

“A few months ago,” Cyrene answers. “She moved in with March. It’s so lonely now.”

“You should go out,” Phainon suggests. “Meet some new people, you know?”

“I know plenty of people,” Cyrene protests. “And I don’t like going out.”

“Hm.” Phainon shrugs. “Work on getting a girlfriend, then, yeah?”

Cyrene doesn’t say anything for a moment, as they approach the front of her house. “Phainon, love comes when you’re not looking for it.” she says, after her moment of deep thought.

Phainon snorts, stepping forward to help her with the door after she unlocks it, keys jingling with all the trinkets she attached to it. “Well. There’s always that girl from the ranch.”

Cyrene blushes instantly, pushing him inside. “Phainon!” She hushes, eyes wide.

“What? It’s not like she’s gonna hear you all the way from over here.”

Cyrene flicks the lights on, and Phainon only has a few minutes to take in his surroundings before he’s nearly tackled to the ground again, this time by a big ball of white fur. He laughs as Snowy licks at his face, somewhat relieved that he had remembered him after all this time.

“I’m ready to have your dog out of here,” Cyrene mumbles as she reaches down to unbuckle her sandals.

“You love Snowy,” Phainon argues, ruffling the fur on his head.

He carries his suitcase upstairs after Snowy has calmed down, navigating to his old room like it’s second nature. Cyrene changed it into a guest room years ago, after he’d moved out, and had mentioned working on turning Eve and March’s room into an office in the last couple of months.

Everything is exactly how he remembered it. The double bed with more pillows than Phainon would ever need, made perfectly with Cyrene’s spare pink bedsheets. There’s an indent in the center of it, littered with sparse white fur, where Snowy had presumably been sleeping.

He puts his suitcase down and takes in the silence surrounding him as soon as the door shuts. Everything is the same, and yet it feels so different. He’s back home, but it’s only temporary, and he hates that. As much as he can’t wait to move in with Mydei officially, he doesn’t think he’s ready to live in Penacony for the rest of his life.

“Stop by the market on your way home, yeah?” Cyrene calls from the living room as Phainon pauses to put his shoes on by the door. “I’ll text you a list of groceries I need.”

He has a meeting with Aglaea today, who he had reached out to weeks ago when he was first planning his stay in Okhema. Cyrene had already been awake when Phainon came downstairs, meticulously painting the world map of her next book.

He agrees, and leaves. It’s only noon, and the sun is already beating down on him. This part of Okhema, he certainly didn’t miss.

Okhema is a walkable city—Cyrene only got her car recently, and he sold his parent’s old car for extra money when he initially moved here. He used

to take Snowy for walks through the market, until all the shopkeepers knew his name.

It’s a fifteen minute walk to Aglaea’s concert hall, and Phainon is almost sweating from the heat by the time he arrives. The doors are as grand as they were the first time Phainon walked through them, with Marmoreal Palace engraved in elegant cursive into the rich mahogany wood.

The inside is empty, with no shows or rehearsals today, so he navigates his way through the front lobby and into the backstage area, finding his way to Aglaea’s office.

“Phainon,” she says, as she hears him open the door. “It’s nice to see you again.” She sits at her polished wooden desk, and not a single piece of furniture has budged since Phainon was in here last.

“Miss Aglaea,” he responds. He can’t help but notice the way she doesn’t stare directly at him, like she used to. She faces him, but her eyes seem to be unfocused and glazed over. He swallows down the dread he feels. “Hi. You look well.”

She smiles a little, but it doesn’t quite spread to the rest of her face. “Thank you, Phainon. Have a seat.” He obliges, sinking into the leather armchair across from her desk. “As I’m sure you’ve heard, my illness has only gotten worse since you’ve left.”

Phainon nods. “Right.”

“My eyes are not what they used to be,” she continues. “But this must be an unforgettable performance. If not, I will be forced to retire.” Her face sours at the word, lips curling as she says it.

“What?” Phainon demands, pulling backwards in shock. “You’re quitting?” He remembers what Mydei said to him nearly half a year ago, in that grocery store. Aglaea was not the kind of woman who would let something like this stop her.

Aglaea’s frown deepens even further. “Terminated would be a more accurate word for it.”

“They’re going to fire you because you’re sick? Didn’t you found this place? Who would be firing you?”

She sighs deeply, closing her eyes as her head drops forward. One of her perfectly styled curls falls out of its hold, bouncing in front of her face. “Cease your questioning, Phainon. I have everything under control.”

“Do you?”

Aglaea lifts her head, silencing Phainon with an icy stare. “I do.”

“Right…” Phainon swallows. “Okay.”

She takes her time choosing her next words, hands clasped so tightly in front of her that her knuckles are turning white. “A blind conductor,” she begins, voice strained, “is nothing to a sighted one.”

“That’s bullshit—”

“Let me finish, Phainon,” Aglaea is the closest to snapping that Phainon had ever seen her. “The council funding this organization simply believes their money would be better off going to a more reliable conductor. At the end of the day, I do not have much power over their decisions.”

Phainon bites his tongue, so he doesn’t say something that might frustrate her even further.

“Of course, you and I both know that one does not need to see the music to know it,” Aglaea says, “but they will not budge. So I have decided that my next concert simply must be outstanding.” She picks her loose curl up from in front of her face, tucking it back into place behind her ear. “With you here, I know I have nothing to worry about.”

Phainon’s throat has gone incredibly dry, and he swallows thickly as he tries to process all of this. A year ago, he would have accepted in a heartbeat. Post his injury, though, he’s not so sure. “I don’t know,” he confesses,

unable to look at her head on. “I’m flattered that you think I’m right for this, but…I don’t think I can deliver the expectations you have of me. Not anymore.”

Aglaea doesn’t react to that. It was an impressive quality of hers, the inability to show very strong emotions past mild discontent and slight humor.

“Are you sure this is the only solution?” He continues. “I—I could try to convince them to let you stay. Caenis is dead anyways, right?”

Aglaea’s jaw twitches. “That old hag was long overdue as it was. And your arguments will make no difference, Phainon.”

“Well…” Phainon starts, unsure what else to say. “I could try?”

She shakes her head. “If it makes you feel any better, I did assume you would think you couldn’t do it.” That doesn’t make Phainon feel better at all, but he doesn’t say anything as she continues. “Which is why I’ve hired someone to help you.”

“What?”

Aglaea’s lips curl. “Anaxa.” She says his name like she’s spitting out poison. “He refused to see me in person—an issue I did not press any further, I suppose—but he has agreed to take up teaching you again. With little trouble.”

“You…” Phainon squints at her, unsure what to make of this situation. “You two are talking again?”

“Desperate times,” Aglaea mutters, voice sour.

Phainon had planned to pay Anaxa a visit soon anyways, given that he was also back in Okhema after the spring semester at Paperfold ended. He wonders why Anaxa hadn’t reached out about this, if it was something he and Aglaea were planning.

Unfortunately, it is convincing. He wants to help Aglaea, after all.

“I just…” he fiddles with his hands under Aglaea’s desk. “I can’t understand why you don’t just want to hire a reliable pianist to do this for you.”

“It’s simple. Your recovery and comeback will have a reception around the world. If you do this, it will be that much more successful.”

He knows that sort of means she’s using him, but he’s surprised to realize how little this bothers him. “Um,” he starts. “Can I think about it?”

Aglaea smiles—or rather, musters up the closest thing she can to a smile. “Of course,” she says. “But I thought I might pitch some repertoire before you make your decision.”

Phainon curses in his head, because he knows that no matter what Aglaea is about to pull out, it will convince him. There’s only a handful of pieces he’d say no to, and Aglaea is aware of all of them.

“First,” she says, ruffling through one of her cabinets. “I thought Tchaikovsky might be nice.”

“Fuck,” Phainon says, out loud this time. Sure enough, she places sheet music he instantly recognizes before him: Tchaikovsky’s first piano concerto. Playing this would mean that he’s played two out of his three favorite piano concertos of all time: Rachmaninoff, Moszkowski, and Tchaikovsky. He would love nothing more than to play this piece.

“I also have a Brahms,” Aglaea places another option in front of him, “or Prokofiev.”

“Fuck,” Phainon says again. Only good options are being laid before him, and it upsets him deeply that he can only choose one for this concert.

“If this goes well, we can always prepare the ones you don’t choose for concerts in the future.”

“Oh my god,” Phainon mutters. “You’re joking.”

“Is that a yes?”

“Yes,” Phainon says, without much further thought. “That one. The Tchaikovsky.”

Phainon is in the middle of brushing his teeth, getting ready for bed when Mydei calls him. His phone lights up with Mydei’s profile photo, and he rushes to pick it up with the toothbrush still hanging out of his mouth.

“Hello?” He asks as Mydei’s face comes into view. His voice is muffled as he tries to talk with his mouth full of toothpaste froth.

Mydei cracks up when he sees him. He’s in a black hoodie Phainon has never seen before—new CALAMITY merch, upon closer inspection—and his phone is propped up on some kind of table. There are two boxes of sushi in front of him, and he holds a pair of chopsticks haphazardly in his hands. “You could’ve picked up when you were done brushing your teeth, you know,” he says when he’s done laughing.

“And miss your call? Nuh uh,” Phainon turns back to the mirror, finishing up what he was doing as he hears Mydei crack open both of his lunch containers on the other end.

“We just got to our hotel for the night,” Mydei explains. “Big show tonight. I’m nervous.”

Phainon raises an eyebrow, though he knows Mydei can’t see him as he leans forward to spit into the sink. “You’re nervous?” He asks, mid rinsing his mouth out with water.

“Sold out arena.”

“So?” Phainon pats his mouth dry with a nearby towel. “Your last show was a sold out arena too.”

“Yeah, but that was opening night.”

“I’m not understanding your logic.” Phainon picks up his phone, exiting the bathroom and heading down the hall to the guest bedroom.

Mydei sighs and puts a piece of sushi in his mouth. Phainon could comment on his poor chopstick skills, but his aren’t much better, so he opts to stay silent. “How’s Okhema?” He asks, through a mouthful of food.

“Lively.” Phainon turns on the lamp on his bedside table and pulls his sheets aside, crawling in.

“Aglaea is well?”

Phainon takes a deep breath. “Well…” he starts, turning to the side and resting his phone against the other pillow in the bed. It’s not a very flattering angle of him, but it will do. “She’s dealing with a lot right now.”

“Oh yeah?” Mydei eats another piece of sushi. “Besides her illness?”

“That’s the main problem,” Phainon swallows, and explains everything to him. The source of her funds, her eyesight, the ultimatum, and Tchaikovsky.

Mydei has stopped eating entirely when he finishes. He looks hard into his phone, like he’s trying to get something out of Phainon through the screen. “And you said yes, right?”

Phainon looks down. “I…yeah, I did.”

Mydei exhales, leaning back in the chair he sits in and running a hand through his hair. “Thank god.”

“It’s not like I wanted to,” Phainon protests, which has Mydei glaring at him. “I just couldn’t pass up this opportunity, for Aglaea.”

“But it’s going to be fine, and you have nothing to worry about,” Mydei says. He’s picked up his chopsticks again, and stabs a piece of sushi with both of them. He might as well just use his hands at this point. “You said Anaxagoras is helping you?”

“Anaxa,” Phainon says, laughing. “And yes.”

Mydei whistles. “Looks like you have your work cut out for you, then.”

Phainon knows he’s right. Herta was cruel to Mydei, but none of the music teachers at Paperfold were exactly kind. Anaxa would draw the line at a lot of things Herta chose to do, but he wasn’t above being a harsh teacher by any means. “Yeah, well, so do you.”

Mydei shrugs. “It hasn’t been that bad so far.”

“Because you’ve played one show. Just wait.”

“Like you’d know.”

“I’ve been on tours before!” Phainon bursts, offended.

“Where you only played weekends. Not the same.”

They talk for another hour, before Mydei eventually hangs up. He needs to be at the venue soon, and Phainon needs to fall asleep. As much as he would like to stay up into the early hours of the morning to watch Mydei’s concert, he has his first meeting with Anaxa tomorrow. To say he’s excited would be overselling it.

Anaxa’s house is a disaster.

From the moment Phainon steps inside, everything immediately makes sense to him. Of course the man would live in a place like this. His walls are lined with bookshelves stuffed to the brim with books about everything from astrophysics to music theory. There’s loose paper everywhere, some of them filled with frantic scribbling that vaguely resembles sheet music.

He had known Anaxa’s head was somewhat of a mess, but his house seems to emulate exactly what his mind is like. Nothing shocks him quite like the eye patch he wears when he answers the door, though.

“Woah,” Phainon says. “What happened to your eye?”

“I cut it out and mailed it to Aglaea,” Anaxa says bitterly. “Come in.” He doesn’t give Phainon any more of an explanation than that. It leaves Phainon wondering if he should really enter this man’s house.

“Um, what?”

Anaxa rolls his eyes—eye, now—in frustration. “I said come in.”

Phainon listens, stepping inside gingerly. It had only been a little over a year since he graduated with his master’s degree at this point, meaning it hadn’t been that long since he’d seen Anaxa last. He didn’t think he was crazy enough to do anything of the sort.

With a small, terrifying realization, Phainon wonders if this has something to do with Aglaea’s illness, and the way she’s losing her own eyesight. Maybe he was rubbing his vision in her face. Or maybe it was an act of solidarity. Neither of those options make any sort of sense to him.

Despite Phainon’s wariness, Anaxa does nothing to clear anything up. He’d cut out his own eye and mailed it to Aglaea, and that was that. Anaxa isn’t one to jest, so Phainon has no choice but to take him at his word.

There’s little fanfare in this reunion. Anaxa brings him to his “living room”, which is filled with more books and papers, the only piece of furniture being the oldest piano Phainon has ever seen in his life. He wonders if it’s in tune, and presses middle C. It is. Anaxa gives him an unimpressed look, like he knows Phainon had doubted him.

He tosses the Tchaikovsky onto the rack, pulling up a chair from his kitchen to sit beside him as Phainon takes a seat on the bench.

“You haven’t practiced,” he says, crossing one leg over the other. He leans back, arms crossed, like he’d rather be anywhere else.

“Obviously.” Phainon opens the book, flipping to the first page. He can’t help the grin that breaks over his face as he sees the opening chords. “Cyrene doesn’t own a piano.”

“You need to find a way to get one, then,” Anaxa yawns. “I want you practicing at least forty hours a week outside of our lessons.”

Phainon swallows. It’s actually less than he was expecting Anaxa to say. They only have a few months to prepare this piece, anyways. He nods, thinking he could probably just practice at the Marmoreal Palace in a private room.

The first lesson is brutal, infinitely worse than Phainon remembers his teaching to be. He wonders if Anaxa was always like this and he had merely forgotten, or if he had gotten stricter over their time apart.

Part of it is that Phainon has never sightread during a lesson before. The expectation throughout his school years was always that he would arrive at the lessons with the piece practiced, and Phainon followed this rule religiously. Now, he didn’t have a chance to practice beforehand, but Anaxa isn’t any kinder to him because of it.

It also might be worse than Phainon remembers because Phainon is worse than he remembers. The piece is difficult, easily the most difficult thing he’s played recently. Piano had just been a hobby to him for the last few months. This is unlike anything he’s had to learn for a long time, and it shows.

He leaves Anaxa’s house feeling discouraged all over again. Anaxa hadn’t said anything like that outright, but it doesn’t stop the way he ends up feeling. He’s not sure if he can do this. He used to be able to, sure, but all the evidence before him only points to one outcome: he hasn’t made a full recovery, after all, and this is it for him.

He heads to the Marmoreal Palace immediately after, using the old code he had to Aglaea’s practice rooms to get into one. She’s not there today, but the place is crawling with musicians regardless. He tries to sneak in without getting caught, but it’s fruitless. Every musician in Okhema knows who he is. Today is the first time he wishes they didn’t.

He spots Tribios before she sees him, standing in the door of her practice room as she struggles to get her horn case over her shoulder. He intends to

hurry past her, but she calls out his name just as he turns his back, and he has no choice but to greet her.

“Oh! It’s really you!” She exclaims, coming over to greet him with her case successfully slung over one shoulder. “Aglaea mentioned you were going to play with us again. I told her I’d believe it when I saw it!” She laughs heartily, and as always, it doesn’t fail to put a smile on Phainon’s face, too.

“Tribios,” he says, and she pulls him into a hug. “It’s been a while, hasn’t it?”

“So, you are really going to be the soloist for the Tchaikovsky?”

Phainon nods. “For some reason,” he says, laughing awkwardly. She doesn’t laugh back. “Miss Aglaea already mentioned it to the rest of you?”

“Just me,” she winks. “An email will be sent out with seating and parts for the rest of the orchestra in the next few days. We don’t rehearse until next week.”

“Ah,” Phainon says. That makes it real. It’s already real, now, but once the rest of them know, it’s really going to be solidified.

“Well, it was so nice to see you, Phainon, but I really have to go,” Tribios says, glancing at her watch. “I need to pick up the triplets from their lesson. Can you believe they’re old enough for those now?”

“Seriously?” Phainon’s eyes widen. He’d met Tribios’ children a few times, when they were mere toddlers. He supposes they wouldn’t be much older than that, now, but it’s still surprising. “What are they playing?”

“Piano, for now.” Tribios rolls her eyes. “They’re not old enough for anything else. But Tribbie is set on clarinet, Trinnon on flute, and Trianne on trumpet…so we’ll see how it plays out.”

“Wow, all winds,” Phainon huffs. “Hopefully at least one of them will stick with piano…”

Tribios laughs. “No, Phainon, we’re a wind family. Sorry.”

“Clearly,” Phainon eyes her horn. “I’ll see you around then, Tribios?”

“I’m so, so happy you’re back, Phainon,” she says, bowing her head to him slightly. It’s a gesture that thoroughly throws Phainon off. “We all are.”

Phainon gives her his thanks, and she hurries off towards the elevator. He’s not sure why he was trying to avoid her so hard earlier. She was one of the longest members of the Marmoreal Orchestra, and helped Aglaea a lot with planning and selecting repertoire. It was just as much her orchestra as it was Aglaea’s, and everyone loved her. Phainon was not excluded from this.

“Oh my god, Phainon?”

He takes a deep breath before he turns around. He recognizes that voice as one of his old classmates, Piso. He and another classmate, Livia, were both summer session percussionists in Aglaea’s orchestra after they’d graduated from the Grove. The three of them were never best friends by any means, but shared a lot of classes and had gotten to know each other well as musicians.

He doesn’t say anything at first, meeting both of them for the first time in a few years. He hadn’t played for Aglaea during the summer in a while, and is surprised at how different both of them look.

“Holy shit,” Livia says. “You look good, Khaslana.”

“Are you playing?” Piso asks, eyes wide. “We heard about your injury. Everyone was heartbroken that you might never come back.”

Phainon shows them his scarred hands, and they both wince. “I’m back, though,” he reassures them. “But no spoilers. You’ll get the email in a few days, I hear.”

“Oh, we know about the Tchaikovsky,” Livia waves him off. “What’s in question is the soloist. Some people were saying Caenis, like she’d crawl out of her grave—”

“What—” Phainon chokes. “Who told you?!”

“Oh, um…” Livia rocks back and forth on her heels. “Was it Chartonus?” She asks, turning to Piso.

“Chartonus?”

“Oof, yeah, it might’ve been,” Piso winces. “He definitely didn’t say that about Caenis though.”

“I heard that part from Bartholos.”

“Are you—Livia!” Piso lightly smacks her shoulder. “And you believed it?”

“I mean…there was some doubt in my mind, for sure…”

Phainon snorts. Being a temporary member of the orchestra, he’s not fully involved in the interpersonal drama between members, much as he’d like to be. All that he knows is that Chartonus is a near mute bassoon player and Bartholos pops in occasionally to cover a piccolo part.

From what he’s heard from Hysilens, drama between string players might be a whole different beast that neither Livia nor Piso know much about, or have any desire to tackle.

“Anyways,” Piso says, resting his hands on his hips. “I heard you’re dating Mydei.”

Phainon sighs. “Guys…”

“Is it true?” Livia asks, eyes glimmering. “Maybe you could get him to do a show with us…he’s never played for Miss Aglaea before…”

“He’s not going to do that.”

“Are you sure? There was quite a bit of piano on that new album of his. Plus, we haven’t seen Cifera or Castorice in so long.”

“I really hate to burst your bubble, but I think they’re all pretty satisfied with the kind of music they’re making right now.”

“I told you, Livia…” Piso groans.

“But is it true?” Livia continues, shushing him. “Are you two really together?”

Phainon scratches the back of his neck awkwardly. “Hasn’t he been pretty open about it online?”

“She’s convinced he’s doing it as fan service,” Piso mutters under his breath.

“Uh, no.” Phainon crosses his arms. “We’re together.”

“Will he be here?” Livia demands. “For the Tchaikovsky?”

“Hopefully.”

“Okay, Livia, I think we should go.” Piso grabs her arm, pulling her away. “Stop fangirling dude, he’s a real person,” he mutters as he drags her down the hallway.

Phainon snickers under his breath as he lets himself into the nearest practice room, finally clear of all the people he used to know.

Conflicting emotions swirl through his brain as he sits on the piano bench. He’s still discouraged, but the unconditional support from his old friends has motivated him like nothing else could. He doesn’t want to let them down.

He doesn’t allow himself to practice for too long. He’d already witnessed how that could ruin someone firsthand during Mydei’s sophomore year of college. If he’s going to see this through, he can’t let this piece destroy him.

Okhema is filled with music lovers. Phainon has been aware of this for many years, but had forgotten just how deep it runs in his absence. As the weeks pass, people recognize him more and more. The whole orchestra

knows of his return now, and word is beginning to spread throughout the townspeople.

Market owners thank him as he visits their shops for putting in the work to ensure Aglaea stays in business. Phainon wonders how she had gotten to the point of potentially stepping down when most of the public opinion was in her favor to begin with, but he knows most of her funding has come from the Council of Elders in the past. They have all the real power here, and it upsets Phainon to his core.

An old violinist, the concert master before Hysilens took her spot, finds him one day and offers to buy him a coffee. He accepts, of course, not one to pass up a free meal. She recoils when she sees his hands. Phainon knows they’re ugly, but they work. That’s all that matters to him.

The weirdest interaction he has happens nearly a month after he first returned to Okhema, though. He’s eating lunch by himself in the Marmoreal Diner. He had just gotten out of his fourth lesson with Anaxa, which left him requiring some serious recovery time.

A group of four men he’s never seen before approach him. They all seem to be Phainon’s age or older, and they somehow know who he is. If they’re members of Aglaea’s orchestra, they’re recent.

“...Hello?” Phainon asks. He holds his sandwich awkwardly in the air, not quite having made it to his mouth before they stopped by his table.

“Excuse me, are you Phainon Khaslana?” One of them says. He has a heavy Kremnoan accent, but his Okheman is extremely polished.

Phainon nods. If they are Kremnoan, then Mydei must know them, somehow. He supposes that might be a gross generalization, but he’s not sure why they would approach him for any other reason.

“I’m Ptolemy,” he continues. “This is Peucesta, Leonnius, and Perdikkas… we’re Mydeimos’ friends from high school. I’m not sure if he’s mentioned us before.”

“Oh,” Phainon puts his sandwich down. “He, um, he might have…” he says quietly. Mostly, he’d mentioned Hephaestion. But Phainon isn’t sure if that’s something they would like to hear right now.

Leonnius clicks his tongue, and mutters something under his breath in Kremnoan. The only word Phainon picks up on is Mydeimos.

Perdikkas nudges him with his elbow, giving him an equally incomprehensible response.

“I apologize,” Ptolemy says, flashing Phainon a reasonably apologetic grin. “Anyways, we heard you were playing with the Marmoreal Orchestra this session as a soloist, so we thought we’d come say hello.”

“What brings you guys to the area, then?” As far as Phainon knew, the group of them had met each other in Kremnos and rarely left. He figured they still played for a Kremnoan orchestra.

“We play for Miss Aglaea now,” Peucesta speaks up. “We found out that our orchestra was being funded by Mr. Nikador, so we quit.”

“Mydei’s father,” Phainon says slowly. He doesn’t know how that man is doing now. He hopes it’s terrible.

Leonnius has something to say about that, too—this time, the only word he recognizes is Mydei. Perdikkas mutters “stop” in Okheman. Phainon doesn’t really like those two.

“Yes,” Ptolemy says. “Anyways, we thought we might ask you how he’s doing. We haven’t really heard from him ever since Hephaestion…oh, um, did he mention that?”

“Hephaestion’s death broke Mydei’s heart,” Phainon says softly. “Of course I know about that.”

“Doesn’t give him an excuse to cut the rest of us off,” Leonnius rolls his eyes. So he did know Okheman. Interesting.

“Speak for yourself. He answered my text congratulating him on the new album,” Perdikkas shoots back.

“So this is a competition, now? Whose shoulder did he cry on when Hephaestion died, huh?”

“Okay, I’m sure Mydei still cares about all of you deeply,” Phainon says, trying to stop whatever is going on between all of them. “He’s busy, and hasn’t been to Kremnos in years. I think there’s a lot of bad memories associated with that place.”

Ptolemy sighs, rubbing both his hands down his face. “Ignore them. I was trying to have a friendly conversation here.”

Phainon snorts. “He’s happy,” he says, and that causes all four men to stop talking over each other and look at him. “Mydei, I mean.”

“Really?” Peucesta asks, blinking. “His album was concerningly melodramatic.”

“Because he deals with shit by writing songs about it,” Phainon explains. “He loves his band. They’ve given him the world.”

“He does look like he’s having the time of his life in his performances,” Perdikkas points out.

“I don’t understand why he ever gave up piano,” Leonnias sighs, slumping into the spot next to Phainon. Alright, then. Phainon tries to inch away as discreetly as possible. “The six—five—of us could’ve been something, man.”

“No we couldn’t. No cellist.” Ptolemy crosses his arms, giving him a stern look. “And you do know why he quit. He told us. After Gorgo died.”

“Look, Mydei is still the same person he was six years ago. He still overworks himself. He still cares too much about being perfect. But he wasn’t just your friend because of Hephaestion or because he was unhappy, he genuinely liked you guys.” Phainon stirs around his drink mindlessly.

He’s not sure if what he’s saying is even true, given how rarely Mydei spoke about them. But he’s sure it is. Mydei isn’t a fake friend, and he never would be. “Seriously, reach out. It’s not that hard.”

Peucesta sighs heavily, then comes to sit across from Phainon. It’s not long before the other two are sitting down too, filling up Phainon’s booth.

“I always thought he was going to marry you,” Peucesta confesses.

Phainon’s eyes go wide. “What?”

“Ugh, enough of this, Peucesta,” Perdikkas scoffs. “Mydeimos is only— how old? Twenty-three?”

“Doesn’t matter,” Peucesta shrugs. “I think you two are soulmates.”

“Oh,” Phainon’s not really sure what to make of that. “Not Hephaestion?”

This gets laughter out of three of them, the only one remaining silent being Ptolemy. He doesn’t seem like the type to laugh very much.

“Hephaestion and Mydeimos were like oil and water,” Leonnias explains. “It never would’ve worked out.”

“Wait, what?!” Phainon chokes out, bewildered. “Mydei never said anything like that?”

“Because they loved each other,” Ptolemy chimes in. His voice has gotten notably sadder. “You can love someone and be incompatible.”

“Also, Mydeimos would beat our ass if he heard us say that,” Perdikkas adds. “That’s what almost happened the last time one of us brought it up.”

“What made them so incompatible?”

“Hephaestion was…spirited,” Ptolemy says carefully, like he’s trying to put it as kindly as possible.

“He was arrogant,” Leonnias cuts in. “His family was full of Kremnoan traditionalists. Well—most of ours were, honestly, but he didn’t really lose those beliefs somewhere along the way like we did.”

“Mydeimos has always been a lot more sensitive than he seems when you first meet him,” Peucesta continues. “Don’t tell him we said that, though.”

Phainon laughs. He supposes that much is true. And he’d never call Mydei sensitive to his face.

“Hephaestion would have made fun of him like crazy if he saw how Mydeimos reacted when he died,” Leonnias explains. “Anyways. That’s just what we think.”

“Ew, are you crying?” Perdikkas mutters, in a mock voice that Phainon can only assume is his best Hephaestion impression. It sends the three of them into a fit of laughter again. Ptolemy cracks a smile this time, but that’s it.

“Anyways, if you want to marry him, you have our blessing,” Peucesta finishes.

“That’s…kind of you,” Phainon says. He’s still not sure what to make of this entire interaction. “But that probably won’t happen for many years.”

Peucesta shrugs. “Still.”

Mydei’s old group of friends aren’t the only people who want to talk to him. CALAMITY is a popular band all throughout Amphoreus, and while Okhema never really knew Mydei, they did know Cipher and Castorice. Phainon isn’t sure where Hyacine grew up, but is realizing quickly that it wasn’t in Okhema. She attended the Grove, but graduated before Phainon, Cipher, and Castorice did. So they’d never crossed paths until they happened to attend the same college in Penacony.

Everyday when Phainon leaves Cyrene’s house, he runs into at least one person that wants to talk to him. Sometimes they keep him for a while, sometimes they just ask how he is. Most of the time, they congratulate him on recovering from his injury. Phainon smiles and doesn’t say anything about how doubtful he still feels about the whole situation.

He’s used to Anaxa’s harsh teachings now, and doesn’t take the insults to heart anymore. He knows Anaxa only wants the best for him, and that it would only do Phainon good to listen to what he has to say.

In late July, Phainon attends his first rehearsal with the Marmoreal Orchestra. It’s held on a hot Tuesday evening. Everyone has stopped playing by the time Phainon walks on stage, at exactly seven PM. A few people clap. Phainon wants to disappear at the first moment of applause.

“Enough,” Aglaea says, shutting them down instantly. “He’s late.”

“I am on time,” Phainon argues. Getting to rehearsals early was much more important for the others than for the pianist.

As if proving his point, the strings proceed to tune for two minutes. He doesn’t know why, but the humidity was rough for string players. Hysilens had once told him she would take summers off, if it didn’t hinder her playing.

“Ladies and gentlemen, Phainon Khaslana.” Aglaea says, once they finish. No one claps this time. “As you know, he will be our soloist for the Tchaikovsky this season. If you wish to welcome him back, do so during our break and please refrain from interrupting the rehearsal to catch up. Thank you.”

Phainon has already run into most of these people—except for Hysilens, surprisingly. She sits right behind him, in first chair, and it makes him a little nervous. He doesn’t think his arrival is a surprise to anyone at this point. Still, he never fails to be flattered by the overwhelming kindness with which they welcome him back. He hadn’t thought he was this big of a deal to the people of Okhema until now.

“Today will likely be tedious and frustrating, as we need to work out the cues and get used to playing alongside our soloist. If I hear a single complaint out of anyone’s mouth, you will be asked to leave until next season. I have replacements on standby for every part.”

Phainon thinks back to his time playing with Herta’s orchestra at Paperfold. If she were the conductor today, this would be a genuine threat she would make. In Aglaea’s case, it’s merely her idea of a joke.

“Alright. Movement one, please.” Phainon scrambles to open his sheet music, finding his spot on the keys. The nerves hadn’t quite gotten to him until right now.

Aglaea gives them a measure of rest before they’re cued in. The opening horns blare throughout the concert hall, shocking Phainon with their volume. When the rest of the orchestra joins in shortly after, Phainon shakes his head in disbelief. The first rehearsal always had this sort of effect on him. He can hardly handle the euphoria it brings him to be in a room full of equally talented and devoted musicians, coming together to perfect one of his favorite pieces of all time.

He almost misses his entrance, it being as early into the piece as it was, but he gets there just in time. The strings play above his opening chords, and much as he wants to look around him, he doesn’t dare take his hands off the keys.

He catches Aglaea gesturing to stop just before his first solo part starts, and everyone immediately stops. He sighs lightly, marking something into his music. He’d missed a couple notes. Probably the nerves, because the beginning was straightforward enough where that shouldn’t be happening.

“Yes, thank you,” Aglaea puts her baton down, tucking her hair behind her ears as she thinks. “Phainon, you nearly missed your entrance. Be more attentive next time.” Phainon nods. He’d foolishly thought she hadn’t noticed that. “Strings, let’s do that again. It was messier than I would like.”

Phainon didn’t think so, but that’s why Aglaea is the conductor, and he is not. She has an ear for the details of things that he lacks when it comes to

orchestral pieces.

They run the main melody with just strings once. Aglaea deems it acceptable this time, but Phainon knows they will likely have to run that more after he leaves.

“From the top, please,” Aglaea continues. “I won’t stop this time, unless we fall apart.”

Phainon nearly cringes at the sound of that. He can play the whole piece at this point, but not well. Aglaea knows it will be rough, but that won’t stop her from ripping him to shreds. Even in that perfectly composed manner of hers.

True to her word, Aglaea doesn’t stop. Not when he misses half the notes in his hardest runs, not when the timpani misses their entrance by a beat or the strings turn into a jumbled mess of notes. It’s just as messy as you would expect the first full rehearsal of a piece to be.

Silence settles over the hall as Aglaea lowers her baton, each musician instantly relaxing. Phainon rests his forehead on the sheet music rack, dejected. The orchestra was beautiful, even if it wasn’t perfect. But it had been horrible on his part.

“Alright,” Aglaea says quietly. Phainon watches her put on glasses out of the corner of his eye, holding up the score so she can study it to the best of her ability. “Phainon.”

His heart lurches. He’s not ready for whatever she has to say to him.

“You rushed every solo.”

Phainon exhales.

“Your octave jumps were dragging. Work on getting up there quicker.”

Phainon nods, biting the inside of his cheek. He hopes he hadn’t disappointed the rest of the orchestra. They were so excited to play with him again, only for him to bring them that.

“You need to count your triplets better. You didn’t get a single one right.”

Phainon nods again.

“...The cadenza was good.”

Phainon looks up. Compliments from Aglaea were rare, though not unheard of. She only gave them when she truly meant it.

“I do think you have improved.”

Now Phainon sits up, furrowing his brows. “What?”

Aglaea lifts both her hands up to the orchestra, palms clasped together. “Applause, everyone.”

Some people clap. The rest of them slam their feet on the ground, with enough vigor to make the whole room shake. Phainon has never been this confused in his life. Once it subsides, he doesn’t have anywhere to hide his rapidly reddening face. “Thank you,” he says sheepishly.

“Don’t thank us,” Aglaea says. There’s clearly something else she wants to say, but she holds herself back. Thank Anaxa, Phainon thinks. That must have been what it was.

“Alright.” Aglaea picks up her baton again. “Let’s work backwards. Rehearsal J.”

The rest of the rehearsal is the most productive three hours Phainon has had in a long time. They break for fifteen minutes halfway through, which flies by with how many people approach Phainon to talk to them. None of them say he sucked. Although he supposes that if they thought that, they probably wouldn’t say it to his face. He can only hope they’re not saying it behind his back, either.

He leaves Marmoreal Palace at ten on the dot, feeling better than he has in weeks. His back hurts, and he’s exhausted, but he’s also filled with giddiness that he doesn’t think will go away for multiple days.

He notices he has a missed call from Mydei from an hour ago, so he pulls out his headphones and calls him back during the walk back to Cyrene’s place.

Mydei picks up on the third ring, from somewhere in the Luofu. Phainon isn’t sure what the exact time difference is, but he knows it must be late there.

It certainly looks like it. Mydei is sprawled across his hotel bed, hair still damp from the shower. “What’s up?” He says, through a yawn.

“You called me,” Phainon answers. “You look exhausted.”

“You look…” Mydei pauses, staring into the screen for a moment. “Good.”

“Thank god,” Phainon laughs. “Seriously, though. How are you?”

Mydei yawns again. “I’m thriving.”

“Are you really?”

“No. I miss my cat.”

Phainon snorts, thinking about Kokopo III. He couldn’t take her with him to Okhema, so Mydei had to hire a catsitter. He doesn’t think Kokopo III minds very much.

“How was rehearsal?”

“Um,” Phainon can’t stop the grin that breaks out over his face, just thinking about it. “Really good, actually. If you’d believe it.”

“I wouldn’t believe it if you said it was bad.”

“Aglaea said I improved.”

Mydei gasps. “No way. Say it.”

“Say what?”

“That I was right.”

“No.”

Mydei lets it go, and the conversation drifts elsewhere. Phainon talks about his latest lesson with Anaxa. Mydei still can’t get over the fact that he cut out his own eye, and doesn’t understand how Phainon can. But he’d never known Anaxa to the extent that Phainon had. It didn’t seem all that uncharacteristic.

Mydei explains how Aventurine put Cipher on “hotel arrest” after she nearly died on their day off in the Luofu. He talks about culture shocks, the newest venues, how amazing everything has been. He still looks exhausted, and Phainon can tell he’s overworked right now, but he’s undeniably happy. The sort of happiness that Phainon has yearned for his whole life.

“Oh, also…” Mydei trails off. When Phainon looks down at him, he’s chewing on his lip. “Never mind.”

“Mydei.”

“Fuck, stop.” Mydei breaks out into a grin, unable to stop himself. “Stop. It’s a surprise.”

“You’re writing a new song?” Phainon asks. Mydei’s almost always writing something. It wouldn’t be much of a secret if he was.

“No.”

Phainon raises an eyebrow.

“Okay, maybe.”

“The fuck does maybe mean?”

Mydei laughs once, stretching himself out along his mattress. He rolls over, now on his elbows, holding his phone up in front of him. “I was inspired.”

“By?”

“You.”

Phainon sighs. “Stop, Mydei.” He doesn’t think he can handle another song written for him. Love Song was already too much.

“I haven’t started writing yet,” Mydei continues. “I just have ideas.”

“Oh my god.”

“I didn’t think this was such a big deal to you.”

“I don’t need all these songs written in my honor,” Phainon says quietly. “Even the one was unnecessary.”

“Too bad. I’ll write whatever I want.”

Phainon groans, tilting his phone down so Mydei can only see the top of his forehead.

“Too late. I already saw you blushing.”

Phainon immediately disconnects the call, laughing to himself as he thinks about Mydei’s reaction. Five seconds later, he gets another call.

The next week flies by. He goes to his lesson with Anaxa, where they work on the long list of things Aglaea had told him to improve. The next rehearsal on Tuesday goes by slower than the first one had, and Phainon is only there for half of it this time. But as he leaves, he opens his phone to a text message from Mydei.

He’s sent Phainon an audio file, along with one text that simply reads “how’s this?”

Phainon sighs, connecting his headphones again, and plays the audio file.

The song is undeniably beautiful, even at the demo state it exists in right now. The audio quality of Mydei’s message is rough and grainy, and seems to have been recorded with his phone propped up on one end of the piano. His voice barely comes through in the background, and Phainon can only hear snippets of lyrics.

It’s subdued, and not very upbeat. Phainon chalks that up to the level of production that’s been done on it thus far. He thinks if Mydei were to play any other song on the album with just him and a piano, they were bound to sound much more melancholic and relaxed than they do on the record.

Still, Phainon replies telling him he loves it so far. He gives him a suggestion to shift to a major key. Mydei responds seconds later, saying “hell no. shut up and focus on your own shit.”

Phainon snorts, hearting the message and putting his phone back in his pocket.

The weeks continue to pass, and that’s the last time he gets any sort of update on the song. Whenever Phainon asks, Mydei remains intentionally vague. He tells him it’s coming along and that he thinks Phainon will like it. But he doesn’t send him any more demos. When Phainon asks his band mates, they say they’ve barely worked on it and that Mydei has sworn them to secrecy.

As August starts to come to a close, Phainon has already accepted that he’s going to hear the song when everybody else does. Which is fine. Obviously, he’d prefer to be a little more special than that, but Mydei has never really been one to share his early or in-progress versions of things.

The Tchaikovsky has started to come together better than Phainon could have ever anticipated. The first movement is already perfect, and they’ve set it aside in the last few weeks to focus closer on things from the second and third movements. One rehearsal, Phainon stays past when they need him and sits in the audience to listen to their other repertoire.

The strings are opening the concert with Dvorak’s Serenade for Strings in E Major. It’s exactly the kind of thing Aglaea liked to pick back when

Phainon was younger—lithe, and graceful. The second movement is a beautiful waltz that gets stuck in Phainon’s head for hours afterwards.

After the Tchaikovsky, the full orchestra is closing the concert with Prokofiev’s fifth symphony. It looks incredibly challenging for the violins. Phainon knows this piece, of course, but hasn’t ever seen it live, and the fourth movement leaves him slack-jawed when they do a run through.

He can’t wait for the concert now. He doesn’t think he’s ever been this excited for a show before, and he’s done some incredible shows. Somehow, this tops even Rach 2—but he thinks that’s only because Rach 2 wasn’t done with the right orchestra.

September 3rd, 3870.

Phainon sits backstage, waiting for the strings to finish up the Serenade. He’s dressed in his nicest suit, the Tchaikovsky sheet music resting open in his lap. He’s using his last few moments to study it, before he plays it all from memory. He’s been looking forward to this for months now, sure, but that does little to quell his anxiety.

Tribios sits next to him, fanning herself off with her own folder of music. She’s already said several things meant to calm him down. None of them have worked.

Mydei is out there. The whole band is. He didn’t get a chance to see them with his early call time, and the fact that they almost didn’t make it on time. But they had. Mydei had pulled strings to shift their departure from Castrum Kremnos to be a day earlier, rather than on the day of their closing show in Okhema. Just so they could make it to the concert.

The time comes for the rest of the orchestra to join the strings on stage, leaving Phainon in an empty room. He takes a deep breath, one that’s shaky on the exhale, as he gets to his feet. His knees shake so violently he fears he might lose his balance.

Aglaea enters, dressed in a simple black suit. She nods at Phainon, and takes his hand. “You worked so hard for this,” she says, in the kindest tone Phainon has ever heard from her. “You’re about to make it all worth it.”

Phainon nods, allowing himself to be led right outside the side doors to the stage. They listen to the full orchestra tune for a few moments, before they eventually fall silent.

“Good luck,” Aglaea whispers.

Phainon pushes the doors open, and the applause starts.

He puts the most charismatic grin he can muster on his face as he walks out towards the piano. He bows before them, then turns to shake Hysilens’ hand before they both sit down.

Moments later, Aglaea walks out, too. She bows before the podium as the audience claps for her, too, then steps up to face the orchestra. Phainon watches her closely as she feels out the tempo in her head. She picks up her baton, and the orchestra lifts their instruments. A measure of rest later, the horn solo sounds out around them, and Phainon places his hands on the keys in position for his entrance.

The moment he starts playing, all of his nerves dissipate. He and the orchestra are one, and he’s never felt like he belongs more than he does at this moment.

He thinks of Mydei in the audience, but not enough to allow it to distract him. He’s playing for Mydei, sure, but he’s also playing for Aglaea. He plays for all of Okhema. For every fan that’s ever attended one of his shows. For everyone that’s ever loved this piece, and for everyone that’s ever loved classical music as a whole. What he really wants is to do one of his favorite pieces of all time justice.

Not once does he mess up. His fingers don’t slip, he doesn’t miss notes. He times all his solos perfectly, his hands jump between octaves easily, and his triplets are all the right rhythms. Most importantly, though, his cadenzas are perfect.

By the end of the third movement, he doesn’t even feel tired. In fact, he can’t believe how much time has passed, despite how short it feels. As the last notes ring out throughout the concert hall, he finds that he wishes he had savored the moment more than he had. It all came to an end too quickly.

As soon as he takes his hands off the keys, the audience erupts. People are cheering. More than half the concert hall is already on their feet. Phainon feels like he wants to cry.

Aglaea motions for him to stand up. For a moment, Phainon thinks he is hallucinating, but the closer he looks, the more he can tell that there really is a small smile on her face.

He stands, bowing deeply as he faces the audience. It sounds like thunder behind him when the orchestra joins in, slamming their feet on the ground. When he rises, he clasps his hands to his chest. He can’t believe this level of support. He doesn’t think he’s ever experienced anything like it.

The orchestra stands next, and another wave of cheers sounds out from the audience. He’s supposed to shake Hysilens’s hand and leave the stage soon, but he’s way too giddy to follow the formalities. So he steps around the piano bench and pulls her into a hug instead.

“Okay, this is weird,” she says into his ear. He can only barely hear it over the sounds of the audience. “Okay. Enough. Leave.”

Phainon lets go, and she shakes her head as she sits back down. He then reaches over the piano to shake Aglaea’s hand, too, thinking that it might not go over very well if he hugged her, too.

The audience is still applauding for them as he walks off stage. He faces them, waving with both of his hands all the way until the doors, where he

finally disappears backstage.

There’s a sound worker back there who shakes his hand, too, and congratulates him. Phainon is so filled with happiness that he feels like he could explode.

He waits back there for them to play through the Prokofiev. He can barely sit still, but manages regardless. The worker gives him a copy of the program, and he stares at his headshot underneath the blurb about the Tchaikovsky in disbelief. He can’t believe he actually did it.

Nearly forty-five minutes later, Aglaea comes offstage first. Phainon can hear the applause as the door opens, but it quickly fades out as it closes behind her.

“Come on,” she says, pulling him up to his feet. “One more time.”

Phainon follows her out the doors again. The applause hasn’t even subsided a little bit—if anything, when he comes back out, it only gets louder.

He bows again, unsure what else he can do to convey how grateful he feels. He wishes he could give a speech, but it’s not that kind of show. He also wishes he had prepared an encore. But nearly all of his time for the past four months was spent preparing the Tchaikovsky, and that had obviously paid off.

After what feels like an eternity, the applause finally subsides. Phainon waves at the crowd again as he walks off, retreating to the green room where he had left his sheet music.

The rest of the orchestra files in shortly after. They swarm him, clapping him on the back and giving him gracious handshakes. Half of them don’t even wait to put their instruments away before they approach him to offer their congratulations.

It feels like an eternity before he finally makes it out. He intends to give Aglaea her sheet music back, and finds her in the lobby stuck in a conversation with Anaxa, of all people. He spots Phainon first, stepping

away to shift Aglaea’s attention. She looks irritated when she first turns around, but beams when she sees Phainon.

“Bravo, Phainon,” she says, shaking his hand one more time.

“Yes, bravo,” Anaxa chimes in. Aglaea shoots him her most venomous glare. Phainon supposes that despite working together for this concert, they still failed to reconcile their differences. Oh well.

When he hands her the sheet music, she pushes it back towards him and tells him to keep it. He shrugs, not wanting to press the issue. Aglaea has her ways of getting more library copies, anyway.

As soon as Phainon steps away, he hears them instantly resume their bickering. He doesn’t care to listen to the basis of their argument. It was more than likely that it wasn’t anything remotely important, anyway.

He’s stopped a few more times as he tries to scan the crowd to find Mydei. He finally spots him in the corner, grouped up with the rest of his band and Cyrene. He seems to be arguing with Cipher. Castorice and Cyrene are catching up off to the side, and Hyacine appears to be searching for Phainon. They make eye contact, and she turns to get the others’ attention.

Phainon rushes over before anyone else can stop him. Mydei turns, and his eyes light up when he spots Phainon. He pushes Cipher off to the side and comes forward, pulling Phainon into a tight hug.

Neither of them say much of anything. Phainon buries his face into Mydei’s neck, and they squeeze each other so tightly that neither one of them can breathe.

Mydei smells nice. Fruity, like pomegranate. It’s probably a new cologne, but it makes perfect sense on him, and Phainon can’t figure out why.

“I missed you,” Mydei says quietly.

“I missed you more,” Phainon answers. His voice is muffled against Mydei’s shirt.

Mydei kisses him as they pull away. “That was incredible,” he says. He looks teary-eyed. Phainon thinks he might be, too. “I knew you could do it. I knew you’d get through it, Phainon.”

“Stop,” Phainon whispers, waving him off. He looks at the three girls behind him, all of them waiting their turn to congratulate Phainon, too.

Hyacine comes up to hug him, next after Mydei steps aside. “I’m so proud of you,” she nearly squeals. “You made a full recovery, didn’t you?”

“I…” Phainon shakes his head. He can hardly believe it, too. “I guess?”

Cyrene says something about how she can’t wait for him to move out of her house. Phainon doesn’t think she actually feels that strongly about it. Castorice gives him her heartfelt congratulations next, with Cipher speaking up last. She mumbles something about how she “actually” enjoyed it.

“Don’t listen to her, Phainon,” Mydei groans, rubbing at his temples. “She was yawning the whole time and kept saying, ‘I could do that’.”

“Oh my god, I was not,” Cipher rolls her eyes.

“Isn’t there someone you should be talking to?” Mydei asks, turning on her fully.

“Wait, who—oh, fuck.” Cipher leans backwards, slamming her head against the wall. “Mydei, don’t make me do that.”

“I’ll go with you,” Castorice says. She pulls Cipher away, who protests the whole time. Phainon isn’t sure who they were talking about until he sees them disappear in Aglaea’s general direction.

“Well,” Hyacine says brightly, looking between Phainon and Mydei. “We’re staying at Cyrene’s tonight. So I guess we’ll be going?”

“Wait, what? What about my room?” Phainon demands.

Cyrene shoots him a deeply unimpressed look. “Sorry. Girl’s night.”

“You’re kicking me out?!”

“No,” Mydei cuts in. He crosses his arms, raising an eyebrow as he looks at Phainon. “You’re coming with me.”

“Oh. That’s fine, actually,” Phainon decides. He can’t believe he needed that to be spelled out for him so explicitly.

Hyacine and Cyrene head outside to wait for Cipher and Castorice to finish up. Phainon doesn’t know how long that would take, with Cipher speaking to Aglaea for what, as far as Phainon knows, is the first time in several years.

Mydei tags along as Phainon searches throughout the concert hall, finding everybody he needs to say his goodbyes to. He meets Tribios for the first time, and signs Livia’s shoe. Then, Phainon drops him off with his old group of friends and leaves them to catch up by themselves.

People mainly want to speak with both him and Aglaea. It takes far too long for the lobby to clear out, and by the time it does, he’s lost track of all the papers he’s signed and conversations he’s had. There are few that stick with him like the children who claim he’s inspired him.

He meets back up with Mydei when he’s done, snaking his hand around his shoulders. He’s in some kind of conversation with his old friends, all of them laughing—even Ptolemy. So he really did have it in him, then.

“Ready?” Phainon asks.

Mydei nods. He promises his friends he will keep in touch—to Phainon’s relief—and they bid him goodbye as both Mydei and Phainon finally head towards the doors.

“Good?” Phainon asks him. The hotel is in walking distance, so Mydei merely grabs his hand and starts guiding him there.

“It was nice to speak with them again,” Mydei admits. “Thank you.”

“So, how have you been?”

Mydei sighs heavily. “You know how I’ve been.”

“Yeah,” Phainon says, shrugging. “One more show.”

Mydei turns to look at him. “You’re going, right?”

“Of course.”

“Okay, good. If you weren’t, all my plans would fall through.”

“Your plans?”

“Stop asking questions.”

Phainon has a sneaking suspicion this has something to do with the song he wouldn’t reveal anything about. But Mydei has never been one to give away information when he doesn’t want to, so Phainon listens to him and shuts up.

The next morning, Phainon wakes up sweating. He groans as he sits up, rubbing his eyes to adjust to the bright morning light filtering in through the open windows. He smells terrible, and doesn’t immediately recognize the room he’s in, until he remembers the events of last night.

It’s Mydei’s hotel room. Why in the world he had decided to open the windows during an Okhema summer, he has no idea.

He rolls over to check the time on his phone. It’s nearly ten in the morning, and Mydei is nowhere to be seen. He had a habit of sneaking off in the mornings if he got bored when Phainon didn’t wake up early enough.

Phainon pays it no mind, pulling himself out of bed. He needs a shower, badly. He doesn’t think Mydei would care.

He can’t find Mydei’s toiletries, so he showers with the ones provided by the hotel. They’re terrible, but at least Phainon is clean.

The only clothing he has is the suit he wore last night, which just so happens to be strewn across the floor. So he rummages through Mydei’s suitcase and throws on a pair of shorts and a CALAMITY t-shirt that he is honestly offended he doesn’t own yet.

When he emerges from the bathroom, Mydei is back. He sits at the hotel desk, writing something in his notebook. He looks up when he hears the door open, and immediately lets out a deep sigh.

“You stole my clothes.”

“What did you expect? I’m not wearing that suit again.”

Mydei sighs again, turning back down to his notebook. “Come here.”

Phainon doesn’t need to be asked twice. He’s peering over Mydei’s shoulder in an instant, making sense of the music he appears to be writing out. It looks like a piano part, and vaguely familiar. He hums, thoughtful, and leans even closer.

“Can you play this?” Mydei asks. “Or—I mean, I know you can,” he tries again. “I meant…can you play this, tonight?”

Phainon tears his eyes away from the sheet music, looking at him now. “What?”

“For my show,” Mydei tries. He looks sheepish, unwilling to make eye contact with Phainon for longer than a second at a time. “I want you to play with me.”

“At your show,” Phainon says slowly. “Tonight.”

“Yes, that’s what I said.”

Phainon takes the notebook in his hands, backing up until he sits at the end of the bed. “This is…” he starts, as he starts to be able to hear the melody Mydei has written in his head. It sounds achingly familiar, and sends chills down his spine. “Tchaikovsky.”

“It’s in a different key…” Mydei says, like he’s been caught doing something he shouldn’t.

It is, but that doesn’t make much of a difference to Phainon. Mydei’s song is in C minor, while Tchaikovsky’s piano concerto is in B-flat minor. Regardless, the melody is the same. “When did you write this?” Phainon asks.

“Today.”

“You wrote this…today, and want me to play it tonight.”

“Yes, everything else in the song is the same. It’s just the piano solo that I switched for one inspired by your performance.”

Phainon is in disbelief. He flips through the previous few pages, scanning the rest of the song that Mydei had written. He can’t play it in his head unless he really focuses all his attention on it, but it looks promising nonetheless. The bridge builds more around the piano than the vocals. He had written this song with Phainon in mind, likely struck by more inspiration during Phainon’s concert last night. It nearly brings tears to his eyes.

“Mydei…”

“So can you do it?”

Of course Phainon can do it. The music is simple enough that he could sightread it right now with no problems. But that wasn’t what caused Phainon to hesitate.

“You don’t have to,” Mydei adds, when left with Phainon’s silence. “I just thought…I don’t know what I thought. I missed you.”

He doesn’t need to say much more than that. Phainon understands, and he knows Mydei doesn’t want to elaborate any further than he already has. He had thought Phainon was going to come on tour with him, and now, on his final show, he wants to share a bit of both of them with the audience. This

song was the perfect mix of the two of them. Phainon can’t imagine anything better.

“When do we rehearse?”

Mydei grins, taking his notebook back out of Phainon’s hands. “Now.”

“What?”

“You heard me. We can take the bus.”

“Take the bus where?”

“The venue is ours until four. Get your shoes.”

The stage crew barely looks up when Mydei waltzes inside, merely giving him small nods. So he did have permission, but that didn’t make Phainon feel any better about being here right now.

“Did you book this?” Phainon asks, just to make sure.

“Oh, come on,” Mydei says, pulling him out on the stage. Phainon has been to this arena before, but he’s never seen it in this state. Nor has he been on the stage before, staring out into thousands of empty seats. It feels surreal.

The rest of the band is already there. Cyrene sits in the first row of chairs, their only audience member. She waves at Phainon when he walks out.

Cipher gags as he passes. “Ew. You smell like him.”

“I didn’t have any clothes,” Phainon protests. She plays something on her bass in lieu of a response, and pretends she hadn’t heard him.

“Okay, positions,” Mydei says, clapping his hands together like he’s a show director. “Phainon, your sheet music is on the piano. Go.”

“How long did you have this planned?”

“Months,” Hyacine answers. “We were really hoping you’d say yes.”

Phainon shakes his head, going to sit at the piano. It’s much worse quality than the one he had been playing last night. It’s not a full grand, for one, and it has a shitty sound to it that Phainon doesn’t particularly like. But it’s in tune, so he can’t complain too much.

The first run through sucks, and there’s no other way to put it. Phainon had thought he understood Mydei’s vision for the song through the sheet music he had scanned earlier, only to find that he was completely wrong. He gets lost just before his entrance and comes in unsure, which causes Mydei to forget the lyrics because now everyone else is confused and not just him.

“Phainon, what was that?” Mydei asks, turning to face him with one hand on his hip. “I thought you said you could play it?”

Phainon flips back to his first entrance, playing through his entire part at double speed just to prove that he knows how to play it. “Clearly it’s everybody else’s fault,” he says once he’s done.

Mydei shakes his head. “Again.”

Unfortunately, the four of them have all developed a language between each other that they can communicate with. They know each other’s playing styles better than anything, they know each other very well as both musicians and people, and they’ve already spent years working together to create music.

Phainon is new. He knows all of them, sure, but he hasn’t really worked with any of them. He doesn’t know how to read what everybody else is thinking and hasn’t perfected communication with everyone mid-song like he has with someone like Hysilens.

It takes a while before the music starts sounding like something. It’s a lot of trial and error, and little arguments between band members. Phainon observes from the side and notices that arguing seems to be the main form

of communication, especially between Mydei and Cipher. But neither Hyacine or Castorice stay quiet when they have something to say, either. When they direct their criticisms towards Phainon, too, he starts to think his feelings of inadequacy were asinine.

It’s nearly three in the afternoon when they get it perfect for the first time. As the last strum of Hyacine’s guitar rings out into the arena and eventually fizzles into nothing, nobody dares to be the first to say something.

Mydei is staring into space, Hyacine wipes at the corners of her eyes. From far out in the audience, Cyrene starts clapping enthusiastically.

“Okay, yeah, that was good.” Cipher finally says.

“Fluke,” is Mydei’s response. “Two more times.”

Phainon nearly slams his head into the keys. He’s not certain, but he has a sneaking suspicion that this was something Madam Herta used to say to him.

He thinks he was joking, but then Mydei really does make them play it through two more times. The lack of comments the rest of the band have on this makes Phainon think this is something Mydei does to them often.

“Please don’t say one more time,” Phainon says, after the third time.

Before Mydei can, if he even wanted to, one of the sound workers comes onstage and asks them if they’re ready to do a sound check now.

Phainon jumps offstage, into what will soon be the pit of the audience in just a few hours, and walks all the way back to where Cyrene is sitting while they start their sound check.

It’s surprisingly fun to watch. Mydei is the pickiest, to no one’s surprise, and keeps asking them to adjust things, especially on the piano. He supposes it’s difficult to get the piano to stand out against the much louder instruments.

“I’m happy for you,” Cyrene says, yawning. “You’ve really made it now.”

Phainon sighs wistfully, propping his feet up onto the chair in the row before them. “I’m going to miss Okhema,” he admits. “Do you think Mydei would be okay with moving here eventually?”

“Oh, Phainon.” Cyrene rolls her eyes as she turns to look at him. “Mydei would do anything for you.”

“Anything?” Phainon raises an eyebrow. “I don’t know. He has so many more opportunities in Penacony.”

“Not after this album,” Cyrene says. “He can go wherever he wants. Success will follow.”

Phainon swallows. CALAMITY was extremely popular in Penacony, but they loved the band in Amphoreus just the same, since each of the members came from there. And moving didn’t necessarily mean he had to cut ties with his record label. Phainon supposes they can just communicate virtually.

At the end of the day, though, there were orchestras in Penacony that Phainon could play for—not to mention, there were orchestras in Penacony he’s played for before. And he has connections after graduating from Paperfold. It was just Aglaea’s orchestra that he wasn’t ready to cut ties with.

Phainon knew this was a small conflict compared to what they’ve already gotten through together. In the grand scheme of things, it wasn’t a very big deal at all.

Phainon waits backstage for most of the show. From behind the door, he hears everything: the screams of the crowd, the way Mydei talks to them in between songs, and Cipher’s bass. He hears her bass most of all.

He watches from a tiny screen they have so the workers can monitor the stage from inside. Mydei has changed since opening night. His stage

presence is electrifying. He exudes confidence—he’s been overly confident since the day Phainon met him, but this is on a whole new level. He looks like he’s exactly where he belongs.

By the time they’ve reached the final few songs on the setlist, the energy inside the arena feels uncontainable. Phainon isn’t even on stage, and he can feel it. Adrenaline pumps through his veins like it never has before.

Mydei steps up to the microphone after a few moments basking in their cheers. His hair is damp with sweat, and three of the buttons on his shirt are undone. Phainon can’t wait for this show to be over, so he can finally have him to himself.

“Before we finish up tonight, I want to play something new.”

Their cheers nearly have the floor beneath Phainon’s feet shaking. He can feel his heart beating in his throat as he prepares himself to walk out on stage. He doesn’t know if he can handle a crowd this large. He’s performed in his fair share of pretentious concert halls, but this is a different situation entirely.

“It’s, um,” Mydei starts, and the cheering instantly subsides. Everyone is listening carefully to what Mydei has to say. “A love letter to music…and the person who reminded me why I fell in love with music in the first place. I call it Play It With Feeling.”

Phainon wishes the floor would swallow him whole. He can barely handle it when Mydei says things like this to his face, never mind to an audience of thousands.

“And he happens to be in the area, so I asked him to join me tonight.”

The crowd explodes. Phainon thinks he can hear Hyacine say something in response to the volume, but it barely registers over the sounds of their screams.

“Phainon?”

He isn’t sure what to expect as he pushes the door open and walks out on stage, but they somehow get even louder. He tries to look into the crowd and wave, but the spotlight in his eyes is blinding.

Mydei finds him, used to stages like these, and wraps an arm around his shoulders. He’s wet. Phainon doesn’t know what it says about him that it doesn’t disgust him.

Mydei asks him something, but Phainon can’t quite make out what it says. The microphone rests at his side, hanging from his free hand. It doesn’t pick up what they say to each other.

Phainon turns to him. He looks even more stunning from up close, in his stage makeup. “You’re beautiful,” he whispers in Mydei’s ear, unable to say anything else.

Mydei doesn’t say anything to that, merely nudging him towards the piano. “I guess he’s nervous,” he says, to the crowd this time. A mix of laughter and cheering sounds in response.

Phainon sits at the piano, lighting tapping one of the keys. It plays much louder than he was expecting around them, and he nearly jumps. He supposes that makes sense, though.

Mydei spends some time connecting his microphone back to the stand. “Are we ready?” He asks, voice a little quieter than before as he turns to look at each of the band members.

Phainon gives him a thumbs up. He’s not sure if there’s an agreed upon gesture between them, but he supposes a thumbs up is pretty much universal.

With little warning, Hyacine plays the opening riff.

The audience falls into dead silence. Phainon is impressed at how easily they seem to be able to wrangle a rowdy crowd into obedience.

When Mydei starts singing, Phainon feels as though he could hear a pin drop in the audience. They all hang onto his every word as no one but him and Hyacine play the opening verse of the song.

In fact, it’s so quiet that Phainon feels afraid to breathe, for fear of ruining what they have. And then Castorice joins in on light, barely there taps of her drums. Cipher’s part is equally subtle. When Phainon finally starts, it’s behind all of them, only growing into a crescendo as the rest of the band fades away.

And then Mydei finishes, and Phainon takes over, with the chords leading into the part he’s sampled from Tchaikovsky. He plays it just as he had last night. It doesn’t feel any different, playing with Mydei’s band versus playing with Aglaea’s orchestra.

Mydei starts singing again, and the rest of the band comes back a thousand times louder. Phainon feels like he’s fighting to be heard on top of their instruments. The climax is much more exciting live than it had been in their rehearsals.

He takes his hands off the keys just as all the other parts fade out, too. Silence falls around them as Mydei pulls his microphone off the stand, bringing it close to his lips as he finishes the final verse, with no one but Hyacine accompanying him. Just as they had in the beginning.

He turns to Phainon as he sings the final line of the song. Phainon holds his eye contact, afraid of what might happen if he didn’t.

For a brief, terrifying moment, it feels like no one but he and Mydei are on stage. The rest of the lights fall into darkness, illuminating just the two of them.

And then all the lights are on again, and the crowd’s roaring sounds in the background, breaking Phainon out of his thoughts. He had been so focused on Mydei alone that he didn’t register the song ending.

Mydei pulls him to his feet, bringing him to the front of the stage and forcing him to bow. He didn’t even know they did that at rock concerts.

“Phainon Khaslana, everybody,” Mydei nearly yells into his microphone. They get impossibly loud at that. Phainon isn’t used to hearing applause this rowdy.

Mydei pulls him into a hug, mic once again discarded at his side. “I love you,” he says into Phainon’s ear. Just loud enough for him to hear it this time.

Phainon pulls away. “I love y—”

Mydei surges forward, kissing him on the lips. Phainon can faintly hear the crowd lose their mind.

He doesn’t care. He has never cared about any of them. Here, with Mydei, making music, is exactly where he’s meant to be his whole life.

He’s never been so sure about anything else.
